# Introduction, Motivation, Pedagogy, and Ideas About Learning

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-2](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-2)

Everything has changed, yet at the same time so much has remained the same. In the past, aspiring scientists, whether in the natural or social sciences, would specialize in their discipline while at the same time taking a number of undergraduate and graduate courses in statistics and research methods ranging from theoretical to applied depending on the flavor of the course and the preference of the instructor. In addition to the typical introductory and usually relatively superficial statistics course that virtually every undergraduate must enroll regardless of specialization (e.g., biology, psychology, business, etc.), advanced undergraduate and graduate students are typically required to take a one-half semester of studying foundations (e.g., probability, hypothesis-testing, etc.) leading up to the analysis of variance (ANOVA) while the second half of the year would be typically spent studying more advanced ANOVA models and simple linear and multiple regression as well as possibly including a survey of the generalized linear model (e.g., logistic and Poisson regression). Such exposure would provide the student with a basic understanding of *what’s going on* in applied statistics sufficient to get their foot in the door to conducting and interpreting their own analyses for theses and dissertations, or at minimum and probably more realistically, be able to converse with someone (e.g., supervisor) able to *guide* them in conducting and interpreting their own analyses. After such a year-long sequence, a multivariate analysis course might also be offered that would feature topics such as *multivariate analysis of variance* (*MANOVA*), *discriminant analysis*, *principal components analysis* (*PCA*), *factor analysis*, among others, including possibly *path analysis* and *structural equation modeling* for students in the social and allied sciences. Much of the above coursework would feature, to varying extents, the use of software, such as Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), Statistical Analysis System (SAS), and more modernly, R, and possibly even Python.

## 0.1 The Paradigm Shift: What Has Changed

What has been described above as the typical course of study for the advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate student is now *out of date*. *It is no longer enough*. *It is grossly incomplete*. *It is archaic*. You get the picture! In the last 20–30 years, certainly post-2000, a machine learning and data science *Kuhnian paradigm shift* has occurred. In the age we find ourselves in, applied statistics courses are desperately in need of a *makeover*. They are in need of a major “updating,” overhaul, and renovation, not necessarily because foundational elements of modern data science and machine learning differ *that much* from the traditional univariate and multivariate essentials presented in the typical science curriculum, but mostly because the very landscape of what we may more generally call *data analysis* has changed. What is called “data analysis” today is much broader than prior to the data science and machine learning revolution, yet at the same time the foundations of these areas are often found in statistics. For the applied scientist or practitioner, 4exposure to traditional courses in statistics that do not incorporate data science and machine learning theory and concepts are now, *incomplete*.

### 0.1.1 A Wide Divide

Consider the current reality – it is entirely possible for a student to graduate from an applied science program having taken a typical statistics sequence yet upon graduating be completely unfamiliar with what is going on in *machine learning* and having little to no idea what *artificial intelligence* is despite the fact that many of the concepts and features learned in their statistics courses are directly applicable to what is occurring in these fields. Indeed, many of the concepts studied in statistics can be considered *foundations* to these modern fields. Hence, the student from a statistics course sitting down to lunch with a student from a machine learning course would soon realize that many of the things they are learning in their respective courses overlap a great deal, and in many cases, may even be very much the *same*. They begin to share notes and compare jargon used from each field and quickly realize the extensive *overlap* of their coursework. They are presumably coming from different disciplines yet may be talking very much about the same things! If they fail to connect and realize this, it may be more to do with the *jargon* used in each field than anything else.

Now, the above is not to suggest that jargon alone is what differentiates these fields. *Far from it*. Machine learning, and its underachieving and overpromising parent *artificial intelligence*, are their own respective fields, and as we will see in this book have already made tremendous advances and contributions for disciplines that are still relatively quite young. However, the overlap, especially at the level of *foundations*, is undeniable. Depending on one’s historical and philosophical perspective, one might even say that in many cases statistics gave *birth* to these fields. When a student or even researcher in machine learning speaks of a “learner” to a student just coming from a statistics course as though it is a “new” concept, the reaction of the statistics or science student should not be one of confusion and ignorance. Instead, it should be one of *recognition* of the similar foundations learned in their respective courses. Of course, the student of statistics, coming from an introductory lecture on the analysis of variance, for example, has just been subjected to a *statistical learner* as well, and it would be a shame if that student were unable to identify with the concept brought to the lunch table by the machine learning student. Indeed, those seemingly simple and “basic” *t*\-tests were kind of “machine learners” themselves in their own right and in the most general sense. Translated to a dummy-coded regression, weights are optimized, and if we feed more data through the *t*\-test or corresponding regression “algorithm,” those scalars get optimized further. *That simple model is learning based on experience*. The statistics student needs to appreciate what the machine learning student is talking about and vice versa, the machine learning student would do well to get in touch with some of his or her own roots in statistical theory.

## 0.2 A Unified Vision: The Bridge

Though machine learning and artificial intelligence are disparate fields, it is high time for a *unified introduction and top-down overview* of these areas for the student of the social and natural sciences. It is well time to construct a *bridge*. For *specialists* in statistics or machine learning the awareness of these bridges is (or should be) old news. But to the newcomer or applied science student, without a roadmap it can be exceedingly difficult to know or even recognize the *landscape*. You may not even know what forest you are in, which makes it terribly difficult to even recognize or navigate the trees.

A unified treatment of these areas should include a strong introduction and overview of topics in *univariate*, *bivariate*, *multivariate*, *machine learning*, *design and analysis of experiments*, along with select topics from *measurement theory*. To this last point, before one analyzes data or designs 5the next fancy algorithm, one should be intimately interested and invested into what *one is actually measuring*. This is true whether one is measuring emotional intelligence or one is measuring product preference via an online retailer. The customer may have “clicked” on product *A* because they *thought* they preferred it over product *B*, until it arrived on delivery day and they realized what they actually preferred was the *image* it falsely represented on the computer screen. In the end, their preference was for the *image*, the *perception*, the *idealization*, the *feeling*, not the *product*, yet the data point is advertised to have recorded *preference for the product*. *The measurement mechanism has failed*. Hence, what was measured in that impressive terabyte SQL database was not what we originally thought. It isn’t communicating what you think it is. Measurement issues abound in science and research, and a good course in statistics and machine learning should address them to some extent regardless of whether that course is for social or natural scientists. *Measurement is the first principle of good science*. Methods to analyze those measurements, of which much of this book is about, are second to that top priority.

What is more, modern texts on statistical and machine learning often tout the discipline as somewhat “novel” even though, of course, it overlaps a great deal with traditional and *classical* statistics in both univariate and multivariate domains. To reiterate, a presentation of machine learning that ignores this foundation or goes “skimpy” on the statistical side of things makes it possible for the graduate student to take a computer science course, for instance, yet fail to realize that many of those same foundational elements can also be found, and often have their *origins* in, *classical statistics*. For example, “unsupervised learning” in the name of techniques such as principal components analysis sounds “new,” but actually had its origins in 1901 with Karl Pearson. It’s a *learning algorithm* now, whereas it used to be simply a *statistical technique*. Oh my, have times changed! Karl Pearson would look befuddled had we told him his minimizing of squared perpendicular distances was a “learning algorithm.” Education needs to emphasize *history*, where these things came from and how they morphed into the verbiage and jargon of today. Very little is truly “new.” Most is usually a mixture of historical elements and ideas.

## 0.3 The Data Science and Machine Learning Invasion: Questions and Answers

Data science, machine learning, artificial intelligence have all invaded society with more pandemonium than even the Beatles in the 1960s. Even for those well-versed in traditional statistics, today’s climate of new topics can make even the experienced professional feel like a novice in the sea of new quantitative language. Questions that regularly arise from students and researchers (and the internet) confronting these areas for the first time include – *What exactly is machine learning? What’s the “machine” in machine learning? Is it basically the same as statistics? If not, how exactly is it different? Where does “Big Data” fit into all this? What is data science? Isn’t data science simply statistics with computation? How is data science the same or different from computational statistics? Is data science a fad that will soon pass?*

The above are only a few of the questions that students and researchers may have about this new quantitative climate and how to incorporate all of these ideas into their work and general understanding of what denotes the larger umbrella of *data analysis* these days. Or at minimum, be able to come across articles that feature these kinds of things and not feel like an outsider as though one were reading theoretical physics for the first time. The book you hold in your hands aims to reveal not only the inner workings of these methods to some extent (and albeit at a *relatively* rather shallow and superficial level, all considered), but also to provide a sense of the “big picture” of *what’s going on* in today’s general quantitative climate.

*The biggest picture, seeing all else from the top of the mountain, provides the greatest perspective*. The infinite set has infinitely many subsets and so the learner should aim to understand the 6largest structures possible. This can be a painful process! As an analogy, jazz is inordinately complex, that is, until one sees the bigger picture. Then all the “special case” theory are just details, difficult details, but details nonetheless. The elements that make up the wider vision are important, but seeing the overall framework is vital to understanding and appreciating those smaller pieces.

## 0.4 Who Should Read This Book?

This book was written for a course in multivariate statistics *and* machine learning for the scientist or practitioner. It was also written for specialists in the area who may benefit from some of the teaching and insight regarding how topics are presented and linked, the “undertones” that exist connecting the various methodologies that the reader may not have been aware of when originally studying and learning these techniques for the first time. The book is a “*big picture*” perspective on these fields. If the applied statistics course for scientists is being taught in room one and the machine learning course in room two, this book is the hallway in between.

### 0.4.1 Textbook Limbo

Having been an instructor of a multivariate course for the better part of twenty years, I have become frustrated in trying to find the ideal resource that reflects today’s mix of *multivariate*, *machine learning*, and *data science* more generally. Even within the realm of traditional multivariate texts, some books feature a discussion of factor analysis and latent variable models while others do not. Many traditional texts on multivariate analysis are quite rigorous in their development of say, *principal components analysis*, yet leave out discussion of these important factor-analytic and latent variable models of which entire books and monographs have been written in both applied statistics and psychometrics. On the other hand, modern machine learning texts are virtually obligated to discuss factor-analytical models under the more general rubric of *manifold learning*. While it is not irregular for instructors to use several different books in teaching a course, it can be difficult for introductory courses to suddenly switch gears from one text to another simply because one text omits an important and fundamental methodology. Personally, I have always found it virtually impossible to find the “right text” for my more advanced multivariate courses.

The current text, perhaps unrealistically, attempts to “cover it all” to some extent, so that upon completion of the book the student will have their *foot in the door* into this “modern empire” of statistics, machine learning, data science, etc. After studying this book, the reader should have a fair idea of *what’s going on* in multivariate statistics *and* machine learning and be able to hopefully use this book as an entry point into the literature. The book can also be used as a reference or refresher for researchers already somewhat familiar with the material.

Demonstrations using software (R and Python) are provided to get users *started* (and *started only*) in applying these techniques to their own data. Most of the software applications are relatively easy and straightforward, adapted directly from R packages and Python sources so the user can follow up with these resources to learn more about the cited examples. They are on familiar “toy” data sets and not some arcane data sets that would be difficult to follow up on for further study, demonstrations, and exploration.

By featuring examples adapted from R packages and online Python sources it hopefully encourages students and readers to more fully “explore” the source’s capabilities. In most cases, the examples we feature in the book are mere “snapshots” and incomplete demonstrations of what the package or Python library is capable of simply to get the proverbial “ball rolling.” In this way, it is hoped that the book serves as a “gateway” for either further class or independent learning and guides students in the direction of the skills required by today’s data scientists, which includes adapting to new packages and libraries almost *daily*. Upon encountering a novel data problem, 7the phrase “*I think R or Python has a package or library for that*,” becomes a common thought in tackling the data or research problem of the day. *Learning new things daily is what data craft is all about*.

To reiterate and emphasize, it is extremely important to realize that these demonstrations and examples are only meant to provide the reader with, once more, a *foot in the door* into these applications in getting started. The code is but a mere gateway to so much more that is *possible*. Statistical analysis and machine learning isn’t a *cookbook*, and very few if any textbook examples historically ever map on one-to-one to what is actually needed in *real research*. There are very good reasons why most R packages are upward of well over 100 pages, some well over 300–400! The skill of the data scientist is being able to be *creative*, *flexible*, and posessing a keen awareness of where to “dig” to follow up on the fairly trivial examples presented in this book and others. *Data can be a mess*. *Modeling it can be even messier*. In practice, each data set is unique and often requires a unique approach. Software demonstrations in this book are merely “glimpses” into the computational aspects and serve to demonstrate some of the theoretical development in the book.

### 0.4.2 Theoretical vs. Applied vs. Software vs. “Cookbooks”

In the statistics textbook market, there are numerous kinds of books for sale. Some are very technical books on the theory of statistics and their mathematical elements, the field of so-called *mathematical statistics*. These books usually feature virtually no scientific or software applications. Their emphasis is primarily on theoretical aspects of statistics and proving theorems. While at first glance these books might appear “deep,” they are often only deep *mathematically* and not in the development of *statistical ideas*, though a mathematical statistician would likely say the ideas are *in* the mathematics, which at that more advanced level is entirely correct. Software books on the other hand give minimal explanation and theory, assuming the reader already “knows what they are doing,” as it were, as it pertains to understanding the material. For example, those big bulky SAS manuals have traditionally been of this sort in that they “recap” the concept somewhat and then go on to show the reader how to implement a methodology in software. Lastly, the “cookbook” is even more incomplete in that such books simply tell the reader *what to do* via software instruction without telling them *why*. The most ideal of books at an introductory level is probably one that contains *some theory*, *some application*, and *some software*. The book you hold in your hands contains that mix.

#### 0.4.2.1 Watered-Down Statistics

The study of statistics can be terrifying for most who are not aspiring quantitative specialists. It’s scary for the specialist as well, the only difference is that they have learned to push through the fear and swim among the sharks daily. All of this is for good reason, *statistics is difficult*, the complexity of which is only fully realized once one begins working with statistical formulae and applying them to data, or reading more advanced literature on statistics. As an example, I was recently asked by a researcher whether Cohen’s *d* values can be compared across data sets. That is, can we say one study with *d* equal to 0.6 had a larger effect than another study with *d* equal to 0.5? The answer is, as are so many answers in statistics, *yes and no* and more complex than first thought would suggest. A few perturbations of data points in one study and the effects could be reversed; a slight change in the standard deviation can have a rather substantial effect on the standardization of the mean difference. So, yes, they can be compared across data sets, *but not without a keen awareness of what went into each computation and knowledge of each data set*. Many answers are of this nature in statistics, such that the answer usually comes with *caveats*, sometimes many of them. For reasons such as this, when students actually embark on understanding statistics, it is rarely black and white, 8and gray zones can, well, make one feel as though they have bees in their heads. *The seemingly simple problem can become quite complex very fast*. *Understanding statistics and how it should and should not be applied and interpreted on data is hard*. Figuring out optimal experimental designs can also be exceedingly challenging.

So, what’s the solution? Make it easier of course! Anyone can write an “easy” statistics book, just as easily as one can *completely misrepresent the discipline and the inherent complexity of statistics and quantitative science more generally*. Books like that fly off the shelves and are sold mostly to individuals who do not want to study nor learn statistics in the first place and are merely looking for an *escape route*. Consequently, they learn “some” statistics, but at risk of it being terribly misunderstood. A little knowledge is a dangerous thing. Memorizing that the mean “is a measure of central tendency” with a formula showing the user how to compute it is dangerous. How so? For one, the *arithmetic mean* is only one of many *possible* means and it often doesn’t adequately indicate the center of the distribution! “Incomplete” statistics books (e.g., software and cookbook manuals) are fine for those who are already aware of the complexities of statistics because they can navigate around the shortcomings in such books, but they are nothing short of *malpractice* if used in teaching as *primary* (not *secondary*) sources for students coming to the discipline for the first time. Without unpacking and working with statistical formulae to truly understand what they reveal vs. what they do not, statistics teaching is more likely to *mislead* than it is to properly *educate*. Alleviating anxiety by teaching “easy statistics” is unethical as such teaching completely misrepresents the subject. *These students are not learning statistics. They are learning something else*. The “easy books” can certainly be useful in a course, but should never replace a *primary* and more rigorous resource.

### 0.4.3 Prerequisites to Reading This Book

The prerequisites to reading this book are modest. We assume the reader has had at least one introductory statistics course at the undergraduate level. Preferably, the student will have also had an introductory course at the college level in calculus and linear algebra, or at least some *exposure* to these areas. The introductory course in statistics is mandatory, while the calculus and linear algebra courses are optional but preferred. The necessary prerequisites are reviewed in [Chapter 2](#c2.xhtml#c2) and as needed throughout the book, but at a quicker pace than would be the case in a truly introductory course in these subjects. For instance, we may refresh the reader on why we are passing to the limit, but we assume the reader has had exposure to limits and derivatives before. Likewise with concepts from linear algebra, we discuss the *why* behind the concept and may re-introduce it briefly, but it would be beneficial if the reader has seen the concept before. From a generally applied perspective, it suffices that the reader has a sense of where the mathematics used “fit” in the bigger picture instead of presenting the mathematics as a sole topic as would be the case in an appendix or simply referring the reader to a book on pure linear algebra devoid of statistical application, for instance.

## 0.5 Pedagogical Approach and the Trade-Offs of Top-Down, Bottom-Up Learning

We would like to spend some time justifying the pedagogical approach used in the book and how it is similar to and different from other approaches that might be employed in teaching material of this sort. We also wish to give instructors and students ideas for how to learn this and similar material. It is hoped that both instructors and students will find this discussion fruitful in contextualizing their own teaching and learning. Nothing in what follows is meant to be rigid or dogmatic regarding how statistical and machine learning methods should be taught or assimilated. What follows is only meant to serve as an invitation to explore and discuss these approaches.9

### 0.5.1 Top-Down, Bottom-Up Learning

There can be said to be two ways of learning the material of multivariate statistics and machine learning (Deisenroth et al., [2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000080)). There are risks inherent in both approaches. The first approach is what we will call a *top-down approach*, where students are instructed from the highest and most general “overview” global perspective on what these methods accomplish and how they can be used. For example, when teaching principal components analysis, one could instruct students that PCA is designed to assess the dimensionality of the variables subjected to analysis. The description, though partially correct, is at the same time grossly incomplete. A *bottom-up approach*, on the other hand, would be that of beginning with fundamental mathematics such as essential ideas of vectors, matrices, and most importantly, linear combinations, which quite naturally leads into the definition of what a component actually *is*, that of the aforesaid *linear combination*. But again, quite incomplete without a blending of the aforementioned top-down perspective regarding the “big picture” from the top of the mountain, which is *dimension reduction*.

As an instructor, given that we only have a limited amount of time with students (or readers), we want them to take away the most essential *lessons* that they will carry with them for a *lifetime* and provide for them a *foundation* on which they can generalize and extend their abilities and understanding. We do not want them to get lost in the trees and not recognize the forest. The top-down approach with regard to PCA (as just one example of a technique) is incomplete of course because it neglects to *contextualize* PCA as *one* such technique for assessing underlying dimensionality, and of those techniques, only assesses *linear dimensions*. PCA, put into proper context, is but a special case of a wide variety of dimension-reduction techniques. The danger with so-called “cookbook” approaches to statistics and data analysis is that a student could come away from a course in multivariate statistics believing that PCA is *the one and only* technique for dimension reduction, which would be blatantly false. Not only does it deprive the student of learning, it is embarrassing for them to discuss or present the method in a public forum if they are asked about the method to any degree and hold fast and true that PCA is *equivalent* to dimension reduction rather than simply one *option* for it.

Hence, even if one begins with a top-down approach, either in teaching or learning, one should quickly get to the “bottom” to make these important distinctions, and the further the “bottom” we go, the more we get into the technical details, differentiations and distinctions, right up to necessary qualifiers such as *the assumption that we are discussing only applies to real numbers*, as an example. That’s probably too far, but the point is that students should be taught proper *context* in learning statistics and machine learning.

> *Much of our thinking is grounded in metaphor and the art of substituting symbols, whether those symbols be words, pictures, or even musical tones.*

Equally, the problem with a *bottom-up approach* is that there can be so much focus spent on distinctions that the student may never grasp the bigger picture that PCA (to use the same example) is a dimension-reduction technique in the first place and how it can be applied to address scientific questions. After a semester of vectors, matrices, and other mathematics which may or may not include proofs, the student could feasibly come away from the course not truly understanding in any global way *what PCA is for*, *when it can (and cannot) be used*, and *what the* *big picture* *is* behind it. I have had first-hand experience in meeting many students who have had calculus, linear algebra, some statistics under their belts, yet who are unable to have a discussion about what these subjects are truly *about* because they were too busy intaking technical computational detail and 10solving problems blindly or by rote computational heuristics via planned and patterned “problem sets” that they never quite grasped the bigger picture of what they were even “doing.” *Zero insight into the bigger picture*.

The pedagogical approach adopted in this book is to be mindful of the bottom-up, top-down distinction and not emphasize one *too much* at the expense of the other.

### 0.5.2 Ways of Writing a Book: Making It Pedagogical Instead of Cryptic

Perhaps the best way to become an overnight genius is to write a book nobody understands then claim authority over the knowledge! That is one approach to writing a book, albeit a poor one and very egoistic. Alternatively, one can write a book that many if not most understand and become known as a great communicator of challenging material. We have all come across mathematics texts that were “unreadable,” and the only audience for the book was between the ears of the author, while at the same time we have come across books that are far too general and appealing to too wide of an audience as to entirely misrepresent the subject.

Mathematics (or at minimum, mathematical *symbolism*) should not be avoided in a book like this, yet at the same time making such mathematics purposely *cryptic* benefits nobody. Rigor should not be avoided in teaching, but students should be instructed on *why* such rigor exists, the importance of differentiating concepts instead of blanketing them in imperfect understanding. The student should be given the opportunity to appreciate why rigor is prized by the mathematician or analytical philosopher in the first place.

### 0.5.3 Standing on the Shoulders of Giants: A Companion to Advanced Texts

Aside from this book being a stand-alone introductory textbook and reference to multivariate statistics and machine learning, it can also be thought of as a *companion* to understanding other texts based on the same or similar topics. The author’s aim was to make this text stand alone in its own right, but also be a “gateway” to understanding what the “next level” books discuss, so that the reader may follow up from this book and get into those more advanced texts with relative (or at least *more*) ease.

For example, if you are a newcomer to statistical learning, understanding existing standards in the field such as *Elements of Statistical Learning* (Hastie et al., [2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)), *Probabilistic Machine Learning* ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)) or *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning* ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)) can be at minimum difficult and daunting and at most impossible without a good teacher at your side. One of the aims of this book is to be that *companion*, that *teacher* to provide an interpretation of the concepts discussed in those higher-level books. With our emphasis on foundations, our hope is that the reader can then excursion into more advanced sources as well as begin perusing the research literature themselves having a foundational base from which to grow.

### 0.5.4 Making Equations “Speak”

The simplest of examples from introductory statistics will illustrate the style we adopt throughout the book. The reader will undoubtedly be familiar with the classic *z-*score:11

  
$$z = \\frac{y - \\mu}{\\sigma}$$  

The reader will also likely remember being taught that converting to *z-*scores standardizes a distribution such to have a mean of zero and standard deviation equal to one. Perhaps such was the extent to which this concept was explored. If you look at the *z*\-score more closely, however, what is it *exactly*? We see that it is a *ratio*, a ratio of *y* − μ to *σ*. But what is *y* *− μ*? It is a *deviation*, a deviation from the mean to be more precise. What is *σ*? It is another deviation, this one the *standard deviation*. Hence, we see the *z*\-score is a comparison via a ratio of *two deviations*, one that you are computing based on *y −* *μ* to one that is “average” or “standard” in the data, that of *σ*. Hence, if the observed deviation is about as large as the average deviation, then *z* is equal to approximately 1. If it is much larger, then *z* will be much greater than 1. This is one interpretation regarding what a *z*\-score is actually communicating.

As much as possible throughout the text, space permitting, we seek to *unpack* the meaning behind equations to appreciate what they are communicating. Equations and formulas are, after all, *concepts*, and concepts should be explored for all of their meaning.

### 0.5.5 The Power of Problems

It is often said that in learning any technical area such as statistics, working out problems is the way to mastery. Tackling problems is not the only way to learn, but it definitely helps focus energy on elements of what you are learning. One can read on a topic to no end, but until you come across problems that take time, energy, brainstorming, and experience to solve, the learning may remain latent. That is, it hasn’t consolidated yet, akin to preparing for a life event yet not truly knowing if you are truly prepared until the event actually arises. I have taught many students who brazenly believed they understood statistics, that is, until asked to explain even basic statistics at a dissertation defense. As is true with life in general, *reality is the true test of one’s knowledge*. “Training” will only get you so far, as every athlete knows.

Each chapter in the book contains a brief set of problems, most are open so that the student can think more globally about the concepts learned to see where it takes her. Most are of the “discussion type.” Intellectual exploration of ideas is encouraged throughout this book, and problem sets attempt to foster this activity. The selection of problems is relatively arbitrary and we encourage instructors to expand or customize existing problems to suit the needs and scope of the course they are teaching. In the author’s own teaching, problem sets are usually improvised or customized to each lecture or class, and we encourage instructors to do the same. An “open problem” can easily turn into a more rigorous closed-answer analytical one with just a few additional elements. The problems in the book should be considered nothing more than good “starting points” to *initiate discussion* and are relatively few in number given space considerations for the book. If the reader or instructor would like more targeted and specific problems of a technical or analytical nature, they should feel welcome in contacting the author who would be more than happy to provide problem sets to suit the needs of their specific course.

### 0.5.6 Computing Languages

R and Python are the dominant languages currently in use for statistics, data science, and machine learning. Hence, they are the languages used for demonstrations of techniques in this book. However, it should be emphasized that *this book is not about computing*, and the reader should realize that computing languages come and go, but *foundations* are generally consistent. “Digging up code” in manuals and the internet is (relatively) easy, even if it can be time-consuming and test our patience! Understanding *why* you want to dig such code up is much more difficult and requires actually understanding the underlying principles and concepts upon which the code is based. The emphasis of this book is on *understanding first*, *computing second*.12

Due to the sheer number of topics we treat in this book, we do not provide code for *every* topic. Instead, we are selective, providing code and examples for topics as a general survey of how Python and R can be used for various applications. For one method, we may provide code examples in both Python and R, while for others, only for Python or R individually. Not only was this to keep the book of manageable size and focus on the most important matters (i.e., explanation of what the actual procedures accomplish), but it is also for the reason that some procedures are simply more amenable to one software package over the other. R is featured a bit more throughout the book than is Python. As an instructor using the book, they should feel free to bypass examples using the software they have not adopted.

### 0.5.7 Notation Used in the Book

Half of the battle with reading a book on multivariate statistics or machine learning can be making out the notation used. Even if you are experienced in the area, you can spend a great deal of your time trying to figure out how the author is using this or that notation. What a waste of time! We avoid that as much as possible in this book. Mathematics is a beautiful subject in its own right and to those who dislike it, it is nonetheless a necessary evil to understanding multivariate and machine learning, but *abuse* of mathematics is all too rampant; otherwise great texts ruined because the author does not explain what the mathematics mean or the symbols used in describing such mathematics. We try to avoid those pitfalls the best we can in this book, though we no doubt do so imperfectly.

Our use of subscripts is purposely non-consistent throughout the text. At times, we subscript *variables*, whereas other times we do not. To use a simple example of this approach, a *z*\-score can be defined as

  
$$z = \\frac{y - \\mu}{\\sigma}$$  

or like this,

  
$$z = \\frac{y\_{i} - \\mu}{\\sigma}$$  

where *y* is now purposely indicated as a variable, *y* [i]. Both *y* and *y* [i] denote a variable in this context, and both forms are acceptable for this and other statistics and equations featured throughout the text. As well, the transpose of a matrix **A** can be denoted **A** *^T* or just as well simply as **A**′. In places using **A** *^T* seemed more “natural” than **A**′, whereas in other places **A**′ was preferred as it is a bit less cumbersome. Random variables versus *realizations* of those random variables is also not always consistent. For example, formally, for a given random variable *X*, a realization of that random variable could be notated as *x* [i], such that *X* = *x* [i], however using uppercase throughout the text we found would be too cumbersome and overall preferred the smaller notation *x* or *x* [i] even when potentially referring to a random variable. Lastly, in a regression context, *βx* or *βx* *[i]* was, in general, deemed preferable to *βX* simply because again we favored the smaller *x* notation regardless of whether or not *x* was considered fixed or random.

## 0.6 Nobody Learns a Million Things: The Importance of Foundations and Learning How to Learn

A great teacher once said, *geniuses chunk information, that’s what makes them so smart*. Contrary to how undergraduates (and beginning graduate students) often perceive their professors, no 13person, even those running around with PhDs, can know *everything* (some even know very little!). But the smart ones *know where to look*. They know which “mental folder” to open and pursue. What is even more vitally important is that they will have a sense of when they are right or wrong. They will also get a sense of when the answer is unachievable or uncertain. The maturity to achieve these milestones is no small feat and is gained through experience. The undergraduate knows a lot, but the seasoned scholar is much more tentative with her own knowledge. *Knowing when you don’t know is probably the most important of all knowledge.*

The philosophy adopted in this book is that it is far better to learn and understand a *few things* really well than to try to learn *everything*, which as mentioned, is always impossible for anyone. With the explosion of statistical learning and such in the current climate, it can be tempting for a book writer to present a “catalogue” of methods, a wealth of “facts” the reader can access anytime they wish. And though, as mentioned, this approach has its place and there are a number of excellent books that already attempt this, for an introductory text or university course a better approach would be to emphasize the more common and *foundational principles*, the rest of which become derivatives and extensions or special cases of these majestic pillar areas. Such is the approach taken in this book. Though our approach is generally “top-down” in that we seek to give the reader a bird’s eye view of what is going on in statistics and machine learning, we prioritize communicating the *foundations* upon which most other topics one could come across are then “learnable.” Without the foundations in place, one’s understanding of new things has no legs to stand on. *Good education starts with strong foundations*.

### 0.6.1 Essential Philosophy of Science and History

Understanding the mathematics of multivariate statistics and machine learning is insufficient for the scientist. One must also have a grounding in the scientific *context* in which these tools are used. Ask the average student in the sciences (or surprisingly, even in mathematics) what philosophy is, and you will probably get some version of pop culture’s interpretation similar to the response you would get if you asked the same question regarding the nature of psychology (“oh yeah, I’ve heard of Freud”). However, closer to truth and the position advanced in this book (and my other books) is that *philosophical thinking is the basis upon which all other knowledge is derived or created*. All of the concepts, statistical and mathematical formulas that we will see in this book have *foundations*. Those foundations are conceptual and very deep. Concepts, even “rigorous” ones do not arise or evolve as concrete objects. Instead, they are first “mushy” and imperfect. There is perhaps no better example of this than the evolution of calculus and the idea of *limits*. The limit concept was not “invented” by Newton or Leibnitz, but instead evolved over a couple thousand years. The great inventors helped “finished the job” as it were (along with several mathematicians afterward), but it should always be understood that they completed a project that was in the works for a very long time. So it is with even advanced statistics and machine learning. The foundations to these “modern” tools often go back centuries. Knowledge is a *progression*, it usually does not simply arrive “on the scene” without prior development.

Why is understanding and appreciating philosophy of science so important and relevant for the scientist? Consider the issue of causation. Statistical analysis could never reveal causation. Causation, whatever it may mean in the first place (for centuries, philosophers have debated the issue), concerns itself mostly with *research design*, at least in experimental science. Further, methods such as neural networks, at least historically, have been more focused on simply getting predictions and classifications “right” without feeling the need to know “why” those predictions are accurate. Analysts using neural networks have more or less been satisfied with the unknown function remaining a “black box” as it were. In many areas, we’re not trying to necessarily create a 14mathematical “causal” model as one would, in say, biology, but instead are simply trying to create an algorithm that will predict or classify successfully and minimize error and misclassifications in doing so. One is more tolerant of the prediction equation being a “black box” than in sciences where explaining the predictors is of paramount importance. For instance, understanding what factors predict the orbit of a satellite is not simply a black box problem. We have to know “why” so that we understand variations in trajectories.

Consider how a student might learn statistics or machine learning in a typical course. They perhaps take a course on the subject, study the materials used in the course, and then most likely prove results associated with those objects or apply those objects to empirical problems often using software. Presumably, one can learn what correlation *is* through its formulaic definition just as one can learn what a *group* is in abstract algebra and then go on to utilize that concept in solving problems. All this is fine and good, but a more *thorough* and *deeper* understanding of these topics can be achieved by studying their *history*. Pearson’s correlation is not merely a formula in a textbook. Understanding correlation means appreciating and understanding where it came from, how it evolved, and ultimately how it revolutionized both statistics and science. This can be said to be true of virtually all statistical and mathematical objects.

Indeed, the seeming infinite regress that occurs when one begins questioning, as though one is a child, eventually brings one to philosophical and historical inquiries. What you typically see in textbooks, including the current one you are reading, is the current “state of the art,” of a discipline. But beneath that state of the art is a long history of *ideas*, *concepts*, *controversies* that culminated in the “polished” object you currently see in your textbook. Pragmatically, there is a need to cut that search off at some point, but if you question further about the objects you are learning you will eventually become a philosopher and historian, because, quite simply, there is *nowhere else to go to learn of the true foundations*. As we will emphasize throughout this book, *true understanding is found in the foundations*, though we stop well short of examining historical and philosophical underpinnings. The point we make is merely for the student to recognize the importance of understanding statistics and machine learning in proper historical and epistemological *context* and to be aware that these directions can be pursued, should one choose well beyond this book.

### 0.6.2 Beyond the Jargon, Beyond the Hype

We hold that the purpose of education is to see inside of the “black box” down to its simplest of principles instead of mapping one’s perception of a mathematical tool to some sophisticated and overblown ideas of what that tool actually *is* and what it can do. A few Google searches will convince anyone “in the know” that artificial intelligence and machine learning are continuously marketed as being mysteriously complex. Let the world think what they will. The job of the student and aspiring professional is to learn what these things actually *are* stripped down to their most basic and essential fundamental principles. This is what “expertise” actually is, awareness of what is going on *inside* of the *perceived complexity*, not being part of the populace that has false perceptions, misunderstandings, and misguided glorifications about the tool.

As an example, consider the word *algorithm*. The *idea* of an algorithm is not new. It is *ancient*. *Algorithms have existed forever*. Even the Babylonians were working with algorithms ([Knuth, 1972](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000195)). Yet without understanding just what *is* an algorithm, the newcomer might be fooled by today’s climate into thinking they are “modern” in some sense. One might even use the word algorithm and automatically associate it with cutting-edge technology. True, modern algorithms are new, but the *concept* is old, and being aware of this can help demystify the nature of the algorithm in today’s modern climate. Conceptual understanding knows no label, it often cannot be encapsulated in a single word or phrase or definition. It is more of an *idea*. All otherwise “precise” 15definitions arise from much *fuzzier* concepts. And if we traced concepts such as algorithms all the way back, we would certainly discover that the earliest of peoples were in fact thinking algorithmically. *Modern ways of describing concepts or ideas do not necessarily imply those things or ideas are modern*.

## 0.7 The Power and Dangers of Analogy and Metaphor: Ways of Understanding

Every explanation is a *way of understanding something, no matter how near or distant the explanation may be*. At first this may seem like a radical point of view. Understanding what is a chair can be helped by understanding what a bench is, but the study of the bench is not the “end game.” It too is a way of understanding something. The concept of a “bench” is elusive, the definition is only an *approximation to understanding its nature*. The sooner we realize this, the sooner we can accept analogies and metaphors as vehicles to understanding concepts in statistics and machine learning, while also appreciating that the truest “forms” (to be somewhat Platonian about it) are not in the mathematical equations. Those too are *approximations*.

As an example, suppose a student takes a course in linear algebra to understand the objects of that subject. Suppose they wish to understand what the *rank of a matrix* is all about. The rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent rows or columns of a matrix. Is that the “end game” to understanding rank? No! It is but an *approximation*. Not only is there a multitude of ways of conceiving rank from different angles in mathematics, the reason *why* rank exists is much deeper. There is a wider *context* to understanding rank, just as there is a wider context to understanding anything else, whether that be in mathematics, statistics, machine learning, or English literature for that matter.

Consider the following analogy that might help in understanding what rank is:

> *Rank is sort of an indication of whether the matrix under consideration contains overlapping “information.”*

Of course, the above is not the full story, but the point is that it *approximates* the full story, at least to some degree. The concept of “information” as a generalization of a column or row vector is a weak generalization of what a column or row vector is, but the analogy helps “encapsulate” the concept and serves a purpose so long as one realizes there is always more to learn about the concept.

The danger, of course, is that all formalism gets lost and all that remains are imperfect, imprecise, and inexact analogies. The purpose of using analogies and metaphors is not to “water down” the material; it is simply to approximate true forms a bit more closely to bring the student into the *neighborhood* of the actual object, where encapsulating the “true” object is somewhat elusive. Defining the arithmetic *mean* as *where most of the data falls* is a terrible definition and just as terrible of an approximation. Settling on that definition in undergraduate statistics would be doing a tremendous disservice to students. Hence, one must be very cautious in using analogies and metaphors too liberally, even with the awareness that all definitions, even the ones closest to the concept, are nonetheless of the analogy/metaphor type, even if at first glance they do not appear so.

Throughout the book we use analogies and metaphors in places while usually emphasizing that they are just that, *approximations to understanding the true concept*. They are “ways” of trying to get *closer* to the object. So long as that is understood, such tools may be helpful and useful in understanding. Indeed, one of the dangers of focusing too heavily on precision and formality is that the concept might be lost altogether. As discussed, concepts are “fuzzy,” they exist within a 16philosophical “cloud” of sorts where the well-defined object can experience a degree of interpretation without losing the essence of what it actually is.

### 0.7.1 The Infinite Regress of Knowledge: A Venture into What It Means to “Understand” Something and Why Epistemology Is Important

Statistics, data analysis, and machine learning are *hard*. Anyone can compute a correlation coefficient or have software do it for them. That is not the difficult part. The difficult part is making sense of empirical observations and applying analytical mathematical approaches in trying to understand something elusive we call *reality*. Many students are amazed at how difficult a statistical problem can become when given just a little thought. Others simply think we’re making the problem difficult on purpose and never learn to appreciate finer distinctions. Rigorous courses in statistical consulting spend a long time assessing and debating over statistical problems that end up having potentially very complex solutions, much different from the typical and overly simplified undergraduate solution obtained by referring back to the course textbook to see if the “right answer” has been achieved. The icy winter driveway pales in comparison to how “slippery” statistics can be when applying them to data. Entire conclusions can be flipped around by looking at the data in a slightly different *way*.

But how does this thing called *understanding* work? It has been my experience that many times “breakthroughs” in understanding, those “ah ha!” moments are about things students have been told before, perhaps many times, but now it has finally been learned “anew” in a much, much deeper way. It is grasped at a much deeper level, and seemingly for the first time. Technical understanding parallels other types of understanding, such as how to navigate through life and the proper mental mindset for peace and success. “*Life is what you make it*” is what we have always been told, yet one day we finally “get it” and realize the truth and depth of that maxim to its fullest. We learn it for the very first time even though we have heard it all our lives.

Understanding does not typically occur *linearly*; it usually occurs in *leaps and bounds*, or through “steps” as in the step-like function of [Figure 0.1](#intro.xhtml#f0.1), where one day the understanding and grasp of the material seems to hit a new unexpected level, seemingly almost overnight.17

![Figure 0.1 Statistical understanding rarely occurs linearly, but instead in leaps and bounds as indicated in the step-like function. The upward arrow represents a “Eureka” moment where new understanding seemingly occurs in an instantaneous “leap.”Return to text.⏎](images/fig0.1.jpg)

*Figure 0.1* Statistical understanding rarely occurs linearly, but instead in leaps and bounds as indicated in the step-like function. The upward arrow represents a “Eureka” moment where new understanding seemingly occurs in an instantaneous “leap.”[Return to text.⏎](#intro.xhtml#re_f0.1)

As practical advice as you embark on your learning of statistics and machine learning, *do not try to understand everything at once*. Allow for “approximation” and “iteration” as you study. Allow for fuzziness each time you look at it. *Do not let perfection be the enemy of* *good* but rather study these things often with a fresh perspective and hopefully the fuzziness will begin to be replaced by understanding.

In this respect, we follow general and excellent ideas provided by [Hubbard and Hubbard (2002)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000161) in their advice on how to read mathematics more generally:

> Reading mathematics is different from other reading … there are two parts to understanding a theorem: understanding the statement, and understanding the proof. The first is more important than the second … . If you’re still having trouble, skip ahead to examples. This may contradict what you have been told – that mathematics is sequential, and that you must understand each sentence before going on to the next. In reality, although mathematical writing is necessarily sequential, mathematical understanding is not: you (and the experts) never understand perfectly up to some point not at all beyond. The “beyond,” where understanding is only partial, is an essential part of the motivation and the conceptual background of the “here and now.” You may often (perhaps usually) find that when you return to something you left half-understood, it will have become clear in the light of the further things you have studied, even though the further things are themselves obscure.”
> 
> (p. 2)

#### 0.7.1.1 Epistemological Maturity

One focus of the book is to situate statistical models and other *ideas* within a wider *context*. For example, set theory is often regarded as one of the most unifying areas of mathematics (though many would say now that *category theory* eclipses that perspective). A sign of maturity in knowledge of statistical and related models is being aware and understanding the more *global structures* of which smaller structures are special cases. These global structures can be more difficult to “see” as one considers more complex models. However, a simple example will illustrate the concept.

Most readers familiar with the analysis of variance will readily be aware that the between-subjects *t*\-test can be considered a special case of the wider between-subjects ANOVA model. This is what we mean by *maturity* – one sees the higher-order structure from which others can be deduced and situated. This process continues for increasingly complex models. While at first many users of statistical methods may prefer a “cookbook approach” for simply selecting the “correct” method for a given problem, the maturity of the user in relation to statistics becomes evident when they realize there is never only a *single* way to analyze data. The cookbook approach is not necessarily always *wrong*; it is usually simply grossly *incomplete*.

If the student understands statistics at a higher level beyond the recipe book, not only do they become aware of different possibilities when analyzing data, their ability to interpret research findings skyrockets. The student no longer assumes that PCA is *equivalent* to dimension reduction, for instance, and thus when the conference speaker reports, “Our PCA did not reveal any components with eigenvalues greater than unity on the correlation matrix we analyzed, hence, the data are not amenable to dimension reduction,” the knowledgeable researcher is immediately aware of the incorrect conclusion to the research report. *The PCA did not reveal linear dimension reduction, the bigger picture of whether underlying dimensions exist in the data has not yet been answered, and may even be unanswerable, since the underlying manifold may not yet have been uncovered*. *The discovery of dimensionality depends greatly on the tool used in the search*. This is no trivial 18difference in conclusions, it is the difference between an *incorrect* vs. *correct* interpretation of the research outcome. *The distinction matters*.

The above is a perfect example of the hierarchical thinking we are attempting to generate in this book. Statistics is slippery; you can think you know it, you can think the formula or data say one thing, but underlying that conclusion is a new *base rate*, a new *denominator*, and if you’re not aware of that underlying base, you are bound to conclude it is winter because you are standing in your walk-in freezer! The ratio 2/4 = 0.5 is with certainty, until we consider that fraction relative to the new base of 5, then (2/4)/5 = 0.1. We were so sure 0.5 was the final answer until we incorporated the new base. Context is everything when it comes to statistics, mathematics, and science more generally. The narrow view of looking at only a few of the many variables in existence can seriously bias the conclusion. Of course, the best of mathematicians, statisticians, scientists, and researchers know this, it is second nature to them. But to the student of these areas, this is what is most important in learning: *there is always context to any conclusion*; *change the context, and the conclusion usually changes as well.*

## 0.8 Format and Organization of Chapters

A survey of each chapter follows:

*   *[Chapter 1](#c1.xhtml#c1)* features a discussion of the philosophical foundations of the methods featured in this book as well as the more broad topics of statistical learning and machine learning.
*   *[Chapter 2](#c2.xhtml#c2)* features an overview of the mathematical and statistical foundations required for the rest of the book. We discuss the “pillars” of statistics and machine learning, namely probability, statistics, linear algebra, calculus.
*   *[Chapter 3](#c3.xhtml#c3)* features a (very) brief introduction to R and Python software. Both software packages are used throughout the book in providing brief “snippet” demonstrations of techniques.
*   *[Chapter 4](#c4.xhtml#c4)* denotes the actual beginning of the statistical and machine learning segment of the book. We begin with a discussion of familiar univariate ANOVA models.
*   *[Chapter 5](#c5.xhtml#c5)* surveys simple linear and multiple linear regression models, effect sizes for such models, mediated and moderated regression models, principal components regression, partial least-squares, and canonical correlation analysis. Regression is the bedrock of many statistical and machine learning methods and much of this chapter lays the foundation for material to be discussed later in the book.
*   *[Chapter 6](#c6.xhtml#c6)* features a discussion of regularization in regression. We introduce the concept of regularization, then discuss the most common ways of regularizing a model, which includes ridge, lasso, elastic net. We also survey least-angle regression.
*   *[Chapter 7](#c7.xhtml#c7)* features a discussion of nonlinear regression models, including polynomial regression, splines, kernel regression, and others. We also relate some of this material to neural networks discussed later in the book.
*   *[Chapter 8](#c8.xhtml#c8)* features a discussion of the generalized linear model, which includes the popular logistic regression, Poisson model, and others. Generalized additive models and discriminant analysis are also discussed. We close out the chapter with a discussion of the nonparametric technique of *k*\-nearest neighbors.
*   *[Chapter 9](#c9.xhtml#c9)* surveys support vector machines (SVMs) as a competitor to discriminant analysis for when the response is binary. We discuss SVMs for both the linearly separable case and non-separable case, which will necessitate using kernels to address the nonlinearity in way of expanding the feature space.
*   *[Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml#c10)* features a discussion of decision trees and committee machines, including bagging, random forests, and boosting.19
*   *[Chapter 11](#c11.xhtml#c11)* features dimension-reduction techniques such as principal components analysis and manifold learning more generally. Independent components analysis and probabilistic PCA are also surveyed, in addition to nonlinear dimension-reduction techniques such as kernel PCA. Principal curves, multidimensional scaling, self-organizing maps, locally linear embedding, isomap, sne, and *t*\-sne are also discussed.
*   *[Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml#c12)* surveys the method of exploratory factor analysis, including the many caveats and potential problems in interpreting factor analysis. Independent factor analysis, nonlinear factor analysis, and mixtures of factor analysis are also discussed.
*   *[Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml#c13)* features a discussion of confirmatory factor analysis, path analysis and structural equation modeling. These models can be interpreted as extensions of regression and exploratory factor analysis and can be considered a special case of the wider dimension-reduction or manifold learning paradigm.
*   *[Chapter 14](#c14.xhtml#c14)* is about cluster analysis and data segmentation. We survey such methods as *k*\-means and hierarchical approaches to cluster analysis, including density-based clustering as well as mixture models.
*   *[Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml#c15)* surveys the method of neural networks. We develop the neural network from first principles of regression, then contextualize neural networks relative to other statistical and machine learning approaches such as projection pursuit.

# 1 First Principles and Philosophical Foundations

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-3](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-3)

In this first chapter, we introduce and survey “big picture” topics that are pertinent to the fields and evolution of statistics and machine learning. These areas of study, just as is true of virtually all areas of inquiry, rest on deep *philosophical assumptions*. To get “deep” is to get philosophical. To the uninformed, the word “philosophy” might bring to mind someone casually questioning the meaning of life or similar pursuit whether in a university classroom or on a Sunday afternoon hammock. Even worse, to the naïve the word might bring to mind something one does if one is determined to not gain employment! To the educated, however, philosophical foundations are everything and are at the very core of virtually all knowledge. *Anything studied enough, questioned enough, critically evaluated enough, will find its way to philosophical assumptions and foundations, into “mushy” territory where distinctions are made not in terms of symbols such as in mathematics, but in pre-symbolic forms in terms of “ideas” that often cannot be easily operationalized. Transforming the “mushy” into “rigorous” is, in many cases, brutally difficult*.

## 1.1 Science, Statistics, Machine Learning, and Artificial Intelligence

Attempting to distinguish between what exactly *statistics*, *machine learning*, and *artificial intelligence* are can seem like a trivial waste of time for knowledgeable researchers. However, for the student, a comment on these distinctions, if there are any, is very important as they are the ones coming to these fields for the first time and do not have the luxury of seeing things in the perspective of a rearview mirror to be able to note which distinctions are important and which are indeed, trivial; that is, which features are overlapping versus which are unique to their respective areas.

Historically, numerous attempts have been made to define just what *is* artificial intelligence, and none of them are truly satisfactory. None can be said to have truly “captured” the concept, in large part because whenever one tries to define something so precisely one usually misses the mark, akin to trying to get a hold of a single observation on a continuous scale – *the more you zero in on it, the more elusive it appears*. Hence, as is true of most things, artificial intelligence is a *concept* that cannot be truly captured by precise definitions and vague language. Even defining precisely what mathematics is can take up a dissertation! The best one can do is get a general *sense* of what it is and what it is not and go from there. Still, we may be able to settle on the following imperfect definition:

> *Artificial intelligence is the science of machines, usually computers, carrying out tasks that would typically require something called “intelligence” if the same task had been performed by a human being.*21

Artificial intelligence (AI) can hardly be considered a “science” in the spirit of laboratory science. Proponents of *weak AI* hold that a machine is intelligent if we can get it to carry out sophisticated tasks. Proponents of *strong AI* hold that artificial intelligence is the ability of machines to “mimic” human intelligence. Of course, strong AI may not even be achievable, but weak AI is possibly so, especially with the rise of machine learning.

*Machine learning* is often defined as the ability of computers to learn from data without having to be explicitly programmed. Machine learning is related to artificial intelligence because an intelligent system should, at minimum, be able to adapt to changes in its environment, which is precisely what machine learning algorithms purport to do. While machine learning is largely associated with computer science, much of its history can also be found in cybernetics and control science. More recently, the origins of machine learning are often associated with the psychologist Frank Rosenblatt who essentially conceived of a learning machine that we would today call a basic *neural network* ([Fradkov, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000107)). It was work on the backpropagation algorithm in the 1980s that truly initiated modern interest in neural networks more specifically and when eventually combined with the cheap availability of parallel computing and memory, the stage was set for the “gold rush” of machine learning in the 2000s ([Fradkov, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000107)).

Where does *statistics* fit into all this? How closely is machine learning related to statistics? The following are a couple of quotes from experts in the area that highlight the closeness of statistics and machine learning:

> Machine learning is essentially a form of applied statistics with increased emphasis on the use of computers to statistically estimate complicated functions and a decreased emphasis on proving confidence intervals around these functions.
> 
> ([Goodfellow et al., 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000131), p. 95)

> If the statistics field had incorporated computing methodology from its inception as a fundamental tool, as opposed to simply a convenient way to apply our existing tools, many of the other data related fields \[such as machine learning (ML)\] would not have needed to exist – they would have been part of statistics.
> 
> ([Friedman, 1997](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000110), p. 27)

Then there is the field of *computational statistics* which is described as *computationally intensive methods in statistics* ([Rizzo, 2019](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000303)) and which focuses on such techniques as the bootstrap and numerical algorithms that overlap a great deal with the subject matter of machine learning. Some even distinguish between *statistical computing* vs. *computational statistics*, the former having more emphasis on numerical methods and algorithms while the latter featuring additional topics such as exploratory analysis, data partitioning, and others ([Rizzo, 2019](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000303)).

When one browses the literature on statistics and machine learning, one will definitely notice differences. Machine learning “feels” more about the *algorithm* than it is about the *data*. For example, in statistics we use linear regression to model data, but in machine learning we are studying how effective linear regression is when compared to other “algorithms.” The computer science perspective is the theoretical study of algorithms, how they perform, how complex they are, their computational efficiency, how much they can store in memory, etc., whereas statistics feels more about fitting a precise scientific model to data. Of course, both overlap a great deal, but have slightly different *flavors*. We should always remember, however, that the computer is nothing more than an electronic machine that speeds up computation in either case. Much of computer science has little to do with the computer. It has everything to do with mathematics and statistics, to which computer scientists have contributed to immensely.22

As we will see throughout the book, many effective machine learning algorithms have been inspired by age-old mathematical ideas for *function approximation*. Indeed, one does not need a machine at all to do machine learning. The stranded person on a deserted island can (at least in *theory*, a lot of theory!) perform simple machine learning just as the high-tech computer scientist, but without the benefit of automation or an electronic machine. “Machine learning” is simply a name to reflect that many processes are *implemented* by a machine, namely, the computer. But make no mistake, machine learning itself, the *concept*, is as old as it gets. Yes, the Greeks were doing “machine learning” in some capacity long before humans “invented” it.

### 1.1.1 Mathematics, Statistics, and Computation

There is sometimes the perception by nonspecialists that “math is math” and that there is little creativity, in a sense, in developing such math. The author has served on student committees where the perception of mathematics is that it is *static*; *it is what it is* and not subject to invention, creativity, amendment, or reconstruction. Of course, this perception of mathematics is wholly false, as creativity in mathematics is what mathematics is all about. However difficult mathematics is, the mathematics itself is entirely (mostly) logical, and solutions are often correct or incorrect, at least at relatively elementary levels. The high-school student completing the problem set quickly looks at the back of the book to see if she got the solution correct. If the solution at the back of the book does not match the solution she obtained, her answer is deemed incorrect and she must then figure out why. Rarely is there flexibility in the solution for elementary problem sets. The “feedback loop” is relatively clear and straightforward.

The further away we move from mathematics, mathematical statistics, etc., the more we stumble upon areas where clear-cut and unique solutions often do not exist. Instead, there are often a *variety of solutions available*, some better than others, and many dependent on the preference or analytical style of the practitioner. This is often the most frustrating of experiences for the newcomer to applying mathematics and statistics to empirical problems. “Good solutions” are not unique and usually require the practitioner to infuse a mixture of methodological and philosophical thinking into the effort of arriving at the *best* solution. That is, the mathematical solution is only the *beginning*; she must now interpret what that solution *means* in the context of the scientific problem. This is where students often have difficulty, struggling with regards to what is the most “optimal” (in some sense) solution. Rigorous thinking is good, but in most things you also have to allow for compromise in “gray” areas and swim in a degree of flexibility. Within *pure* mathematics, most is quite rigorous, but only if fundamental philosophical issues are ignored that are at the foundations of such surface rigor. Deeper study into the philosophical assumptions of mathematics and one is no longer doing mathematics.

### 1.1.2 Mathematical Systems as Narratives to Understanding

One reason, I believe, that students can be “put off” by mathematics isn’t because of the difficulty of the subject. It is because they do not appreciate or understand what mathematics actually *is*. It can be very difficult to motivate someone to do something when they do not know what it is you are asking them to do and why. Asking a student to compute the quadratic formula to solve a quadratic equation is one thing, but explaining to them *why* solving for roots is such a big deal in the first place is quite another. Most students are excellent at blindly working the formula (basic arithmetic is really not *that* hard), but understanding the “why” beyond such rote manipulation is much more challenging.

Mathematics can be perceived in many ways, but we find it most useful for the student to perceive mathematics as a *narrative*. It is a *way* of explaining something, just like other narratives are 23ways of explaining other things. Of course, mathematical ways are often more *defined*, *exact*, and *precise*. A linear equation is quite precise, whereas using the English language to describe how your day went is quite vague. It is worth noting that not all things we describe are amenable to description using mathematics. The climate of one’s soul is probably not amenable to mathematical description, for instance. Self-concept is probably not amenable to mathematical description despite psychologists’ efforts to measure such things.

Mathematics, much beyond the early teachings of it merely being computation is often said to be about *form*, *structure*, *symmetry*, *equivalences*, *analogy*, and so on. However, these properties are not unique to mathematics. All of these elements are present in ventures such as music, art, physics, and even psychological theory. The only difference in the last of these is that rigor is much more difficult to implement, that is, the “rules” are not nearly as rigid. What makes mathematics unique is the relative *simplicity* (not *complexity*) in definitions that allows for rigor and communication among participants in the discipline. For instance, a *function* can be crisply defined in mathematics. Attempting a definition of the soul in philosophy or psychology can take up a dissertation.

## 1.2 The Scope of Data Analysis and Data Science: Expertise in Everything!

The field of data analysis and data science can easily feel overwhelming. Why? *Because you need to know everything!* At least it can feel that way. As has been discussed many different times by a number of authors, data science lies at the intersection or heart of so many specialty areas. To understand deep learning, for instance, you must have a strong grasp of statistical principles. But the machinery (not necessarily the *concepts*) underlying statistics is mathematics and if you venture into more foundational issues within mathematics itself you will soon encounter philosophical and historical issues, so you should to some extent be aware of those areas as well. But we’re not done. Not even close. You also need to be a computer scientist to some extent so you can apply all of this theory to the computer, understand the strengths and limitations of the computing you are doing, and be comfortable enough with code that you can improve or tweak a program if needed, or at minimum know if it needs tweaking and where to look for answers. So, so far, you’re to some extent a *mathematician*, *statistician*, *philosopher*, *historian*, and *computer scientist*. That’s a tall order for anyone.

But we’re still not done. Data science is applied to substantive areas such as business or a science (e.g., economics, psychology, sociology, biology, physics, astronomy), so you need to be an expert, to some extent, in the area of application as well. It becomes very difficult to know where and how to apply the technical elements you’re learning if you are unfamiliar with the discipline and the problems that the discipline seeks to solve. If it’s a scientific area, then you are also required to have knowledge and experience in areas of *research design*, *experimental* vs. *non-experimental designs*, *cross-sectional* and *longitudinal models*, and so on. Indeed, as we will discuss in this book, most if not all of machine learning does not make even one mention of design issues, and so it is possible that an expert machine learner may be somewhat naïve about important distinctions such as that between *experimental* vs. *quasi-experimental designs*, and so on. These design issues rear their heads daily in fields such as biology and psychology. Couple all of these areas with the problem of measurement such as in sciences like psychology or economics with latent variables, and you then need to also be an expert at psychometrics or measurement theory more generally. This is all to say that the expertise required to be a good data scientist can feel overwhelming and essentially impossible to ever achieve.

### 1.2.1 Theoretical vs. Applied Statistics and Specialization

There exists a *paradox of specialization*, such that if you focus too much on one area at the expense of others, you then become out of balance.
