# 2 Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-4](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-4)

In this chapter we provide an overview of the general mathematical and statistical background required for understanding the rest of the book. Most readers of this book will arrive with a varied background; some may be coming to this book having taken prior mathematics, statistics, and methodology courses, while others may only have the bare minimum introductory first- or second-year statistics course as their only preparation that they took likely as a follow-up to introductory courses in linear algebra and calculus which they may or may not have understood. Sadly, in today’s climate, it is very common for students to be able to pass a course in calculus, for example, without being able to describe what calculus is even *about* afterward; one can apply the power rule of differentiation to the function *f*(*x*) = 2*x*² to get *f*′(*x*) = 4*x*, but one may not understand at all the work that has been just performed. What does *f*′(*x*) mean here? How should 4*x* be interpreted? It has been remarked by many that far too much mathematics education is about *computation* rather than truly *understanding*. For such readers who may not have been encouraged to *understand* in prior coursework, some or much of the material surveyed in this chapter may not quite be “review” and will instead essentially be introduced for the first time. Readers with a limited background are encouraged to supplement their study of these topics with references provided throughout and suggested readings at the close of the chapter.

As mentioned in the previous chapter, the foundations of statistics and machine learning are not really in mathematics. Mathematics only serves as the *vehicle* by which such concepts are communicated. For instance, in a simple linear regression problem, the “idea” is to minimize error in prediction. That’s the *concept*. To operationalize the concept requires more than words or a general idea; it requires *precise symbolic definition and representation*, that is, *mathematics*. The two are not one and the same. And while statistics and mathematics are challenging in their own right, the more significant challenge as it concerns the applied scientist is to understand *why* the given mathematics is being used in the given context. This helps to motivate the big-picture ideas behind the mathematics.

As an example, *kernels*, while all the rage in modern machine learning, are in fact quite old and not new to linear algebra and can be used in a variety of contexts well beyond machine learning. But why use them at all? What is the general “theme” underlying their use? The general big-picture idea to using them is to both facilitate computation while also providing a shorthand to approximating functions in higher dimensions. The underlying mathematics allows us to define what this looks like *symbolically*, but understanding *how*, *why*, and *when* to use kernels is the more “global” picture that is most important to grasp. “Big-picture” understanding is what is needed most and which is most often lacking from typical undergraduate *and* graduate courses, especially in quantitative courses targeted to applied scientists. Students need to be taught *why*, not just *how*. When one understands the “why” the how either reveals itself or can be dug up. Learning the *how* at the 61expense of the *why* is not pedagogically meaningful, yet sadly is often encouraged in the teaching of students. Students are not *robots*; they are *creative minds* and should be educated as such.

The technical “underground” of statistics, multivariate statistics, machine learning, and data science more generally is typically found in what are often regarded as the three “pillar” areas of mathematics: *probability and statistics*, *linear algebra*, and *calculus and optimization*. Indeed, it is not out of the ordinary for a statistician or researcher to simultaneously be somewhat of a “mini expert” in linear algebra or calculus, or both, since so much of linear models and multivariate modeling has its technical basis in these areas. As an example, consider the topic of *eigenvalues* and *eigenvectors*. These objects show up throughout statistics and machine learning, yet one can also study them in their own right, far removed from any applied statistical use. *They are mathematical objects in and of themselves*. As discussed at the outset of this book, the researcher or scientist, or more generally the “user” of these methods must be continuously aware of how much of a “sub-area” to study while also keeping focused on the primary area of their investigation. For example, too much of a focus on linear algebra eventually detracts from their applied experimental science, whatever that specialization may be (e.g., biology, psychology, forestry, chemistry, etc.).

## 2.1 Mathematical Previews vs. the “Appendix” Approach

### *2.1.1 Why Previews Are Better*

Too often requisite mathematical underpinnings in books like this are given either as a disconnected review of fundamentals or as an appendix. All the “good stuff” is packed away in the appendix for the reader to look up as needed. This approach is limiting, however, as it fails to connect the material to the more substantive areas of the text. Our approach is to provide an overview of these technical fundamentals but most importantly, *preview where we will see them again throughout the book*. This last point is especially important. It does little good for the reader to learn or review a bunch of seemingly “abstract” mathematics if it is not properly *motivated*. At least not in an *applied* sense. Of course, the reader may not always readily fully appreciate the preview as it will be an incomplete description of the new concept (if it is indeed new to the reader); however, it will still serve the purpose of exposing the concepts to the reader as a preview of where such mathematics are used in statistics and machine learning. These early foundations help make understanding the pillars of statistics and machine learning (probability, linear algebra, calculus) a more *continuous* process rather than a *discrete* one. In this sense, the foundations *are* the method, but one is largely unaware of this until they see the foundations “in motion” or “at work” when studying the method later in the book, then returns back to these earlier pages to better recognize the connections that were being previewed.

As an example, the concept of a *linear combination*, taught in the abstract, may come across as an arcane and pointless symbolic mathematical object, until one realizes that so much of multivariate statistics and machine learning are about these very objects. If the reader is coming to the book with virtually no prior experience, then they will not appreciate our preview of where linear combinations will be used later in the book. On the other hand, if they are coming to the book with such prior experience, they will likely immediately recognize the connection which may help “tie” together concepts for that reader.

As another example, understanding the problems associated with *linear dependence* in a regression problem will only truly make sense once we get to linear regression, even though the concept of linear dependence is introduced and previewed in the current chapter. Books like this one are written in a more or less linear fashion, but *the understanding of these subjects is not always linear*. Chapters later in the book may help make something “click” in earlier chapters, and the reader should be pedagogically open to these types of connections.62

### 2.1.2 About Proofs

We avoid formal proofs in this chapter and throughout the book. However, this does not imply that basic proofs cannot be constructed based on the details we do present. Proofs are often a lot “closer” in proximity to the reader’s capacity than they may at first realize, especially if they are truly grasping the material.

As an example, it is well known that the Pearson correlation coefficient is bounded by limits of −1 and +1. Why this is so we explain in the book, though the explanation would not constitute a “formal proof.” However, if desired, a proof can be constructed from pieces of the explanation, and this typically makes for a great exercise. As gifted educator Morris Kline has said numerous times in reference to teaching calculus, it is better to understand the *intuition* behind the object than to learn a rigorous proof, at least on first reading and exposure. Indeed, historically, physicists and other scientists have relied on this approach quite heavily in the invention of new concepts. The mathematical and statistically specialized communities rightfully have high and very rigorous standards for what denotes a “formal proof,” (they should be applauded for their appreciation of rigor), but it is important for the reader to recognize that they themselves are sometimes not that far off from that “ideal” formal justification in at least some cases. *Approximations are okay*, so long as one realizes they are not the be-all and end-all and may lack formality. So long as the approximation does justice to the concept, you’re fine. If the approximation leads you astray from the concept, then that’s a problem.

Where results are very important, we provide the requisite technical references to more formal proofs and justification. For example, understanding what the *central limit theorem* is and why it works is most important in an applied sense, but if one were adamant on learning “why” via formal proof and had the ambition to work through it, select references are provided that further justify the theorem. Understanding why and how a theorem is “proved” and not the details of the proof may be enough, even for the curious reader. Proofs can be complex, but the *idea* of proof is (generally) not.

What is a proof, exactly? A quote by Abbott ([2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000001), pp. 8–9) on famed mathematician Hardy is helpful here:

> As Hardy indicates, there is an artistic quality to mathematics of this type, which may or may not come easily, but that is not to say that anything especially mysterious is happening. A proof is an essay of sorts. It is a set of carefully crafted directions, which, when followed, should leave the reader absolutely convinced of the truth of the proposition in question. To achieve this, the steps in a proof must follow logically from previous steps or be justified by some other agreed-upon set of facts. In addition to being valid, these steps must also fit coherently together to form a cogent argument. Mathematics has a specialized vocabulary, to be sure, but that does not exempt a good proof from being written in grammatically correct English.

Hence, a proof is a way of justifying that a mathematical statement is correct; it is an argument of sorts, just as arguments abound in other areas of inquiry (e.g., science, history, politics, etc.). Mathematical proofs, however, are much more rigorous because they are on objects that we can operationalize as specific quantities and variables.

One final point for now before we begin. Obviously, it is impossible to cover all the mathematics used in statistics or machine learning in one single chapter. It is even not possible to cover it all in one single *book*, or series of books, or encyclopedia! You get the idea. Our primary goal here is to simply survey the most *common*, *relevant*, and *foundationally important* prerequisite mathematics and statistics for an understanding of the contents to follow in the remainder of the book. 63A related goal is to provide additional insight for readers who may already have an introductory grasp of these topics and to help such a reader see the bigger picture. For example, has the reader ever appreciated how similar basic neural networks are to other statistical methods? As mentioned at the outset of this book, one of the chief goals is to emphasize such *connections* to augment the student’s understanding of these more global notions.

## 2.2 Elementary Probability and Fundamental Statistics

Probability theory is the quantification of uncertainty and is at the foundation of most statistical and machine learning ideas. As R.A. Fisher ([1925](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000100), [1935](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000101)), the “father of statistics” put it, we may not be able to make *certain* predictions, but we can often rigorously quantify the degree to which we are *uncertain*. This is a powerful idea, one that essentially revolutionized how scientific thought and conclusions are “packaged.” We may not know whether it will rain tomorrow, but the extent to which we can quantify our uncertainty regarding whether or not it will rain nonetheless provides us with knowledge and gives us a “handle” on the problem. We have become relatively *certain* about the *uncertainty*. That’s a big idea. Historically, the invention or discovery of probability was somewhat of a paradigm shift, not only in science, but in everyday communication.

Ideas and concepts of probability go back at least to the ancient Greeks and probably much before then, as most important ideas do. However, probability was only mathematically formalized into a system relatively recently beginning in the 1600s. Most mathematical (and other) inventions have histories where the key concepts germinate over time. Few innovators truly work alone and few important ideas are unmotivated by other equally important ideas. The formalized interpretation of probability, considered in proper context, was more of a *culmination* of ideas that germinated for centuries.

## 2.3 Interpretations of Probability

There are generally three schools of probability: *classical*, *frequentist*, and *subjective*. Classical views are, for the most part, not really part of mainstream probability. The probability of getting a “1” on a roll of a die is 1/6 since there are six sides to the die and all *appear* to have equal probability. That’s an example of the classical view. Historically, frequentist and subjective notions have dominated statistics and hence also more or less dominate machine learning.

For the *frequentist*, probability is a long-run frequency; that is, if you want to know the probability of something, you need to *experience* the event over repeated trials and take the fraction of times the event occurs to the total number of trials. The typical classic and easy example is that of flipping a coin. If we flip the coin 100 times and get 50 heads, we say the probability of heads is equal to 50/100 = 0.5, even though theoretically this is only an *approximation* to the true probability. The 0.5 is not the true probability. For the true probability under this approach, we would require flipping the coin an *infinite* number of times. From this perspective, true probabilities are only arrived at *in the limit* as sample size grows infinitely large, that is,

  
$$\\lim\\limits\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}\\frac{n\_{H}}{N} = p\\left( H \\right)$$  
(2.1)

Unfortunately, “infinitely large” could never be a reality, and hence one weakness of the relative-frequency approach is that obtaining such a large number of trials is nothing more than a fanciful idea, even if it does serve as a useful working model for defining probabilities. Many scholars have critiqued the relative-frequency interpretation of probability precisely on this basis.64

The *subjectivist*, also commonly known as the *Bayesian* (since Bayesians typically adopt a subjective viewpoint of probability), takes probability to be an *opinion*, a *degree of belief* and hence does not require the unrealistic and unattainable infinite number of trials idea that is mandatory for the frequentist to accept. As we will see later however when we survey Bayesian statistics, subjective probability has its problems as well.

The key point to take away from this discussion so far is that the nature of probability has historically, and is still currently, open to debate. You are understanding this point correctly; *nobody knows what a probability actually is!* All that can be offered is an *interpretation* of probability. Which interpretation is correct is not a debate we will have here, and in fact, if you studied and wrote a dissertation on the topic, you’d most likely end up in the same place you started. That is, probability is a relatively elusive concept, and the best we can do is simply adopt a *way* of thinking about it. The frequentist and subjectivist notions of probability dominate modern science.

## 2.4 Mathematical Probability

Regardless of the interpretation of probability adopted, virtually all probability theorists agree on the fundamental mathematics of probability. That is, while the nature of probability (i.e., frequentist vs. subjectivist) is and has been up for debate for literally centuries, the essential mathematics underlying fundamental probability are usually not contested, except perhaps by true rebels and nonconformists! Hence, in what follows in our brief presentation of mathematical probability, there are no true “debates.” Most are “on board” with these basic notions and definitions. Much of modern probability is based on the *theory of sets*, which we do not review here, except as it applies directly to the concepts we do present.

The probability of the event *A* is denoted *P(A)*, and is a number between 0 and 1:

  
0 ≤ *P*(*A*) ≤ 1  
(2.2)

The *complement* of *A* denoted $\\overline{A}$ is the probability that *A* does not occur. Since the probability of the entire sample space, by definition (and convenience) must equal 1, this implies that

  
$$P\\left( \\overline{A} \\right) = 1 - P\\left( A \\right)$$  
(2.3)

The *joint probability*, that is, of *A* and *B* occurring at the same time is denoted

  
*P*(*A*∩*B*)  
(2.4)

If *A* and *B* cannot occur simultaneously, then

  
*P*(*A*∩*B*) = 0  
(2.5)

and we say the two events *A* and *B* are *disjoint* or *mutually exclusive*. Examples of mutually exclusive events include the events “head” and “tail” on the flipping of a single coin since one cannot obtain a head and a tail on the same flip.

To know if two events are mutually exclusive, one must know about the *context* or *physical model* of the problem. For example, the events “heads” and “tails” are not *intrinsically* and *organically* mutually exclusive events; they are only so under the model of a *single flip*. For successive flips, they are not typically mutually exclusive. The only absolutely necessary criterion for mutually exclusive events is as stated in (2.5), that of *P*(*A*∩*B*) = 0, and hence so long as this condition 65is satisfied, even in the abstract, the two events are mutually exclusive. Knowledge of temporal conditions of the physical model imposed serves to help us know whether the condition is met.

Why is this point so important? Why are we going on about it? The reason is that physical models (which include *temporal sequences* as a special case) are special cases or circumstances of a more general “real-world” context. Abstract mathematics (or philosophy, for that matter) does not require such a basis in reality. To emphasize the point, if the aliens come one day and have no conception of time, the concept of mutual exclusiveness would still be “communicable” by simply drawing the idea in [Figure 2.1](#c2.xhtml#f2.1) with Venn diagrams on a sheet of paper.

![Figure 2.1 Depiction of mutually exclusive events, non-overlapping circles.Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.1.jpg)

*Figure 2.1* Depiction of mutually exclusive events, non-overlapping circles.[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.1)

The depiction in [Figure 2.1](#c2.xhtml#f2.1) is what mutual exclusiveness *is*, at least from a geometrical point of view. Knowing whether mutual exclusiveness applies to the objects under study must come from the *context*. If there is only one flip of the coin, head and tail are mutually exclusive events. If there are two flips, they are not. *Context matters*. Everything happens in a given context; this includes scientific, mathematical, statistical, and machine learning matters. This “theme” will return time and time again throughout this book and it is worth emphasizing and repeating here:

> Context Matters!

### 2.4.1 Unions and Intersections of Events

The probability of *A* or *B* occurring on a given trial is denoted by their union,

  
*P*(*A*∪*B*)  
(2.6)

and is equal to the sum of probabilities of *A* and *B* minus their intersection,

  
*P*(*A*∪*B*) = *P*(*A*) + *P*(*B*) − *P*(*A*∩*B*)  
(2.7)

where *P*(*A*∩*B*) defines the probability of the intersection.

It is easy to see that for mutually exclusive events, where *P*(*A*∩*B*) = 0, the union of *A* and *B* is equal to66

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {P\\left( A \\cup B \\right) = P\\left( A \\right) + P\\left( B \\right) - P\\left( A \\cap B \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = P\\left( A \\right) + P\\left( B \\right) - 0} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = P\\left( A \\right) + P\\left( B \\right)} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

This is sometimes referred to as the *special rule for the addition of probabilities*, that is, where the intersection is equal to 0 and we can simply compute the union by adding probabilities. To be on the safe side, it is good advice to always plan on subtracting an intersection from the addition to ensure for yourself that there is no overlap. It is obvious and easily provable that the intersection of a number of sets must be a subset of their union as the overlap, no matter how large, cannot be larger than the sum of all sets. The reader may recall that a *subset* can consist of the entire set, whereas a *proper subset* must be smaller than the full set.

## 2.5 Conditional Probability

Most phenomena in science are not about probabilities; they are instead about *conditional probabilities*. We rarely care about the probability of an event occurring; we care more about the probability of an event occurring, *given something else has already occurred*. This “conditional” statement translates to a reduction in the original sample space from what it originally was for the unconditional probability estimate. The probability of cancer is interesting, but the probability of cancer *given that you do or do not smoke two packs of cigarettes per day* is much more interesting. Virtually every problem and finding in science, no matter how simple or complex the model or lack thereof, can be translated into a statement of conditional probabilities.

Conditional probabilities add the aforementioned “context” to the problem since unconditional probabilities, while often accurate in and of themselves, can be grossly misleading. In passing, this is precisely why some detest statistics, because depending on what other factors or conditions are imposed on a problem, one can draw one of many conclusions. For instance, while the probability of perishing from COVID-19 may be 0.05, the probability of one dying given that one is an otherwise healthy 30-year-old is likely significantly less. Unconditional probabilities are, in a sense, “averages” across objects and conditions, and as we will discuss later, averages can be grossly misleading. Conditional probabilities are specialized *focused slices* within that spectrum. They help us narrow in on the probability estimate of most interest and provide that necessary context to the problem. The difficulty is that in many or most problems, there is no theoretical limit to how much context can be included which makes arriving at the “true” conditional probability in many situations very difficult or even impossible. At worst, a lack of context will simply make the probability estimate unmeaningful and very misleading. The probability of a human being currently eating baby formula is very low. It’s a silly probability estimate because we have not conditioned it on age and thus have not provided proper context to the problem. The probability estimate is accurate. The lack of context to the problem is foolish and makes the unconditional probability estimate *uninteresting*.

The concept of so-called *risk factors* also evolves from the general principle of conditional probabilities. For instance, when a practitioner asks about the past suicidality in your family as a way of estimating your own probability of suicide, she is attempting to narrow the sample space such as to ascribe past suicidality as a risk factor in estimating your own risk of suicide. The concept of risk factors plays a significant role in many branches of epidemiology and science in general. When you hear the word “risk factor,” think “conditional probability.”67

Mathematically, the conditional probability of *A* given *B* is defined as

  
$$P\\left( A \\middle| B \\right) = \\frac{P\\left( A \\cap B \\right)}{P\\left( B \\right)}$$  
(2.8)

while the conditional probability of *B* given *A* is given by

  
$$P\\left( B \\middle| A \\right) = \\frac{P\\left( A \\cap B \\right)}{P\\left( A \\right)}$$  
(2.9)

depending on which variable we are conditioning the other on. Using conditional probabilities and simple algebra, we can now define the aforementioned intersection between *A* and *B* more formally:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\,\\,\\, P\\left( B \\middle| A \\right) = \\frac{P\\left( A \\cap B \\right)}{P\\left( A \\right)}} \\\\ {P\\left( A \\cap B \\right) = P\\left( A \\right)P\\left( B \\middle| A \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = P\\left( B \\right)P\\left( A \\middle| B \\right)} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

That is, the probability of *A* and *B* occurring simultaneously (i.e., *P*(*A*∩*B*)) is equal to the product of an unconditional probability – either *P*(*A*) or *P*(*B*) – with a conditional probability where it is also true that

  
*P*(*A*)*P*(*B*|*A*) = *P*(*B*)*P*(*A*|*B*)  
.

### 2.5.1 Unconditional vs. Conditional Statistical Models

As emphasized in our discussion of unconditional vs. conditional probabilities, much of statistical modeling in the end is about conditional probabilities. In most cases, however, we do not evaluate such probabilities in a vacuum. Rather, we evaluate them relative to a particular *statistical model*. Hence, when we write the unconditional probability of *P*(*A*), it will now be understood that we are assuming a statistical model, whether that statistical model is specified explicitly or not.

Referring to our previous example, the unconditional probability of cancer is, by itself, though useful, rather uninteresting, and would denote a much too simplistic statistical model similar to the idea of predicting overall suicide rates in a regression context based on no predictors would also be much too simple of a model. The *intercept-only model* is limiting. To enrichen the model, we should want to include *covariates* and variables to provide a meaningful *context* to the evaluation of the probability. This is the very essence of much of statistical modeling, to *provide a context for evaluating and estimating particular probabilities of most interest*. Many statistical models are, in the end, nothing more than generalizations of ideas of conditional probabilities. Of course, that’s a simplification, but it’s a good start to understanding statistical modeling.

Going from conditional probabilities to statistical models, we need to generalize our notation. Instead of speaking of the unconditional probability *P*(*A*), we need to speak instead of the unconditional *model*, not simply *probability*. The conditional model is given by the following,68

  
*p*(*y*|*θ*)  
(2.10)

where the response is now *y* and the parameter vector is now *θ*. The model is unconditional because there are no covariates. We now add a covariate *x* as follows:

  
*p*(*y*|*x*,*θ*)  
(2.11)

which yields a conditional model where now *y* is “conditioned” on *x*, for which the parameters in *θ* will be estimated. Under the circumstance where *y* and *x* are independent, then *p*(*y*|*θ*) = *p*(*y*|*x*,*θ*). Contrarily, when *y* and *x* are dependent, then it should be obvious that *p*(*y*|*θ*) ≠ *p*(*y*|*x*,*θ*).

## 2.6 Probabilistic Independence

From the definition of conditional probability, we can quite easily obtain the concept of statistical or probabilistic independence. If *P*(*A*) = *P*(*A*|*B*), then events *A* and *B* are said to be *independent*, which implies that knowing *B* has occurred tells us nothing about the probability of *A* occurring. Note that the qualifier “has occurred” implies a temporal dimension, but as was the case for mutual exclusiveness, we need not assume a temporal context at all. All we really require is a reduction in the sample space so that the event of interest is referenced to that *reduced space* instead of to the original wider space.

We can easily see from the rule for joint events that if *A* and *B* are independent, then

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {P\\left( A \\cap B \\right) = P\\left( A \\right)P\\left( B \\middle| A \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = P\\left( A \\right)P\\left( B \\right)} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(2.12)

since if *A* and *B* are independent, then *P*(*B*|*A*) = *P*(*B*). That is, if we can assume events *A* and *B* are independent, then we can simply multiply their unconditional probabilities in determining *P*(*A*∩*B*). This is known as the *multiplication rule for independent events*. If we cannot assume they are independent, then we cannot simplify the rule and must always invoke the conditional probability *P*(*B*|*A*) rather than simply *P*(*B*) in the second term. That is, the more complete rule for computing the probability of the intersection is the first above, that of

  
*P*(*A*∩*B*) = *P*(*A*)*P*(*B*|*A*)  

The multiplication of unconditional probabilities is simply a special case of the above more general rule. But how do you know if events *A* and *B* are independent or not? We discuss this issue next.

### 2.6.1 Everything Is about Independence vs. Dependence!

Whenever new concepts are introduced in statistics, they are often so fundamental that it is tempting to conclude that the whole discipline revolves around them. We just experienced this idea in our discussion of conditional probabilities, concluding that everything is about conditional probabilities. Even more fundamental is the idea of *independence versus dependence*. The unifying principle of these concepts cannot be overstated. It is what probability and thus virtually all statistics and science are about. On the one hand, statistically, probabilistic independence is at the heart of many probability calculations and often simplifies matters a great deal. On the other hand, in terms of real scientific empirical objects, establishing independence can be extremely difficult (and many times impossible) to demonstrate, and instead is often simply an *assumption* that 69must be (conveniently, and even unrealistically in many cases) made, often on reasonable grounds given the experts concluding the independence have knowledge of the system(s) they are working with. Determining empirically that two events are independent can often be next to impossible. Statistical modeling is about making *assumptions*, often lots of them.

As an example of what we are talking about, consider an airplane system. Probabilistic independence is a sought-after goal when conceptualizing and manufacturing aircraft components and running failure analysis scenarios. Engineers purposely design airplane systems to be as independent as possible so that *a failure in one system does not change the probability of a failure in another system*. Why is this so important? Well, consider the possibilities when flying on an airplane; it would be a terrible thing if the probability of a failure of one engine increased the probability of a failure of a second engine, or if the probability of the landing gear detracting was not independent of the probability of the hydraulic system working. In these cases, it would take but one failure to influence other failures, and hence a single failure could, in theory, take down the airplane through a chain reaction of events. Hence, as much as possible, system events on airplanes are designed to be probabilistically independent. The probability of one engine failing should, ideally, not have an effect on the probability that the plane experiences a decompression, for instance.

But how do these experts “know” the systems are independent? They don’t! Well, not for *certain*, anyway. However, rational argument, a *plausible argument*, knowledge of the systems under consideration, increasing empirical evidence, and making assumptions that align with such knowledge typically lead such professionals to conclude that operating the flaps on the wings, for instance, is independent of the ability of the fuel tank to hold fuel, just as a failure of the landing gear to retract is independent of the plane’s engines to generate power. Of course, these seem like “obvious” assumptions to make, but the point is that they are often nonetheless *assumptions* (assumptions often supported by increasing amounts of evidence, in this case). The goal of science is to reject “obvious” assumptions with newly established empirical evidence that potentially counter or challenge existing assumptions.

For instance, it was once assumed that a simple cigarette could never cause any harm, just as it was once assumed that chemicals used in paint (e.g., benzene) could never pose a threat to our health and the health of our pets. Social media was never thought to be associated with depression and anxiety in our children. Science is about cutting through “established” beliefs with evidence that suggests such “establishment” should be rejected. Newtonian mechanics was once assumed correct until Einstein’s “unlikely” theory led us to believe differently. The point is that all scientific “fact” is tentative to new evidence and revision, and the idea of probabilistic independence is no different. We can assume events to be independent to get on with business (and fly the plane, for instance), but we must always allow the possibility that they are not, subject to new evidence. It was once assumed that a thin layer of icing on wings could never influence the capacity of the plane to stay airborne. We now know differently, largely due to experiencing (i.e., data) planes fall from the sky because of a thin layer of such ice. Such has encouraged us to “update” our belief about the impact of ice on wings, which is why that 20-minute delay we are so impatient about as travelers (while de-icing equipment clears our wings) could be saving our lives. The 20-minute delay is a “good thing” and has been informed by prior deaths and tragedies, that is, *experience*.

## 2.7 Marginal vs. Conditional Distributions

As we have seen, the concept of conditional probabilities is vitally important to both statistics and science. However, we have also discussed that conditional probabilities are often applied to statistical *models*, not individual probabilities. With these two elements, we can generalize concepts 70of conditional probabilities to that of *joint* and *conditional distributions*. Further, for a continuous distribution, the marginal *probability density function* (PDF) over all possible values of *y* can be obtained from the joint PDF by integrating out all other *p* variables that may be present and summing (via integration) over all possible values of *y*,

  
*f*(*x*) = ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)*f*(*x*,*y*)*d**y*  
(2.13)

The PDF integrates to 1, that is,

  
*f*(*x*) = ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)*f*(*x*,*y*)*d**y* = 1  
(2.14)

In the discrete case, we can simply visualize summing up or down a 2 × 2 table across *categories* of the second variable. As was the simpler case for the rule of independence for individual probabilities, random variables are *independent* if the joint PDF is equal to the product of marginal PDFs. If the joint PDF is not equal to the product of marginal PDFs, then the two random variables are said to be *dependent*.

## 2.8 Independence Implies Covariance of Zero, but Covariance of Zero Does Not (Necessarily) Imply Independence

As we will discuss in more detail later, the covariance between variables is a measure of the extent to which the variance of one variable is *linearly* associated with the variance of another. The covariance is given by

  
$$Cov\_{xy} = \\frac{\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right)\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)}{n}$$  
(2.15)

For any two variables that are statistically independent, this necessarily implies a covariance equal to 0. However, the converse is not necessarily true. That is, a covariance equal to 0 does not necessarily imply that two events are independent. They may turn out to be independent, but the covariance equal to 0 is not enough to imply it. This is because the relationship between the two variables may simply be one that is *nonlinear*. *The covariance between two variables is a measure of linear association or relationship only*. Hence, two variables may be strongly dependent or related to one another, yet still have a covariance (and hence, also *correlation*, though as we will see later the two are not equivalent) equal to 0. This is one reason why interpreting a measure of covariance or correlation should never be done without also inspecting a scatterplot of the association. *Always plot your data!* This is worth repeating:

> **Always plot your data!**

Numerical summaries are never enough. As an extreme instance and very insightful example of this effect, we refer to *Anscombe’s Graphs in Statistical Analysis* ([Anscombe, 1973](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000012)) in [Figure 2.2](#c2.xhtml#f2.2) which consists of three different data sets that yield identical summary statistics.71

![Figure 2.2 From Anscombe, F. J. (1973). Graphs in Statistical Analysis. The American Statistician. Copyright © 1973 American Statistical Association, reprinted by permission of Informa UK Limited, trading Taylor & Francis Group, https://www.tandfonline.com on behalf of American Statistical Association.Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.2.jpg)

*Figure 2.2* From Anscombe, F. J. (1973). Graphs in Statistical Analysis. The American Statistician. Copyright © 1973 American Statistical Association, reprinted by permission of Informa UK Limited, trading Taylor & Francis Group, https://www.tandfonline.com on behalf of American Statistical Association.[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.2)

Remarkably, all four plots share the same means on *x* and *y* ($\\overline{x} = 9.0$, $\\overline{y} = 7.5$), regression of *y* on *x* (slope of 0.5), regression equation *y* = 3 + 0.5*x*, sum of squares $x - \\overline{x} = 110.0$, regression sum of squares (27.50), residual sum of squares (13.75), estimated standard error (0.118), and *R*² = 0.667. If such a demonstration does not convince the reader to always plot their data, nothing will!

Other examples of this effect abound (see [Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259), p. 42 for examples). In short, *visualization is a must for good data analysis and exploration, not an option*. Let’s put this another way; if you are not visualizing your data in at least *some* capacity, you are usually conducting a *poor data analysis*. There are special cases where one may be able to circumvent visualization, but the point is that visualization will tell you things about your data that numerical summaries may never. Numerical summaries alone will never provide the widest or most complete picture or understanding of the data, and as we have said already ad nauseam by now, and will continue to repeat throughout the book, all variables exist in a wider *context* of other variables. Visualization helps provide a description of that context, which is why so much effort is put toward developing new visualization techniques in statistics. As we will see later in relation to manifold learning, multivariate visualization can be especially challenging and difficult, and as the dimensionality of the data increases, can be virtually impossible.

We will revisit covariance and correlation in more detail shortly.

## 2.9 Sensitivity and Specificity: More Conditional Probabilities

Another area where conditional probabilities are featured and used is when determining the sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic tests. A diagnostic test is a *sign*. It is a piece of *data*. It is a moment of *experience*. It is not a deterministic indication that the disease or condition is present. A classic and modern example of this is diagnosing COVID-19. A diagnostic test may indicate the presence of the virus, but there is also associated with that a probability that the disease is not present. A test that detects the disease when the disease is present is called the *sensitivity* of the test. A test that fails to detect a disease that is not present is called the *specificity* of the test. Good tests have strong sensitivity and specificity though the two will seldom, if ever, be perfect or equal to one another.

Of course, we desire any test to have maximum sensitivity and maximum specificity. That is the ideal we shoot for. Where things go wrong with diagnostic tests is when a test indicates the virus or condition is present when the virus or condition is not present. This is known as a *false positive*, or more commonly in the statistical literature as a *Type I error* in hypothesis testing. On the other hand, a test that fails to detect a virus when the virus is present has committed a *Type II error*. 72Which is the worst error? Which error has the greater consequence? Such, of course, depends, again, on the *context of the problem*. Context matters! Again! Which is most important depends on which type of error the scientist wishes to minimize. Surely, we do not want to misdiagnose the virus. Yet at the same time, diagnosing the virus when it is not present can lead to many problems, such as emotional distress, financial costs, the inconvenience of further testing, etc. Indeed, this has been one of the controversies surrounding habitual mammogram testing, for example; some argue that due to the error rates involved, yearly mammograms may be doing more harm than good. The risks of diagnosing a disease when none exists are real and can have great consequences. At the same time, missing a condition when the condition is present can likewise have serious consequences. Which error is more consequential largely depends on the situation, context, and the inclination of the scientist or subject.

## 2.10 Bayes’ Theorem and Conditional Probabilities

There is perhaps no better or more important of an example of conditional probabilities as with Bayes’ theorem. Recall that we mentioned at the outset of this chapter that the two primary camps in statistics are those of the frequentist and subjective perspectives. Maximum likelihood estimation, the most common method for estimating parameters, generally stems from and is governed by a frequentist approach in which the probability of the data given a parameter is evaluated, that of *p*(*y*|*x*), where here *y* is the data and *x* is the parameter (in place of the notation *θ* for our discussion here). The conditional probability *p*(*y*|*x*) is referred to in frequentist probability as the *likelihood*.

In Bayesian reasoning, the probability of the parameter given the data is instead evaluated, that of *p*(*x*|*y*). Bayes’ theorem inverts conditional probabilities from *p*(*y*|*x*) to *p*(*x*|*y*):

  
$$p\\left( x \\middle| y \\right) = \\frac{p\\left( y \\middle| x \\right)p\\left( x \\right)}{p\\left( y \\right)}$$  
(2.16)

where *p*(*y*|*x*), as before, is called the *likelihood*, *p*(*x*) is the *prior probability*, and *p*(*x*|*y*) is the *posterior probability*. The denominator, *p*(*y*) is the *total probability* of the data, or evidence more generally.

An even more meaningful way to interpret Baye’s theorem is by replacing *x* with *T* (theory) and *y* with *D* (data):

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\, p\\left( x \\middle| y \\right) = \\frac{p\\left( y \\middle| x \\right)p\\left( x \\right)}{p\\left( y \\right)}} \\\\ {p\\left( T \\middle| D \\right) = \\frac{p\\left( D \\middle| T \\right)p\\left( T \\right)}{p\\left( D \\right)}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

That is, *p*(*T*|*D*) is the probability of the theory given the evidence or data. The difficulty with Baye’s theorem is that one must enter a *prior probability*, which can be quite subjective in nature. Note that no matter the strength of the data, if the prior probability *p*(*T*) is equal to 0, then the posterior probability will also equal 0, since,73

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {p\\left( T \\middle| D \\right) = \\frac{p\\left( D \\middle| T \\right)\\left( 0 \\right)}{p\\left( D \\right)}} \\\\ {p\\left( T \\middle| D \\right) = 0} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

The big idea in Bayesian analysis is that contrary to frequentist approaches where parameters are regarded as fixed constants, Bayesian analysis treats parameters as *random variables*.

### 2.10.1 Bayes Factor

In the case where we have two competing models, *M*[0] and *M*[1], we can form the *Bayes factor*, which is a ratio of likelihoods of the data under these two hypothetical conditions:

  
$$B = \\frac{p\\left( D \\middle| M\_{1} \\right)}{p\\left( D \\middle| M\_{0} \\right)}$$  
(2.17)

where *p*(*D*|*M*[1]) is the probability of the data under the condition of the alternative hypothesis, *M*[1], and *p*(*D*|*M*[0]) is the probability of the data under the condition of the null hypothesis, *M*[0]. If the two likelihoods are the same, then we would, obviously, expect *B* to equal 1, whereas if *M*[1] is preferred over *M*[0] then we would expect *B* > 1. The Bayes factor provides a competing alternative to classical frequentist statistics that focuses on the *p*\-value as a means of making a decision between the two states. According to Jeffreys, a Bayes factor greater than 10 indicates strong evidence for *M*[1] while a Bayes factor greater than 100 indicates exceptionally strong evidence for *M*[1] ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). However, as always, the size of the ratio should be evaluated, at least in part, relative to the context of the investigation. A Bayes factor of 2 in some research settings may be considered relatively large, whereas a Bayes factor of 10 in another research setting may be considered trivially small. Have we mentioned before that context matters?

### 2.10.2 Bayesian Model Selection

Suppose we run a host of competing models and wish to select the “best” one in some sense. The qualifier “in some sense” is necessary here, as selecting a “best” model is in no way a straightforward task and will usually depend on much more than a single criterion for selection.

By a Bayesian approach, that model should be the one that maximizes *p*(*m*|*D*), where *m* is now the model and *D* is, as before, the data:

  
$$p\\left( m \\middle| D \\right) = \\frac{p\\left( D \\middle| m \\right)p\\left( m \\right)}{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}{p\\left( D \\middle| m \\right)p\\left( m \\right)}}$$  
(2.18)

We recognize in the above the quantity *p*(*D*|*m*), which, when unpacked, is equal to

  
*p*(*D*|*m*) = ∫*p*(*D*|*θ*,*m*)*p*(*θ*|*m*)*d**θ*  

and is called the *marginal likelihood* (Murphy, 2022). If *p*(*D*|*m*) holds strong under different settings of the parameter *θ*, then *m* is likely to be considered a reasonable model. The key to the marginal likelihood is the summing (via integration) across a variety of parameter values (*θ*). This is why it is called “marginal,” as a result of the summation over all values of *θ*. If it were for a particular value of *θ* = *θ*[*i*], then it would be “conditional” instead of marginal. Under the condition of two competing models *m*[1] and *m*[2], should *p*(*D*|*θ̂*[1],*m*[1]) and *p*(*D*|*θ̂*[2],*m*[2]) both be large, Occam’s razor requires us to select the model that is simplest. Marginal likelihoods then help us select a suitably complex model, which has analogies to cross-validation and other model selection guidelines in a frequentist context (see [Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259), pp. 179–180 for details). However, 74marginal likelihoods can be difficult to compute in practice because they require integrating over the entire parameter space ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). The *Bayesian Information Criterion* (BIC) can be considered a kind of approximation to the log marginal likelihood, which, as we will see later in the book, is used in many contexts, including regression and cluster density estimation, among others.

### 2.10.3 Bayes’ Theorem as Rational Belief or Theorizing

Bayes’ theorem is not a trivial idea. Far from it. By itself, Bayes’ theorem tells us how, as *rational agents*, we should update our belief about *T* in light of new *D*, where *T* is nothing more than a belief or theory and *D* is nothing more than experience in its fullest generality. Bayes’ theorem is not a statistical idea; first and foremost it is a *philosophical* one. Bayesian inference essentially tells us how a rational agent *should* update their belief in light of new experience. “Should” equates to being *rational*. It is not equivalent to how human beings *actually* update their beliefs. Indeed, much psychological research has been conducted on human subjects to demonstrate that human beings are far from being Bayesian.

As one might imagine, this idea has made Bayes central to not only statistics, but also other areas where the study of rational behavior is of primary interest. The application of Bayes’ theorem, whether formal or informal, is a way of being “intelligent” about updating one’s belief. *Game theory*, *psychology of beliefs*, *economic theory*, etc., are all areas that, in the end, study human behavior. Sub-specialties of these domains have interests in learning whether human beings update their beliefs in correspondence with what Bayesian theory would prescribe. The *Bayes estimator* tells us which action to take, if acting *rationally*, to minimize the risk of making a wrong decision. Maximizing expectation, however, is not always equivalent to maximizing *utility*, and hence Bayesian decision theory will often have us maximize the latter instead of the former, except if the problem is relatively simple and both expectation and utility coincide. Utility, simply put, is a measure of how beneficial this or that action is to the agent, not simply evaluated based on probability or mathematical expectation. Not buying that overpriced post-pandemic McDonald’s hamburger may maximize budgeting constraints, but buying it because it tastes *so good* maximizes utility. A fiscally poor and irrational choice, but has much utility for the buyer and thus becomes rational from that perspective. Utility theory is a fascinating area of investigation. For an excellent discussion, consult [Winkler (2003)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000388).

While Bayes’ theorem is generally useful, it should be remarked that it could introduce bias and discrimination into the process of updating belief. For example, the high probability of a black person committing a crime may be justified by reference to Bayes’ theorem because for a given crime, past crimes may have featured a disproportionate number of blacks, causing the prior probability to skyrocket. Bayes’ theorem is rational updating of belief, but it may be considered discrimination to use it in this particular *context*. Likewise, the probability of a mass in a dog being cancerous may be high upon application of Bayes’ theorem, given the age and breed of the dog. While Bayes’ theorem is doing its work, it can also be terrifying that a dog is put down because of their breed and without the result of a biopsy. The prior probability makes a cancer diagnosis more likely, perhaps even highly probable, but if it’s a decision of *life vs. death* for the dog, putting the dog down on the “gamble” that it is cancer is an unwise action. *The cost of making an error in this regard may be too high, even if the posterior probability is exceedingly high*. *Bayes theorem can only estimate the probability of the theory; it cannot, by itself, tell you how to act*, *nor is a posterior probability ever equal to unity in most real-world applications*. Further, it must always be remembered that we do not know anything about the current event; we only know about *past events*, and the prior probability in Bayes’ theorem, even if estimated correctly, is not about the current event under consideration. *Calculate Bayes’ theorem with reckless abandon, but use, and most importantly* 75***interpret Bayes’ theorem with caution*** . As a result of the prior probability potentially having an overwhelming influence on the posterior, work has been done on what are called *noninformative priors* ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)), which, as the name suggests, attempts to reduce the influence of the prior.

We will revisit Bayes’ theorem often in this book, such as when determining the optimal decision boundary when discussing *discriminant analysis*, or when considering *Naïve Bayes* as a nonparametric alternative to classification. The idea of including prior information in a model is not new and can be witnessed throughout statistics and science, as well as more modernly with machine learning. For instance, a new paradigm in machine learning called *physics-informed machine learning* has the goal of informing machine learning models using physically relevant prior information (Pateras et al., [2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000282)). That is, the model or algorithm is “informed” by prior knowledge of the object or system that is being modeled.

## 2.11 Law of Large Numbers

The law of large numbers is a fundamental law in statistics that in words essentially says *the larger the sample size, the closer one gets to the true probability of an event*. As a simple example, getting 9 heads out of 10 trials yields an estimate of the probability of heads equal to 9/10 = 0.90. The estimate of the probability of heads is not that great in this instance because it is based on only a few observations, that is, a relatively small sample. As sample size *n* increases, the approximation gets better, until in the limit as *n*→∞, the true probability is known. The limit, in this case, infinity ∞, is never achieved. The true probability, at least in this frequentist perspective, will never be known. All we really have are estimates. The bigger the sample size, in general, the better the estimate.

The law can be formalized as follows for the case of the sample mean $\\overline{y}$ when used as an estimator of the population mean, *μ*: for any *ε* > 0, the probability of any deviation of the kind $\\overline{y} - \\mu$ goes to 0 as *n* increases, eventually without bound, that is, *n*→∞. Alternatively, we could express the same thing by saying for any |*ε*|>0, the probability that $\\overline{y} - \\mu$ is between  − *ε* and *ε* goes to 0 as *n*→∞. Incidentally, it is worth noting that infinity, ∞, is not regarded as a number in mathematics, but is simply a *concept*. The symbol for positive infinity in R is Inf.

The law stems from a relative-frequency interpretation of probability and more pragmatically means that *if you want to know the true probability of an event, the more data you collect, in general, the better your estimate of that probability*. Note that this does not necessarily imply that collecting more data is always advisable. A million data points can do no worse than a thousand, unless of course the cost of collecting such extra observations is prohibitive and one can conclude about just as much knowledge from the initial sample of a thousand than the million. While the law of large numbers wants us to collect more data, it is a theoretical argument only. It may not be practical in reality. That thing we call the “real world” and is the unpleasant distraction from the theoretical mathematician often interferes with our capacity to collect more data and if the identical conclusion can be drawn with lesser data points, then collecting more data may simply be a waste of time and resources. Limiting theorems such as the above are attractive, but we must not get lost in their beauty at the expense of practical, real-world considerations.

An implication of the above is that statistical *power curves* tend to asymptote (horizontally) as sample size increases, and hence the cost of collecting more data may simply not be worth it. In the age of big data and the facility by which large data sets can be collected, these truths still hold, but since collecting data can be done rather cheaply these days in many contexts, such costs are unlikely to deter businesses such as *Amazon* from collecting terabytes of data and hence ignore power curves altogether. When “Big Data” is available, power curves are left in the wind. In such contexts, data is far too easy to come by to be concerned with power curves.

However, in other settings, such as smaller experimental ones where collecting data may be very difficult and vastly expensive, establishing just how much information is needed to draw 76conclusions is a very worthwhile activity. For example, if your units of observation consist of children with a particular rare disorder, each single data point may be extremely difficult to collect and the difference between 20 and 25 observations may be a huge undertaking. Collecting data may be prohibitively expensive. The development of small-sample statistics in the early 1900s made it possible to study populations without having to sample huge numbers. This was the gift of inferential statistics. We seem to be coming full circle in the current climate where collecting bigger data sets is the norm in some areas (definitely not all), mostly due to the facility by which such data can be collected (i.e., electronically) and easily stored. Early inferential statistical procedures were originally designed to circumvent this activity and make the most out of small data. Will the age of “small data” ever return? Let’s imagine what that might look like in the following fictional academic news report headline:

> An amazing new quantitative technology is being popularized for which one only requires very small samples to make generalizations to much wider populations. We call this new age of data analysis, SDA, or “Small Data Analysis.”

Increasing sample size can also have an influence on Bayesian posteriors. For example, in choosing a model, for small sample size, a posterior may indicate one model, whereas as sample size grows, a competing model may have a higher posterior due to the increase in information. *Weak* vs. *strong* laws of large numbers can also be distinguished though not discussed here. For details, see [Shao](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000334) (2023) for a clear but relatively theoretical discussion. [Casella and Berger (2002)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000055) also feature a discussion (p. 235).

### 2.11.1 Law of Large Numbers and the Idea of Committee Machines

One indirect application of the law of large numbers that we will revisit later in the book is contained in the idea that *average prediction functions converge to expected prediction functions*. For instance, ten prediction functions, when averaged, get us closer to the true expected (i.e., in terms of long-run probability) prediction function than any of the single prediction functions. That is, *when we combine many weak learners, we often achieve better predictions than the capacity of any of the weak learners that make up the combination*.

An analogy to sports would be that a team of weak players produces a better outcome than any of the individual teammates. Indirectly, the law of averages is present in this statement, since it implies that the greater the *n*, where “*n*” in this case is the number of prediction functions (players), the better we will converge to the true function. This idea of combining so-called “weak learners” to produce a stronger learner generally falls under the general category of *committee machines*.

## 2.12 Random Variables and Probability Density Functions

A *random variable* is a mathematical variable that is associated with a probability distribution. More precisely, a random variable is a function from a sample space into the real numbers ([Casella & Berger, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000055)) such that for any “slice” or interval, that is, for any subset of the sample space is called an *event*. The function must as well be *measurable* ([Mohri et al., 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000253)) though measurability of functions is well beyond the scope of the current text. We simply make mention of the word “measurability” here to denote the fact that not all functions are measurable, and hence saying that random variables are a function onto the real numbers is incomplete. Deeper and more sophisticated definitions of a random variable will first distinguish between *measurable* versus *nonmeasurable* functions (e.g., see [Shao](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000334), 2023).77

As an example of a random variable, consider the variable *x*[*i*] having values 0, 1, 2, 3. The variable *x*[*i*], as it currently stands, is often called a *mathematical variable*. The descriptor “mathematical” is usually implicit, but such a variable may often be called such in a statistics text simply to distinguish it from a random variable. As the reader will recall, it is a variable because *x*[*i*] can take on different values in the set. If *x*[*i*] could only take on a single value (e.g., 0 or any other value), it would not be a variable but instead would be a *constant*. It becomes a *random* variable when we associate probabilities with those values in the set such that they sum to unity. For instance, the aforementioned *x*[*i*] is now a random variable in the table below, where each value of *x*[*i*] is now associated with a probability of 0.25:

 
| *x*[*i*] || *p*(*x*[*i*]) |
| --- | --- |
| 0 || 0.25 |
| --- | --- |
| 1 || 0.25 |
| 2 || 0.25 |
| 3 || 0.25 |
|  || ∑ = 1.0 |

Note that there is no requirement that probabilities be equal across values of *x*[*i*] for *x*[*i*] to be a random variable. The only requirement is that the sum of probabilities is equal to 1.0. That is, we could have just as easily distributed the probabilities as 0.20, 0.40, 0.30, and 0.10 to illustrate the concept.

## 2.13 Convergence of Random Variables

Where a random variable “is going” is often of theoretical interest. That is, we often would like to know what value a random variable *converges to* in the limit. As sample size increases without bound to infinity, that is, *n*→∞, we would like to know properties of this convergence.

We say a sequence of random variables *converges in probability* to a random variable *x* if:

  
$$\\lim\\limits\_{n\\rightarrow\\infty}p\\left\\lbrack \\middle| x\_{n} - x \\middle| \\geq \\varepsilon \\right\\rbrack = 0$$  
(2.19)

In passing, note we have used the word *infinity* above, and do so as well in other places in the book. And while it seems convenient to use it and the spirit of what is meant by statements such as *n*→∞ is quite easily understood, the concept of infinity itself is quite rich historically and comes with it many philosophical difficulties and challenges, many of which are still ongoing today. Our inclusion of it in no way is meant to trivialize the depth of the object. Indeed, a dissertation with the title *The History and Theory of Infinity in Philosophy and Mathematics* would be no easy undertaking! Some hold that concepts of infinity, coupled with abstraction and proof, open the gateway to advanced mathematics ([Stillwell, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000349)). Make no mistake as well, by our mention of *philosophy of mathematics*, we are in no way meaning to communicate anything less than extremely rigorous. An in-depth study of infinity would not only require deeper mathematics, but also deeper philosophy. Whether such philosophy utilizes symbols (as does mathematics) has no bearing on the depth required to investigate such a topic.

## 2.14 Probability Density Functions

A *probability density function* is a function *f* that is associated with a continuous random variable *x* and that integrates to one:78

  
*p*(*a*≤*x*≤*b*) = ∫[*a*]^(*b*)*f*(*x*)*d**x* = 1  

The probability of any particular value in a *continuous probability density* has a limiting value equal to 0. That is, *p*(*x*\=*x*[*i*]) = 0. Continuity is defined very precisely and rigorously in mathematics using epsilon-delta definitions; however, intuitively, continuity can be thought of as drawing a curve without lifting one’s pencil from the page. Because it is a probability density function, its CDF is also regarded as *absolutely continuous*, where absolute continuity implies, among other things, that we can integrate for all values of *a*, *b*. The distinction here between absolutely continuous vs. simply continuous has no bearing on the work we do in the current book. However, to the real analyst in mathematics, such a distinction is very important.

At first consideration, this may seem like an odd result. *How can any particular value in a continuous distribution have (limiting) probability equal to 0?* To make this more intuitive, consider the probability between any two particular values, *a* and *b*, to equal a number greater than 0. As the distance *a* − *b* decreases, the probability of that interval gets smaller and smaller, until in the limit the distance *a* − *b* is such a thin slice that the probability of that thin slice is, theoretically, equal to 0. Numerically, one can think of this as the impossibility of grabbing hold of a number with an infinite number of decimals; only an *interval* of numbers can be seized; any particular number in that interval is elusive. One can also liken the idea to that of *Zeno’s paradox*, in which as one approaches an object, the distances are continuously “halved” on route to that object, until one gets so close to that object that the distance between the person and the object has a limiting value of zero.

If the probability distribution is of a *discrete* rather than a *continuous* variable, then it usually goes by the name of a *probability mass function*. In such distributions, we can assign a positive probability of a given value of the random variable, *p*(*x*\=*x*[*i*]) ≠ 0, unless of course the probability of a particular value of *x* is, in actuality, zero. The point, however, is that the probability of any particular value does not *need* to be zero as was the case for a continuous distribution. In a discrete distribution, we can assign probabilities to specific events. In a continuous distribution, we can only assign probabilities to *intervals*. That is, in a continuous density, the “events” are, in actuality, the interval “cuts” along the real line.

An example of a discrete vs. continuous probability distribution is given in [Figure 2.3](#c2.xhtml#f2.3).79

(b) Example of a continuous distribution where only ranges of values of x can be assigned probabilities.
