## 2.15 Normal (Gaussian) Distributions

Normal distributions and densities in statistics are everywhere. They are often called “Gaussian” because of their innovator, Friedrich Gauss. Not only do many physical phenomena approximate normality, but assuming normality theoretically provides a great deal of convenience in deriving new statistics and sampling distributions. Normality of a single variable is referred to as *univariate normality*, for two variables is *bivariate normality*, and for greater than two, *multivariate normality*. We survey each of these densities below.

### 2.15.1 Univariate Gaussian

The univariate normal density is given by

  
$$f\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\sigma\\sqrt{2\\pi}}e^{- {(x - \\mu)}^{2}/2\\sigma^{2}}$$  
(2.20)

There are two parameters in the univariate density, that of *μ* and *σ*², where *x* is simply the “input” value and *π* and *e* are constants. The density (or crudely, “area”) under the normal distribution integrates to 1,

  
$$\\int\\limits\_{- \\infty}^{\\infty}{N\\left( x \\middle| \\mu,\\sigma^{2} \\right)dx = 1}$$  

If we set *μ* = 0 and *σ*² = 1, the normal density is called the *standard normal density* and is the classic *z*\-distribution that appears at the back of most introductory statistics texts and serves to reveal various areas (proportions) under the curve. Having a single “standard” distribution to refer to provides a single “scale” from which other distributions with different *μ* and *σ*² can be transformed via *z*\-scores. When we compute a *z*\-score,

  
$$z = \\frac{x - \\mu}{\\sigma}$$  
(2.21)

we are transforming the given distribution to have a mean equal to 0 and standard deviation equal to 1 where (*x*−*μ*)²/*σ*² = (*x*−*μ*)(*σ*²)^( − 1)(*x*−*μ*). Hence, for a given *μ* and *σ*², the “action” of the univariate density is a function of its exponent. If we take the reciprocal of *σ*², that is, 1/*σ*²,we obtain the *precision* of the distribution ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032), p. 24). As we will see later, writing the exponent in the way of (*x*−*μ*)(*σ*²)^( − 1)(*x*−*μ*) will translate nicely in going from univariate to multivariate dimensions.

The transformation to *z* is an example of a *linear transformation* (the meaning of which we review shortly). It being an example of a linear transformation means that conversion to *z* does not change the shape of the distribution of the original data. This is very important! At first glance it can seem that conversion to *z* should *normalize* a distribution and hence give it a normal shape. But this intuition is incorrect and is a perfect example where what one feels *should* be correct is, in actuality, not. Intuition in mathematics and statistics can be a boon but at times a dangerous thing which is why proofs are usually required before a statement is considered true.80

### 2.15.2 Mixtures of Gaussians

Mixture models are those that combine different distributions, typically *linearly*, at arriving at a probability estimate. Oftentimes those individual distributions are Gaussian, and hence *Gaussian mixture models* are quite common. We write a mixture of Gaussians as

  
$$p\\left( x \\right) = {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\pi\_{k}}N\\left( x \\middle| \\mu\_{k},\\Sigma\_{k} \\right)$$  
(2.22)

The components *k* = 1 through *K* of a mixture model are the different *k* distributions that are “mixed” into a single distribution, each having its own mean *μ* and covariance matrix ∑ and where *π* is the mixing parameter or “weight” applied for each distribution. Combined, we wish to model the probability of *x*, *p*(*x*). The sum of mixing proportions must equal 1, that is, ${\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\pi\_{k}} = 1$ and where 0 ≤ *π*[*k*] ≤ 1. We can also impose equality constraints in a mixture distribution such that certain parameters are set to be equal across distributions, such as that of equal covariance matrices in a multivariate setting ([Goodfellow et al., 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000131)).

A Gaussian mixture model is a *universal approximator*, which, as we will see when we survey neural networks, implies that any smooth function (or density) can be approximated to any small degree of error given enough components ([Goodfellow et al., 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000131)). Hence, given enough mixtures of distributions, function approximation becomes a certainty just as with neural networks; if we are given enough hidden layers and nodes, they too become universal approximators. Mixture models, as we will see, are also useful in methods ranging from random effects models to cluster analysis to neural networks and beyond and are much more general than simply mixing normal densities. Our example here is of normal densities only for the reason that we are currently surveying the normal distribution. Mixtures for discrete variables, for instance, might include mixing Bernoulli distributions ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)).

### 2.15.3 Evaluating Univariate Normality

Many methods and techniques have been proposed for evaluating the normality of distributions. Perhaps the most useful are simple graphical and visualization techniques; however, inferential methods exist as well to estimate how likely it is the current sample distribution was selected from a population distribution that is normal. Tests for univariate normality include the *Kolmogorov-Smirnov test*, the *Shapiro-Wilk test*, the *Anderson-Darling test*, and many others. According to [Bilodeau and Brenner (1999)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000030), the Shapiro-Wilk test has been found to be the best omnibus test. We assume the reader has some experience with interpreting these tests, especially the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests. Further details can be found in [Denis (2021a)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000087).

We can demonstrate the Shapiro-Wilk test very easily in R:

```
> shapiro.test(rnorm(100, mean = 5, sd = 3))
```

```
  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
```

```
data: rnorm(100, mean = 5, sd = 3)
W = 0.99085, p-value = 0.7331
```

The null hypothesis is that the population from which the sample data were drawn is normally distributed. Since the *p*\-value is not even close to a traditional cut-off, such as *p* < 0.05 (*p* = 0.7331), we do not have evidence to reject the null. Note that this in no way confirms the population to be normal, but it does not give us evidence to suggest it is *not* normal.81

There are many ways and packages available for plotting all kinds of densities in R. For example, we can easily obtain a plot of the normal distribution in R by the following (Figure 2.4):

```
> x <- seq(-3, 3, length = 100)
> y <- dnorm(x)
>plot(y)
```

### 2.15.4 Multivariate Gaussian

As we have just seen, in the univariate density,

  
$$f\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\sigma\\sqrt{2\\pi}}e^{- {(x - \\mu)}^{2}/2\\sigma^{2}}$$  

the exponent featured  − (*x*−*μ*)²/2*σ*². When we generalize the univariate Gaussian to the multivariate setting, we replace observations *x* with vectors *x*, *μ* with *μ*, and individual variances, *σ*² with covariance matrices *Σ*:

  
$$f\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\left. \\left( \\sqrt{2\\pi} \\right)^{p} \\middle| \\sum \\right|^{1/2}}e^{- (x - \\mu)'\\Sigma^{- 1}(x - \\mu)/2}$$  
(2.23)

For *μ* = 0 and *Σ* = *σ*²*I*, where *σ*² = 1, this is the parallel setting for the standard normal distribution with *μ* = 0 and *σ*² = 1, where now *I* is the identity matrix. But how exactly is *Σ* = *σ*²*I* the analogous condition to *σ*² = 1? Recall that when *Σ* = *I*, this means that all values along the main diagonal are equal to 1 and all elsewhere is equal to 0 indicating that there is zero pairwise covariance between all variables. This implies that all variances in the multivariate density for *Σ* = *I* are equal to *σ*², where *σ*² = 1 in this case, just as *σ*² = 1 is true for the univariate density under a standard normal distribution.

We can easily compare respective univariate and multivariate densities. In the univariate density, note that the density begins with82

  
$$\\frac{1}{\\sigma\\sqrt{2\\pi}}$$  

In the multivariate setting, this is generalized to

  
$$\\frac{1}{\\left. \\left( \\sqrt{2\\pi} \\right)^{p} \\middle| \\sum \\right|^{1/2}}$$  

and now reflects *volume* as opposed to *area* as was the case in the univariate setting due to the now multidimensional space occupied by the multivariate density. The reason why it reflects volume instead of area is because we are now working in greater than two dimensions (i.e., think of a cube or cuboid, for example, instead of a square). The univariate distribution is often referred to as a *one-dimensional* distribution *statistically*, but such refers to the *number of variables* being studied, which is one. On paper, *geometrically*, the distribution occurs in *two* dimensions.

But what of the bivariate density? The bivariate density is simply a special case of the multivariate density for the case of two variables and hence, we find it more convenient to simply regard it as a multivariate density. However, it can also be written in the following form:

  
$$f\\left( x\_{1},x\_{2} \\right) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\frac{1}{\\sigma\_{1}\\sigma\_{2}\\left( 1 - \\rho^{2} \\right)^{\\frac{1}{2}}}\\exp\\left\\{ {- \\frac{1}{2\\left( 1 - \\rho^{2} \\right)}\\left\\lbrack {\\left\\lbrack \\frac{x\_{1} - \\mu\_{1}}{\\sigma\_{1}} \\right\\rbrack^{2} - 2\\rho\\left\\lbrack \\frac{x\_{1} - \\mu\_{1}}{\\sigma\_{1}} \\right\\rbrack\\left\\lbrack \\frac{x\_{2} - \\mu\_{2}}{\\sigma\_{2}} \\right\\rbrack + \\left\\lbrack \\frac{x\_{2} - \\mu\_{2}}{\\sigma\_{2}} \\right\\rbrack^{2}} \\right\\rbrack} \\right\\}$$  
(2.24)

where *ρ*² is the squared correlation between variables *x*[1] and *x*[2]. For further details on the bivariate density, see Johnson and Wichern ([2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173), p. 151).

The multivariate density is significant for many reasons, most of which parallel the reasons for the popularity of the univariate density in statistics and science more generally. However, there is an added feature of importance as regards the multivariate density, and that is, if we can assume multivariate normality, we can be assured that *any linear combination of the random vector* *X* *is also normally distributed*. While this may seem like an intuitive result, it has huge implications for statistical inference in multivariate models. The theorem also implies that conditional distributions will be multivariate normal as well.

### 2.15.5 Evaluating Multivariate Normality

Assessing multivariate normality is exponentially more difficult than assessing univariate normality due to it being a higher-dimensional problem. The best advice for such evaluation is probably given by Johnson and Wichern ([2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173), p. 177):

> It will become clear that our investigations of normality will concentrate on the behavior of the observations in one or two dimensions (for example, marginal distributions and scatter plots). As might be expected, it has proved difficult to construct a “good” overall test of joint normality in more than two dimensions because of the large number of things that can go wrong. To some extent, we must pay a price for concentrating on univariate and bivariate examinations of normality: We can never be sure that we have not missed some feature that is revealed only in higher dimensions … for most practical work, one-dimensional and two-dimensional investigations are ordinarily sufficient. Fortunately, pathological data sets that are normal in lower dimensional representations, but nonnormal in higher dimensions, are not frequently encountered in practice.83

Still, there are tests that can be used to evaluate normality, even in the multivariate domain. A generalization of the Shapiro-Wilk test can be used, as well as a more recent test called the *Henze-Zirkler test*. See [Zhou and Shao (2014)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000405) for details. The consequence of not ensuring multivariate normality is that the asymptotic distribution of many statistical tests becomes much more complicated ([Bilodeau & Brenner, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000030)). Recall that the asymptotic distribution is that obtained as *n*→∞.

In practice, researchers often use visualization and graphical techniques to verify univariate (e.g., *Q-Q plots*, *histograms*, etc.) and bivariate normality (e.g., scatterplots), and if such are more or less *approximately* satisfied, they then make the inferential “leap” to assuming that multivariate normality holds as well. However, it needs to be emphasized that while multivariate normality implies bivariate and univariate normality, the reverse is not necessarily true. That is, univariate and bivariate normality does not automatically imply multivariate normality. Hence the aforementioned “leap” required. Univariate and bivariate normality may increase the probability of multivariate normality, but it does not necessarily imply it.

## 2.16 Binomial Distributions

When a variable has a binary outcome, such as pass vs. fail, and whose probability of a success is constant or *stationary* over a series of trials, the binomial distribution is a plausible distribution for modeling such data. A random variable *x* is binomially distributed if *x* can take on one of two binary-valued numbers. For convenience, we denote these numbers 0 and 1; however in theory they could be any two numbers. We assume that 1 occurs with probability *π* and 0 occurs with probability 1 − *π*, where of course *π* is bound by limits 0 and 1 as is true of all probabilities.

The binomial density is given by

  
$$p\\left( x;n,\\pi \\right) = \\frac{n!}{x!\\left( n - x \\right)!}\\pi^{x}\\left( 1 - \\pi \\right)^{n - x}$$  
(2.25)

where *x* is the number of outcomes that we are modeling, *n* is the total number of trials, and *π* is the probability of a success on any given trial. A classic example of the binomial in practice is modeling the probability of getting 2 heads out of 5 flips on a fair coin (i.e., where “fair” implies *π* = 0.5). This probability is easily computed,

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\,\\, p\\left( x;n,\\pi \\right) = \\frac{n!}{x!\\left( n - x \\right)!}\\pi^{x}\\left( 1 - \\pi \\right){n - x}} \\\\ {p\\left( 2;5,0.5 \\right) = \\frac{5!}{2!\\left( 5 - 2 \\right)!}\\left( 0.5 \\right)2\\left( 1 - 0.5 \\right){5 - 2}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = 0.3125} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

Knowing that the probability of getting 2 heads out of 5 flips of a fair coin is equal to 0.3125, or about 31% of the time, such can help us evaluate the null hypothesis that a given coin is fair. Surely, if the coin is producing 2 heads out of 5 flips, this would give us no reason to suspect the coin is *not fair*. On the other hand, had the coin produced, say, 0 heads out of 5 flips, such would have yielded a probability of 0.03125. That is, the probability of getting zero heads out of five flips on a fair coin is quite low. It is so low that it might suggest we reject the null hypothesis that the coin is fair and infer the alternative that it is not, or at minimum, that the probability of heads is *not* equal to 0.5.84

We can compute binomial probabilities very easily in R. For the case of 2 heads out of 5 flips with a stationary success set at 0.5, the probability is computed as

```
> dbinom(2, 5, 0.5)
[1] 0.3125
```

The mean of a binomial distribution is *n**π*, that is, the number of trials multiplied by the probability of success on any given trial. For the above data, this number is 5(0.5) = 2.5. That is, on 5 flips, we would expect an average of 2.5 heads. Of course, since the variable is a discrete one, this interpretation should be made with caution as it is not possible to obtain “fractions” of heads. Recall that averages do not care about fractions. The mean number of persons per household may very well be 3.4, impossible as this number is for human beings (or any discrete objects, for that matter).

The variance of a binomial random variable is equal to *n**π*(1−*π*). For example, the variance of a binomial distribution with probability *π* = 0.5, and as before *n* = 5, is equal to *n**π*(1−*π*) = 5(0.5)(1−0.5) = 2.5(0.5) = 1.25, with standard deviation (square root) equal to 1.118.

### 2.16.1 Approximation to the Normal Distribution

The binomial distribution approximates the normal distribution for large number of trials, and in the limit, converges to the normal distribution. We can easily demonstrate in R how increasing *n* approximates normality via the plots in [Figure 2.5](#c2.xhtml#f2.5).

![Figure 2.5. Binomial distributions; as the number of successes increases from 5 to 100, the distribution increasingly takes on a smooth and normal shape.Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.5.jpg)

*Figure 2.5.* Binomial distributions; as the number of successes increases from 5 to 100, the distribution increasingly takes on a smooth and normal shape.[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.5)

Notice that as *n* increases for the same probability *p* = 0.5, the distribution increasingly resembles a smooth normal distribution. This is just one example, and perhaps the simplest and easiest to demonstrate, of how virtually all distributions in statistics are related. Many distributions converge to others under sufficient conditions. The Poisson distribution, to be surveyed shortly, in the limit converges to the normal distribution as well.

## 2.17 Multinomial Distributions

The binomial distribution just surveyed is actually a special case of the more general multinomial distribution:85

  
$$p\\left( x\_{1},...,x\_{k} \\right) = \\frac{n!}{x\_{1}!x\_{2}!...x\_{k}{}\_{!}}\\pi\_{1}^{x\_{1}}\\pi\_{2}^{x\_{2}}...\\pi\_{k}^{x\_{k}}$$  
(2.26)

where now *π*[1]^(*x*[1])*π*[2]^(*x*[2])...*π*[*k*]^(*x*[*k*]) are the different probabilities associated with individual events *x*[1], *x*[2],*x*[*k*]. That is, instead of having only two possibilities on the discrete variable (binomial), the variable now has several possibilities, each having their own respective probabilities, *π*[1], *π*[2], … *π*[*k*].

## 2.18 Poisson Distributions

The Poisson density is given by

  
$$p\\left( x/\\mu \\right) = \\frac{e^{- \\mu}\\mu^{x}}{x!}$$  
(2.27)

where *e* is a constant and x is the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time. The expectation (i.e., mean) of the Poisson density and that of its variance are both equal to *μ*. For further details on the Poisson density, see Casella and Berger ([2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000055), p. 92).

## 2.19 Chi-Square Distributions

The chi-square density is given by

  
$$f\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{1}{2^{v/2}\\Gamma\\left( v/2 \\right)}x^{\\lbrack(v/2) - 1\\rbrack}e^{- x/2}$$  
(2.28)

where *Γ* is the gamma function and *v* are the degrees of freedom of the density. The chi-square distribution of a random variable is equal to the sum of squares of *n* independent and normally distributed *z*\-scores (see [Fisher, 1922](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000099) for details):

  
$$\\chi\_{n}^{2} = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}z\_{i}^{2}} = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\frac{\\left( x\_{i} - \\mu \\right)^{2}}{\\sigma^{2}}}$$  

A final thought on statistical distributions and densities. Not surprisingly, there are many more than we have highlighted here in our brief review. Most times, the type of problem you are modeling will quite naturally dictate or strongly suggest the density you should use to model the given phenomenon. The key is recognizing from the problem you are facing which statistical distribution might be most *appropriate*. Such insight can be difficult and often depends on relying on one’s experience or expertise in the given substantive area. It is not unusual, however, for an analyst to spend some time contemplating which density would be best in modeling this or that phenomenon, especially when the problem is difficult.

## 2.20 Expectation and Expected Value

When we talk about “expectation” in statistics, we are generally referring to the long-run average behavior of a random variable. Since we are dealing with a random variable, this idea necessarily invokes and implies the *probability* concept. The expected value of a function *g* is the sum (or 86integral) of that function multiplied by its corresponding probability, for a continuous random variable,

  
$$E\_{X}\\left\\lbrack g\\left( x \\right) \\right\\rbrack = {\\int\\limits\_{x}{g\\left( x \\right)p\\left( x \\right)dx}}$$  
(2.29)

For a discrete random variable, the expectation is

  
$$E\_{X}\\left\\lbrack g\\left( x \\right) \\right\\rbrack = {\\sum\\limits\_{x}{g\\left( x \\right)p\\left( x \\right)}}$$  
(2.30)

The expectation for a discrete variable is different from that of a continuous variable since, with a discrete one, we can assign individual probabilities to values of the variable and sum up products, *g*(*x*)*p*(*x*). With a continuous variable, products are technically also summed, but they require integral calculus to do the summation and not simply sigma as in the discrete case.

We can compute expected values of single random variables as above, but we can also compute expected values of elements of vectors and matrices as well. The expectation of a random matrix is the expectation of each of its random variables,

  
$$E\\left( X \\right) = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {E\\left( x\_{11} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{12} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{1}{}\_{p} \\right)} \\\\ {E\\left( x\_{21} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{22} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{2}{}\_{p} \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {E\\left( x\_{n1} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{n2} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{n}{}\_{p} \\right)} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  
(2.31)

Since *E*(*x*[11]) through to *E*(*x*[*n*][*p*]) is equal to *μ*[11] to *μ*[*n**p*], we can write:

  
$$E\\left( X \\right) = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {E\\left( x\_{11} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{12} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{1}{}\_{p} \\right)} \\\\ {E\\left( x\_{21} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{22} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{2}{}\_{p} \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {E\\left( x\_{n1} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{n2} \\right)\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\, E\\left( x\_{n}{}\_{p} \\right)} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {\\mu\_{11}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\mu\_{12}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\mu\_{1}{}\_{p}} \\\\ {\\mu\_{21}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\mu\_{22}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\mu\_{2}{}\_{p}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\mu\_{n1}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\mu\_{n2}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\mu\_{n}{}\_{p}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  
(2.32)

## 2.21 Measures of Central Tendency

Observing every data point in a data set, especially for large data sets, provides a weak summary of that data and we usually wish instead to summarize the data with one or two measures that, in some sense, “represent” the data. We emphasize “in some sense,” because no single measure could ever summarize any data *perfectly*. To understand what central tendency means with regard to a particular measure used, one must understand in some depth the measure, that is, the abstract “idea” of what central tendency might mean. Of course, if the data set consists of only say, 2–3 data points, then inspecting the data set *point by point* is well advised and it makes little sense in trying to reduce such data into a smaller set of summary statistics. Usually, however, our data sets are medium-sized to very large, and graphical or numerical summaries are required in getting to know our data.

Measures of central tendency are *data reduction measures*; they take a set of observations and reduce such data down to a single measure.87

### 2.21.1 The Arithmetic Mean (Average)

The arithmetic mean is without question the most popular measure of central tendency. The arithmetic mean is given by

  
$$\\overline{x} = \\frac{1}{n}{\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}x\_{n}}$$  
(2.33)

Note that the arithmetic average consists of summing all observations, and then dividing by how many numbers went into that sum. Hence, the mean is often regarded as the *center of gravity* in a distribution. Since it is the center of gravity, it is also true that the sum of deviations from the mean is equal to 0; that is,

  
$$\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right) = 0$$  
(2.34)

The fact that deviations from the mean sum to zero is one reason why such deviations are typically squared (or absolute values taken under some circumstances) when producing the variance or standard deviation.

For a random variable, the mean is given by

  
*μ* = ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)*x**f*(*x*)*d**x*  
(2.35)

where *x* will denote a specific value of the variable and *f*(*x*) is the density under the curve for that value, and for discrete random variables,

  
$$\\mu = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}x}p\\left( x \\right)$$  
(2.36)

where *p*(*x*) will be the probability of the specific value *x* since with discrete random variables we can assign an individual probability to *x*, whereas with continuous variables recall, we cannot.

The arithmetic mean is only one of many means that can be computed on a set of data. Other means include the *geometric mean* and the *harmonic mean*. The geometric mean is given by

  
$${\\overline{x}}\_{g} = \\left( {\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}x\_{i}} \\right)^{\\frac{1}{n}} = \\sqrt\[n\]{x\_{1} \\cdot x\_{2} \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot x\_{n}}$$  
(2.37)

Note that in the geometric mean, we are taking products of values (via the product operator, $\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{}$) instead of sums as in the arithmetic mean and taking the root equal to the number of observations *n* (i.e., 1/*n*).

The harmonic mean is given by88

  
$${\\overline{x}}\_{h} = \\frac{n}{\\frac{1}{x\_{1}} + \\frac{1}{x\_{2}} + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\frac{1}{x\_{n}}} = \\frac{n}{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\frac{1}{x\_{i}}}$$  
(2.38)

The important point is that when someone reports computing the mean on a set of data, be sure to inquire *which* mean is being computed. Typically, when the word “mean” is used, it refers to the arithmetic mean, but not always. In the reporting of scientific research, it would be irresponsible of a researcher to not specify which mean is being reported if it were *not* the arithmetic mean. Further, though the arithmetic mean is often advertised as a measure of *central* tendency, it only reveals the center of a distribution in the sense of $\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\left( {x\_{i} - \\overline{x}} \\right) = 0}$, and in no other sense. In a perfectly normal distribution, the mean will be at the center of the distribution with symmetrical and equal areas on each side of the distribution. In a skewed distribution, however, the mean will no longer be at the “center” of the distribution and will simply fall where the condition $\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right) = 0$ is satisfied. For example, consider the location of the arithmetic mean in the distribution in [Figure 2.6](#c2.xhtml#f2.6).

![Figure 2.6 A distribution with a slight positive skew, where the mean is being “pulled” by larger scores toward the upper end of the distribution, where \\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right) = 0 is satisfied. Key to note is that \\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right) = 0 does not necessarily imply \\overline{x} is in the geometric “middle” of a distribution, nor does meeting this condition necessarily imply the distribution is normal in shape.Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.6.jpg)

*Figure 2.6* A distribution with a slight positive skew, where the mean is being “pulled” by larger scores toward the upper end of the distribution, where $\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right) = 0$ is satisfied. Key to note is that $\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right) = 0$ does not necessarily imply $\\overline{x}$ is in the geometric “middle” of a distribution, nor does meeting this condition necessarily imply the distribution is normal in shape.[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.6)

Note that the mean is *not* at the center of the distribution, however it is still defined as a measure of “central tendency.” If you memorize “*mean* = *central tendency*,” you will never truly understand the mean! The only way to understand it is to inspect its structure and appreciate what it actually *does*. This is true of all equations and formulas in statistics and machine learning. *Never rely on “verbal” definitions to describe them; only their equations and formulas reveal what they actually accomplish*.

It is a good computing exercise to compute the mean the “long way” in R or Python (try devising a function to generate the mean). In Python, we can easily compute the mean by using numpy.mean():89

```
import numpy as np
x = [10, 20, 30]
np.mean(x)
Out[56]: 20.0
```

The mean of the observations 10, 20, and 30 is, not surprisingly, equal to 20.

#### 2.21.1.1 Averaging Over Cases: Why Thinking in Terms of Averages Can Be Dangerous

Means and averages are much more than about the above computations. Though averaging incorporates all deviations from a center point, it simultaneously ignores individual information. If averaging is held as a *policy* to govern by, then it will naturally and necessarily ignore important individual cases. The “spirit” of an average need not be numerical either; it can be entirely conceptual as the following example illustrates.

Consider the case of canine vaccines. Many states require all dogs to be vaccinated routinely every one to three years. However, there is increasing evidence, some published, and some based on clinical observation and experience, that over-vaccinating may have detrimental health effects. If this is the case, then why have a blanket policy of vaccinating all dogs every one to three years? The answer is an easy one, because of *convenience and a lack of attention paid to each particular case*. Since the goal of vaccination is to not only protect any individual dog but also to offer protection to all human beings, the policy of vaccination is very general. But this greatly ignores individual cases. Not all dogs are the same and not all dogs have the same behavior patterns. For the dog whose owner doesn’t know where the dog is at 11 p.m. as the dog roams about the neighborhood searching for mischief and wrestling with potentially rabid foxes and raccoons, the one-to-three-year vaccination policy is a good one! However, for the dog who is primarily an “inside dog” who goes outside only periodically and is in virtually no danger of contracting the disease due to hypervigilant supervision by his owner, the one-to-three-year policy is overkill *for that particular dog*. Averaging makes things “easy” and allows a *blanket policy*, and essentially discriminates against cases that do not “fit” into requiring the policy. The law says your 11-year-old senior dog requires vaccination, yet science may suggest doing so is a bad idea because the dog is elderly, has medical conditions, and in all probability the prior vaccination is probably still providing immunity (a titer test for immunity may be a better option). Given such risk factors, vaccinating again would be somewhat reckless, yet by the “easy” and convenient policy of averages, the law often does not take into account these individual cases.

The moral of the story is that while thinking (and computing) in terms of averages can be productive, it can also be very dangerous. *Individual case analysis* is almost always better, despite how more expensive and time-consuming such an analysis may be. *Means and averages are balance points, yet often, “balancing” should not be of primary interest*. Case studies and more focused analysis should be the priority when the data, resources, and time allow it. Indeed, this is one criticism against numerical “summative” statistical research in general, that it focuses too heavily on the *common person* rather than the *individual person*. In clinical settings, case studies will typically do away with averages and instead focus on the individual.

Averages can also be dangerous when it comes to interpreting data. For instance, our interpretation of the mean implicitly assumes *linear interpolation* between values. For example, consider the mean of two numbers, 2 and 4. The mean is, of course, 3. Denoting 3 as the “center of mass” assumes that the distance and importance between 2 and 3 and 3 to 4 is the same, which in this case is linear. Linear interpolation, in general, can be risky because the intermediate values may not be 90linear, but are often assumed to be out of convenience. This is a simple idea but can have drastic and important consequences when interpreting real data.

### 2.21.2 The Median

Another measure of central tendency is that of the *median*. The median is the data point that divides the ordered data set into exactly two equal parts. The computation of the median will depend on how many observations are in the data set. For instance, if *n* is odd, then the location of the median *ỹ* is equal to (*n*+1)/2, yielding a median value equal to

  
$$\\widetilde{y} = y\_{(\\frac{n + 1}{2})}$$  
(2.39)

If *n* is even, then the location of the median is between (*n*/2) and (*n*/2) + 1, yielding a median of

  
*ỹ* = \[\[*y*[*n*/2]\]+\[*y*[(*n*/2)]+1\]\]/2  
(2.40)

While means can be said to be sensitive to extreme observations, medians are not. Medians, and other median-like statistics (such as quartiles), are said to be *robust* to extreme or outlying observations. Because medians only consider the “middle” value of the distribution, one can easily change other values in the data set while still retaining the same median. For example, the median of the data set 9, 10, 11 is 10, while the median of the data set 9, 10, 100 is also equal to 10. If a researcher reports the median of their data, ask to see a plot! Resist engaging in the cognitive bias that the median (or the mean, for that matter) implies a normal distribution. “Normality” is a theoretical notion. Empirical normality never truly exists; it can only be *approximated* by the theoretical ideal, that is, by the mathematical definition of a normal density.

Recall that the arithmetic mean is not robust to extreme scores or outliers. That is, since the mean is a weighted sum of deviations, even changing one value in the distribution will alter the mean. Is this a benefit or drawback? Such will depend on what you want the measure to accomplish. The scientist is, of course, interested in the data, but without knowledge of the functions (e.g., mean, median, etc.) *imposed* on such data, statistics computed on that data become amenable to misunderstanding and misinterpretation.

## 2.22 Measures of Variability

Measuring the variability in an empirical or theoretical distribution can take many forms, some better than others depending on the context of the situation and the characteristics of the data. Measures such as the *range*, *interquartile range*, which is equal to the 75th minus the 25th percentile, *semi-interquartile range*, equal to the 75th minus the 25th percentile divided by 2, and others are useful as “median-like” measures of variability. Being median measures, they are insensitive and robust to outlier observations, and hence, if such influence is not desired when summarizing a data set, these types of measures come highly recommended. Most commonly, however, we wish to calculate more sensitive measures that utilize the arithmetic mean as their locus or center from which we take deviations. For this reason, the variance and standard deviation dominate statistics as measures of variability, which we now review.91

### 2.22.1 Variance and Standard Deviation

The sample variance is defined as

  
$$S^{2} = \\frac{\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right.} \\right)^{2}}{n}$$  
(2.41)

where $\\overline{y}$ is the mean of the distribution and *y*[*i*] any particular data point in that distribution. The sample size is given by *n*. The sample variance requires us to sum squared deviations from the mean and take the average of that sum. The sample variance with *n* in the denominator is a *biased estimator* of the population variance, *σ*²,

  
$$\\sigma^{2} = \\frac{\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\mu \\right.} \\right)^{2}}{n}$$  
(2.42)

where now *μ* is the population mean to replace $\\overline{y}$ in the aforementioned sample variance. Formally, *S*² is a biased estimator because its expected value does not equal the population parameter, *σ*². More succinctly, we write *E*(*S*²) ≠ *σ*². To make it an *unbiased estimator*, we can correct the denominator by subtracting a *degree of freedom*, which yields,

  
$$s^{2} = \\frac{\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right.} \\right)^{2}}{n - 1}$$  
(2.43)

and now makes it true that *E*(*s*²) = *σ*². The positive square root of the sample variance is the *sample standard deviation s*,

  
$$s = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right.} \\right)^{2}}{n - 1}}$$  
(2.44)

which provides a measure of average deviation from the mean, now no longer in squared units as was true for the variance. As an example, if the standard deviation for a distribution is computed to be equal to 5, we can conclude that o*n average, scores deviate from the mean by five units*. However, without knowing the characteristics of the distribution and whether it is normal or not, we cannot use the normal density to compute proportions under the curve. That is, we cannot automatically assume that nearly 68% of cases fall within +1 or −1 units (i.e., a single standard deviation on either side of zero). We need to know more about the *shape* of the distribution in order to make such statements.

The variance and standard deviation so far discussed are for empirical variables, not theoretical random variables. For a continuous random variable, the variance is given by

  
*σ*[]² = ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)(*x*−*μ*)²*f*(*x*)*d**x*  
(2.45)

If the variable is *discrete*, then we can associate a probability *p*[*i*] with any particular value *x* in the distribution, yielding92

  
$$\\sigma\_{}^{2} = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\left( x - \\mu \\right)^{2}p\_{i}\\left( x \\right)}}$$  
(2.46)

In Python, the variance can be computed by numpy.var(). In R, the var() function will return the variance.

### 2.22.2 Mean Absolute Deviation

The reader may wonder why squared deviations of the kind $\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)^{2}$ are taken when computing the standard deviation. Indeed, we must take at least *some* function of the deviations since taking the sum of deviations, $\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)$, will always result in a value of zero, no matter the extent of variability or dispersion present in the distribution. That is, recall it can easily be shown that ${\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)} = 0$ for any conceivable distribution, which thus makes it a poor measure of dispersion. Why do we always get zero? The reason is because deviations from the mean are made up of both positive and negative deviations which *balance out* when taking the sum. By squaring deviations, we eliminate the negatively-signed differences and hence obtain a value greater than zero *only if there is indeed variability present in the distribution*. If there is no variability, then $\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right.} \\right)^{2} = 0$ will be true but only because there is indeed no variability, not because it is a constant for any distribution of data we may consider.

Squaring deviations is not the only operation that will negate negative deviations. We could have also taken a simpler function, that of absolute values of deviations. That is, taking absolute-valued deviations,

  
$$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left| {y\_{i} - \\overline{y}} \\right|$$  

would have also generated a value greater than zero only in the situation where there is variability in the distribution. So why take squares? Why not take absolute deviations instead? It turns out that taking squared deviations is mathematically more tractable and facilitates differentiation easier than would absolute values. However, it should be emphasized that taking absolute-valued deviations is permissible and is done in many contexts, especially those in which outliers in the distribution may make the squared sum especially large. That is, squaring a deviation magnifies its deviation much more than taking an absolute value. For example, a deviation of 4 has a squared value of 16, whereas it only has a value of 4 in absolute value. Hence, if you wish to minimize the influence of outlying data, then taking absolute deviations may be preferable in some cases to taking squared deviations. There is a whole literature on taking absolute-valued deviations in a variety of statistical and machine learning methods. Such a procedure is usually called *least-absolute-value (deviation) regression* in a linear model context.

## 2.23 Skewness and Kurtosis

The *skewness* of a distribution is a measure of the general shape of that distribution away from the typical bell-shaped normal distribution and is given by93

  
$$\\gamma = \\frac{E\\left\\lbrack \\left( y\_{i} - \\mu \\right)^{3} \\right\\rbrack}{\\left( {E\\left\\lbrack \\left( y\_{i} - \\mu \\right)^{2} \\right\\rbrack} \\right)^{3/2}}$$  
(2.47)

A distribution that is positively skewed has a tail that stretches out toward the right (i.e., higher scores), while a distribution that is negatively skewed has a tail that stretches out toward the left (i.e., lower scores). A distribution with an absence of skew may have a single mode (i.e., the classic normal distribution) or may have several modes (e.g., a bimodal distribution). *A lack of skew in a distribution should not automatically be associated with or imply a normal shape*. For example, the distribution in [Figure 2.7](#c2.xhtml#f2.7) exhibits virtually no skew.

![Figure 2.7 Bimodal distribution exhibiting virtually no skew. It is a mistake to assume that a distribution with no skew necessarily implies a unimodal normal distribution.Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.7.jpg)

*Figure 2.7* Bimodal distribution exhibiting virtually no skew. It is a mistake to assume that a distribution with no skew necessarily implies a unimodal normal distribution.[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.7)

To reiterate, it can be easy to assume that upon hearing a distribution has no skew to visualize a normal distribution with a single mode. However, this could be in error, as the plot in [Figure 2.7](#c2.xhtml#f2.7) reveals. *An absence of skewness does not necessarily imply a single mode*. This is one more reason to always plot data. Numerical summaries are usually never enough to draw strong conclusions about distributional characteristics.

The *kurtosis* of a distribution measures the general “tailness” of that distribution ([Upton & Cook, 2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000368)) and more succinctly the behavior of the distribution’s tails with regard to how “heavy” they are, meaning how much mass exists in the tails ([DeCarlo, 1997](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000078)). It is given by

  
$$k = \\frac{E\\left\\lbrack \\left( y\_{i} - \\mu \\right)^{4} \\right\\rbrack}{\\left( {E\\left\\lbrack \\left( y\_{i} - \\mu \\right)^{2} \\right\\rbrack} \\right)^{2}}$$  
(2.48)

A distribution is said to be *mesokurtic* if the distribution exhibits kurtosis typical of a bell-shaped curve, *platykurtic* if the distribution has lighter tails and is often flatter toward the center of the distribution when compared to the normal, and *leptokurtic* if the distribution exhibits heavier tails and is often more narrow in the middle of the distribution, typically making it more “peaked” than what would be expected in the normal density. While degree of “peakness” of a distribution is not the formal definition of kurtosis, the heaviness of tails often to some extent (though definitely not *always*) corresponds to whether the distribution is wider or more narrow toward the center of the distribution. However, associating kurtosis entirely with the peakness of a distribution has largely been jettisoned.94

## 2.24 Coefficient of Variation

The *coefficient of variation* is yet another measure of dispersion in a data set, and essentially “scales” the standard deviation *σ* by the value of the mean, *μ*. It can be useful in this regard to know how the standard deviation for a set of data (sample or population) relates to the size of that data’s mean. Hence, if we report the standard deviation equal to 2, knowing what the mean is can help us assess the extent to which a standard deviation of 2 is considered “big” or “small.”

The coefficient of variation is given by

  
$$CV = \\frac{\\sigma}{\\left| \\mu \\right|}$$  
(2.49)

where *σ* is the population standard deviation and |*μ*| is the absolute value of the population mean. As an example, for *σ* = 5, the coefficient of variation when *μ* = 5 is much smaller (i.e., 1) than if *μ* = 1 (i.e., 5). Hence, comparing standard deviations of distributions without incorporating respective means may, in some cases, be misleading, and a useful practice when comparing variability in distributions is to also incorporate the coefficient of variation into the discussion.

## 2.25 Statistical Estimation

Classical (and Bayesian, for that matter) statistics is all about *estimation*. Unless we have entire populations, we cannot know, for certain, the parameters of those populations and instead must estimate them using sample data. Recall that if you have the population data at your disposal, there is nothing to estimate, as one can simply compute descriptive statistics on the parameters of interest. This is sometimes misunderstood by newcomers to statistics, many of whom, upon learning about significance tests and *p*\-values become in a hurry to conduct such tests on every data situation they encounter, all too proud to report *p*\-values! However, a significance test on population parameters provides no additional insight beyond observing the parameters themselves. Significance tests are only meaningful when performed on sample data and when we wish to know something about the population parameters from which the sample data was presumably collected.

We say that *θ̂* is an estimator of the population parameter *θ*. More precisely, it is a *point estimator* because it seeks to estimate one particular and specific value of the parameter, *θ*. In general, an *estimator is any function of the sample data that is used to estimate a population parameter*. When we apply the estimator to some data and obtain a value for it, for instance, applying the mean estimator and obtaining a numerical mean, we say that the *estimator* has produced an *estimate*. Point estimators are almost always *statistics* (since they are computed on samples), but statistics are not always point estimators. As an example, if we compute the mean salary of a university department, such a mean is a descriptive statistic on the sample; however, it is not a point estimator because we are not using it to estimate any parameter.

An estimator is *unbiased* if the expectation of *θ̂* is equal to *θ*, that is,

  
*E*(*θ̂*) = *θ*  
(2.50)

In contrast, an estimator is biased if the above equality does not hold,95

  
*E*(*θ̂*) ≠ *θ*  
(2.51)

with the amount of bias being equal to the difference between the expectation and the actual parameter value:

Bias = *E*(*θ̂*) − *θ*(2.52)

Many estimators exhibit bias in samples but are not *asymptotically* biased. That is, as sample size grows indefinitely, bias eventually vanishes. More succinctly, an estimator is asymptotically unbiased if bias tends toward zero as sample size increases toward infinity. We can express this more formally as,

  
$$\\lim\\limits\_{n\\rightarrow\\infty}\\left( {E\\left( \\hat{\\theta} \\right) - \\theta} \\right) = 0$$  

where in the above recall that *E*(*θ̂*) − *θ* is the degree of bias present. As *n* increases, bias increasingly disappears, and is nonexistent in the limit. That is, *E*(*θ̂*) = *θ* in the limit as *n*→∞.

The *variance* of an estimator is a measure of how much the estimate would change if we changed or perturbed the data. That is, in repeated sampling where we experience random fluctuations in sample data, the variance of an estimator captures how much the estimate changes as a result of this fluctuation. We define the variance of an estimator as:

  
*V**a**r*[*θ̂*] = *E*(*θ̂*²) − (*E*(*θ̂*))²  
(2.53)

It seems intuitive to conclude that favorable estimators are those that have minimal to no bias while simultaneously having minimal variance. In most cases, this is the ideal to shoot for. However, as we will see later in the book, such estimators are not always most favorable for all situations. There are times where purposely allowing bias into an estimator is actually a “good thing” if it helps reduce variance. Of course, the most ideal situation would be to both reduce variance and reduce bias, but this is usually an unattainable goal. As bias decreases, we usually experience an upshoot in variance, and as variance decreases, an upshoot in bias. This *trade-off* is well known in statistical circles and not surprisingly goes by the name of the *bias-variance trade-off*. Biased estimators include those of the *ridge* and *lasso*, which are detailed later in the book. For now, we unpack in more detail the bias-variance trade-off.

## 2.26 Bias-Variance Trade-Off

We just mentioned that two things we need to be concerned about regarding an estimator are its bias and variance. We can unpack this idea into the following fundamental identity:

  
*E*(*y*[0]−*f̂*(*x*[0]))² = *V**a**r*(*f̂*(*x*[0])) + \[*B**i**a**s*(*f̂*(*x*[0]))\]² + *V**a**r*(*ε*)  
(2.54)

where *E*(*y*[0]−*f̂*(*x*[0]))² is the expected test mean squared error (MSE) at the value of the predictor, *x*[0]. It is important to realize here that the variance and bias in this context refer to the *statistical learning method or model*, not the data. That is, we are not interested in the variance of the sample data in this context; we are interested instead in the variance generated by using such and such statistical *methodology* or *model estimate*. Variance is how much the estimated function, *f̂*, would 96change if a different training data set was used, or if the current one was “perturbed,” and bias is how “off” the learning method is in actually capturing the true function, *f*(*x*[0]). The more flexible the method, the higher the variance, while the lower the bias. The relative change of these two quantities will influence test MSE. As flexibility increases, bias initially decreases faster than the variance increases ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)). However, beyond this initial state, an increase in flexibility impacts the bias much less but instead increases the variance, at which point test MSE likewise increases. The objective is to have both low variance and low bias as much as possible; however, a reduction in bias often results in an increase in variance, and vice versa.

### 2.26.1 Is Irreducible Error Really Irreducible?

It is typically held that variance of a statistical method, *V**a**r*(*f̂*(*x*)), can be mitigated or reduced; however, *V**a**r*(*ε*) is considered to be *irreducible variance*, which implies it cannot be mitigated and we are essentially “stuck” with it. That is, *V**a**r*(*ε*) is sometimes regarded as a *constant* that cannot be decreased. But is *V**a**r*(*ε*) truly irreducible? No! Yes, we can find a better function to fit, that is, *f̂*(*x*) to better approximate the “truth” in the form of *f*(*x*), which will get us closer to *E*(*y*−*f̂*(*x*[0]))² = 0, but we can also reduce *ε* via *measurement*, or at minimum, make *ε* less *variable*. It is only “irreducible” in the sense that it may be independent of the function one is fitting, but it is not irreducible in the sense of simply reducing the overall squared error. That is, *ε* exists not solely as a result of not fitting the “correct” function or using a better statistical learning technique, but can decrease simply by an improvement in *measurement*. Reducing *V**a**r*(*ε*) becomes a realistic possibility.

Are we theoretically able to get *ε* completely to zero? Probably not, but such will depend on what we consider *ε* to actually “be” at a deeper philosophical level. If one believes in *true chance* or *true error*, then it may be impossible to get error down to zero and we will always have at least *some* fluctuation. As noted in James et al. ([2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168), p. 19), “the irreducible error will always provide an upper bound on the accuracy of our prediction for *Y*. This bound is almost always unknown in practice.” While this is true, our point is merely that this does not take into consideration whether error can *theoretically* ever go to zero. More formally, we may write,

  
lim[*V**a**r*(*ε*) → 0] = *E*(*y* − *ŷ*)²\=\[*f*(*x*)–*f̂*(*x*)\]²  

That is, as *V**a**r*(*ε*)→0 in the limit, we simply obtain the squared difference between the observed *f*(*x*) and estimated *f̂*(*x*) functions (note that we dropped *V**a**r*(*ε*)). This “ideal” is theoretically possible as we find ways to decrease *ε* and its *V**a**r*(*ε*). While this is a hugely interesting topic on a psychometric and philosophical level, we will not explore the issue further here.

## 2.27 Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Maximum likelihood is, historically, the most common method of estimating parameters in a variety of statistical models and contexts. It is due primarily to [Fisher (1922)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000099) though in concept at least, its origins and germination span several hundred years before Fisher ([Stigler, 1986](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000348)). The idea of maximum likelihood is very simple. Suppose you have observed data in the form of a sample. Maximum likelihood asks the question:97

> *What values of parameters should we choose, that would maximize the likelihood function of such data?*

Note carefully that the data have already been observed. The question we are asking is what value for parameters of interest *would have made such data most likely*?

As a simple example, consider flipping a coin ten times and observing five heads. The five heads constitute the observed data. What parameter value for the probability of heads would have given this observed result a “maximum likelihood” of occurring? The answer, of course, is the probability of heads equal to 0.5, or, more succinctly, *p*(*H*) = 0.5. An alternative parameter value such as *p*(*H*) = 0.4 would have made the data *less likely* than *p*(*H*) = 0.5, and hence *θ̂* = 0.5 is the maximum likelihood estimator in this case. The estimates for the parameter values (e.g., *p*(*H*) = 0.5) are referred to as *maximum likelihood estimates*.

More formally, the maximum likelihood estimator, or MLE, is defined by

  
$$\\left. {\\hat{\\theta}}\_{mle} \\triangleq \\underset{\\theta}{\\arg\\max}p\\text{(}D \\middle| \\theta\\text{)} \\right.$$  
(2.55)

which simply expresses the argument value (i.e., arg ) that makes the data *D* most likely given the parameter value, *θ*. That is, maximum likelihood (ML) provides which value for *θ* makes *p*(*D*|*θ*) (the *likelihood function*) most probable. The logarithm of a function is a monotonically increasing function, which means that whether we take the likelihood or the log of the likelihood essentially amounts to the same thing in terms of assessing the size of likelihoods. For technical reasons, and for convenience, taking the log is useful, and hence the log-likelihood is given by

  
log *L*(*θ*) = log *p*(*D*/*θ*)  
(2.56)

In practice, it will often be the negative of the log-likelihood that is *minimized* instead of the log being maximized,

  
$${\\hat{\\theta}}\_{mle} \\triangleq \\underset{\\theta}{\\text{arg}\\min}\\text{-log}\\, p\\text{(}D/\\theta\\text{)}$$  
(2.57)

which is generally known as the *error function* ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)).

All of the above is quite general. For instance, we can unpack these elements for the multivariate situation specifically in which we desire maximum likelihood estimators. Hence, suppose we seek maximum likelihood estimates of *μ*, the multivariate mean, and *Σ*, the covariance matrix, that will maximize the likelihood of the data. In the multivariate setting, the aforementioned estimates are found by

  
$$\\hat{\\mu} = \\overline{y}$$  

for the multivariate mean vector, and98

  
$$\\left. \\hat{\\Sigma} = \\frac{1}{n}{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right.} \\right)\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)'$$  

which can also be given by $\\frac{n - 1}{n}S$, where *S* is the sample covariance matrix. For justification for these particular maximum likelihood estimators, see Rencher and Christensen ([2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295), p. 99). Maximum likelihood requires us to select the parameters that *maximize* the joint density evaluated at the observations ([Johnson & Wichern, 2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173)). The maximizing parameter values, as before, are called *maximum likelihood estimates*. That is, the maximum likelihood estimates of *μ* and *Σ* are those values, *μ̂* and *Σ̂* that maximize the likelihood function *L*(*μ*,*Σ*). In practice, as in the univariate case, often the negative of the log of the likelihood is computed. As mentioned, maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing error ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)).

### 2.27.1 Why ML Is So Popular and Alternatives

Maximum likelihood estimators possess many favorable properties. It is the default estimation for many if not most statistical and machine learning problems. For instance, it is commonly used in neural networks (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000131)).

Despite its popularity, maximum likelihood is by no means the *only* method of estimation in statistical modeling and machine learning. Numerous other methods have been advanced to accommodate data situations for which assuming multivariate normality is unrealistic. For instance, *quasi-maximum likelihood* (QML) is a method of estimation advanced in structural equation modeling featuring nonlinear terms such as quadratic effects ([Klein & Muthén, 2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000188)). *Two-stage least-squares* estimation for nonlinear SEM models has also been advanced ([Holst & Budtz-Jorgensen, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000156)). *Adaptive Gaussian Quadrature* (AGQ) has also been proposed for estimating nonlinearity in SEM models. The *method of moments* is an alternative approach to ML estimation when the solution is either unavailable or computationally difficult ([Murray, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). *Online recursive estimation* is yet another possibility (Murray, 2022). All of these estimation methods are complex and discussions of them could fill an entire chapter or even book.

The key takeaway from this discussion is that when it comes to estimation methods, though maximum likelihood is probably the most popular method, there are numerous alternative methods which are already in existence and others which are being developed in statistics and machine learning. Hence, when one comes across the term “estimation,” one should be curious to learn what *type* of estimation is being referred to as it will not always be maximum likelihood.

### 2.27.2 Estimation and Confidence Intervals

In classical statistics, we can either attempt to estimate a particular point in a distribution, such as the arithmetic mean, or we can attempt instead to estimate an *interval* of values. Theoretical statistics tells us that the expected value of the sample mean, $\\overline{y}$, is equal to the population mean, *μ*. That is, $E\\left( \\overline{y} \\right) = \\mu$. However, we also know that the probability of “hitting” the precise value of the population mean has a limiting value of zero. Hence, we seek usually to build an *interval* of values around the sample estimator and instead of seeking *point predictions*, we will use an *interval estimator*, the most common of which is the confidence interval.

The *confidence for the mean* is given by

  
$$\\overline{y} \\pm z\_{\\alpha/2}\\frac{\\sigma}{\\sqrt{n}}$$  
(2.58)

where *z*[*α*/2] is the critical value of *z* given the desired accuracy for the confidence interval. For a 95% interval, that value is 1.96, and so we have99

  
$$\\overline{y} \\pm 1.96\\frac{\\sigma}{\\sqrt{n}}$$  

Recall that seldom do we actually know the value of *σ* and must instead estimate it based on sample data. When we use the sample standard deviation *s* as an estimator of the population standard deviation *σ*, the mean is no longer distributed as *z*, but instead is distributed as a *t*\-statistic, and hence the confidence interval becomes:

  
$$\\overline{y} \\pm t\_{\\alpha/2}\\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}$$  
(2.59)

Confidence intervals are by no means limited to means. Interval estimators can be used for a variety of statistics. In many cases, analytical solutions tell us how to construct the standard errors for such intervals. In other cases, standard errors are intractable and difficult or even impossible to calculate. When we cannot compute standard errors directly, one option is to *bootstrap* samples of observations and determine interval bounds via repeated sampling. We discuss the bootstrap shortly.

Be sure to note that as was true for the point estimator, an interval estimator is the random variable. The parameter that is being estimated is not the random variable. While there are a few different ways of interpreting confidence intervals in practice, the most correct way is to refer to the *procedure* for computing such intervals of which one interval has been calculated. Hence, the most correct interpretation of a computed 95% interval on data becomes

> *The probability that the given interval, based on the procedure used to compute the interval, covers the parameter, is 0.95. Repeating the procedure of calculating intervals this way would result in 95% of them covering the true parameter.*

There is a whole literature on the correct interpretation of confidence intervals and how researchers presumably always get it wrong. Yes, formality matters here, but the above is not the only way a confidence interval can be conceptualized, especially in a real research setting. The above interpretation is rather awkward when it comes to interpreting real research, but is arguably near the most theoretically correct interpretation. For a brief discussion on this point and a brief argument for why competing ways of interpreting confidence intervals may be useful in practice, consult [Denis (2020)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000086).

## 2.28 The Bootstrap: A Way of Estimating Nonparametrically

Perhaps more than any other statistical technique, the bootstrap is the one that has benefited the most from the computer age revolution and the speed and facility that such computation provides. Though theoretically the bootstrap would still be possible without computers, it would be so laborious and impractical computationally that it is fair to say the technique would have likely forever been abandoned and have never risen to fame. Thanks to computation, however, the bootstrap has, in the world of statistics and machine learning, become a “household name.”

The origins of the bootstrap are usually credited with [Efron (1979)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000093) and is actually a special case of what is generally known as the *jackknife* which came before it, but is far more applicable and generalizable than the jackknife. The jackknife itself can be thought of as a *linear expansion method* (called the *delta method*) for approximating the bootstrap ([Efron, 1979](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000093)). As noted by [Efron and Hastie (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000094), “Before computers, applied statisticians needed to be Taylor series experts in 100laboriously pursuing the accuracy of even moderately complicated statistics” (p. 155). The jackknife, originating in 1957, was a first step toward a computational approach to standard errors.

The basic idea of the bootstrap is to capitalize on computing power to draw repeated samples from a sample that, for the given bootstrap scenario, serves as a *pseudo-population*. We include the bootstrap here in our discussion of estimation as it is yet another way to estimate parameters of a distribution; while the methods we have just surveyed do so *parametrically* through time-tested analytical formulae, the bootstrap is a *nonparametric* way of estimation through simulations of resampling using the computer.

Even more generally, bootstrap methods are a special case of the wider family of *Monte Carlo methods*, which is a general name given for *resampling*. To be clear, the bootstrap is not *equivalent* to Monte Carlo methods by any stretch, as many other techniques that utilize Monte Carlo sampling exist. However, in applied statistics and machine learning circles the bootstrap is undoubtedly one of the more popular *applications* of the general Monte Carlo technique. As a result of the bootstrap typically being used for estimation, we have included a discussion of it here instead of under Monte Carlo techniques, but including it under a general discussion of Monte Carlo techniques would not have been wrong.

### 2.28.1 Simple Examples of the Bootstrap

As discussed, *the bootstrapped sample is to the original sample as the original sample is to the population*. Why would we ever want to sample from a sample? There are a few reasons, but one primary reason is that obtaining things like standard errors and such *analytically* is sometimes not feasible and in many cases, actually impossible. True, we know what the standard error is for the mean, for instance, equal to

  
$$\\frac{\\sigma}{\\sqrt{n}}$$  

but we are less sure, for instance, what the standard error is for the *median* (i.e., the standard error for the median is less *exact*). That is, the standard error of the median is less *analytically available*. However, thanks to the bootstrap, we can assess “empirically” the standard deviation of medians (i.e., the standard error of the median). This is a chief benefit to being able to bootstrap, that of being able to “simulate” statistics empirically via resampling that have no analytical sampling distribution or that deriving such sampling distributions proves very difficult. In theory, we could “invent” a new statistic tomorrow that has no known sampling distribution and simply bootstrap the statistic via resampling to determine its “behavior” over the long run. This is perhaps the biggest reason why the bootstrap is such a “big deal” in statistics.

More formally, assume we have a training set, denoted by *Z* = (*z*[1],*z*[2],...,*z*[*N*]), where any given *z*[*i*] corresponds to data on *x*, *y*, that is, *z*[*i*] = (*x*[*i*],*y*[*i*]). Imagine now we resample from *Z* a total of *B* = 100 samples. We will refer to these samples as the *bootstrapped samples*. To use our example of the standard error, we would compute standard deviations on each of the bootstrapped samples and observe standard deviation behavior over the 100 samples. This would denote the standard error we want to compute. However, we need not necessarily be computing standard errors; we could be computing virtually *anything* on these bootstrapped samples. As mentioned, bootstrapping is widely applicable to virtually any statistic, even those for which deriving sampling distributions is impossible.

As an example, we could compute linear regressions on the bootstrapped samples and observe the behavior of the linear equations across the samples, or any other models or statistics. This is the 101power of the bootstrap and Monte Carlo simulation in general; *it allows us to resample repeatedly and build a distribution of functions of the data, whatever those functions may be*. The bootstrap in this regard is very flexible and has wide application. It is *nonparametric*, meaning it assumes nothing about the population, making it extremely flexible and well-suited for creative ventures pertaining to whatever you wish to calculate on the repeated samples. Bootstrapping *allows you to create an actual empirical distribution of computed statistics instead of deriving a theoretical one analytically*.

More formally, consider once more *Z* = (*z*[1],*z*[2],...,*z*[*N*]). Suppose we compute some quantity on *Z*, that is, some function of *Z* which we will appropriately denote *f*(*Z*). Suppose that function *f*(*Z*) is the variance of *Z*, that is, *V**a**r*(*Z*) defined as

  
$$f\\left( Z \\right) = Var\\left( Z \\right) = \\frac{\\sum\\limits\_{b = 1}^{B}\\left( Z\_{}^{{}^{\*b}} - {\\overline{Z}}^{\*b} \\right)^{2}}{B}$$  

where *Z*^( \* *b*) is a particular computed bootstrapped sample and ${\\overline{Z}}^{\*b}$ is the *mean* of all bootstrapped samples. Notice carefully that *V**a**r*(*Z*) here is just an ordinary variance but computed on the *B* bootstrapped samples. All of this looks familiar based on our earlier study of the variance. For instance, if we wished for the more typical estimator, we could use *B* − 1 instead of *B* in the denominator,

  
$$f\\left( Z \\right) = Var\\left( Z \\right) = \\frac{\\sum\\limits\_{b = 1}^{B}\\left( Z^{\*b} - {\\overline{Z}}^{\*b} \\right)^{2}}{B - 1}$$  

It is easy to see then that *V**a**r*(*Z*) is yielding a measure of variance around bootstrapped samples.

### 2.28.2 Why Not Bootstrap Everything?

As we have seen, the bootstrap is quite universal and general and can be applied in many different contexts. Indeed, we can literally bootstrap virtually any function on a sample if we have sufficient reason for doing so. It does not need to be something familiar, such as a mean, median, or other well-known statistic. This is precisely the advantage of the bootstrap, in that it allows us to estimate statistical quantities for which we may have literally no theory to guide us and for which there may be no chance of ever knowing the sampling distribution without resampling.

So, why isn’t the bootstrap used more often? Why don’t we bootstrap virtually *everything*? The reason is that except when assumptions are violated, analytically-derived solutions may produce more favorable results than resampling. Computer simulations can be inexact when compared to timeless analytical derivations. Hence, when statistical theory is available and analytical solutions possible, *classic formulas may dominate bootstrapped approaches*. As a general guideline as to when or not to bootstrap, first check to see if an analytical solution is available and use it if it is a valid one that is strongly supported theoretically. Second, try the bootstrap. Of course, there is never any harm in trying out both approaches and comparing results.

When bootstrapping, the question that also naturally arises regards how many replicates are sufficient to get a reasonable estimate of the distribution of the bootstrapped statistic. Though there is some debate on this, a general recommendation is in the neighborhood of *B* = 50, and rarely greater than 200 ([Rizzo, 2019](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000303)). Bootstrapping also allows for replacement, and hence one bootstrapped sample might contain the same sampling element as another bootstrapped sample. The 102probability that a data point is not included in a sample is equal to 1 − (1/*n*) which implies that the probability that the given data point is not included in *n* samples is equal to (1−1/*n*)^(*n*), which is a well-known approximation to 1/*e* in the limit as *n*→∞ ([Aggarwal, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000005)).

Bootstrapping in Python can be easily performed using *SciPy*. Bootstrapping in R can be performed several ways. One way is by using the *bootstrap* package (Original et al., [2019](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000276)).

### 2.28.3 Variations and Extensions of the Bootstrap

There are numerous variations on the bootstrap. Among these include the *leave-one-out bootstrap*, where the accuracy of an instance is computed using all the data except that instance ([Aggarwal, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000005)). Kleiner et al. ([2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000190)) proposed a sub-sampling method called *bag of little bootstraps* (BLB) to help deal with the massive data that may be too large for computer memory or take too long to analyze efficiently. In the BLB approach, one draws a number of subsamples of a given size on each sample from the original collected data set. For each of the subsets, a number of bootstrapped samples are chosen and we compute statistical methods on those subsets (e.g., computation of the mean). These are thus, the point estimates. These measures are then combined by averaging to yield the overall point estimates and quality measures.

The *fractional bootstrap*, also known as the *Bayesian bootstrap*, draws random weights and instead of applying such to resampling units, applies them to the actual data. For details and implementation in R, see the *fwb* package ([Greifer, 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000133)).

## 2.29 Elements of Classic Null Hypothesis Significance Testing

For better or for worse, much of classical statistics is based on the method of *null hypothesis significance testing*, or “NHST” for short, which provides the basis for rejecting a hypothesis if the data are unlikely to have occurred under the presumed model. This yields the classic “*p*\-value” from which a scientist decides “yay” or “nay” whether to retain or discard the null. The null hypothesis, contrary to misconception, is not necessarily the hypothesis of a null result or zero effect, nor is it necessarily the hypothesis of equality in a comparison scenario of two populations. R.A. Fisher, the inventor of ANOVA, coined the null hypothesis to be the hypothesis to be *nullified* if observed data contradict it. More specifically, if the probability of an observed statistic is relatively small in light of the null, the null is rejected and a *statistical alternative* hypothesis is inferred. The designation of “statistical” in *statistical alternative* is important. A statistical alternative hypothesis is a statement of “not the null,” and is *not* a statement confirming the researcher’s substantive alternative hypothesis. Classical null hypothesis significance testing, or really any *statistical* theory, does not have the ability to confirm a research hypothesis. Misunderstanding this point can easily lead to misunderstanding the results of a significance test.

As an example to illustrate the point, suppose we posit a null hypothesis that the mean IQ of a population is equal to 100. That is,

  
*H*[0] : *μ* = 100  

The statistical alternative hypothesis is that the mean is not equal to 100; that is,

  
*H*[1] : *μ* ≠ 100  

But why would it not be equal to 100? Perhaps because the investigator treated the group with a magic pill that would increase their IQ. In this context, that is the *research alternative hypothesis*. 103Note that *rejection of the null and inference of the statistical alternative hypothesis is not equivalent to inference of the research alternative*. The null hypothesis does not know “why” it is being rejected; it is simply being rejected based on the low probability of the test statistic. Hence, a rejection of the null could “happen” under a lot of conditions, especially if the study or experiment were done poorly. If the null is rejected under a properly done experiment, then inference of the statistical alternative naturally leads to a strong inference of the research alternative, but that “leap” is not automatic, and making it so can easily lead to inference of an incorrect research alternative. For instance, under a poorly performed study, perhaps it wasn’t the magic pill at all that was the effective agent; perhaps the increase in IQ was due to increased sunlight due to a change in seasons or a change in diet among participants that simulated an increase in IQ because of greater cognitive processing power.

To emphasize the abstraction that exists in the classical null hypothesis significance test, we can express the parameter value (or vector, in the case of multivariate models) as belonging to a particular parameter space under the null, *Θ*[0], from which the parameter value is a member of that set,

  
*H*[0] : *θ* ∈ *Θ*[0]  
(2.60)

against an alternative hypothesis that the parameter value is a member of an alternative set,

  
*H*[1] : *θ* ∈ *Θ*[0]^(*c*)  
(2.61)

where *Θ*[0]^(*c*) is the complement to *Θ*[0] and whose membership is that of *not the null*. Why the abstraction? To make things unnecessarily abstract and mathematical? No! This symbolism demonstrates the most *general framework* of the null hypothesis significance test and emphasizes that the complement to the null hypothesis *is* an abstraction. It is not “concrete.” Otherwise said, rejection of the null hypothesis does not necessarily mean anything other than inferring the complement to the null in terms of an abstract parameter space! Allowing this idea to sink in will prevent the reader from making egregious scientific inferences when rejecting a null hypothesis that are habitually made even by professionals in various fields. A rejection of the null does not imply the research alternative; it merely indicates the complement to the null *statistically* (not *substantively*).

Classical significance levels used in most scientific investigations include 0.05 and 0.01, though there is absolutely no statistical or philosophical grounds for using these levels. Fisher himself simply denoted the 0.05 level as “usual and convenient” in the establishment of evidence to contradict the null. Still, there is a long history of misunderstanding what 0.05 actually means, and often researchers incorrectly treat 0.05 as a “yes” vs. “no” decision on the presence of an *effect* in the experiment, which is a serious misunderstanding. Not only does 0.05 not necessarily indicate the presence or absence of a meaningful effect, but there is simply nothing “special” about 0.05. As many have noted before, surely God loves the 0.06 level as much as the 0.05.
