is in the kernel or null space of $\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 1} \\\\ {2\\,\\,\\,\\, - 1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 1} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$ as a result of $\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 1} \\\\ {2\\,\\,\\,\\, - 1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 1} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {- 2} \\\\ {- 1} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\, 3} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} 0 \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$. That is, *T*(*x*) = 0. In words, the kernel of a linear transformation is the set of vectors that maps the transformation to zero.

### 2.37.7 Trace of a Matrix

The *trace* of a matrix *A*, denoted tr(*A*), is the sum of elements along the main diagonal:

  
$$\\text{tr}\\left( A \\right) = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}a\_{ii}}$$  
(2.98)

where *a*[*i**i*] denotes the values along the main diagonal. Traces only exist for square matrices. Among the properties of traces include the following:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\text{tr}\\left( A \\right) = \\text{tr}\\left( A^{T} \\right)} \\\\ {\\text{tr}\\left( A + B \\right) = \\text{tr}\\left( A \\right) + \\text{tr}\\left( B \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\text{tr}\\left( {AB} \\right) = tr\\left( {BA} \\right)} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

The trace of a matrix multiplied by a constant *c* is also equal to that constant times the trace of the matrix, and we write,

  
tr(*c**A*) = *c*tr(*A*)  

All of these relations can be easily verified by the reader. Traces play a meaningful role in multivariate statistics. For instance, at times we are only interested in values along the main diagonal of a matrix such as when we wish to consider only variances in the covariance matrix and ignore covariances in the off-diagonal. Instead of communicating “sum all the diagonal entries of the matrix to get the total variance,” we simply say “compute the trace of the matrix.” The trace will be featured when we consider multivariate test statistics, for instance, later in the book.

The trace of a matrix in R can be obtained by sum(diag()). In Python, matrix.trace() in numpy() will generate the trace.

## 2.38 Linear Combinations

If there is one mathematical element or object that is common to virtually all of statistics and machine learning, it is that of a *linear combination*, which is defined quite simply as133

  
*l*[*i*] = *a*[1]*y*[1] + *a*[2]*y*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *a*[*p*]*y*[*p*]  
(2.99)

The above is very generic. Usually in statistics we will see linear combinations with alternate identifiers. We use the symbol “*l*[*i*]” to stand for “linear combination.” We can see that a linear combination is actually a sum of products, *a*[1]*y*[1] through *a*[*p*]*y*[*p*] depending on how many variables we are summing. In the sum, *a*[1] through *a*[*p*] are scalars, which are usually real numbers. We can see that each variable *y*[1] through *y*[*p*] is being “weighted” by a given scalar. Our first impression here might be that variables receiving a greater weight have more “importance” (in some sense) than variables receiving less weight.

Where do we see linear combinations in statistics and machine learning? Everywhere! As an example, as the reader will surely already recognize, recall the simple linear regression model,

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[1] + *ε*  
(2.100)

We can see that the above is nothing more than a linear combination, comprising of an intercept, *β*[0], which is a constant scalar, and a variable *x*[1] that is weighted by the scalar *β*[1], then trailing off with an error term, *ε*.

Linear combinations are utilized all over the place in ANOVA-type models as well. Consider the following linear combination between population means,

  
$$C\_{i} = c\_{1}\\mu\_{1} + c\_{2}\\mu\_{2} + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot + c\_{J}\\mu\_{J} = {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}{c\_{j}\\mu\_{j}}}$$  
(2.101)

The linear combination becomes a *linear contrast* when we impose the constraint that the weights, *c*[1] through *c*[*J*] must sum to 0, that is,

  
$$\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}{c\_{j} = 0}$$  
(2.102)

Another place where we see linear combinations in statistics is in principal components analysis, or “PCA” for short. In fact, a principal component *is* a linear combination of the sort,

  
*y*[*i*] = *a*[1]*x*[1] + *a*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *a*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  

As we will see later in the book, the coefficients *a*[1] through *a*[*p*] will be values of the eigenvector resulting from the eigen decomposition performed to obtain the components, and the *x*[1] through *x*[*p*] will be variables on which the PCA is being performed.

The *span* of a set of vectors is the set of vectors in a vector space consisting of all linear combinations of those vectors, while the *basis* of a set of vectors is the number of linearly independent vectors that span the space, which means out of all vectors in the space, the basis is the minimal number of vectors that can, essentially, generate the space. There are typically lots of vectors in a vector space, but the *basis* vectors are those for which all those other “less important” vectors can be generated. This is why basis vectors are so important. The basis vectors are essentially the “boss” of the vector space.

Linear combinations are also featured in the committee machine of *boosting*, where one weights classifiers by scalars to generate a stronger learner from a series of weak learners. We feature a discussion of boosting later in the book.134

## 2.39 Determinants

Determinants play a central role in linear algebra and statistics. Determinants are only defined for *square* matrices. While determinants can be calculated for increasingly large matrices, they are most easily demonstrated for small matrices. For example, the determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix *A* can be easily computed as follows:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} \\left| A \\middle| = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {a\_{11}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{12}} \\\\ {a\_{21}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{22}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack \\right. \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = a\_{11}a\_{22} - a\_{12}a\_{21}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(2.103)

When would such a computation be useful in statistics? We note immediately that through the subtraction of the product *a*[12]*a*[21], the determinant becomes useful for matrices such as the covariance matrix in which we wish to consider variances in the product *a*[11]*a*[22] but then subtract out the product of covariances in *a*[12]*a*[21]. In the case where covariances are equal to 0, it follows that the determinant is computed simply as

  
*a*[11]*a*[22] − *a*[12]*a*[21] = *a*[11]*a*[22] − 0 = *a*[11]*a*[22]  

As we will see shortly, this is one reason why the determinant is an ideal measure for constructing an overall “generalized” version of variance in a covariance matrix.

For 3 × 3 matrices and beyond, the computation of the determinant becomes increasingly unwieldy and is, not surprisingly, best left to a computer (even very higher-order determinant calculations can be time-consuming for computers). Still, there is intuition that can be gleamed from computing a determinant for a 3 × 3 matrix (we leave it to the reader to extract the algorithm):

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} \\left| A \\middle| = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {a\_{11}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{12}\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{13}} \\\\ {a\_{21}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{22}\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{23}} \\\\ {a\_{31}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{32}\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{33}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack \\right. \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = a\_{11}\\det\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {a\_{22}\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{23}} \\\\ {a\_{32}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{33}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack\\left( - 1 \\right)2 + a\_{12}\\det\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {a\_{21}\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{23}} \\\\ {a\_{31}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{33}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack + \\left( - 1 \\right)3 + a\_{13}\\det\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {a\_{21}\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{22}} \\\\ {a\_{31}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{32}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack\\left( - 1 \\right)4} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(2.104)

Geometrically, we can also easily visualize the determinant in this case as the subtraction of shapes (areas). For example, consider the matrix *A* defined as

  
$$A = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {3\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 2} \\\\ {1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 3} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  

The determinant of *A* is equal to (3)(3) – (2)(1) = 7. As described in [Young (2023)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000401) and shown in [Figure 2.12](#c2.xhtml#f2.12), this subtraction can be visualized as the subtraction of corresponding areas (i.e., the larger area (3)(3) minus the smaller (2)(1)).135

![Figure 2.12 Determinant as a subtraction of areas. For this matrix, the smaller area (2) is being subtracted from the larger (9).Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.12.jpg)

*Figure 2.12* Determinant as a subtraction of areas. For this matrix, the smaller area (2) is being subtracted from the larger (9).[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.12)

[Figure 2.12](#c2.xhtml#f2.12) is for the 2 × 2 case and hence the measure of *area* is suitable for geometrical representation. In matrices of 3 × 3 or greater, we shall require a measure of *volume*, and hence, for the general case, we will typically speak of the *volume* of a matrix instead of that of area. From this geometrical interpretation, we see then that *the determinant is the factor by which the volume of a matrix increases or decreases*. A determinant equal to 0 corresponds to a *parallelogram* (in the 2 × 2 case) having zero area or *parallelepiped* (in the 3 × 3 or higher case) having zero volume ([Young, 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000401)). As an example, consider the 3 × 3 matrix in [Figure 2.13](#c2.xhtml#f2.13) with corresponding drawn parallelepiped.

![Figure 2.13 Parallelepiped with determinant (and hence, volume) equal to 0.Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.13.jpg)

*Figure 2.13* Parallelepiped with determinant (and hence, volume) equal to 0.[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.13)

We see that the parallelepiped has collapsed upon itself and contains no volume since the determinant of the corresponding matrix is equal to 0. These notions of area and volume are not of terrible interest in this abstract sense but will be very useful as we consider statistical measures that feature determinants later in the book. Certainly, in virtually every multivariate method, one will find determinants somewhere.

A few of the many properties of these measures have been established, which include the following: |*A*|=|*A*^(*T*)|, |*c**A*|=*c*^(*n*)|*A*|, |*A**B*|=|*A*||*B*|. A determinant equal to 0 implies the matrix is not invertible, which means the matrix is *singular*. This has consequences for statistical procedures (such as regression) that typically require an inverse. The matrix is called *nonsingular* if it is invertible and hence |*A*|≠0. Determinants also have numerous relationships with other objects in linear algebra. For instance, the determinant of a *diagonalizable matrix* is equal to the product of its eigenvalues, where diagonalizing a matrix, in this context, means transforming the matrix such 136that the values along the main diagonal are the eigenvalues of the matrix and all other values are equal to 0. More generally, a diagonal matrix is a matrix such that all entries off the main diagonal are equal to 0. Hence, a matrix with eigenvalues down its main diagonal and all other values in the matrix equal to 0 is a diagonal matrix.

Matrix decompositions include the *LR decomposition*, *Cholesky decomposition*, and *QR decomposition*, which are also used as efficient methods for computing determinants. For details, see [Strang (1993)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000351).

Determinants in R can be easily computed. For example, the following computes the determinant of an identity matrix:

```
> A <- diag(x = 5)
> det(A)
[1] 1
```

In Python, we can compute the determinant of a matrix using numpy():

```
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
```

  
$$\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 2} \\\\ {3\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 4} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack = 4 - 6 = - 2$$  

```
np.linalg.det(a)
Out[336]: -2.0000000000000004
```

## 2.40 Means and Variances of Matrices

Recall that the goal of statistical inference is largely to estimate parameters. In a univariate context, we often wish to estimate the population mean, *μ*. A good estimator of *μ* is that of the sample mean, $\\overline{y}$, since recall that $\\overline{y}$ is an unbiased estimator of *μ*. That is, the expectation, *E*, of $\\overline{y}$ is that of *μ*, $E\\left( \\overline{y} \\right) = \\mu$. Likewise, we saw that *E*(*s*²) = *σ*².

Vectors and matrices are simply larger objects than these comparative univariate counterparts, and hence it makes sense that we should want to estimate means and variances on these objects as well. Not surprisingly, the expectation of a mean vector, $\\overline{X}$, is that of a population vector, *μ*, and we write

  
$$E\\left( \\overline{X} \\right) = \\mu$$  
(2.105)

However, contrary to simply estimating a variance, *s*² as we did in the univariate case, in the multivariate case we not only have variances, but also *covariances*. The variances and covariances you will recall are packaged up in the covariance matrix, *Σ*. As usual, we typically do not have the population covariance matrix at our disposal and need to estimate it. An unbiased estimator of *Σ* can be obtained as a function of the sample covariance matrix, *S*[*n*]:

  
$$E\\left( {\\frac{n}{n - 1}S\_{n}} \\right) = \\Sigma$$  
(2.106)

It can easily be shown that the bias of the estimator, *S*[*n*], is equal to  − (1/*n*)*Σ* ([Johnson and Wichern, 2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173), p. 121).137

## 2.41 Determinant as a Generalized Variance

As a result of the covariance matrix incorporating both variances and covariances, we can establish a generalized version of the variance that parallels the univariate case. A measure that is often used to denote a generalized variance in a multivariate setting is the determinant of the covariance matrix, |*S*|. For a visualization of the generalized variance, see Johnson and Wichern ([2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173), p. 125).

It should be emphasized that |*S*| only provides a measure of variance and like *s*² in the univariate setting does not by itself provide any information as to the *pattern* of the data or direction. That is, without visualization, a report of |*S*| simply gives us a sense of the volume of the space; *it does not by itself tell us which directions are most prominent or emphasized in the data*. This is not surprising since as mentioned the reporting of a univariate variance *s*² does not either by itself give us information on the *particular* distances between data objects or points; it only provides an *average* of those (squared) distances. A generalized variance of |*S*|=0 implies the entire space has collapsed onto itself with a corresponding volume equal to 0. A volume greater than zero is indicated by |*S*|>0.

Instead of the determinant of the covariance matrix, we can also conceive of a *total* variance as the sum of univariate variances along the main diagonal of the covariance matrix,

  
*s*²[11] + *s*²[22] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *s*²[*p**p*]  

where *s*²[11] through *s*²[*p**p*] are variances in the corresponding covariance matrix. More concisely, this version of the variance is simply the *trace* of the covariance matrix. Note that this interpretation does not include covariances and hence is not a true measure of “multivariate” variance in the same spirit as that of the generalized variance, |*S*|.

## 2.42 Matrix Inverse

The inverse of a matrix plays a fundamental role in matrix algebra and parallels the notion of an inverse in ordinary scalar algebra. To understand what an inverse is, consider a simple example from scalar algebra. The inverse of the number 6 is that number which, when multiplied by 6, will equal 1. That number, of course, is ⅙, since ⅙ multiplied by 6 yields 1.

The concept is analogous in matrix algebra. The inverse of matrix *A* is that matrix *A*^( − 1) such that *A**A*^( − 1) = *I*. For two matrices *B* and *A*, if *B**A* = *I*, then *B* is called the *left inverse* of *A*. For another matrix *C*, if *A**C* = *I*, then *C* is the *right inverse* of *A*. An invertible matrix has both a right and a left inverse (which are identical) and hence in this book, whenever we speak of the inverse of a matrix, the distinction between left vs. right inverse is immaterial. In this book, the inverse of a matrix is simply *the one and only inverse*.

Computing inverses in numerical linear algebra is “big business” and some mathematicians have devoted much of their lives to developing new and better algorithms for approximating inverses. Thankfully, for simple matrices, computing inverses is relatively easy and straightforward. As an example, consider the generic matrix A:

  
$$A = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {a\_{11}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{12}} \\\\ {a\_{21}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{22}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  

The inverse of *A* is equal to138

  
$$A^{- 1} = \\frac{1}{a\_{11}a\_{22} - a\_{12}a\_{21}}\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {a\_{22}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, - a\_{12}} \\\\ {- a\_{21}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{11}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  
(2.107)

An inverse for a matrix exists only if the determinant of that matrix is unequal to 0. If the determinant is equal to 0, then the inverse does not exist. Hence, for the simple square 2 × 2 matrix *A* above, we require

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {A = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {a\_{11}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{12}} \\\\ {a\_{21}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, a\_{22}} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = a\_{11}a\_{22} - a\_{12}a\_{21} \\neq 0} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

The properties of inverse matrices are many. A few of the more important ones are the following:

(*A*^( − 1))^( − 1) = *A*, the inverse of the inverse of a matrix is the original matrix. This parallels what we would expect in simple scalar algebra, since the inverse of 1/*a* is equal to *a* and so the inverse of the inverse of 1/*a* is 1/*a.*

(*A*^(*T*))^( − 1) = (*A*^( − 1))^(*T*), the inverse of the transpose is equal to the transpose of the inverse.

(*A**B*)^( − 1) = *B*^( − 1)*A*^( − 1), the inverse of a product is equal to the product of inverses in reverse order.

|*A*^( − 1)|=1/|*A*|, the determinant of the inverse is equal to the reciprocal of the determinant.

In R, we can get the inverse by the function solve(). For example, if A is a square matrix, the inverse is computed as solve(A). In Python, we can compute the inverse using numpy().linalg.inv():

```
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
np.linalg.inv(a)
Out[337]:
array([[-2. , 1. ],
[ 1.5, -0.5]])
```

If *A*^( − 1) does not exist, such as with rectangular matrices, a pseudo-inverse may be used known as the *Moore-Penrose inverse*. For details, see [Rencher and Christensen (2012)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295).

### 2.42.1 Nonexistence of an Inverse and Singularity

To emphasize the point already made, the most important property (or “consequence”) of inverses, for our purposes anyway, is that if the inverse of a matrix does not exist, then it implies that that matrix has a determinant equal to 0 and is thus deemed *singular*. Hence, it is generally a “big deal” in statistics when a matrix is not invertible. An additional consequence is that a non-invertible matrix also implies a *dependency* within the matrix; that is, not all rows and columns are linearly independent. We discuss linear independence and dependence shortly. In brief, for now, matrices that are singular and have linearly dependent columns or rows, or even nearly so, are statistically generally regarded as *ill-conditioned* and not “well-behaved.” Non-invertible matrices can provide a lot of problems when it comes to statistical analyses.139

## 2.43 Quadratic Forms

A quadratic form is nothing more than a polynomial for which *all* terms (not just *some*) are of the second degree. An example of a quadratic form is *y* = *x*[]² + *z*[]². The following polynomial *y* = *x*[1]*x*[2]*x*[3] is not a quadratic form since it involves a cubic form ([Hubbard & Hubbard, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000161)). In vectors and matrices, as we will soon elaborate on, an important quadratic form is that of *x*′*A**x*, for which if *x*′*A**x* > 0 for all vectors *x* ≠ 0, it indicates that *A* (symmetric) is positive definite. We will come across quadratic forms in one way or another throughout this book mostly implicitly and “behind the scenes.”

## 2.44 Positive Definite Matrices

Referring to the matrix representation of quadratic forms above, *x*′*A**x*, it is easy to see that for *x* = 0, *x*′*A**x* = 0. Now, consider the case where *x*′*A**x* ≥ 0, where *A* is a symmetric nonzero matrix (since zero matrices are, by definition, also symmetric). As already noted when discussing quadratic forms, if the only way for equality to hold for *x*′*A**x* ≥ 0 is for *x* to be the zero vector, then *A* is called *positive definite*, which implies that the quadratic form *x*′*A**x* will be positive, that is, *x*′*A**x*\> 0.

The above result has important and pragmatic implications. Most pragmatically for statistics and machine learning in an applied sense, positive definite symmetric matrices are those for which *all eigenvalues are strictly positive*. *Semi-positive definite* matrices, on the other hand, have some (at least one) eigenvalues equal to 0 and all others positive, while indefinite matrices have at least one eigenvalue that is also negative. A further implication of positive definite matrices is that such matrices have all row and column vectors linearly independent, which implies that the matrix is of full rank and hence nonsingular, and this equates to the determinant of the matrix being nonzero.

## 2.45 Inner Products

One of the most significant foundational aspects of linear algebra is that of *inner products*, also generally known as *dot products*. Though the two terms are often used interchangeably, as we do as well in this book, they are not exactly the same. The dot product can be considered a *special case* of the more general Euclidean inner product, where dot products are usually restricted to finite Euclidean spaces of ℝ² or ℝ³ but where *Euclidean inner products* are generalizable to higher dimensions, including to infinite-dimensional vector spaces ([Anton & Rorres, 2000](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000013), p. 163). Inner products are at the heart of many computations in linear algebra and hence are also heavily used in statistics and machine learning. For example, covariance and correlation are based entirely on the notion of a dot product. The *kernel trick* featured in support vector machines and other algorithms also features the inner product, where, as we will see, computation of the kernel in the original dimensionality of the data points generalizes to an inner product space in higher dimensions.

An inner product is defined as

  
*x*′*y* = *y*′*x* = *x*[1]*y*[1] + *x*[2]*y*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *x*[*m*]*y*[*m*]  
(2.108)

where *x*′*y* = *y*′*x* indicates commutativity. The inner product is also distributive where for three vectors, *x* ⋅ (*y*+*z*) = *x**y* + *x**z*. A vector space together with an inner product is called an *inner product space* ([Roman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000306)).

Recall that the *length* of a vector *x* can be expressed as the square root of its inner product,140

  
$$L\_{x} = \\sqrt{x\_{1}^{2} + x\_{2}^{2} + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot + x\_{n}^{2}} = \\sqrt{x'x}$$  

For two random vectors, *x*, *y*, the *Cauchy-Schwarz inequality* holds that

  
|⟨*x*′*y*⟩| ≤   ||x||        ||y||  
(2.109)

which in words says that the absolute value of the inner product, *x**y*, is equal to or smaller than the product of individual lengths ([Bilodeau & Brenner, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000030)). Equality exists in the case that *x* and *y* are linearly dependent (i.e., scalar multiples since there are only two vectors). A proof of the inequality can be found in Garcia and Horn ([2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000122), p. 93).

In Python, we can easily compute the inner product:

```
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([0, 1, 0])
np.inner(a, b)
Out[342]: 2
```

A *Hilbert space* is an abstract vector space with an inner product that is complete under the metric that is induced by the inner product ([Roman](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000306), 2008, p. 327). Formality matters here, but we can make this definition much more practical. Pragmatically, as it regards statistics and machine learning, a Hilbert space is essentially a kind of feature space ([Mohri et al., 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000253)). The concept of inner products here is key because it forms the basis of the aforementioned kernel function or *kernel trick*. The idea of the kernel trick is to compute a given kernel using raw data in the original space (called the input or “data space”) so as to tell us something about the inner product of vectors in the higher “feature” space. That is, *the kernel function in the data space essentially reproduces kernel Hilbert spaces*. In this way, the elements of the kernel function “live” in the more abstract higher-dimensional Hilbert space, which allows us to compute kernels in low dimensions to tell us something about inner products in higher dimensions, that is, in the feature space. We extend this discussion of the kernel trick shortly.

## 2.46 Linear Independence

The idea of linear independence is of fundamental importance and has wide implications in statistics and machine learning. Consider two vectors, *x* and *y*, weighted by scalars *c*[1] and *c*[2],

  
*c*[1]*x* + *c*[2]*y* = 0  

If both *c*[1] and *c*[2] are both equal to 0, then the equality is easily shown to be true. This is the *trivial* case, and hence not very interesting. If, on the other hand, we can find scalars *c*[1] and *c*[2] both not equal to 0 such that the equality still holds, then the vectors *x* and *y* are said to be *linearly dependent*. It essentially means, *for the case of only two vectors*, that we can write one vector as a *scalar multiple* of the other. In the case of more than two vectors, linear dependence implies we can write one vector as a linear combination of others in the set. If we cannot find such a set of scalars (other than zero), then the set of vectors is *linearly independent*.

As mentioned, the above example features only two vectors. We can generalize this principle of linear independence and dependence to a much broader set of vectors, indeed, *k* vectors,141

  
*c*[1]*x*[1] + *c*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *c*[*k*]*x*[*k*] = 0  

If there exist scalars *c*[1] through *c*[*k*] not all zero such that the above equality holds, then the vectors *x*[1] through *x*[*k*] are said to be *linearly dependent*. Otherwise, the set of vectors is linearly independent. Linear independence basically implies that we cannot write one vector as a linear combination of any others in the set, for which in the special case of two vectors in a set, the linear combination necessarily implies a scalar multiple. It is important to note that linear dependence or independence is relative to the *set of vectors* only. For example, two vectors are not themselves *intrinsically* linearly dependent or independent without considering the set in which they are featured. That is, the vector (0, 2, 4) is not by itself linearly independent or dependent; its status must be concluded *relative to the set in which it is referenced*. If that vector is the only (nonzero) vector in the set, then it is still regarded as linearly independent, but it is only so *relative to the set*, which in this case, consists of no other vectors.

## 2.47 Rank of a Matrix

The maximum number of linearly independent rows or columns of a matrix is the matrix’s *rank*. A fundamental, if not surprising result of linear algebra is that *row rank* will always equal *column rank*, which also implies that the matrices *A* and *A*^( − 1) (if it exists) have the same rank. Throughout our study of statistics, we will typically be interested in matrices of *full rank*, which implies that the total number of columns or rows is inclusive in the rank of the matrix.

As an example, if we have a 3 × 3 matrix and say it is of “full rank,” then it means the number of linearly independent rows (and columns) is equal to 3. If we say a matrix is less than full rank, or “rank deficient,” then it suggests the rank of the matrix is less than the number of columns or rows. Rank-deficient matrices have one or more columns (or rows) that are linear combinations of other columns (or rows). For instance, the following matrix is less than full rank:

  
$$A = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 2\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 3} \\\\ {1\\mspace{6mu}\\,\\,\\, 2\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 5} \\\\ {1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 2\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 6} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  

It is less than full rank because the second column is simply a scalar multiple of the first. That is, the second column is exactly a factor of twice that of the first column. The rank of the matrix is 2 because there are only two linearly independent columns (and rows). Rank is also equal to the dimensionality of the largest submatrix **A** (i.e., deleting certain rows and columns) that has a nonzero determinant ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). In an applied sense, the rank of a matrix gives us a sense of how much information is “duplicated” in the matrix. A matrix of full rank tells us that each row (or column) is providing “unique” information. A matrix less than full rank tells us that there is, essentially, “overlap” in the matrix in terms of information. Though this is a nonrigorous way of conceiving rank, it is nonetheless helpful in grasping the concept in an applied sense.

As an example of computing the rank of a matrix in Python, we can use numpy(), where in the following the rank of the matrix is equal to 1:

```
np.ones(4)
Out[345]: array([1., 1., 1., 1.])
from numpy.linalg import matrix_rank
matrix_rank(np.ones(4))
Out[347]: 1
```

142 

## 2.48 Orthogonal Matrices

Orthogonal matrices are those square matrices for which when we multiply by its transpose, we obtain the identity matrix. As an example, *X**X*^(*T*) = *I* = *X*^(*T*)*X* implies that *X* is an orthogonal matrix. If *X*² = *X*, the matrix is regarded as *idempotent* ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). For vectors, we can more simply define orthogonality as when the inner product *x**y* = 0. Orthogonality also implies perpendicularity, which is expressed by *x*⊥*y*. *Orthonormal* vectors are orthogonal and have length equal to 1; hence if *x* is orthonormal to some vector, then it stands that ||*x*||=1.

## 2.49 Kernels, the Kernel Trick, and Dual Representations

Kernels play a significant role in machine learning and we see them in techniques such as *neural networks* and *support vector* *machines* (SVMs). Indeed, the “kernel trick” is something that quickly becomes common territory as one studies machine learning. In general, *kernel functions* (as distinct from the kernels featured earlier in relation to matrices) are used to define *similarity* between data objects. Kernels of inner products are often taken to determine the similarity of input data so that a linear classifier can be used to solve what is essentially a nonlinear problem. In support vector machines, the kernel trick was first introduced by Boser et al. ([1992](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000041)).

Even though much of the emphasis of statistics is on linearity, nonlinear problems pervade scientific practice. Attempting to model such nonlinearity via polynomial transformations, for instance, or other *basis function transformations*, as we will see later, can be complex, timely, and computationally infeasible. By taking kernels of input data, however, what was originally linearly *inseparable* data now becomes *separable* without having to actually mathematically go to those higher dimensions. That is, the kernel trick will allow us to stay in 2-D, for instance, when the data are only separable, for example, in 3-D. Essentially, the *kernel trick* or *kernel substitution* ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032), p. 292) allows one to take an infinite-dimensional problem and reduce it to a finite dimensional problem ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)).

The kernel function *k* is defined by

  
  *k*(*x*,*x*′)  = *k*(*x*′,*x*) = *ϕ*(*x*)^′*ϕ*(*x*′)  
(2.110)

where the inner product *x*, *x*′ is a measure of *similarity* between two vectors, and hence the kernel function is considered a measure of such “likeness” of data. That is, the kernel function essentially measures how similar observations are to one another. As shown in (2.110), the kernel function here is also symmetric such that *k*(*x*,*x*′) = *k*(*x*′,*x*). Computations of *k*(*x*,*x*′) take place in the original data space, but equate to the inner product *ϕ*(*x*)^′*ϕ*(*x*′) in the feature space.

Of the only key requirements of kernels is that they be *positive definite* as it can be shown that positive definite kernels induce an inner product in a Hilbert space ([Mohri, 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000253)). The reader may recall that positive definiteness ensures that the eigenvalues of **K**, the *kernel matrix* in this case, are (strictly) positive. What is more, *for a positive definite kernel, such will always produce (or “associate with”*) *a kernel matrix that is positive semidefinite* ([Mohri et al., 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000253), p .108). A variety of kernels exist, such as *polynomial kernels*, *Gaussian kernels*, *sigmoid kernels*, and others. Of importance to remember with regard to kernels is that they need not be actually computed as inner products in the original data space *x*, *x*′ for them to imply an inner product *ϕ*(*x*)^′*ϕ*(*x*′) in the feature space. *Many other kernels are possible that do not computationally and directly calculate the inner product in data space*. *What is important is that the kernel expresses a degree of similarity in the data space, such that it induces an inner product space in the feature space.*

To better illustrate the kernel trick, consider the data in [Figure 2.14](#c2.xhtml#f2.14) depicting two classes.143

![Figure 2.14 Data on two classes that are clearly not linearly separable.Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.14.jpg)

*Figure 2.14* Data on two classes that are clearly not linearly separable.[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.14)

Of course, the data in [Figure 2.14](#c2.xhtml#f2.14) is not linearly separable; that is, we need a swishy curve to separate the two groups. By computing the *kernel* of the data however, *in its original dimensionality*, we essentially transform this nonlinearity into a linearly separable problem in the feature space. But why should this work? Why does the kernel trick do what it does?

The reason why the kernel trick works is related to *Mercer’s theorem* ([1909](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000248)), which essentially yields the following very important result:

> *A kernel can be used to approximate a function when it is known that the function exists even if knowledge of what that function is, is incomplete or not known*.

That is, the kernel essentially contains a wealth of information even about higher dimensionalities for which we may be currently unaware. The fact that we can work on the problem in its original configuration or via a kernel is known as *dual representation* ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)). In words, the so-called “kernel trick” essentially communicates the idea: *You’re working on a complicated problem in higher dimensions, you’re not possibly even aware of what those dimensions are, or even how many there might be, but if you compute the kernel in your existing lower-dimensional space you can learn a lot about those higher dimensions without ever having to go there* ***explicitly*** . By way of fictional analogy, the kernel might allow you to stay and compute in this 3-D spatial universe while potentially learning something about a different one (e.g., a universe possibly in five dimensions).

As stated earlier, the utility of kernels is based on the fact that many data sets that we work with are not linearly separable. *Applying a kernel (hopefully) makes the data linearly separable and also allows for a solution that is convex* ([Goodfellow et al., 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000131)). Convex solutions (as we will discuss later in more detail) are desirable because they have *global* minima and hence the algorithm will not get “stuck” in *local* minima. That is, an important implication of Mercer’s condition is that it establishes the convexity of the optimization problem for support vector machines and similar algorithms ([Mohri et al., 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000253)). Hence, a global minimum is assured in optimization.

To consolidate what the kernel trick does, it is helpful to remember the following:

> *Nonlinearly Separable Data in Original Data Space + Kernel Trick* = *Linearly Separable Data in the Feature Space*144

[Aggarwal (2015)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000005) summarizes the kernel trick concisely in the following way in relation to support vector machines; however, the following quote is applicable to a much broader set of statistical and machine learning methods well beyond SVMs:

> The kernel trick leverages the important observation that the SVM formulation can be fully solved in terms of dot products (or similarities) between pairs of data points. One does not need to know the feature values … all computations are performed in the original space and the actual transformation does not need to be known as long as the kernel similarity function is known.

### 2.49.1 When Are Kernel Methods Useful?

Based on the above discussion, it stands to reason that kernels are most useful when dealing with data that are not linearly separable in the data space. If we did not have the kernel trick at our disposal we would need to map the data to higher dimensions of nonlinearity, that is, *enlarge the feature space to account for the complexity of the data*. This can be time-consuming, complicated, and sometimes not even doable. By using a kernel transformation, we do not need to map the data to higher dimensions at all but instead can simply use the kernel trick, which essentially means computing kernels in the *original dimensionality* of the problem instead of trying to enlarge the feature space ourselves. Kernel functions are, in general, and as already emphasized, less concerned about the actual data than they are about how *similar* data points are to each other ([Alpaydin, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000009)).

Yet another way of conceptualizing kernels is that they can also be seen as a way to express or “encode” prior knowledge. Consider that if *x*[*i*] and *x*[*j*] are similar before applying a function to them, then it will generally imply that functions of those observations, *f*(*x*[*i*]) and *f*(*x*[*j*]) are also similar. Indeed, in many procedures, the specifying of the *kernel matrix* is essentially somewhat akin to specifying a kind of “Bayesian” *prior knowledge*.

## 2.50 Systems of Equations

Many problems in statistical modeling at their core reduce to solving systems of linear equations. What is a “system” in this respect? A system is simply a *set of equations* for which we are seeking a solution for the variables that will solve the set of equations *simultaneously*. The idea of a *set* here is, as the reader is already likely familiar, a collection of objects, the objects in this case being *equations*. The solution set for one set of linear equations consisting of two equations will likely be different from the solution set for those same two equations but with a third equation added to the set. Once again, *context matters*.

A simple example will suffice to demonstrate the principle of solving a set of linear equations. Consider the following two linear equations:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {4x\_{1} + 4x\_{2} = 5} \\\\ {2x\_{1} - 4x\_{2} = 1} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

When we plot these two equations, we obtain the linear system depicted in [Figure 2.15](#c2.xhtml#f2.15).145

![Figure 2.15 The solution set to the linear system is where the lines intersect.Return to text.⏎](images/fig2.15.jpg)

*Figure 2.15* The solution set to the linear system is where the lines intersect.[Return to text.⏎](#c2.xhtml#re_f2.15)

The *solution set* is where the *intersection* occurs between the two lines. A system of linear equations such as this can be solved using the technique of *Gaussian elimination*, where the matrix is reduced to what is known as *reduced row-echelon* form which allows one to easily see the solution. We do not review Gaussian elimination here due to space limitations but also because it is not terribly enlightening from an applied statistics point of view.

We can solve systems of linear equations in R quite easily. For example, consider the following two equations set up in R, where first we designate the two coefficients for *x*[1] and *x*[2] on the left-hand side of the equation:

```
> left_matrix <- matrix(c(5, 2, 4, 6), nrow=2)
> left_matrix
```

 
|  || \[,1\] || \[,2\] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \[1,\] || 5 || 4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \[2,\] || 2 || 6 |

Next, we define the *y* values on the right-hand side:

```
> right_matrix <- matrix(c(35, 36), nrow=2)
> right_matrix
```

 
|  || \[,1\] |
| --- | --- |
| \[1,\] || 35 |
| --- | --- |
| \[2,\] || 36 |

We next solve the equation:146

```
> solve(left_matrix, right_matrix)
```

 
|  || \[,1\] |
| --- | --- |
| \[1,\] || 3 |
| --- | --- |
| \[2,\] || 5 |

We can see that the solutions to the linear system are 3 and 5. That is, we have just solved the equations

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {5x\_{1} + 4x\_{2} = 35} \\\\ {2x\_{1} + 6x\_{2} = 36} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

for which when we substitute solutions *x*[1] = 3 and *x*[2] = 5 we obtain,

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {5\\left( 3 \\right) + 4\\left( 5 \\right) = 35} \\\\ {2\\left( 3 \\right) + 6\\left( 5 \\right) = 36} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

In Python, suppose we want to solve the following system of equations:

24a + 4b = 35

8a + 4b = 94

```
a = np.array([[24, 4], [8, 4]])
b = np.array([35, 94])
print(np.linalg.solve(a,b))
[-3.6875 30.875 ]
```

The solutions to the above equations are thus −3.6875 and 30.875.

There are a variety of methods useful for solving systems of linear equations, including the *elimination method*, *substitution method*, and *graphical method*. Regression analysis is an example of solving a system of equations when an exact solution is not achievable and hence an *approximation* is required, typically that of ordinary least-squares. The approximation is required as a result of there being too many equations to provide a unique solution. That is, the set of equations is *overdetermined*, meaning that there are too many equations because of the scatter of the data and as such many lines *could* be fit. However, we only wish to fit a single line, and that will mean approximating weights for *β*[0], the intercept, and *β*[1], the slope.

Many times when considering systems of equations, some equations will be a consequence of others. That is, one equation may reveal the same *information* as one or more other equations. For example, if two equations are scalar multiples of one another, then one equation, as previously discussed, essentially duplicates the “information” provided by the first. Such can be visually depicted by two lines taking up the same space (i.e., laying on top of each other). As an easy example, consider the following two equations:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, x\_{1} + x\_{2} = y} \\\\ {2x\_{1} + 2x\_{2} = 2y} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

Clearly, the second equation is simply a scalar multiple of the first and as such provides no new “information” to the system. As previously discussed in terms of vectors, the equations are said to be *linearly dependent*.147

Note that we have only surveyed linear equations above. What made them linear was that each term in the equation was raised to no power higher than one. For instance,

  
*x*[1] + *x*[2] = *y*  

only featured powers to *x*[1], *x*[2] and *y* equal to one. In contrast, the following is a *nonlinear* equation because at least one of the terms is raised to an exponent greater than one:

  
*x*[1]² + *x*[2] = *y*  

Many times in applied problems, systems of equations are *nonlinear*. *Newton’s method* is a classic algorithm used to solve nonlinear equations. For details, see [Hubbard and Hubbard (2002)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000161).

## 2.51 Distance

Virtually all statistical techniques are organizations and re-organizations of the distance metric in some capacity or another. Even the Pearson correlation coefficient can be conceived as a measure of distance between points (we challenge the reader to think about this).

The most common metric for distance is that of *Euclidean distance* given by

  
$$d\\left( O,P \\right) = \\sqrt{x\_{1}^{2} + x\_{2}^{2} + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot + x\_{p}^{2}}$$  
(2.111)

where *d* is the distance between origin *O* and *P*, where *x*[1]² through *x*[*p*]² are coordinates of observations. A strength of Euclidean distances is that they are *rotation-invariant*, which means that the straight-line distance between two points does not change with the orientation of the axis system ([Aggarwal, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000005)).

While Euclidean distance is what we typically think of when we consider distance, there are a host of definitions for distance, including *Minkowski*, *city-block (Manhattan)*, and many others. Distance metrics are especially useful in the technique of cluster analysis that seeks to generate *groups* (in some sense) of cases based on their similarity or distance from case to case. In the context of this and other methods, we will survey a number of distance measures throughout the book. Simple distances in Python can be computed using numpy.linalg.norm(a−b).

## 2.52 Projections and Basis

The projection likely already most familiar to the reader will undoubtedly be that of linear regression, where we take the vector *y*, generate a linear function, and project onto the span of *x* resulting in a new line called the *regression line* containing predicted values, *ŷ*. The fit of the regression line to the swarm of points is essentially as a result of projecting *y* onto the space “inhabited” by *x*. The residual is *y*[*i*] − *ŷ*.

When we speak of an *orthogonal projection*, this implies that for a subspace *S*, *y*[*i*] − *ŷ* is orthogonal to *S*. That is, the residual is perpendicular (orthogonal) to the space *S* “occupied” by the predictors (typically called the *column space*). Said differently, parameter estimates for the regression (which then generate *ŷ*) are chosen so that the residual vector *y*[*i*] − *ŷ* is orthogonal to the space “generated” by the predictors in the model ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)).

The orthogonality, coupled with the Pythagorean theorem, further implies that we can decompose the squared norms of these objects in the following manner,148

  
||*y*[*i*]|| ²\= ||*ŷ*||[2]+||*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*||²  
(2.112)

or more generally for arbitrary observed and fitted vectors where *v̂* is the more general fitted value of the vector and *ŷ* above only a special case:

  
||*v*|| ²\= ||*v̂*||[2]+||*v*−*v̂*||²  
(2.113)

The above identities are important, as they essentially describe what occurs in regression and ANOVA; that is, the total sums of squares can be broken down into that due to treatment and that due to error ([Marden, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000239), p. 89). The “treatment variation” is represented by ||*v̂*||² while the error is given by ||*v*−*v̂*||².

In *principal components analysis*, the goal will be to obtain a subspace onto which we also project observed data onto that subspace. The projected data are *principal component scores* and the new coordinates from which that data are projected are the new *basis vectors*. The original basis, or *canonical basis* as it is sometimes called, are the original coordinates at a right angle. For example, in ℝ³, the standard basis vectors are the following:

  
$$e\_{1} = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} 1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack,e\_{2} = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} 0 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack,e\_{3} = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} 0 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1 \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  

The axes of the standard basis or any other basis need not be at right angles ([Hubbard & Hubbard, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000161)). That is, there is no *absolute* requirement that the above vectors *e*[1], *e*[2], *e*[3] be at right angles, *ontologically*. Historically, and for most problems, the decision to have bases at right angles is very much due to *convenience*. Descartes’ invention of the Cartesian coordinate system in the 17th century allowed algebra to be expressed geometrically where each axis was set perpendicular or orthogonal to one another. Pierre de Fermat (1607–1665) discovered the same coordinate system although his work was published only after his death, and hence Descartes is typically associated with the traditional coordinate system we know today. A mathematician by the name of John Wallis (1616–1703) was one of the first to conceive of the possibility of negative coordinates ([Tanton, 2005](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000352)). Not starting off with pairwise orthogonality of basis vectors would complicate problems tremendously and hence like many other things in mathematics, it is convenient to start with the assumption or constraint of orthogonality of canonical vectors in many cases. It is a convenient and natural starting point to many problems, and indeed, to much of mathematics in general.

The new basis vectors in the case of principal components are *eigenvectors* and possess favorable properties from which the projection is made. Hence, PCA is often regarded at a technical level as a *change of basis* methodology from which we project new scores. It is also generally regarded as a *dimension-reduction technique*, but this dimension reduction “happens” through a change of basis.

## 2.53 The Meaning of Linearity

The word *linear* is perhaps the most common word used in all statistics and machine learning. But what does linear mean, exactly? A linear transformation *T*, as already discussed, is a mapping from ℝ^(*n*) to ℝ^(*m*) such that the following holds for scalars *a* and vectors *x* and *y*:149

  
*T*(*x*+*y*) = *T*(*x*) + *T*(*y*)  
(2.114)

and

  
*T*(*a**x*) = *a**T*(*x*)  
(2.115)

That is, linear transformations are said to *preserve* vector addition and scalar multiplication. Linear transformations, when viewed from a geometrical point of view, are an example of an *affine transformation*. Affine transformations and associated geometry also preserve such things as ratios of distances between points. For example, transforming degrees Celsius into degrees Fahrenheit is an example of an affine transformation because the relative change between say, 10 degrees and 20 degrees Celsius is preserved when we transform to Fahrenheit:

  
^∘*C* = ((^∘*F*)−32)(5/9)  

If one draws the corresponding plot, one will see that the relationship between degrees Celcius and Fahrenheit is indeed linear and the ratios of distances are preserved.

Linear transformations in R and Python are very simple to execute. For example, in Python, suppose we want to determine the aforementioned temperature in Celsius corresponding to a temperature of 32.0 Fahrenheit:

```
F = 32.0
(F-32)*(5/9)
Out[16]: 0.0
```

or, for a temperature of F = 0, we have

```
F = 0
(F-32)*(5/9)
Out[18]: -17.77777777777778
```

## 2.54 Basis and Dimension

We have already discussed informally the nature of a basis. We now put the concept on a formal footing. *A basis is a set of linearly independent vectors in a vector space that spans the space*. Conceptually, a basis essentially provides a “frame of reference” for vectors in a subspace. The dimension of a basis is the number of linearly independent vectors in the given set making up the basis. More formally, a basis is a *maximum linearly independent set* such that if we added one more vector, the set would cease to be linearly independent. That is, if there exists a basis with *n* vectors in a vector space, then there cannot be a basis with more than *n* vectors in that vector space (since by definition, a basis is the *maximum* linearly independent set). This last result is a consequence of the *Steinitz exchange lemma* ([Stillwell, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000349)). Equivalently, a basis is a minimal spanning set such that if we dropped a vector, it would no longer span the given subspace ([Hubbard & Hubbard, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000161)).150

### 2.54.1 Orthogonal Basis

Recall that the canonical basis vectors of the coordinate system generate an *orthogonal basis*, and that since each of the vector’s lengths is equal to 1, it is simultaneously an *orthonormal basis*. In many procedures, the goal is to generate an orthogonal basis from one that may not already be orthogonal. This is a very powerful idea that actually accounts for how many statistical methods operate “under the hood” so to speak.

The *Gram-Schmidt process* is an algorithm used in linear algebra for finding an orthogonal basis. The details of the procedure are not enlightening from an applied point of view. For mathematical details on the approach, see virtually any good introductory linear algebra text (e.g., [Anton & Rorres, 2000](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000013)). The Gram-Schmidt process implies that *if you have a finite inner product space, an orthonormal basis can be constructed in that space* ([Garcia & Horn, 2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000122)). Such a result will serve us well when we survey methods such as principal components analysis, where, as already mentioned, the goal will be to establish a new set of basis vectors with special properties and from which to project the observed data. Principal components analysis is essentially a (linear) transformation of the data onto a new basis. That is, it generates new coordinates from which to visualize and interpret the original data.

The very concept or general idea of a basis can also be made much simpler. Moving away from matrices and eigenvectors, and as a helpful imperfect analogy, consider the “basis” on which numbers are computed. For example, expressing the number 0.5 is relative to one basis (i.e., “frame of reference”), while expressing it as ½ is relative to another ([Hubbard & Hubbard, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000161)).
