The package *nlme* (Pinheiro et al., [2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000289)) can also be used to fit mixed models, as well as the *VCA* package ([Schuetzenmeister and Dufey, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000330)). R’s capacity to fit increasingly complex mixed models is virtually unlimited using these and related packages in R.

## 4.4 Multilevel Modeling

The standard linear model typically estimated by least-squares regression is appropriate for independent observations, which implies that errors will also typically be *independent*. That is, it is assumed that *ε*[*i*], *ε*[*i*′] are independent for *i* ≠ *i*′. The standard linear model is usually not appropriate, or at minimum severely *compromised*, when this assumption is violated.

One type of dependency that naturally arises in applied settings is that of *clustering*, where *ε*[*i*], *ε*[*i*′] are not independent for *i* ≠ *i*′. A classic example of where this type of clustering or dependency surfaces is in classrooms within a school, where students may share the same teacher. We say *students are nested within classrooms*. It would be unreasonable to expect that errors within classrooms are *not* related. However, this is only one potential source of nesting in the hierarchy that we may consider. Classrooms exist in schools, and schools exist in states. That is, schools within the same state, *and their errors*, are likely not independent of one another. As we build the nesting hierarchy from scores to groups, we develop a *multilevel structure to observations*, thus the name *multilevel modeling*. Multilevel modeling allows one to deal with the non-independence of errors that manifest at each level of the hierarchy.

### 4.4.1 A Garbled Mess of Jargon

The jargon and confusion of words and terminology that surrounds random, mixed, and multilevel modeling is nothing short of extraordinary. Historically, statistics is a discipline that has always had a difficult time having consistency in how it defines its terms because many concepts arise independently in different applied disciplines. Mixed models may arise independently in ecology, for instance, while also being developed (or “rediscovered”) in sociology as well. Slightly different names may be given to the models, which makes learning (and teaching) them very difficult for the newcomer. It’s as if in addition to learning the rather difficult method one has to become keen on how the *vocabulary* differs by area of specialization. This not only applies to mixed models, it applies to many statistical techniques; jargon can easily ruin your day in attempting to learn them.

It is exceptionally important however when discussing these models to be very exact and precise regarding what we are referring to. Multilevel models are often casually referred to as *hierarchical linear models*, *random-effects models*, *mixed models*, and other identifiers, and it can become greatly confusing for the newcomer to these models to appreciate or understand what these models are all about beyond these generalities.205

First, we need to make a distinction between *structure* vs. *model*. The term “multilevel” is a *structure*, it is not actually a “model,” though it is referred to as such in the literature (i.e., *multilevel modeling*), for reasons that will become clear shortly. It is best to reserve the word “multilevel” to describe structure, though in what follows we ourselves at times adopt the conventional phrase “multilevel modeling” as well and make no distinction. So long as one understands and appreciates the distinction, no harm is done. However, to the newcomer to multilevel models, a great deal of confusion can arise from not understanding what a *structure* is compared to a *model*. As we will see, multilevel structures can be analyzed in a host of different ways, only one of which is via random and mixed effects.

Second, *a multilevel structure need not necessarily imply a mixed model, nor does a multilevel structure need to incorporate any random effects*. They *usually* do include such random effects, but the definition of what is a multilevel (structure) does not absolutely require it. In reading the literature, however, the newcomer to these models is rarely made aware of this. Multilevel models are automatically assumed to consist of random effects. This implied association is not a necessary one. *As we will see, for a multilevel model to have one or more random effects (other than the naturally occurring error terms), this must be assumed or imposed by the researcher*. *No multilevel structure, by itself, necessarily implies or must otherwise contain random effects*.

As an example, consider the classic case once more of ten students per classroom in which there are five classrooms. Students are nested within classrooms, as students in one classroom will likely share features or common experiences over students in another classroom. They will be more *similar* than students in a competing classroom. Statistically, error terms of students within classroom will not be independent of one another. *We can assume their errors will be correlated*. In practice, if we desired, we could account for the multilevel *structure* by calculating separate regressions on each classroom. We could then compare the regressions by way of computing a product term that incorporates classroom. Notice that there is no random effect implied here and yet we are dealing with the multilevel structure just the same. *The multilevel structure is still intact without requiring any random effects*. It may not be the most “ideal” of solutions in modeling the multilevel structure, but the point is that addressing the multilevel structure does not *necessarily* imply, nor require, the modeling of random effects.

The purest or most accurate definition of a multilevel model often given or implied in the literature is that it *allows for residual analyses at each level of the hierarchy*. And while this is true, there is nothing in a multilevel *structure* that absolutely requires this level of analysis. The emphasis should be on “allows” in the previous phrase, not “necessitates.” Again, notice that we could quite easily analyze each regression or mean structure separately by classroom and assess residuals within each classroom. We do not *require* any random effects to do so. Including random effects, however, is often a very good idea, as we now discuss.

### 4.4.2 Why Do Multilevel Models Often Include Random Effects?

If a multilevel *structure* by itself does not necessarily imply the inclusion of random effects, how do random effects therefore come to rise in a multilevel model? The answer is that the researcher has to *impose* them on the multilevel structure through an assumption of the modeling. Take note again that *we are imposing the random effect(s); they are not necessarily implied in the multilevel structure*. Again, and referring to our previous example, *observed variance in intercepts or slopes in exploratory analysis of data cannot serve as justification alone to model such as random effects*.

To emphasize this important point, consider an excellent description of multilevel modeling by one of the chief leaders in this area:206

> *Given that the intercept and slope coefficients vary randomly over group …*

The above is completely correct, but what does it mean? The key point to recognize from the above is that it is *us* who decides whether such coefficients “vary randomly” or not. The fact that there is *observed variation* in them is not enough. We have to decide to model the intercept and slope as fixed or random based on the *assumptions* we are imposing on the model. If there is no observed variation, we probably would not model them as random effects, but in theory, we still could.

Consider another typical presentation of the multilevel model:

> *Because multilevel models contain a mix of fixed effects and random effects, they are sometimes known as mixed-effects models.*

The problem with the above is that, as mentioned, not only do multilevel structures *not* necessarily require the inclusion of random effects, but that even if they did, they do not *need* to be modeled using a *traditional* mixed-effects modeling approach. A structural equation modeling approach, for instance, could be just as fruitful. Once more, *a multilevel structure does not necessarily imply a fixed, random, or mixed model*.

In summary then, the intercepts and slopes typically found in hierarchical (or “nested” designs) do not know where they “came from.” We have to make those decisions as part of the assumptions we are imposing on our analysis. In writings about multilevel models, authors too often imply that because there is observed variation in intercepts and slopes, it necessarily implies the corresponding effect should be modeled as a random effect. This is simply not the case. Observed variation in statistics, whatever they may be (e.g., intercepts, slopes, means, standard deviations, etc.), is insufficient reason for modeling such as random effects. The decision to model as a random effect has all to do with how the observed realizations are *conceptualized to have originated and how such statistics would likely behave in theoretical repetitions of the experiment*. These are decisions made by the investigator.

> *A multilevel structure does not necessarily imply the presence of random effects. Random effects arise in such structures because the researcher decides to model them (intercepts and slopes) as such, but a multilevel structure need not necessarily imply the inclusion of these effects. Intercepts and slopes could, in theory, even when exhibiting much variation, be estimated as fixed effects.*

### 4.4.3 A Priori vs. Post-Hoc “Nesting”

There is another important and key distinction to make with regard to multilevel ideas and nesting. In appreciating what a multilevel structure actually *is*, it is just as pedagogical to consider what a multilevel structure is *not*. Consider the classic one-way randomized analysis of variance design in which participants (*n* = 5 per sample, e.g., *y*[11] is observation 1 in sample 1) are randomly assigned to treatments (Figure 4.3).207

![Figure 4.3 Classic one-way randomized analysis of variance layout. Each sample is drawn from the same population and observations are randomly assigned to different treatments.Return to text.⏎](images/fig4.3.jpg)

*Figure 4.3* Classic one-way randomized analysis of variance layout. Each sample is drawn from the same population and observations are randomly assigned to different treatments.Return to text.⏎

Are participants nested within treatment groups? Are the errors within treatment groups expected to be related? *No*. Because of the random assignment to treatment groups, an individual’s score *a priori* is not expected to be related to any other individual’s score. Why is the qualifier “*a priori*” essential here? It is important because *after they undergo treatment*, we might indeed observe their errors to be related. For example, if being in the first treatment group involves ingesting a particular dosage of an energy drink, whereas other groups did not receive any energy drink, we would of course expect errors to be related within that first group *relative to other groups*. Those drinking energy drinks will become more “similar” due to the treatment they have received. They are now a “nest” due to receiving the treatment.

However, the above similarity is only apparent *after* the treatment has been administered, not *before*. Before receiving treatment, there was no reason to expect that the score of one participant would be related to the score (and error) of a second participant within that group. Participants in this case are not nested *a priori*, but once the treatment is applied, they are, in a sense, nested *post-hoc*. But this *post-hoc* nesting idea is immaterial to multilevel modeling. It would only play a role if we decided to build on the current study to perform a second one and used the treatment groups as starting points. In such a case, those drinking energy drinks would start out the new study having correlated errors. That is, those receiving the treatment would be more “alike” compared to others not receiving the treatment.

The key takeaway from this discussion is that for hierarchical, multilevel, or nesting structures to exist, errors should be *expected* to be related *prior* to receiving treatment, not *after*. Students in a classroom being taught by the same teacher are *expected* to have related errors well before they receive any treatment or intervention. This is the “likeness” that we wish to account for in multilevel structures. While the classic one-way ANOVA (for instance) can actually be considered a multilevel structure (the reader may want to think of how), the errors within each treatment group are expected to be *independent* even if they become correlated once the treatment is applied and measurement occurs. What is most important for modeling decisions such as this is the *expectation* of how errors will behave *prior* to treatment, not *after*.

### 4.4.4 Blocking as an Example of Hierarchical/Multilevel Structure

When a researcher forces observations into blocks, the so-called *randomized block design*, this is an example and special case of a multilevel structure. *Observations are nested within blocks*. The nesting is *induced* or *created* by the researcher. For instance, if we put all first-grade school 208children in one block and all second graders in another block, it stands that observations within each respective block will be more similar than observations across blocks. The observations are level-one units, while the blocks are level two. For this reason, blocking designs are often analyzed as mixed models where the blocking factor is regarded as random. For readers to whom blocking designs may be entirely new, [Kirk (1995)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000187) provides a good and deep introduction.

### 4.4.5 Nonparametric Random-Effects Model

Most multilevel models include at least one random effect that aids in dealing with the nesting structure and dependencies of observations. In the classic random-effects model, it is assumed that random effects are normally distributed. This assumption, however, may be untenable and we may wish to adopt instead, as we will be doing in many places in this book, a *nonparametric* approach that makes no (or at least *fewer*) assumptions about the distribution of the random effects. The *nonparametric random-effects model* can be considered a special case of the wider *latent class model*. The random-effects regression model is also commonly known as a *mixture model in regression* since it combines a mixture of regressions that helps deal with the potential heterogeneity of groups ([Jiang and Guntuboyina, 2021](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000172)).

As an easy example of a nonparametric random-effects model and to get an idea of how it differs from the classic parametric random-effects model, consider first the typical (parametric) random-intercept model that contains no predictors,

  
*g*\[*E*(*y*[*i**j*])\] = *α*[*j*]  

where it is assumed that the intercept terms *α*[*j*] are normally distributed with a given mean and variance, that is, *α*[*j*] ∼ *N*(*μ*,*σ*²). Traditionally, we would like to estimate the mean *μ* of these intercepts and more importantly their variance (*σ*²). The approach is *parametric* because we are imposing a *probability model* on the intercepts. In a nonparametric approach, we assume that the distribution of *α*[*j*] is indexed by an unspecified discrete mixing distribution of *latent classes*, where the intercept associated with a given class *x* is denoted by *α*[*x*]and the size of the given class is given by *P*(*x*), where *α*[*x*] is the location and *P*(*x*) the “weight” of the given node or class.

Simplified, the nonparametric model is given by

  
*g*\[*E*(*y*[*i**j*]|,*x*)\] = *α*[*x*]  
(4.15)

which is simply the expectation of *y*[*i**j*] for a given class *x*, which will be subject to *P*(*x*). A two-level model in which predictors are included is a natural extension of (4.15), where now *z*[*i**j*] denotes the inclusion of predictors into the model:

  
$$g\\left\\lbrack E\\left( y\_{ij} \\middle| z\_{ij},x \\right) \\right\\rbrack = \\alpha\_{x} + {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{\\beta\_{k} \\cdot z\_{ijk}}}$$  
(4.16)

Key to note is that what makes the model nonparametric is not the inclusion of predictors in *z*[*i**j*], but as was the case in the intercept-only model, the fact that *y*[*i**j*] is a function of a mixing distribution of classes, *x*. To reiterate, *E*(*y*[*i**j*]) is a function of a *probability distribution* in the classic parametric model, whereas it is a function of a *mixing distribution* (classes) in the nonparametric counterpart. Random slopes, in addition to random intercepts, can also be included, giving rise to a full-scale *multilevel nonparametric random-effects model*.209

Multilevel models, as was generally the case for mixed models, are best implemented using R (e.g., *lme4*) software instead of Python. *Latent Gold* is a software program that can estimate latent class models and the special case of nonparametric random-effects models. In R, the package *npmlreg* ([Einbeck et al., 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000095)) can be used to fit these types of models as well.

## 4.5 Repeated-Measures and Longitudinal Models

Often in research studies, measurements are taken over a series of days, weeks, months, or years, or even *epochs*, as in the case of attempting to estimate whether today’s rising temperatures are just normal long-term temperature variation versus human-made climate change. Models that involve a temporal component are often called *repeated-measures models* or *within-subjects designs*, or, more generally, *longitudinal models or time series*. The reader should be aware, however, that longitudinal models can comprise a whole host of models and complexities which can include mixed-effects components as well as elements of structural equation models. As noted earlier, jargon and terminology are often not consistent from discipline to discipline, and hence it behooves the reader to be cautious when coming across these and similar terms to learn exactly what the author or researcher means by them. Making assumptions as to what they mean will typically only lead to misunderstandings!

### 4.5.1 Classic Repeated-Measures Models

For lack of a better terminology, and to differentiate among repeated-measures approaches, we will refer to the repeated measures that typically assumes a *sphericity structure* for the covariance matrix to be that of *classic repeated measures*. The assumption of sphericity is essentially that of equal variances among differences between all possible pairs of within-subject conditions. An even more stringent assumption is that of *compound symmetry* that assumes all variances and covariances in the matrix of within-subject variables are equal. Both of these assumptions give rise to what we are calling the “classic” repeated-measures model to distinguish it from more sophisticated models such as random-effects, mixed-effects, and structural equation longitudinal models and growth curves. *Latent growth models* are a sub-type of the more general *structural equation model* in which the latent variables are typically such things as intercepts and slopes that “give rise” to time points.

Just as we did for classic ANOVA, we assume the reader has had at least some exposure to basic repeated measures under the assumption of a spherical covariance matrix. Hence, we move quickly and simply provide the expected mean squares for the classic model. There is a lot of theory and explanation that goes along with these expected mean squares and for readers unfamiliar, [Hays (1994)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000149) and [Denis (2021a)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000087) are good sources that explain how these expected mean squares arise, including how MS residual is a function of the intraclass coefficient *ρ* below.

The expected mean squares for the classic additive “sphericity” repeated-measures model are thus:210

  
*E*(MS subjects) = *σ*[*e*]² + *K**σ*[*s**u**b**j**e**c**t**s*]²  
(4.17)

  
$$E\\left( \\text{MS}\\,\\text{treatment} \\right) = \\sigma\_{e}^{2} + \\frac{J{\\sum\\limits\_{j}\\alpha\_{j}^{2}}}{K - 1}$$  
(4.18)

  
*E*(MS residual) = *σ*[*e*]² = *σ*[*T*]²(1−*ρ*)  
(4.19)

where *J* is the number of rows for subjects, *K* is the number of columns for treatment, *ρ* is the intraclass coefficient, and *σ*[*T*]² and *σ*[*e*]² are the total and error variances, respectively.

There are numerous ways of fitting repeated-measures models in R. The function aov() in R has easy capabilities for fitting such models (see [Denis, 2021a](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000087) for details). Many packages are also devoted to fitting repeated-measures or longitudinal models, for example the *mmrm* package ([Sabanes et al., 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000318)). Repeated-measures models can also be fit in a variety of ways in Python. Probably the easiest way is via statsmodels using AnovaRM. The following is sample code (output not shown) for a basic one-way repeated measures where the dependent variable is y, the subject variable is person, and the repeated measure is time:

```
from statsmodels.stats.anova import AnovaRM
print(AnovaRM(data=df, depvar=‘y’, subject=‘person’, within=[‘time’]).fit())
```

## 4.6 Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA)

Univariate ANOVA allows for more than a single independent variable or factor but only allows for a single response or dependent variable. The name *univariate* derives from this fact, that of a single response. When there exists more than a single response variable, we enter into *multivariate* territory. Multivariate analysis of variance, or “MANOVA” for short, is defined by having more than a single continuous response variable.

The multivariate hypothesis about mean vectors can be stated as follows,

  
$$H\_{0}:\\left( \\begin{array}{l} \\mu\_{11} \\\\ \\mu\_{21} \\\\ \\mu\_{31} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ \\mu\_{j1} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right) = \\left( \\begin{array}{l} \\mu\_{12} \\\\ \\mu\_{22} \\\\ \\mu\_{32} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ \\mu\_{j2} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right) = \\left( \\begin{array}{l} \\mu\_{13} \\\\ \\mu\_{23} \\\\ \\mu\_{33} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ \\mu\_{j3} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right)... = \\left( \\begin{array}{l} \\mu\_{1p} \\\\ \\mu\_{2p} \\\\ \\mu\_{3p} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ \\mu\_{jp} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right)$$  
(4.20)

which is evaluated against an alternative hypothesis that somewhere among the set of mean vectors is a difference, for example of one possibility, that of a mean vector difference between the first two groups (inequality statement is slightly informal here),211

  
$$H\_{1}:\\left( \\begin{array}{l} \\mu\_{11} \\\\ \\mu\_{21} \\\\ \\mu\_{31} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ \\mu\_{j1} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right) \\neq \\left( \\begin{array}{l} \\mu\_{12} \\\\ \\mu\_{22} \\\\ \\mu\_{32} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ \\mu\_{j2} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right) = \\left( \\begin{array}{l} \\mu\_{13} \\\\ \\mu\_{23} \\\\ \\mu\_{33} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ \\mu\_{j3} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right)... = \\left( \\begin{array}{l} \\mu\_{1p} \\\\ \\mu\_{2p} \\\\ \\mu\_{3p} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ {\\,\\, \\cdot} \\\\ \\mu\_{jp} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right)$$  
(4.21)

### 4.6.1 Suitability of MANOVA

When is it appropriate to perform a MANOVA over an ANOVA? The answer cannot simply be “when there is more than a single continuous response,” despite misleading cookbook approaches to data analysis sometimes advising on such a poor strategy. Indeed, analyzing sex differences on response variables IQ and amount of gasoline consumed in one’s vehicle in the past week would make little sense for the reason that the response “variate,” that is, the combination of variables on the response side, makes little if any substantive “sense.” Can it be analyzed? Yes, but on an applied level, is not a hypothesis we would likely be interested in. The key to MANOVA is not to analyze multiple responses simultaneously; it is to analyze multiple responses that in some sense “go together” to produce a *variate*. Simultaneous analysis of reading speed and grade point average would be a variate of more interest in an applied setting. Or, another example might be skull measurements as a function of prehistoric epoch ([Anderson, 2003](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000011)). The takeaway point is that when one combines multiple responses into a single model, one should have a *reason* for doing so over and above simply producing a multivariate model.

With that substantive rationale and caveat in place, there are *statistical* benefits to conducting a MANOVA over multiple ANOVAs, which include control over an inflating type I error rate. For instance, three different univariate ANOVAs conducted separately carries an increasingly large type I error rate (e.g., 0.05 per test, *p* = 0.05). The probability of making *no type I errors* (*r* = 0) across *n* = 3 tests each set at 0.05 is a binomial random variable,

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, p\\left( r \\right) = \\left( \\begin{array}{l} n \\\\ r \\\\ \\end{array} \\right)p^{r}\\left( 1 - p \\right){n - r}} \\\\ {p\\left( 0,3,0.05 \\right) = \\left( \\begin{array}{l} 3 \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\end{array} \\right)\\left( 0.05 \\right)0\\left( 0.95 \\right)3 = 0.86} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(4.22)

and hence the probability of at least one type I error is equal to 1 − 0.86 = 0.14. More formally, the probability of *at least one type I error* across *k*\-tests can be approximated by

  
*p*(*t**y**p**e*  *I*  *e**r**r**o**r*≥1) = 1 − (1−*α*[*P**C*])^(*k*)  
(4.23)

A single MANOVA on the three response variables conducted simultaneously keeps the type I error rate fixed at whatever *α*is set to for the MANOVA (e.g., 0.05). This is a *statistical* benefit to performing a MANOVA over several ANOVAs; however, if substantively the MANOVA does not make sense, as discussed, a MANOVA model makes no sense to conduct for statistical reasons alone. *The scientific or substantive rationale should dominate over the statistical here*.

### 4.6.2 Extending the Univariate Model: Hotelling’s T²

The easiest and most direct way of extending the univariate model to the multivariate one is via the simple between-subjects *t*\-test and generalization to Hotelling’s *T* ², which is the multivariate counterpart where we model more than a single continuous response variable. This essentially will generalize to more complex models, but we focus on the *t*\-test because it emphasizes the core principles in going from a univariate to multivariate landscape.

Recall the univariate *t*\-test discussed earlier in our review of essential statistics:212

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {t = \\frac{E\\left( {\\overline{y}}\_{1} \\right) - E\\left( {\\overline{y}}\_{2} \\right) - \\delta\_{0}}{\\sqrt{\\frac{\\left( n\_{1} - 1 \\right)s\_{1}^{2} + \\left( n\_{2} - 1 \\right)s\_{2}^{2}}{n\_{1} - n\_{2} - 2}\\left( {\\frac{1}{n\_{1}} + \\frac{1}{n\_{2}}} \\right)}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\, = \\frac{\\mu\_{1} - \\mu\_{2} - \\delta\_{0}}{\\sqrt{\\frac{\\left( n\_{1} - 1 \\right)s\_{1}^{2} + \\left( n\_{2} - 1 \\right)s\_{2}^{2}}{n\_{1} - n\_{2} - 2}\\left( {\\frac{1}{n\_{1}} + \\frac{1}{n\_{2}}} \\right)}}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

Consider now what happens when we square *t*,

  
$$t^{2} = \\frac{\\left( {\\overline{y}}\_{1} - {\\overline{y}}\_{2} \\right)^{2}}{\\frac{\\left( n\_{1} - 1 \\right)s\_{1}^{2} + \\left( n\_{2} - 1 \\right)s\_{2}^{2}}{n\_{1} - n\_{2} - 2}\\left( {\\frac{1}{n\_{1}} + \\frac{1}{n\_{2}}} \\right)}$$  

Next, we express the denominator as an inverse so that there is no denominator:

  
$$t^{2} = \\left( {\\overline{y}}\_{1} - {\\overline{y}}\_{2} \\right)\\left\\lbrack {\\frac{\\left( n\_{1} - 1 \\right)s\_{1}^{2} + \\left( n\_{2} - 1 \\right)s\_{2}^{2}}{n\_{1} - n\_{2} - 2}\\left\\lbrack {\\frac{1}{n\_{1}} + \\frac{1}{n\_{2}}} \\right\\rbrack} \\right\\rbrack^{- 1}\\left( {\\overline{y}}\_{1} - {\\overline{y}}\_{2} \\right)$$  

Finally, we end up with

  
$$T^{2} = \\frac{n\_{1}n\_{2}}{n\_{1} + n\_{2}}\\left( {\\overline{y}}\_{1} - {\\overline{y}}\_{2} \\right)'\\left( S^{- 1} \\right)\\left( {\\overline{y}}\_{1} - {\\overline{y}}\_{2} \\right)$$  
(4.24)

For the one-sample mean vector, the corresponding *T*² is the following:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {T^{2} = \\left( \\overline{y} - \\mu\_{0} \\right)'\\left( {\\frac{1}{n}S} \\right)^{- 1}\\left( \\overline{y} - \\mu\_{0} \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = n\\left( \\overline{y} - \\mu\_{0} \\right)'S^{- 1}\\left( \\overline{y} - \\mu\_{0} \\right)} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(4.25)

*T*² is distributed as $\\frac{\\left( n - 1 \\right)p}{\\left( n - p \\right)}F\_{p,n - p}$, where *p* and *n* − *p* are degrees of freedom, where *p* is the number of variables and *n* is sample size. For details on likelihood ratio tests in relation to *T*², see Johnson and Wichern ([2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173), pp. 217–218). Confidence regions can also be computed for *T*² and multivariate populations (see Johnson & Wicher, [2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173), pp. 220–221).

### 4.6.3 Multivariate Test Statistics

In the univariate ANOVA setting, there is only a single *F*\-test to perform. In the multivariate setting, because of the alternative way covariances of response variables may be structured within groups on the independent variable(s), multiple multivariate tests have been developed and are available in virtually all software. These include *Wilk’s lambda*, *Pillai’s trace*, *Roy’s largest root*, and the *Lawley-Hotelling’s trace*. We provide only a cursory “glimpse” into the variety of multivariate tests. For a full development of how these tests come about, see [Johnson and Wichern (2007)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173).213

Wilk’s lambda, *Λ*, is given by

  
$$\\Lambda = \\frac{\\left| E \\right|}{\\left| H + E \\right|} = \\frac{\\left| E \\right|}{\\left| T \\right|}$$  
(4.26)

where under the null hypothesis,

  
$$\\Lambda = \\frac{\\left| E \\right|}{\\left| 0 + E \\right|} = \\frac{\\left| E \\right|}{\\left| E \\right|} = 1.0$$  

and where *H* is the “hypothesis” matrix and *E* the “error” matrix. Note that Wilk’s is an *inverse criterion*, meaning that if there is no effect, we would expect *Λ* to equal 1.0. This is unlike the *F-*ratio in univariate ANOVA, where larger F’s are preferred over smaller.

On the opposite extreme, if *H* accounts for all of the variation, then,

  
$$\\Lambda = \\frac{\\left| 0 \\right|}{\\left| H + 0 \\right|} = \\frac{\\left| 0 \\right|}{\\left| H \\right|} = 0$$  

Wilk’s lambda can also be expressed in terms of eigenvalues of *E*^( − 1)*H*:

  
$$\\Lambda = {\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{s}\\frac{1}{1 + \\lambda\_{i}}}$$  
(4.27)

where *λ*[*i*] are the eigenvalues extracted from the analysis.

Pillai’s trace is defined as

  
$$V^{(s)} = {tr}\\left\\lbrack {\\left( E + H \\right)^{- 1}H} \\right\\rbrack = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{s}\\frac{\\lambda\_{i}}{1 + \\lambda\_{i}}}$$  
(4.28)

Note that Pillai’s uses all eigenvalues (often called “roots”), *λ*[*i*]. If we use only the *largest* of these roots, this gives rise to *Roy’s largest root*. That is, Roy’s largest root is simply the largest eigenvalue extracted and hence represents only the largest dimension underlying the data. Roy’s largest root is especially useful if one dimension dominates all others, which translates into one eigenvalue being much larger than the others. When the distribution of eigenvalues is more spread out, Pillai’s is more appropriate since presumably more than a single dimension is of interest.

Lastly, Lawley-Hotelling’s trace is simply a sum of eigenvalues and is thus given by

  
$$U^{(s)} = \\text{tr}\\left( E^{- 1}H \\right) = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{s}\\lambda\_{i}}$$  
(4.29)

### 4.6.4 Evaluating Equality of Covariance Matrices: The Box-M Test

Recall that in univariate ANOVA, we were required to evaluate the assumption that all variances were equal. In the multivariate counterpart, we not only have variances to deal with; we also have *covariances*. Hence, the assumption now includes that all covariances across levels (or cells) of the independent variable are equal, that is,214

  
*H*[0]: *Σ*[1] = *Σ*[2] = *Σ*[3]... = *Σ*[*p*]  
(4.30)

where *Σ*[*p*] are the *p* covariance matrices for each population under levels of the independent variable.

There are different approaches to evaluating this assumption. One is simply a crude (yet still useful) visual approach to learn whether the covariance matrices are relatively similar to one another to deem their population counterparts at least approximately equal and proceed with the MANOVA. The *Box-M test* is another approach that evaluates this assumption and is available in R in the *biotools* package ([da Silva, 2021](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000075)) under the boxM test, which can be easily demonstrated directly from the package on the iris data:

```
> library(biotools)
> data(iris)
> boxM(iris[, -5], iris[, 5])
Box M-test for Homogeneity of Covariance Matrices
data: iris[, -5]
Chi-Sq (approx.) = 140.94, df = 20, p-value < 2.2e-16
```

The assumption under the null is that population covariance matrices are equal. For these data, we reject the null (*p* = 2.2e-16) and infer the alternative hypothesis that at least two covariance matrices differ. When covariance matrices differ, it behooves the researcher to have a look at such matrices and to consider substantive reasons as to why they may differ. *Never obtain a statistical result without carefully considering what it might imply about your data on a scientific, not only statistical, level*. For additional theory on the test, see [Johnson and Wichern (2007)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173).

### 4.6.5 MANOVA in Python

We can conduct a basic MANOVA in Python using statsmodels. In the following we conduct a MANOVA on some random data where we generate 20 samples (n\_samples = 20) on five responses (n\_dim = 5) with three levels on an independent variable (n\_classes = 3):

```
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.multivariate.manova import MANOVA
n_samples = 20
n_dim = 5
n_classes = 3
```

We produce the random data using np.random.randn() where X is the independent variable (or “exogenous” variable) side of the equation and y the response variable (or “endogenous” variable):

```
y = np.random.randn(n_samples, n_dim)
X = np.random.randint(n_classes, size=n_samples)
```

Note that the number of classes for X (i.e., 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, etc.) is designated to equal the size of the n\_samples specified in y, so that each case gets assigned a class (we print only a few cases for y):215

```
y
Out[31]:
array([[-0.68321194, -1.17229168, 0.86179734, 1.26790702, 0.53352012],
  [-0.95366322, -1.06883607, 1.13404045, -0.71916984, -1.37089659],
  [ 0.18602881, -0.22453474, 0.02700791, 0.17279279, 0.13939027],
  [-1.45080321, -0.20265485, 0.57581133, -0.39974093, 0.93340395],
X
Out[33]: array([0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0])
```

In the following we specify the endogenous variable (i.e., the *response* variable) as well as the exogenous variable (the *independent* variable):

```
manova = MANOVA(endog=y, exog=X)
print(manova.mv_test())
```

 
| x0 || Value || Num DF || Den DF || F Value || Pr > F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wilks’ lambda || 0.7224 || 5.0000 || 15.0000 || 1.1526 || 0.3765 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pillai’s trace || 0.2776 || 5.0000 || 15.0000 || 1.1526 || 0.3765 |
| Hotelling-Lawley trace || 0.3842 || 5.0000 || 15.0000 || 1.1526 || 0.3765 |
| Roy’s greatest root || 0.3842 || 5.0000 || 15.0000 || 1.1526 || 0.3765 |

We see that none of the multivariate tests reject the null having *p*\-values equal to 0.3765, and hence we do not have sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis of equality of mean vectors.

### 4.6.6 MANOVA in R

Carrying out a MANOVA in R can be done in a variety of ways via several packages. In the following we conduct a MANOVA on the iris data. We construct the dependent variable “variate” by *concatenating* (i.e., joining) the iris features and identify species as the independent variable:

```
> data(iris)
> dv <- cbind(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Petal.Length, iris$Petal.Width)
> iv <- iris$Species
> manova <- manova(dv ~ iv, data = iris)
> summary(manova)
```

```
Df Pillai approx F num Df den Df Pr(>F)
iv 2 1.1919 53.466 8 290 < 2.2e-16 ***
Residuals 147
---
Signif. codes: 0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
```

We see that species yields a *statistically* (not necessarily *substantively*) significant effect (*p* < 0.001).216

To obtain effect sizes, we can use the package *effect size* (Ben-Shachar, [2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000028)) to obtain a partial Eta-squared statistic:

```
> library(effectsize)
> effectsize::eta_squared(manova)
# Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)
Parameter | Eta2 (partial) | 95% CI
-----------------------------------------
iv | 0.60 | [0.54, 1.00]
- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].>
```

We see that the partial Eta squared associated with the *iv* is 0.60, meaning that species explains approximately 60% of the variance in the response variable *variate*, that is, the linear combination of sepal length, sepal width, etc. Next, we conduct a discriminant analysis on species, a kind of follow-up analysis to MANOVA in the way of generating discriminant functions:

```
> library(MASS)
> discrim <- lda(iv ~ dv, CV=F)
> discrim
```

Designating CV=F instructs not to perform leave-one-out cross-validation (CV = T will provide such validation).

```
Call:
lda(iv ~ dv, CV = F)
Prior probabilities of groups:
setosa versicolor virginica
0.3333333 0.3333333 0.3333333
Group means:
```

 
|  || dv1 || dv2 || dv3 || dv4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| setosa || 5.006 || 3.428 || 1.462 || 0.246 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| versicolor || 5.936 || 2.770 || 4.260 || 1.326 |
| virginica || 6.588 || 2.974 || 5.552 || 2.026 |

```
Coefficients of linear discriminants:
```

 
|  || LD1 || LD2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dv1 || 0.8293776 || \-0.02410215 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dv2 || 1.5344731 || \-2.16452123 |
| dv3 || \-2.2012117 || 0.93192121 |
| dv4 || \-2.8104603 || \-2.83918785 |

```
Proportion of trace:
LD1 LD2
0.9912 0.0088
```

217 

We can see that the first discriminant function accounts for a much larger proportion of the trace (0.9912) than the second (0.0088), which implies the first function is more “important” statistically than the second and better differentiates flower groups (i.e., the function has a greater eigenvalue). We are also given coefficients of the linear discriminants. But why are we seeing a discriminant analysis here? Though we introduce and discuss discriminant analysis in more detail later in the book as a *classifier* (if you have never studied discriminant analysis, you may choose to skip to that section now), it behooves us to briefly discuss here how discriminant analysis can be considered the “reverse” of the multivariate analysis of variance.

## 4.7 Linear Discriminant Analysis (as the “Reverse” of MANOVA)

The linear discriminant analysis model (that we have just briefly seen in our MANOVA example) features a binary or polytomous categorical response variable in which a linear combination of predictors is sought that maximizes group differences on the response. Discriminant analysis is sometimes referred to as a *filter model* and a *feature selection method* in the data mining literature ([Aggarwal, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000005)). While at first glance, this may be challenging for the reader to grasp or “see” the big picture, the LDA model can actually be regarded as a “hub” model, that is, a model from which many other models can be considered *scaled-up* or *scaled-down* versions of the LDA model structure.

For one, it can be operationalized in a few different ways, including being the “opposite” of the MANOVA model. This is the interpretation that most interests us here to supplement our discussion of MANOVA and also understand the above output provided in R by the MANOVA follow-up analysis or, crudely, “*post-hoc”* analysis (though it is not strictly a *post-hoc* *test* as we are not attempting to control for any error rates, we are using the word “*post-hoc*” here merely *descriptively*). MANOVA and LDA are often conceived as *opposites* of one another, and many times, a discriminant analysis will be performed as a follow-up to MANOVA to help learn more about the underlying function(s) (called the *discriminant function(s)*) responsible for separating groups so efficiently.

In the above output, we came across via our *post-hoc* of MANOVA a set of discriminant functions (technically, they are not discriminant *functions* yet until we weight the corresponding coefficients with the variables, which is why R calls them *linear discriminants*):

```
Coefficients of linear discriminants:
```

 
|  || LD1 || LD2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dv1 || 0.8293776 || \-0.02410215 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dv2 || 1.5344731 || \-2.16452123 |
| dv3 || \-2.2012117 || 0.93192121 |
| dv4 || \-2.8104603 || \-2.83918785 |

A full understanding of what a discriminant function is will have to wait until we survey discriminant analysis later in the book. However, for now, it is enough to know that we have obtained two discriminant functions as a result of there being three groups in our data (i.e., type of species). LD1 above is nothing more than a linear combination (called *linear discriminant* or more generally *linear discriminant function* after weighting by variables) that is weighted with values of sepal length, sepal width, petal length and petal width (i.e., dv1 through dv4). The linear combination generated by LD1 is thus:218

```
LD1 = 0.82(sepal length) + 1.53(sepal width) + (-2.20)(petal length) + (-2.81)(petal width).
```

In the machine-learning community, LDA is hardly ever conceived as the opposite of MANOVA but instead simply as a “classifier” of group membership and as a similar and potential alternative to logistic regression. However, even more generally, both LDA and logistic can be interpreted as special cases of a wider model, that of the *generalized linear model*, which we discuss later in the book. Under this umbrella, LDA is an application of the generalized linear model in which the response is (typically) binary, yet the model is still *linear*. That is, in this context, the *link function* is simply the *identity function*. This serves to contrast the LDA model with that of the logistic in which the link function is the *log of the odds*. For readers coming to this discussion with some background, this likely makes perfect sense. Without such background however, what we have just said will be entirely confusing and the reader will have to wait until further in the book when we survey discriminant analysis and the generalized linear model in more detail. She may wish to return to this section after that discussion.

We “unpack” the LDA model later in the book where we treat it in much more detail as a classifier. For now, however, we simply wish to note that the unifying aspects of LDA and MANOVA cannot be overstated. Where MANOVA seeks to find mean vector differences, the LDA model seeks to use those linear combinations to distinguish between groups. Extensions and special cases of these models are numerous, and pedagogically, understanding discriminant analysis gives rise to a variety of related models. Indeed, it is not an exaggeration to say that we could, if desired, title an entire book called *Linear Discriminant Analysis and Variations* because of the “hub” nature of LDA.

# 5 Simple Linear and Multiple Regression Models (and Extensions)

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-8](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-8)

Linear regression has historically been the workhorse of statistics and is still so today ([Stigler, 1986](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000348)). What is more, many of the common techniques that are in use today are, in one way or another, *extensions* or *derivatives* of the basic linear regression model. Entire books and treatises are written on linear regression as well as entire courses that study the topic in outstanding depth. This is for good reason; *regression is literally at the center of the universe of statistical modeling and that of machine learning algorithms*. Excellent textbook-length sources on regression analysis alone include [Fox (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106) and [Draper and Smith (1998)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000090).

The history of regression ideas and concepts dates back to antiquity ([Stigler, 1986](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000348)). More recently, the origin of least-squares generally is said to lay with [Legendre (1805)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000215) and later in the same century with [Galton (1888),](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000121) who applied regression to problems of heredity. The essential idea of regression is that of making predictions on one variable based on another (or more) while minimizing some function of the error in making those predictions. Least-squares regression is all about exploiting the correlation between two or more variables with the goal of reducing error in prediction in the one based on knowledge of the other(s). Regression, the *concept*, is the essence of what statistical modeling is all about.

## 5.1 Simple Linear Regression – Fixed Predictor Case

The simplest linear regression model features a single predictor whose values are regarded as fixed in advance. This classic simple linear regression model is given by

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*] + *ε*[*i*]  
(5.1)

where *y*[*i*] is the response variable, *β*[0] is the intercept of the regression line, *β*[1] is the slope, *x*[*i*] is the explanatory or independent variable, and *ε*[*i*] is the error term, that part of *y*[*i*] that is unaccounted for by the systematic part of the model and where *E*(*ε*[*i*]) = 0. The intercept is sometimes referred to as the *offset* or *bias* term. This terminology is common in neural networks discussed later in the book.

The systematic part of the model is *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*], and thus the expectation of *y*[*i*], that is, *E*(*y*[*i*]) = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*] is equal to *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*]. The model has expectation *E*(*y*[*i*]) = *β*[0] when *x*[*i*] = 0 since220

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {E\\left( y\_{i} \\right) = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x\_{i}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}\\left( 0 \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\beta\_{0}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

We note that the model is linear in the parameters *β*[0] and *β*[1]. This is the meaning of *linear* in linear regression. Note that this definition of linearity does not require the model to be linear in the input variable *x*[*i*]. Hence, the following model is still a linear model even though the input enters as a squared term:

  
*E*(*y*[*i*]) = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*]²  

In our model of regression in (5.1), as mentioned, we assume that our predictor is *fixed*. That is, if we were to refit the model on new data and thus replicate the experiment, we would use the same values on our predictor *x*[*i*]. If *x*[*i*] were random, we would presumably use different values since such values were presumably, at least on a theoretical level, drawn from a probability distribution. The theory we develop below assumes a fixed-effects model. For a treatment of random effects in regression, see [Fox (2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 228).

### 5.1.1 Parameter Estimates

Recall that we usually do not know values for *β*[0] and *β*[1] and hence typically require estimating them from sample data,

  
*ŷ* = *β̂*[0] + *β̂*[1]*x*[*i*]  
(5.2)

How shall values of *β̂*[0] and *β̂*[1] be chosen? Certainly not arbitrarily or at random. As is true for most statistical models, parameter estimates are chosen in such a way that they accomplish some goal, which is usually to *minimize* or *maximize* some objective function. In the case of simple linear regression, these estimates are chosen such that they minimize the sum of squared errors around the regression line in simple linear regression and regression *surface* in multiple regression. That is, we wish to minimize the difference between observed and values predicted by the function *f̂*(*x*[*i*]):

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {RSS = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{i} - \\hat{f}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) \\right)^{2}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{i} - {\\hat{\\beta}}\_{0} - {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{x\_{ij}{\\hat{\\beta}}\_{j}}} \\right)^{2}}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(5.3)

The general form of the above loss function is of the type (*a*−*h*)² which is a *quadratic* term, and hence the loss is a *quadratic loss*, often referred to as an *L2 loss*. Regression itself in no way requires us to minimize the L2 loss specifically. We could have instead, for instance, minimized the L1 loss, which is that of taking the absolute value of differences, |*a*−*h*|. Regression that minimizes L1 is often referred to as *robust regression* for the reason that through taking absolute deviations, it places less weight on outlying or more extreme scores (i.e., it is more “robust” to such extremes compared to L2). This is in contrast to the L2 loss, which magnifies extreme deviations through squaring them. Deviations from medians instead of means can also make regression more robust. The takeaway point for now is that there are many possible loss functions one may choose. For instance, yet another loss function is the *Huber loss* (for details, see [Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). The point is that the fact that we are minimizing the L2 loss in classic regression in no way implies that this is *the* one and only loss function that should dominate all work. However, it is undoubtedly the most 221common among loss functions and is typically used as a default. Ideally, however, whatever loss function is chosen should depend on the problem at hand.

The least-squares estimates for *β̂*[0] and *β̂*[1] are found by differentiating the residual sums of squares (RSS) with respect to both *β*[0] and *β*[*j*], of which the solutions can be shown to be equal to

  
$${\\hat{\\beta}}\_{0} = \\overline{y} - {\\hat{\\beta}}\_{1}\\overline{x}$$  
(5.4)

for *β̂*[0] and

  
$${\\hat{\\beta}}\_{1} = \\frac{\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right)\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right.}} \\right)}{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right)^{2}}$$  
(5.5)

for *β*[1]. It is easy to see that computing the slope requires variation in both *x* and *y*. For instance, without variation in *x*, $\\sum\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right)^{2}$ is equal to 0 and hence *β̂*[1] is undefined.

The slope, in the case of zero intercept, can also be written as the inner product of *x* and *y* relative to the inner product of *x*, that is,

  
$${\\hat{\\beta}}\_{1} = \\frac{\\left\\langle {x,y} \\right\\rangle}{\\left\\langle {x,x} \\right\\rangle}$$  
(5.6)

As we will see when we survey multiple regression shortly, the variance of *β̂*[1] is equal to (*X*^(*T*)*X*)^( − 1)*σ*² where *σ*² is estimated by

  
$$\\left. {\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2} = \\frac{1}{N - p - 1}{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{i} - {\\hat{y}}\_{i} \\right.} \\right)^{2}$$  
(5.7)

where *N* is the number of cases and *p* the number of predictors in the model. To compute significance tests on *β̂*[0] and *β̂*[1] we of course require standard errors, which in scalar form can be calculated from

  
$$SE\\left( {\\hat{\\beta}}\_{0} \\right)^{2} = {\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2}\\left\\lbrack {\\frac{1}{n} + \\frac{{\\overline{x}}^{2}}{\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right)^{2}}} \\right\\rbrack$$  
(5.8)

and222

  
$$SE\\left( {\\hat{\\beta}}\_{1} \\right)^{2} = \\frac{{\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2}}{\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right.} \\right)^{2}}$$  
(5.9)

With standard errors computed, we can easily compute confidence intervals for both *β̂*[0] and *β̂*[1] as *β̂*[0] ± 2 ⋅ *S**E*(*β̂*[0]) and *β̂*[1] ± 2 ⋅ *S**E*(*β̂*[1]), respectively.

A test of the null hypothesis that the slope *β*[1] is equal to zero takes the form,

  
*H*[0] : *β*[1] = 0  
(5.10)

against the statistical alternative hypothesis,

  
*H*[*a*] : *β*[1] ≠ 0  
(5.11)

To evaluate the null, we compute a *t*\-statistic,

  
$$t = \\frac{{\\hat{\\beta}}\_{1} - 0}{SE\\left( {\\hat{\\beta}}\_{1} \\right)}$$  
(5.12)

evaluated on *n* − 2 degrees of freedom.

Recall that the correlation *r*[*y**x*] between *x* and *y* is given by

  
$$Cor\\left( x,y \\right) = r\_{xy} = \\frac{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right)\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)}}{\\sqrt{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( x\_{i} - \\overline{x} \\right)^{2}}\\sqrt{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)^{2}}} = \\frac{{cov}\_{xy}}{s\_{x}s\_{y}}$$  

The square of *r*[*y**x*], that is, *r*[[*y**x*]]², is the proportion of variance accounted for in *y* based on knowledge of *x*. For example, for *r*[[*y**x*]]² = 0.70, this means that 70% of the variance in *y* is accounted for by *x*.

Note that many of the equations and formulas just reviewed feature the use of *scalar algebra* and not matrix algebra (though we did use matrices a tiny bit). This is because in the simple linear regression case working with scalars generally suffices. As we turn shortly to multiple regression however, we will require working with matrices, where it stands that all the scalar algebra just surveyed can be just as well presented via matrices. Most books on regression will present the theory in matrices because these books aim for the widest and most *general* presentation of linear regression possible, for which using scalars (e.g., simple linear regression) is but a special case.

If the effect is so small, why is price statistically significant? This is likely occurring due to the sample size of the data. The cars data has a total of 804 observations and hence rejecting the null hypothesis is relatively easy. Recall that the sensitivity of the *p*\-value to sample size is something that should always be kept in mind when interpreting statistical tests. It may be tempting based on the statistical significance of price to say that price is an “important” predictor of mileage, but the multiple R-squared and Adjusted R-squared tell a different story with such small amounts of variance explained. The observed *p*\-value is likely so small simply because of the large sample size.224

## 5.2 Multiple Linear Regression

In a simple linear regression there is only a single response variable and a single predictor. In a multiple regression model, there are several predictor variables that we model simultaneously in predicting the single response. In a *multivariate multiple regression*, there are not only several predictor variables but also several responses modeled simultaneously.

The multiple linear regression model is given by

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[1] + *β*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *β*[*p*]*x*[*p*] + *ε*[*i*]  
(5.13)

where *E*(*ε*[*i*]) = 0 and thus with expectation equal to227

  
*E*(*y*[*i*]) = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[1] + *β*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *β*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  

or when expressed as conditional on *x*,

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {y = E\\left( y \\middle| x\_{1},...,x\_{p} \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\beta\_{0} + {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{x\_{j}\\beta\_{j}\\,}}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

We can more concisely state the above model more generally as a function *f*(*x*),

  
$$f\\left( x \\right) = \\beta\_{0} + {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{x\_{j}\\beta\_{j}}}$$  
(5.14)

where “*f*(*x*)” represents the function *f* given the input of *x*. The summation $\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{x\_{j}\\beta\_{j}}$ allows for as many predictors that we wish to include into the regression model.

As was true for the simple linear regression model, parameter values *β*[0], *β*[1], *β*[2], ..., *β*[*p*] are not known and must be estimated from the sample data; hence the *estimated* multiple regression model is given by

  
*ŷ*[*i*] = *β̂*[0] + *β̂*[1]*x*[1] + *β̂*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *β̂*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  
(5.15)

Parameter values are chosen via ordinary least-squares, which is an optimization problem to minimize the sum of squared errors. The least-squares solution is the following, where *X* is a matrix of predictors and *y* a vector of responses:

  
*β̂* = (*X*^(*T*)*X*)^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*y*  
(5.16)

Though the matrix representation for multiple regression looks more complex than for simple regression, it is not difficult to appreciate the solution. Recall that taking inverses is conceptually equivalent to division in ordinary scalar algebra, and hence if we were to *naïvely* (though mathematically incorrectly) rewrite (5.16) in the most “familiar” way, we could express it as

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\hat{\\beta} = \\left( XTX \\right){- 1}X^{T}y} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\frac{X^{T}y}{\\left( X^{T}X \\right)}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

We now easily see that the numerator contains in a general way a product of *X* and *y* whereas the denominator contains only a product of *X*. Hence, in words, the solution for *β̂* is answering the question of the extent to which *X* and *y* “go together” relative to only *X*. If *X* and *y* are highly *linearly* related (emphasis on *linear* here), then *X*^(*T*)*y* will be much larger than *X*^(*T*)*X* and hence the coefficient for *β̂* will be larger than not. On the opposite extreme, if *X* and *y* are not very much linearly related, then *X*^(*T*)*y* < *X*^(*T*)*X* and *X*^(*T*)*y* will be only a *fraction* of the total “cross-variation” present in *X*^(*T*)*X* in the hypothetical division of quantities. Note that this matrix representation then is nothing more than a generalization of the single variable case in which228

  
$$\\hat{\\beta} = \\frac{Cov\_{xy}}{S\_{x}^{2}}$$  

where in this simpler case *C**o**v*[*x**y*] is analogous, in concept at least, to *X*^(*T*)*y* and *S*[*x*]² to *X*^(*T*)*X*.

The term

  
*X*^† = (*X*^(*T*)*X*)^( − 1)*X*^(*T*),  
(5.17)

that is, with *y* dropped, is the left *pseudo-inverse* of the nonsquare matrix *X* ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259), p. 367). Hence, in cases where the inverse does not exist, a pseudo-inverse may be an option. This is especially useful for nonsquare matrices since ordinary inverses exist only for square matrices. Pseudo-inverses are best computed using the singular value decomposition, or “SVD” ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)).

### 5.2.1 Minimizing Squared vs. Absolute Deviations

Recall that instead of squared deviations from predicted values, one could also take least absolute deviations of the kind

  
|*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*[*i*]|  
(5.18)

But what is the relationship between minimizing (*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*[*i*])² vs. minimizing |*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*[*i*]|? Minimizing |*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*[*i*]| instead of (*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*[*i*])² places less emphasis on extreme scores. That is, when we square *y*[*i*] − *ŷ*[*i*], differences are magnified due to the squaring. If we instead minimize |*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*[*i*]|, large deviations are not so emphasized.

Minimizing |*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*[*i*]| is featured in *least-absolute-value regression*, or “LAV” regression for short. Historically, however, (*y*[*i*]−*ŷ*[*i*])² is usually first choice in a regression context as squares are usually more tractable mathematically than are absolute value deviations ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)).

### 5.2.2 Hypothesis-Testing in Multiple Regression

The null hypothesis under test in the multiple regression model is the following:

  
*H*[0] : *β*[1] = *β*[2] =  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  = *β*[*p*] = 0  
(5.19)

against the statistical alternative hypothesis that at least one of the coefficients, *β*[*j*], is not equal to 0. To evaluate, as we did in analysis of variance (ANOVA), we compute an *F*\-ratio, but not identical to that in ANOVA,

  
$$F = \\frac{\\left( TSS - RSS \\right)/p}{RSS/\\left( n - p - 1 \\right)}$$  
(5.20)

which is evaluated on *p* and *n* − *p* degrees of freedom, where *p* is the number of predictors and *n* is the number of data points. *TSS* and *RSS* are the total and residual sums of squares, respectively. If the probability of *F* under the null hypothesis of *ρ*² = 0 is small, we reject the null hypothesis of no effect and conclude *ρ*² ≠ 0 in the population from which the data were drawn.229
