## 5.3 Geometry of Least-Squares

A picture is worth a thousand words, and this holds true for visualizing how least-squares works. [Figure 5.1](#c5.xhtml#f5.1) is a depiction of the projection of a least-squares line based on two predictors, *x*[1] and *x*[2].

![Figure 5.1 Geometry of least-squares regression, where the response variable y is projected onto the space spanned by predictors x\_{1} and x\_{2}. Used with permission of Springer Nature BV, from Modern Multivariate Statistical Techniques by Alan J. Izenman, © 2008; permission conveyed through Copyright Clearance Center, Inc.Return to text.⏎](images/fig5.1.jpg)

*Figure 5.1* Geometry of least-squares regression, where the response variable y is projected onto the space spanned by predictors *x*[1] and *x*[2]. Used with permission of Springer Nature BV, from Modern Multivariate Statistical Techniques by Alan J. Izenman, © 2008; permission conveyed through Copyright Clearance Center, Inc.[Return to text.⏎](#c5.xhtml#re_f5.1)

We can see the response *y* and its estimated values *ŷ* as a function of *x*[1] and *x*[2], the space *spanned* by these predictors. The projection is the ordinary least-squares estimate. The extent to which *x*[1] and *x*[2] overlap is the extent to which there may be *collinearity* among the predictors and hence they are taking up a similar space. This overview just scratches the surface regarding visualizing regression and is only meant to whet the reader’s appetite should one wish to follow up on the interesting topic of the *geometry of linear models*. For an excellent and much more detailed treatment, see [Fox, *The Vector Geometry of Linear Models* (2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml#c10)).232

## 5.4 Gauss-Markov Theorem: What We Like about Least-Squares Estimates

Why do we like least-squares estimators so much? What is so attractive about them? What is most important about them can be summarized in the *Gauss-Markov theorem*, which asserts that the least-squares estimates of the parameters *a*^(*T*)*β̂* have the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators when the errors are independently distributed with zero expectation and constant variance ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 212). Least-squares estimators are often called “BLUE” which stands for *best linear unbiased estimator*. As noted earlier, the least-squares estimate of *a*^(*T*)*β̂* is

  
*a*^(*T*)*β̂* = *a*^(*T*)(*X*^(*T*)*X*)^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*y*  
(5.21)

for which the expectation is equal to

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {E\\left( a^{T}\\hat{\\beta} \\right) = E\\left( a^{T}\\left( XTX \\right){- 1}X^{T}y \\right)} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = a^{T}\\left( XTX \\right){- 1}X^{T}X\\beta} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = a^{T}\\beta} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(5.22)

The Gauss-Markov theorem holds that for any other linear estimator for which the expectation is *a*^(*T*)*β* (unbiased), for example, *E*(*w*^(*T*)*ŷ*) = *w*^(*T*)*y*, the variance of the least-squares estimates *a*^(*T*)*β̂* is less than or equal to the variance of *w*^(*T*)*y*. For a proof of this theorem, see [Fox (2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 213). An implication of the theorem is that the least-squares estimator has *the smallest mean-squared error out of all the linear estimators we could consider that have no bias* (Hastie et al., [2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)).

### 5.4.1 Are Unbiased Estimators Always Best?

As we will see later, the restriction to unbiased estimators in regression and other methods is not necessarily always a wise one. Recall that the bias-variance trade-off is always at work in estimation. Most of the time, we would like to minimize bias in estimation. At times, however, it may be beneficial to permit some bias into an estimator for the purpose of reducing variance.

Biased estimators such as the *ridge estimator* in *ridge regression* may at times be preferred over an unbiased estimator. One such case when a biased estimator may be preferred is when least-squares estimates are *unstable* ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). That is, if *X* in (*X*^(*T*)*X*)^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*y* is less than full rank, then *singularity* will result, which means the least-squares estimates will no longer be *unique*. When the assumptions of regression do not hold due to collinearity or other problems (e.g., correlated errors), alternative solutions for estimation must be sought. And while exact collinearity may rarely occur, variables that are “almost collinear” can happen quite often depending on the research context. A *biased* estimator can be a better choice when faced with these kinds of conditions as well as for data that are ill-conditioned, meaning that estimated quantities are rather sensitive to small changes in the data ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). Collinearity and instability often go hand in hand, as the effects of collinearity are such that it can produce overly large positive or negative estimated coefficients whose very signs can be reversed under rather negligible changes to the data. Standard errors could be grossly inflated as well, which could yield non-statistically significant effects, whereas if collinearity were not present, those same effects may have been statistically significant.233

In addition to the above, for some data sets, the number of input variables in *X* might greatly exceed the number of observations in the data. Under these conditions, the OLS estimator still exists, but is not *unique*, and hence a biased estimator may be useful in this case. We discuss biased estimators such as ridge and the lasso shortly in the book.

## 5.5 Time Series: An Example of Correlated Errors

The standard linear model assumes independently and normally distributed errors, but the assumption of independence is rarely (if ever) quite right on empirical data. Just like most things in statistics, it is often a reasonable *approximation*, however. Recall that approximations are what statistical modeling is all about. Rarely, if ever, are any assumptions for any model *exactly* met.

When measurements are taken across a *time period*, the assumption of independent errors is usually not satisfied. That is, when the observations comprise a *time series*, *ε*[*i*] are usually *correlated*. Indeed, dependencies among the errors can be very strong in such time-dependent data.

How is this dependency represented in the linear model? Recall in the classic linear model,

  
*y* = *X**β* + *ε*  

where *ε* ∼ *N*(0,∑[*ε**ε*]) and where ∑[*ε**ε*] is the covariance matrix of errors, symmetric and positive semi-definite. However, unlike in the typical non-time series least-squares regression model, the expectation for ∑[*ε**ε*] is not one having zeroes on the off-diagonal. Instead, because measurements are usually related, we expect *nonzero diagonal elements* in the off-diagonal representing the correlated errors, which implies ∑[*ε**ε*]will have *n*(*n +* 1)/2 distinct elements. The dependency of errors in a time series model requires us to incorporate the covariances between time points similar to how we did so in the classic repeated measures models surveyed earlier in the book.

Time series is an enormous topic and we have only scratched the surface here in our cursory overview to give an example of where errors are often correlated in data. Books on time series include those by [Chatfield and Xing (2019)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000058) and [Cryer and Chan (2008)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000072). The package *timeseries* ([Wuertz et al., 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000395)) can be used for time series in R, especially applicable to financial time series. The package *pyts* can be used to fit time series models in Python. Other packages such as *sktime* and *tslearn* can also be used. [Fox (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106) provides a good, if not somewhat technical introduction to time series and comes highly recommended.

## 5.6 Model Selection in Regression: Is There an “Optimal” Model?

One of the biggest problems in regression analysis and related models is that of determining which model to maintain or keep. *Model selection* in statistics in general is a huge problem and is usually not quite as simple as using statistical criteria alone to determine which model to adopt. Research and scientific criteria should always enter the discussion. Too often researchers adopt a “kitchen-sink” approach (i.e., throw in everything but the kitchen sink) to variable selection which often leads to overly complex models, problems of collinearity, and poor generalizability of test data.

Among the statistical approaches, there are generally two common strategies used for selecting a model. Recall that in choosing a model, we are not interested in the model that minimizes *training error*; we are interested in the model that minimizes *test error*. The most direct way to evaluate test error would be to employ a *cross-validation* approach. For example, we could fit our model to 80% of the data and test on 20%. This gives us a direct estimate of the test error because it tells us exactly how the model performs on new data, that is, data the model has yet to “see.” This is a 234first strategy to choosing a model, that of evaluating the fitted model on test data to learn how it performs.

For many reasons, however, we may not want to follow the above direct cross-validation approach. Some of these reasons include the fact that historically, data may have been expensive and sometimes very inconvenient to collect in the given field, and hence training a model on anything less than the full data set is sometimes simply not feasible. Indeed, before computers came along, the idea of setting aside data to test on via fast computation was, of course, not even an option. Hence, what if we decided to not put aside test data and wanted simply to estimate the test error on the training data itself, even if imperfectly? Since we only have the training data, fortunately we can *adjust* the training error rate to, for some measures at least, better reflect test error. We consider these options next.

## 5.7 Effect Size, Model Selection, and Adjusting the Training Error Rate

A rejection of the null hypothesis in regression, crudely, suggests that the regression is predicting better than chance. However, on its own, a statistically significant *p*\-value does not necessarily tell us much more than that, unless of course we have specific knowledge of the inputs to the computed *p*\-value such as sample size, variance, and so on, to help make sense of the *p*\-value finding for the given data set. As is usually the case with significance testing, it is entirely possible to reject a null hypothesis for regression yet it be a *trivial* scientific effect. Such can occur often when sample size is extremely large and hence even miniscule effects cause us to reject the null hypothesis. This is nothing new, as we have discussed in many other places in the book the influence that sample size has on computed *p*\-values. As usual, what is needed is a measure of *effect size*. A good effect size is not sample size dependent. The problem with effect size, however, is that if we compute it only on the training data then we usually get an overly *optimistic* size of effect. This is not surprising and is in line with our understanding of how models fit to training data are generally too optimistic overall.

In what follows we first consider an effect size for training data, then survey a few strategies for measuring size of effect as well as *model selection measures* that better evaluate the parsimony of statistical models, and in some cases (e.g., *Akaike’s Information Criterion*), also help us better estimate test error.

## 5.7.1 R², Adjusted R², C[p], AIC, BIC

Recall that *R*² in regression is given by

  
$$R^{2} = \\frac{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i}^{'} - \\overline{y} \\right)^{2}}{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)^{2}}$$  
(5.23)

The denominator, $\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i} - \\overline{y} \\right)^{2}$ is simply a sums of squares of actual data values from $\\overline{y}$. This quantity will be large or small depending simply on how much variation we have in the current data set. However, look more closely at the numerator, $\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i}^{'} - \\overline{y} \\right)^{2}$; this term expresses the distance between predicted values, *y*[*i*]^′ and the mean of the data, $\\overline{y}$. If this distance is zero, then 235$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( y\_{i}^{'} - \\overline{y} \\right)^{2}$ is equal to 0 and *R*² will equal 0. As this distance increases, *R*² becomes larger, and the quadratic (i.e., squared) nature of sums of squares amplifies the magnitude, especially for deviations that are distant from the mean. Hence, it would appear at first glance that this *R*² statistic is all we really need to choose a model, such that *the larger the value of* *R*²*, the better the model*. But this logic is problematic, since in almost all cases *R*² will necessarily mathematically increase as the number of predictors entered into the model also increases. Hence, models with a greater number of predictors will result in larger *R*² values. The value of 1 − *R*² will give us a measure of what is typically called the *apparent error rate*. What we really want to know is the *actual error rate*.

One way around this difficulty is to interpret, instead of *R*², an *adjusted* *R*² *statistic* given by the following:

  
$$R\_{adj}^{2} = 1 - \\left( 1 - R^{2} \\right)\\left( \\frac{n - 1}{n - p} \\right)$$  
(5.24)

where “*p*” here is the number of parameters in the model, including the intercept term. From (5.24) we can see that as *p* increases relative to a stable *R*², *R*[*a**d**j*]² *decreases* instead of automatically increasing as was the case for *R*². Hence, *R*[*a**d**j*]² essentially “penalizes” the user for including predictors that are not “worth their salt” in increasing *R*².

The *C*[*p*] statistic (“Mallow’s *C*[*p*]”) is another approach to penalizing model fit,

  
$$C\_{p} = \\frac{1}{n}\\left( RSS + 2d{\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2} \\right)$$  
(5.25)

where, as before, *n* is the number of cases or observations, *R**S**S* is the residual sums of squares on the training data, *d* now is the number of predictors (recall that *p* was the number of *parameters* in *R*[*a**d**j*]²), and *σ̂*² is an estimate of error variance using all predictors, usually MS residual. The nature of the penalty in *C*[*p*] is by way of 2*d**σ̂*². Smaller values of *C*[*p*] are preferred over larger values since smaller *R**S**S* implies a better-fitting model. However, this is offset by 2*d**σ̂*², where increasing *d* has the effect of increasing 2*d**σ̂*². Hence, *C*[*p*], if it could speak, would say, “Congrats on getting *R**S**S* down, but that decrease will be penalized by how many *d* it required to do so. If any of your *d* are not sufficiently contributing to the observed decrease in *RSS*, you may want to consider removing them instead of being penalized for including them.”

A similar statistic to the *C*[*p*], and one that is more popular, is that of the AIC (*Akaike’s Information Criterion*) statistic,

  
$$AIC = \\frac{1}{n{\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2}}\\left( RSS + 2d{\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2} \\right)$$  
(5.26)

which is very similar in logic to that of the *C*[*p*]: the only difference is the multiplier $\\frac{1}{n{\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2}}$ instead of $\\frac{1}{n}$ in *C*[*p*]. The penalty is still equal to 2*d**σ̂*², however. In this formulation, increasingly smaller values are preferred over larger values. The following is another version of AIC, the original version given by Akaike ([1974](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000409)),236

  
 − 2ln *p*(*D*|*θ*) + 2*m*  
(5.27)

which is the familiar log-likelihood, ln *p*(*D*|*θ*), however pre-multiplied by −2. For this version of AIC, smaller is also better than larger, as the penalty *m* (number of *parameters* in the model) acts to increase AIC, and if the decrease in  − 2ln *p*(*D*|*θ*) isn’t “worth” the increase by *m*, it makes adding the extra parameter(s) less worthwhile in terms of maintaining model parsimony. However, “smaller is always better” does not always pertain to the report of an AIC statistic; *it depends on how it is formulated*. AIC could, in theory, appear as simply ln *p*(*D*|*θ*) − 2*m* where now a *larger* than not value is preferred. Notice that now the log-likelihood is positive without pre-multiplying it by −2 and as before we are subtracting the number of parameters in the way of *2m*. *Be sure you are clear on how AIC (or BIC) is specifically defined for your particular application (e.g., software, package, etc.) before you interpret it.*

A derivative of both the *C*[*p*] and AIC is the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC),

  
$$BIC = \\frac{1}{n{\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2}}\\left( RSS + \\log\\left( n \\right)d{\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2} \\right)$$  
(5.28)

The BIC often penalizes to a greater extent than the AIC. The key difference in the two statistics is in what follows *RSS* in their respective formulations. In the AIC, that term is 2*d**σ̂*², where in the BIC, it is *l**o**g*(*n*)*d**σ̂*². All else equal, as sample size *n* increases, so does log (*n*) and BIC will typically “punish” more than AIC for the same *RSS* and *σ̂*². As with AIC, be sure you know how the author is defining BIC before concluding that “smaller is better” (e.g., see [Schwarz, 1978](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000328); [Fraley & Raftery, 1998](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000109), where BIC is translated into a “larger is better” statistic).

As the name suggests, BIC originates from Bayesian decision theory and hence is derived from Bayesian principles. It can be shown that choosing a model with the minimum BIC is equivalent to choosing the model with the highest approximate posterior probability ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). What is more, BIC is asymptotically consistent as a selection criterion, which implies that the probability that BIC will select the correct model increases toward unity (i.e., 1) as the amount of information (sample size) on which it is based increases. This is not true for AIC, which will too often select a model that is too rich or complex as information on which it is based increases (i.e., *n*→∞). For smaller sample sizes, BIC typically penalizes much more severely than AIC and hence may choose a model that is too simple ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)).

An additional measure of effect size that is sometimes recommended in regression is that of the *semi-partial correlation* coefficient ([Hays, 1994](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000149)). The semi-partial correlation partials out variance due to other predictors in the model before relating a predictor to the response variable. That is, it is the bivariate correlation between an adjusted variable (predictor) and an unadjusted variable (response). For details, see [Hays (1994)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000149).

### *5.7.2 Comparing* *R*[*a**d**j*]², *C*[*p*], *AIC, and BIC to Cross-Validation*

We have surveyed above a few ways of penalizing training data to assess model fit and model selection. Which measure is best? Should one use any of the *R*[*a**d**j*]², *C*[*p*], AIC, or BIC options, or should one use cross-validation? Cross-validation is usually first choice, since it is a direct estimate of the test error, whereas only *C*[*p*] and AIC rather efficiently, though *indirectly*, estimate test error. Cross-validation also makes fewer assumptions about the underlying model ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)). 237Historically, before high-speed computing power and very large data sets (at least in some fields), performing cross-validation directly was computationally quite difficult or borderline impossible and hence computing measures such as *C*[*p*], *R*[*a**d**j*]², etc. was more feasible and convenient. Today, however, with high-speed computing, cross-validation can be performed with relative ease. Hence, given the availability of relatively cheap computing speed, cross-validation is often the preferred option for model validation. Of course, nothing stops the investigator from simultaneously computing many competing effect-size measures and comparing them to see if they *triangulate* on the same data set. There is no “type I” error rate when computing effect sizes; the researcher can compute as many of them as she would like.

## 5.8 Assumptions for Regression

Virtually all statistical models are founded on a set of assumptions. Verifying assumptions for regression is important because least-squares estimates and inference are only as good as the assumptions on which they are based. Further, techniques have been developed that allow for users to evaluate the impact that data points have on the estimated least-squares solution. Thus, in addition to verifying assumptions such as *linearity* and *homoscedasticity of variance*, residual analyses that evaluate such things as leverage, raw, standardized, and studentized residuals are generally recommended.

Residual analysis in regression is a huge topic and due to space limitations, we do not survey it here. Defining such things as *leverage* and *influence* of data points requires more theoretical development than we can afford here. We also assume the reader may already have at least some exposure to this area in prior courses. We refer the reader to [Fox (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106) for a thorough and excellent treatment of residual analyses, which can become quite complex and is an art unto itself. We cannot escape the topic of assumption analysis entirely, however, and must survey one of the most important areas of assumption-checking in regression and related models, that of collinearity.

### 5.8.1 Collinearity

Collinearity can have serious and deleterious effects on a regression solution. If the columns of *X* are not linearly independent, this equates to *X* not being of full rank, which implies that *X*^(*T*)*X* is singular, the determinant is equal to 0, and the least-squares coefficients, though they theoretically can be estimated, are not *uniquely* defined. Hence, collinearity in regression is a serious problem and we need a way to address it.

#### 5.8.1.1 Variance Inflation Factor

There are a few common ways of assessing collinearity. The first we survey is probably the most popular, that of computing a statistic called the *variance inflation factor*, or “VIF” for short. To understand VIF, we must first consider how we can write the variance of the i*th* partial regression coefficient (Cohen et al., [2003](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000064), p. 423):238

  
$$s\_{\\beta\_{i}}^{2} = \\frac{s\_{y}^{2}}{s\_{x\_{i}}^{2}}\\left( \\frac{1 - R\_{y.12...p}^{2}}{n - p - 1} \\right)\\left( \\frac{1}{1 - R\_{i.12...(i)...p}^{2}} \\right)$$  
(5.29)

where *s*[*β*[*i*]]² is the variance of the *β*[*i*] coefficient, *s*[*y*]² is the variance of the response, *s*[*x*[*i*]]² is the variance of the given predictor *x*[*i*] corresponding to *β*[*i*], and *R*[*y*.12...*p*]² is the coefficient of determination for the entire model with all predictors *y*.12...*p*. The variance inflation factor is the last term in (5.29):

  
$$\\left( \\frac{1}{1 - R\_{i.12...(i)...p}^{2}} \\right)$$  
(5.30)

where *R*[*i*.12...(*i*)...*p*]² represents the explained variance of the predictor in question regressed on the rest of predictors in the model. The extent to which *R*[*i*.12...(*i*)...*p*]² is large is the extent to which the denominator 1 − *R*[*i*.12...(*i*)...*p*]² goes toward zero, and hence is the extent to which VIF will be larger than not. That is, the extent to which the predictor in question shares variance with other predictors in the model is the extent to which the variance inflation factor increases. The variance inflation factor, as the name suggests, measures *the factor by which the variance of the given regression coefficient increases due to its collinearity with other variables in the model*.

A second popular way of assessing ill-conditioning is through the *condition number*. The *condition number* *k* is the square root of the ratio of the largest to the smallest nonzero eigenvalues, that is, $k = \\sqrt{\\lambda\_{1}/\\lambda\_{2}}$, where *λ*[1] is the largest eigenvalue and *λ*[2] is the smallest ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)). If this ratio is large, *X* is considered *ill-conditioned*. It makes sense that a comparison of eigenvalues here can be used as an indicator of ill-conditioning. Consider what it means to have a very wide range between the largest and smallest eigenvalues. It implies that an increasing amount of variance is in one “component” (i.e., *principal component*) only in the data, which implies that there exists a large degree of correlation among variables “coagulating” into that component. Hence, the condition number can serve as an aid in detecting collinearity.

### 5.8.2 Collinearity Necessarily Implies Redundancy Only in Terms of Variance

In our discussion of collinearity thus far, it should be emphasized that two variables that are nearly perfectly collinear are redundant only in terms of *shared variance*, and not necessarily in terms of what they are actually individually measuring. A common misunderstanding when considering collinearity is to assume that two collinear variables are “getting at the same thing” on a substantive level simply because they are highly correlated. And while in some cases this may be true, it is not necessarily so across all cases.

For example, consider the classic case of correlating height and weight. Suppose the correlation is near 0.90. The shared variance between variables is relatively high, but we would all agree that weight is not the same thing as height. More generally, *a statistical measure, whatever the kind, in no way* ***necessarily*** *reflects substantive reality*. Whenever we apply an arbitrary statistical function to any “real object,” it is never a one-to-one relationship. *The statistics are never enough; you have to know what the statistics are being applied to in order to draw the proper scientific conclusion*. A lack of understanding of what statistics *can* vs. *cannot* tell you about empirical data is probably the greatest pitfall for users of statistics who have not considered these wider and deeper methodological and philosophical issues.

## 5.9 Variable Selection Methods: Building the Regression Model

Previously we discussed model fit and model selection measures, such as *R*², *R*[*a**d**j*]², AIC, etc. While we discussed how to potentially choose the best model, we did not discuss *how* to select 239variables for a given model. This latter concern falls under the category of *variable selection* rather than the previously discussed topic of *model selection*. One way to conceive of variable selection in a very general sense is as suggested by [Breiman (2001)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000049), such that a variable is important *if dropping it from the model seriously affects prediction*. And while variable selection may at first glance appear to be simple, it is an extremely complex problem, just as complex as model selection overall. Most variable selection procedures are quite unstable as well, such that tweaking or perturbing the original data even slightly can have a rather drastic effect on the final model ([Breiman, 1996](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000047)).

Variable selection methods include *forward*, *backward*, and *stepwise* techniques, where stepwise can be considered a hybrid version of forward and backward. Stepwise and selection algorithms often go by the name of *wrapper models* in the data-mining literature ([Aggarwal, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000005)). Versions of backward elimination algorithms are sometimes referred to as *recursive feature elimination algorithms* in the data and machine learning environments, and though there are distinctions between these types of algorithms, they pretty much get at the same thing in the end.

Other techniques include *all-possible-subsets*, *forward-stagewise regression*, and others. Both ridge and lasso regression, as we will see in the next chapter, can be considered in some sense variable selection techniques as well, especially the lasso since coefficients are explicitly driven to values of zero, while for ridge coefficients they are simply “shrunk” toward zero. For this reason, ridge is often not considered a “pure” variable selection procedure. However, nothing inhibits the user from simply dropping shrunken coefficients as they near zero or are much less in magnitude than other coefficients in the model. We will return to this discussion when we discuss both techniques in the following chapter.

In typical forward regression, predictors are entered based on some entry criteria, such as statistical significance (e.g., attaining *p* < 0.05). The procedure halts when no more predictors reach that criterion. In backward regression, all predictors begin in the model and are removed once they no longer reach *p* < 0.05 (or whatever level one chooses). Stepwise regression is typically a mix of both forward and backward approaches; however there are many stepwise programs and packages and it behooves the reader to study the details of the package they are using to clearly understand what the stepwise program does or does not do. The algorithms in various packages can become quite complex, which if not understood, provides ample opportunity for drawing false substantive conclusions from the stepwise results.

### 5.9.1 Forward, Backward, and Stepwise in R

There are several ways (and packages) for conducting forward, backward, or stepwise regressions in R. Many packages and routines will often combine routines, so as already emphasized, it is essential that one thoroughly familiarize oneself with the given package to know exactly what is being computed.

For our example here, we feature the *mtcars* data in R once more, on which we conduct both a *forward* and *backward* stepwise regression. Recall that the *mtcars* data contains numerous vehicle specs such as gas mileage (mpg), number of cylinders (cyl), and displacement (disp), among other characteristics of vehicles. We will use the *StepReg* package (Li et al., [2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000219)) to carry out stepwise regression:240

```
> library(StepReg)
> data(mtcars)
> head(mtcars)
```

 
|  || Mpg || cyl || disp || hp || drat || wt || qsec || vs || am || gear || carb |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mazda RX4 || 21.0 || 6 || 160 || 110 || 3.90 || 2.620 || 16.46 || 0 || 1 || 4 || 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mazda RX4 Wag || 21.0 || 6 || 160 || 110 || 3.90 || 2.875 || 17.02 || 0 || 1 || 4 || 4 |
| Datsun 710 || 22.8 || 4 || 108 || 93 || 3.85 || 2.320 || 18.61 || 1 || 1 || 4 || 1 |
| Hornet 4 Drive || 21.4 || 6 || 258 || 110 || 3.08 || 3.215 || 19.44 || 1 || 0 || 3 || 1 |
| Hornet Sportabout || 18.7 || 8 || 360 || 175 || 3.15 || 3.440 || 17.02 || 0 || 0 || 3 || 2 |
| Valiant || 18.1 || 6 || 225 || 105 || 2.76 || 3.460 || 20.22 || 1 || 0 || 3 || 1 |

```
> formula <- mpg ~ .
```

In specifying mpg ~., we are implicitly requesting modeling mpg as a function of all other variables. We will now specify that we wish to conduct a stepwise, specifically:

```
> fit <- stepwise(formula = formula,
+ data = mtcars,
+ type = “linear”,
+ strategy = c(“forward”, “bidirection”, “backward”),
+ metric = c(“AIC”, “BIC”, “SL”))
> fit
```

We have requested above that forward, bidirection, and backward elimination be performed, and hence our output will be quite long. We have also requested AIC, BIC, and SL as the metrics for evaluating the regressions, where “SL” corresponds to “significance level.” Indeed, if we choose to look at the results from the stepwise (fit), we will get a listing of the model selection variables in the data set that is quite long and provides much detail. To at least illustrate some of the output, we obtain a listing of the AIC values under the *forward* algorithm ([Table 5.1](#c5.xhtml#t5.1)):

 *Table 5.1* AIC Value for Steps Using a Forward Algorithm[Return to text.⏎](#c5.xhtml#re_t5.1) 

 
| Summary of selection process under forward with AIC  |
| --- |
| Step || EffectEntered || NumberParams || AIC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 1 || 1 || 149.94345 |
| 2 || wt || 2 || 107.217363 |
| 3 || cyl || 3 || 97.197999 |
| 4 || hp || 4 || 96.664562 |

We can see that at step 4, AIC is the smallest under a forward algorithm. Recall that, typically, the smaller the AIC, the better. The reason we say “typically” here is because recall that AIC can also at times be defined such that increasing values of AIC suggest a better-fitting model. *Always check how AIC is being defined in your specific software application or package before concluding what denotes an increasingly better value*.241

The benefit to using *StepReg* is that we can also visualize the results of the selection process where in [Figure 5.2](#c5.xhtml#f5.2) is shown the effect of *variable removal* (e.g., (-)cyl) on each of AIC, BIC, and SL, this time resulting from the *backward* algorithm:

![Figure 5.2 AIC, BIC, and SL as a function of step, where the effect of removing variables (e.g., (-)cyl) is displayed resulting from the backward algorithm.Return to text.⏎](images/fig5.2.jpg)

*Figure 5.2* AIC, BIC, and SL as a function of step, where the effect of removing variables (e.g., (-)cyl) is displayed resulting from the backward algorithm.[Return to text.⏎](#c5.xhtml#re_f5.2)

```
> plot(fit)
```

We see from the plot that at each step of the function, AIC, BIC, and SL drop in value as predictors are removed. The plot is a powerful way of visualizing the selection process. We see that SL drops rather dramatically toward the latter steps. BIC follows an almost perfect negative linear path across steps.

In Python, forward and stepwise regression can be performed using sklearn’s `SequentialFeatureSelector()` though not demonstrated here. For details, see Python’s sklearn site.

## 5.10 Mediated and Moderated Regression Models

Mediation has a relatively long history in statistics and has been motivated primarily by the substantive interests of social scientists, primarily psychologists. Despite its popularity and hype in 242some fields, it is important to understand what statistical mediation *can* vs. *cannot* do. Moderation, on the other hand, is most generally simply another word for *interaction*. In ANOVA-type models, we usually refer to such as interactions, whereas in regression models it has come to be known as moderation. It is vitally important to realize at the outset that *mediation and moderation do not, by themselves, imply a physical process*. That is, conducting a test of statistical mediation and concluding *Z mediates the relationship between X and Y* is only necessarily true *statistically*; it is not true *substantively* unless one has a substantive rationale or argument outside of the statistical model for inferring such a mediational process. There are countless published articles, even in “high impact factor” journals, where researchers conclude a mediational process simply based on *statistical* mediation, which exemplifies one of many philosophical and methodological abuses of statistics. We revisit and discuss this issue more extensively later.

### 5.10.1 Statistical Mediation

We purposely title this section by the name of *statistical* mediation for the reason that, as mentioned, far too often researchers tend to believe that if they apply a mediation model to data, it can thereby “extract” a mediational *process*. This is simply not the case. In addressing this important issue, let’s first very briefly survey how mediation (and moderation) is defined in the literature. For example, [Little et al. (2007, p. 207)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000225) offer the following definition and distinction:

> Generally speaking, a mediator can be thought of as the carrier or transporter of information along the causal chain of effects. A moderator, on the other hand, is the changer of a relationship in a system.

Pearl ([2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000284), pp. 1–2) claims, “Scientifically, mediation tells us “how nature works” and, practically, it enables us to predict behavior under a rich variety of conditions and interventions.”

The classic mediation model is diagrammed in [Figure 5.3](#c5.xhtml#f5.3), where X is the predictor, Y is the response, and M is the mediator.

![Figure 5.3 Classic mediation model where “M” is a mediator of the relationship between X and Y.Return to text.⏎](images/fig5.3.jpg)

*Figure 5.3* Classic mediation model where “M” is a mediator of the relationship between X and Y.[Return to text.⏎](#c5.xhtml#re_f5.3)

The conditions for “classic” or traditional mediation typically include the following ([MacKinnon et al., 2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000232)):

1.  1\. *X* should bear a relationship to *Y*.
2.  2\. *X* should bear a relationship to *M*.
3.  3\. *M* should be related to *Y* when both *X* and *M* are predictors of *Y*.
4.  4\. The relationship of *X* to *Y* should *diminish* (in absolute value) when *M* is included in the model, presumably as a result of *M* “taking up” the correlation that would have otherwise been “transmitted” (in necessarily some *statistical* sense only) from *X* to *Y*.243

A more complex combination of mediator models is illustrated in [Figure 5.4](#c5.xhtml#f5.4) where we now have three mediators, *z*[1], *z*[2], and *z*[3], and where *ε*[1], *ε*[2], and *ε*[3] are errors.

![Figure 5.4 A three-mediator model. Used with permission of Springer Nature BV, from The Causal Mediation Formula—A Guide to the Assessment of Pathways and Mechanisms by Judea Pearl, © 2012; permission conveyed through Copyright Clearance Center, Inc.Return to text.⏎](images/fig5.4.jpg)

*Figure 5.4* A three-mediator model. Used with permission of Springer Nature BV, from The Causal Mediation Formula—A Guide to the Assessment of Pathways and Mechanisms by Judea Pearl, © 2012; permission conveyed through Copyright Clearance Center, Inc.[Return to text.⏎](#c5.xhtml#re_f5.4)

While including more than a single mediator may seem initially a good idea, it comes with many caveats. The models are only as valid as the assumptions imposed on those models. Indeed, as again noted by Pearl ([2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000283), pp. 2–3), whom we paraphrase:

> The validity of these two methods depends of course on the *assumption* \[added emphasis\] that the error terms … are uncorrelated, otherwise, some of the structural parameters would produce biased results. In randomized trials, where error can be identified with the randomization device, we are assured that error is uncorrelated with other errors and so the regressional estimates will be unbiased … However, randomization does not remove error from e2 and e3.

There is no end to how complex we can formulate a mediation model. For example, [Figure 5.5](#c5.xhtml#f5.5) features a mediation model with a confounder that predicts the treatment, mediator, and outcome. Other than the confounder, the model is a classic three-variable mediation model.

![Figure 5.5 Mediation model with confounder(s).Return to text.⏎](images/fig5.5.jpg)

*Figure 5.5* Mediation model with confounder(s).[Return to text.⏎](#c5.xhtml#re_f5.5)

Other than for rather simple mediation models, models such as these are often best analyzed as *structural equation models*, and hence we will revisit them to some degree later in the book when we survey SEM models in more detail. Estimation in mediation models includes the traditional *coefficient product estimator* ([Hayes, 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000147)). Simulation-based estimators have also been proposed as well as semi-parametric estimators such as the *inverse probability weighting estimator* ([Zhang, 2442023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000403)). The *multiply-robust estimator*, as well as the *double-machine learning for mediation estimator*, have also been proposed. For details, see [Abécassis et al. (2023)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000002).

### 5.10.2 Statistical Moderation

As mentioned at the outset of our discussion of mediation and moderation, moderation analysis is nothing more than analyzing interactions. That is, quite literally, “moderation” is a fancy word for statistical *interaction*. When you conduct an analysis of variance and model the interaction, you are performing a moderation analysis. However, there is so much “hype” about moderation analyses in fields such as psychology and others that it is often advertised as being able to accomplish so much more than it can. Again, to reiterate, nowhere in the *statistical* procedure of moderation analysis is anything necessarily “moderating” anything else in a *physical* or *substantive* sense unless the variables you are working with and your theory suggest such a “physical” process. *Statistical moderation alone does not afford that process in any way whatsoever*. In fact, in many cases, statistical moderation can be rather anticlimactic.

As a basic example of moderation, consider the plot in [Figure 5.6](#c5.xhtml#f5.6).

![Figure 5.6 Illustration of moderation for two groups; slopes are nonparallel.Return to text.⏎](images/fig5.6.jpg)

*Figure 5.6* Illustration of moderation for two groups; slopes are nonparallel.[Return to text.⏎](#c5.xhtml#re_f5.6)

As a result of the slopes being different (*nonparallel*), we have a moderation effect. Of course, in the *sample*, there will virtually *always be a moderation effect*. Do you really think slopes could ever be *exactly* parallel *in the sample*? The real question is whether such an effect can be inferred toward the population, which is the inferential question we are ultimately interested in. We will survey an example of moderation later in the chapter using software.

### 5.10.3 Moderated Mediation

Just as in the test for any other interaction effect, one may be interested in learning whether an entire mediation model holds across values of a moderating variable. More specifically, we may be interested in learning whether an *indirect effect* (i.e., the effect of going “through” the mediator, so to speak) is conditional on values of a moderating variable. This is referred to as *moderated mediation* and more generally is found under the name of *conditional process models* ([Hayes, 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000147)), or again, the search for *conditional indirect effects*. That is, the indirect (or “mediating”) effect is conditional upon some other third variable, illustrated in [Figure 5.7](#c5.xhtml#f5.7).245

![Figure 5.7 Three-variable mediation model conditional upon w.Return to text.⏎](images/fig5.7.jpg)

*Figure 5.7* Three-variable mediation model conditional upon *w*.[Return to text.⏎](#c5.xhtml#re_f5.7)

We see in [Figure 5.7](#c5.xhtml#f5.7) the classic three-variable mediation model, however conditional upon the *w* variable as indicated by the *x**w* interaction. Note that both *w* and the interaction term *x**w* are included due to the *principle of marginality* ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)) which holds that an interaction term should not be included without also including the individual terms that make up the interaction, which in this case is simply the *w* variable.

A *mediated moderation* model is when an interaction between an independent variable and a moderator variable “affects” (statistically) a mediator variable that in turn “affects” (again, only necessarily *statistically*) the outcome variable. According to Hayes ([2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000147), p. 465), “mediated moderation is neither interesting nor meaningful” and ends up being mathematically equivalent under most conditions to moderated mediation. As such, Hayes recommends that questions of mediated moderation should be recast as *moderated mediational hypotheses*.

### 5.10.4 Mediation in Python

Mediation and moderation analyses are probably best left to R or similar software specifically designed for statistics (e.g., SPSS also has macros devoted to performing mediation). However, Python does afford some capabilities for this as well. The following is an example of mediation using the *pingouin* package ([Vallat, 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000371)) in Python. The pingouin package is an open-source package originally written in Python 3 and uses primarily *pandas* and *numpy*.

We first install pingouin via *pip* and then import the mediation\_analysis function:246

```
pip install pingouin
from pingouin import mediation_analysis, read_dataset
df = read_dataset(‘mediation’)
df
Out[216]:
```

 
|  || X || M || Y || Mbin || Ybin || W1 || W2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 || 6 || 5 || 6 || 0 || 1 || 0.0 || 1.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 7 || 5 || 5 || 1 || 0 || 0.1 || 1.0 |
| 2 || 7 || 7 || 4 || 0 || 0 || 0.2 || 1.0 |
| 3 || 8 || 4 || 8 || 0 || 1 || 0.3 || 1.0 |
| 4 || 4 || 3 || 5 || 0 || 1 || 0.4 || 1.0 |
| .. || .. || .. || .. || ... || ... || ... || ... |
| 95 || 5 || 2 || 2 || 1 || 0 || 1.0 || 1.0 |
| 96 || 8 || 4 || 1 || 1 || 0 || 1.0 || 1.0 |
| 97 || 7 || 4 || 5 || 0 || 0 || 1.0 || 1.0 |
| 98 || 2 || 2 || 1 || 0 || 1 || 1.5 || 1.0 |
| 99 || 5 || 4 || 5 || 0 || 0 || 2.0 || 1.0 |

In the following, we will designate X as the predictor, M as the mediator, and Y as the response. We set the significance level (alpha) at 0.05:

```
mediation_analysis(data=df, x=‘X’, m=‘M’, y=‘Y’, alpha = 0.05, seed = 42)
Out[214]:
```

 
|  || path || coef || se || pval || CI\[2.5%\] || CI\[97.5%\] || sig |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 || M ~ X || 0.561015 || 0.094480 || 4.391362e-08 || 0.373522 || 0.748509 || Yes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || Y ~ M || 0.654173 || 0.085831 || 1.612674e-11 || 0.483844 || 0.824501 || Yes |
| 2 || Total || 0.396126 || 0.111160 || 5.671128e-04 || 0.175533 || 0.616719 || Yes |
| 3 || Direct || 0.039604 || 0.109648 || 7.187429e-01 || \-0.178018 || 0.257226 || No |
| 4 || Indirect || 0.356522 || 0.083313 || 0.000000e+00 || 0.219818 || 0.537654 || Yes |

We can see from the above that while the direct path is not statistically significant, the *total* and *indirect* paths are. The *direct effect* is from the exogenous variable to the endogenous one, which for our data is from X to Y. The *indirect effect* is the pathway through the mediator. The *total effect* is the sum of the direct and indirect effects.

The pingouin package can also easily fit mediation with binary variables as well as models with multiple mediators. Mediation models can also be fit with statsmodels.stats.mediation(), though we do not explore these usages here. The package *moderate.mediation* in R ([Qin, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000293)) can be used to fit rather complex mediation models and comes highly recommended for moderated mediation modeling. The package *mediation* (Tingley et al., [2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000360)) also fits a variety of mediation models. Sensitivity analyses for mediation effects can also be performed. See Imai et al. ([2010](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000164)) for details. As a summary on mediation and moderation analyses in R, the package *mediation* (Tingley et al., [2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000360)) is the “go-to” source for all types of mediation analyses using R.

## 5.11 Further Directions and a Final Word of Warning on Mediation and Moderation

Mediation and moderation in statistics is an enormous topic with books devoted to these methods (e.g., see [Hayes, 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000147)). Recent work on mediation includes that of [Ge et al. (2023)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000124) who develop a reinforcement learning framework for *dynamic mediation analysis*. In many cases, treatments are assigned over time and this work seeks to evaluate mediators along a longitudinal trajectory as well as sequential decision-making over an infinite number of decision points. [Pearl (2012)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000283) critically assesses the habitual way of performing mediation, which assumes linearity and independence of errors, and proposes an alternative approach for modeling nonlinear relationships, which includes that with categorical variables. Judd et al. ([2001](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000178)) give details on estimating mediation and moderation models in within-subjects designs.

As mentioned at the outset of our discussion, however, mediation and moderation, if used and more importantly, *interpreted* incorrectly, can do more harm than good. Far too often in the social sciences are mediational and moderation processes concluded simply because statistical evidence supports it.

To reiterate, and as any good methodologist or philosopher of science will tell you, *no statistical method, whatever the kind, can alone indicate a physical process* (Fiedler et al., [2011](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000098)). The problem with using these “power” and “action” words to describe statistical processes is *dangerous*. “Causal modeling” as mediational analysis has sometimes come to be known, is not causal at all unless there is a substantive *context* to induce such causality. There is absolutely nothing wrong with conducting a mediation or moderation analysis, but if more researchers actually understood how *little* it truly tells them about their data instead of recklessly imposing *powers* on their variables that they do not 247*necessarily* possess, the methods would probably be used less than they currently are. *It behooves all researchers to understand the limitations of the statistical procedures they use before using and interpreting them on empirical data. Researchers regularly “empower” statistics to say much more from their data than they are able. Mathematical and statistical models are first and foremost abstractions; they have no knowledge of your empirical observations, they are simply using those numbers as inputs in their computations. Whether the statistical model says anything substantive about those empirical observations is a much more complex scientific and philosophical issue than simply fitting the statistical model. Narratives rarely correspond to “reality” one-to-one.*

## 5.12 Principal Components Regression

Recall that in the typical multiple regression problem, a linear combination of predictors *x*[1] through *x*[*p*] is sought such that it maximizes the correlation with the response variable, *y*. This maximum correlation is expressed via fit statistics such as *R*². As we know already, multicollinearity can have detrimental effects on a regression model. Having several predictors that have high correlations with one another can, for one, *inflate standard errors*. Inflated standard errors reduce statistical power for detecting effects and hence make it more difficult to reject null hypotheses for predictors.

Statistical issues are not the only reason for disliking collinearity. From a scientific point of view, having correlated predictors is a waste of resources. For example, recording your birth date in months and then again in days is a waste of time, as one variable essentially does the job of two. They are essentially duplicates of one another. More precisely, one variable is a linear combination of the other. In such a case, the most likely solution is to simply drop one of the variables from the regression and simplify the model, both to eliminate or reduce collinearity but also to substantively reduce the scientific complexity of the model.

There are alternatives to simply eliminating variables from the set of predictors, however. One relatively popular alternative approach to this problem is to reduce the dimensionality of *x*[1] through *x*[*p*] *before* making a prediction on *y*. Especially if *p* (the number of predictors) is very large, it may make more sense to transform *p* into a smaller number of *components* and then regress *y* onto this smaller number of components. *Principal components regression* attempts to do just this. To understand principal components regression, however, we must first get an idea of what *principal components analysis* is all about.

### 5.12.1 What Is Principal Components Analysis?

A more extensive discussion of principal components analysis (PCA) is reserved for later in the book where we discuss dimension-reduction techniques and manifold learning in more detail, devoting part of an entire chapter to the PCA technique. For now, we only survey the method briefly to learn how it serves the PCA regression technique.

Principal components analysis derives *orthogonal linear combinations* of the variables equal to the number of variables, such that successive linear combinations account for less and less variance in the observed variables. Recall that a linear combination is defined as248

  
*l*[*i*] = *a*[1]*y*[1] + *a*[2]*y*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *a*[*p*]*y*[*p*]  

That is, a linear combination is a *weighted sum of products*, where *a*[1] through *a*[*p*] are the weights applied to observed variables *y*[1] through *y*[*p*]. For our data on *x*[1], ..., *x*[*p*], the linear combination becomes

  
*z*[*i*] = *a*[1]*x*[1] + *a*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *a*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  

where now *z*[*i*] is the name of the linear combination and *x*[1] through *x*[*p*] are the observed variables. A principal component is a unique kind of linear combination such that the weights *a*[1] through *a*[*p*] correspond to values of allied eigenvectors extracted from an eigen analysis performed on the covariance or correlation matrix of variables *x*[1], ..., *x*[*p*]. Hence, if we denote the weights *a*[1] through *a*[*p*] by *e*[1] through *e*[*p*] to represent eigenvector weights, the first principal component is defined as

  
*z*[1] = *e*[1]*x*[1] + *e*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *e*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  
(5.31)

The first principal component accounts for the most variance in the observed variables. The second principal component accounts for the second-most variance in the observed variables but is orthogonal to the first. The goal of PCA is to capture as much variance in the first few components as possible to account for the variance in the set of observed variables. *Principal components regression* uses the first few principal components as predictors in a least-squares sense. In this way, the number of components retained in the PCR (*principal components regression*) can be likened to a *tuning parameter* ([Boehmke & Greenwell, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000033)). As we will see when we survey methods such as ridge and lasso regression, tuning parameters are useful in controlling the balance between the variance and bias of a statistical learning method and are useful in selecting a “best” model from a wider set of possibilities.

Principal components regression, useful as it may at first appear, makes one important assumption that may with empirical data not always hold. By regressing *y* on the set of components, *we are implicitly assuming that the directions of most variance in* *x*[1] *through* *x*[*p*] *are those same directions that are associated with* *y*. While this assumption may not always hold, it is often considered a useful approximation for most data and PCA regression often gives reasonable results ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)). As more precisely stated by [Izenman (2008, p.132)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167):

> The extraction of the principal components is accomplished without any reference to the output variable *Y*, we have no reason to expect *Y*to be highly correlated with any of the principal components, in particular those having the largest eigenvalues. Indeed, *Y* may actually have its highest correlation with one of the last few principal components or even the last one.

Or, as even better elucidated by [Artigue and Smith (2018, p. 9)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000014):

> The promise of principal components regression is that it is an efficient way of selecting a relatively small number of explanatory variables from a vast array of possibilities, based on the correlations among the explanatory variables. The problem is that the eigenvector weights on the candidate variables have nothing to do with their relationship to the variable being predicted. Mildly important variables may be given larger weights than important variables. Nuisance variables may be given larger weights than the true explanatory variables. The coefficients of the true explanatory variables may be given the wrong signs.249

Even though principal components regression provides a simple way to use less than the full spectrum of predictors for the problem, it should *not* be regarded as a feature or variable selection method because of the lack of guarantee that the directions that best explain the predictors will also be the best directions to use for predicting the response. In fact, it is entirely possible to have variables only weakly related to the response, yet as the number of these variables increases, *R*\-squared of 1.0 is nonetheless approached. In general, adding useless predictors, though resulting in an increase in dimensionality, will do so at the risk of overfitting and an increase in test error.

A more in-depth discussion of the above problems can be found in [Jolliffe (1982)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000408). The key takeaway point is that *though PCA regression is guaranteed to derive orthogonal components that maximize variance in the set of predictors, this will not necessarily be equivalent to maximizing* *R*²*between* *y* *and those components that account for the most variance in* *x*[1] *through* *x*[*p*]. For this reason, PCA regression should not be considered a variable selection technique ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)) in the same spirit as techniques such as *best-subsets* or *forward regression*. PCA regression is also not scale-invariant, and hence standardization of predictors is typically (though not *always*) recommended.

### 5.12.2 PCA Regression and Singularity

As we have seen, PCA regression can be useful in situations where we wish to reduce the dimensionality of the predictors before using resulting components as predictors of a response. More to the point, PCA regression can be useful when predictors are highly correlated with one another.

There is another instance where PCA regression may be especially useful, and that is when the matrix of predictors, *X*, is *singular* and hence *ill-conditioned*. Recall that for a singular matrix *X*, it is implied that one row or column is a linear combination of one or more rows or columns. This condition always implies that the determinant of the matrix will equal zero, which implies the inverse of *X* cannot be computed. In such a case, one can substitute a *generalized inverse* when computing least-squares estimates. There are many generalized inverses, but the most common is that of the *Moore-Penrose inverse*, the use of which will yield the generalized inverse regression estimator ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)).

The number of components to keep in PCA regression on the side of *X* can be determined by *Kaiser’s rule*, which says to keep all those components with eigenvalues greater than 1 for the correlation matrix, or by using a cross-validation technique ([Wold, 1978](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000390)). The substantive meaning of derived components can also play a significant role in their selection contingent on whether or not the scientific nature of components matters to the scientist.

## 5.13 Partial Least-Squares Regression

Whereas principal components regression only uses *x*[1] through *x*[*p*] in its construction of components, *partial least-squares* seeks out dimensionality or directions in the data that incorporates both the predictors *and* the response variable. That is, the components found in *x*[1] through *x*[*p*] are not just relevant to the predictor side, but are also relevant to the response *y*. Partial least-squares, or “PLS” for short, is often considered a supervised alternative to principal components regression ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)) since PLS will incorporate the response when determining the best “directions.”

As well described by Izenman,

> PLS searches for a set of components (called latent vectors) that performs a simultaneous decomposition of *X* and *Y* with the constraint that these components explain as much as possible of the covariance between *X* and *Y*. In this manner, the derived variables in PLS are constructed in such a way as to retain most of the information in the *X*[1] through *X*[*p*] variables and is typically obtained via algorithm rather than optimization procedure ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 133).

To unpack what PLS actually accomplishes, recall once more what a linear combination looks like in the typical PCA:

  
*z*[1] = *e*[1]*x*[1] + *e*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *e*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  

In PLS, the coefficients in *z*[1], those of *e*[1], etc., are set to the coefficients resulting from a simple linear regression of *y* on *x* for each predictor. This coefficient (e.g., for *e*[1]) is proportional to the correlation between *y* and *x*[*j*], the given predictor we are considering. That is, in computing the first component, variables *x* that are most strongly related to *y* (in a univariate sense) receive the most weight.

To obtain the second component, *z*[2], each of the variables for *z*[1] are first adjusted by regressing each variable on *z*[1] and taking residuals of what is “left over.” If the first component accounts for all the information in the predictors, the residual will equal zero. More than likely, the first 253component will not account for all information, and hence the residual will be greater than zero. The second component *z*[2] is computed using these residuals, which are *orthogonal* to the first component. The iterative approach continues for ensuing directions (i.e., components) of *z*.

It is clear then why the method is referred to as *partial* least-squares. It is so because it capitalizes on residuals that are orthogonal to previous component values. Hence, if PLS could talk, it would say, “After the predictive part is removed (or ‘partialled’), let’s now regress the new component on what is left over.” Partial least-squares, as is true of principal components regression, is not scale-invariant, and hence standardizing predictors is often advised. However, as noted elsewhere in the book, the decision to standardize should not be made without careful consideration of the nature (and specifically, *scales*) of the variables under study.

### 5.13.2 Partial Least-Squares in Python

Partial least-squares regression can be fit in Python using PLSRegression. The following is a simple example with easy data:

```
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression
X = [[0., 0., 1.], [1., 0., 0.], [2., 2., 2.], [2., 5., 4.]]
Y = [[0.1, -0.2], [0.9, 1.1], [6.2, 5.9], [11.9, 12.3]]
```

We will request a 2-component solution:

```
pls2 = PLSRegression(n_components=2)
pls2.fit(X, Y)
```

We now obtain predicted values based on the two-component solution:

```
Out[5]: PLSRegression()
Y_pred = pls2.predict(X)
Y_pred
Out[7]:
array([[ 0.26087869, 0.15302213],
       [ 0.60667302, 0.45634164],
       [ 6.46856199, 6.48931562],
       [11.7638863, 12.00132061]])
```

The predicted values on each component extracted above are to be read *vertically* in a column. That is, the first component has predicted values of 0.26, 0.60, 6.46, and 11.76.

## 5.14 Multivariate Reduced-Rank Regression

Multivariate reduced-rank regression ([Izenman, 1975](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000166)) is a very general framework for the multivariate regression model and we mention it here only for pedagogical inclusion into the general regression framework. The classic multivariate linear regression model can be stated in its most general way as

  
*Y* = *μ* + *C**X* + *ε*  
(5.32)

where *C* is a matrix of regression coefficients or parameters on which there exists a set of linear constraints. These linear constraints in the case of reduced rank for *C* imply that *C* = *A**B*, where both *A* and *B* are *nonunique full-rank matrices* ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 177), such that we can rewrite the classical multivariate model as

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {Y = \\mu + {CX} + \\varepsilon} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\mu + \\left( {AB} \\right)X + \\varepsilon} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(5.33)

where in (5.33), we have simply substitued *A**B* for *C*. That is, the reduced-rank multivariate model generalizes the classical multivariate model by, as summarized by [Izenman (2008)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), relaxing the implicit constraint on the rank of *C*, which by consequence, allows for dimension reduction. The theme is already familiar by now; a matrix of less than full rank may very well have underlying 260dimensionality “disguised” within it. *By estimating* *A* *and* *B**, we effectively “treat” the reduced-rank condition of* *C*. For a proof of why *A* and *B* are nonunique, see Izenman ([2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 177).

Several statistical models, including *principal components analysis*, *exploratory factor analysis*, *canonical correlation*, *discriminant analysis*, and even *neural networks*, can be conceptualized as special cases of the reduced-rank multivariate model. What is more, the Gauss-Markov theorem for regression discussed earlier in the book generalizes to the multivariate reduced-rank counterpart. Profile analysis and time series can also be conceptualized within the reduced-rank multivariate model.

## 5.15 Canonical Correlation

The canonical correlation is the bivariate correlation between sets of variables. It is, like Pearson *r*, a *linear* correlation. It is the linear correlation between linear combinations of variables. That is, for linear combinations *l*[1] and *l*[2], the correlation between them is given by:

  
$$r\_{l\_{1},l\_{2}} = \\frac{{cov}\_{l\_{1},l\_{2}}}{\\sqrt{s\_{l\_{1}}^{2}s\_{l2}^{2}}}$$  
(5.34)

where *s*[*l*[1]]² and *s*[*l*2]² are variances of the respective linear combinations ([Denis, 2021a](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000087)) and *c**o**v*[*l*[1], *l*[2]] is the covariance between linear combinations *l*[1] and *l*[2]. The nonzero squared population canonical correlations are the nonzero eigenvalues *λ*[*i*] of the following ([Bilodeau and Brenner, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000030), p. 177; [Rencher and Christensen, 2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295), p. 387):

  
*Σ*[*y**y*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*y**x*]^()*Σ*[*x**x*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*x**y*]^()  

As a result of the eigenvalues providing the *squared* canonical correlations, the *unsquared* canonical correlations are thus equal to the *square root* of the eigenvalues, that is, $\\sqrt{\\lambda\_{i}}$.

How are the squared canonical correlations found? There are a few ways of obtaining them, but perhaps the easiest way is through an eigen analysis of *Σ*[*y**y*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*y**x*]^()*Σ*[*x**x*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*x**y*]^(), where such represents the matrix being analyzed in *A* in the classic form of the eigen equality:

  
*A**x* = *λ**x*  

Recall that to find *λ* we set |*A*−*λ**I*|=0, where now instead of simply a matrix *A*,

  
*A* = *Σ*[*y**y*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*y**x*]^()*Σ*[*x**x*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*x**y*]^()  

and so we have

  
|*A*−*λ**I*|=0       →       |*Σ*[*y**y*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*y**x*]^()*Σ*[*x**x*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*x**y*]^()−*λ**I*|=0  
(5.35)

and hence since |*A*−*λ**I*|*x*\=0, where *x* is an eigenvector associated with *λ*, the respective eigenvectors *a* and *b* of *Σ*[*y**y*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*y**x*]^()*Σ*[*x**x*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*x**y*]^() are found by261

  
(*Σ*[*y**y*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*y**x*]^()*Σ*[*x**x*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*x**y*]^()−*λ**I*)*a* = 0  
(5.36)

and

  
(*Σ*[*y**y*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*y**x*]^()*Σ*[*x**x*]^( − 1)*Σ*[*x**y*]^()−*λ**I*)*b* = 0  
(5.37)

That is, the first linear combination is now *l*[1] = *a*′*x* and the second *l*[2] = *b*′*y*. Corresponding canonical variates for each dimension are *uncorrelated*, and each subsequent canonical dimension extracted is uncorrelated to previous dimensions. Izenman ([2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 216) summarizes canonical correlation:

> The CVA technique ensures that every bit of correlation is wrung out of the original X and Y variables and deposited in an orderly fashion into pairs of new variables … which have a special correlation structure. If the notion of correlation is regarded as the primary determinant of information in the system of variables, then CVA is a major tool for reducing the dimensionality of the original two sets of variables.

Not surprisingly, canonical correlation can be interpreted as a special case of the aforementioned reduced-rank regression ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). Variations of canonical correlation include *deep variational canonical correlation* (Wang et al., [2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000380)) that extends and generalizes linear canonical correlation to nonlinear models within a deep neural network parameterization. *Probabilistic canonical correlation* is discussed by [Bach and Jordan (2006)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000017). *Tensor canonical correlation* has also been proposed, where each observation in data consists of multidimensional arrays (tensors) (Min et al., [2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000252)). Relationships between multivariate reduced rank, PCA, and CVA can be found in [Izenman (1975)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000166).

### 5.15.1 Canonical Correlation in R

The package *CCA* in R ([González & Déjean, 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000130)) can be used for canonical correlation as well as a version of regularized canonical correlation. The package also allows for numerous graphical visualizations of canonical correlation. Below is an example adapted from the package’s documentation on the *nutrimouse* data, where gene data is correlated to lipids on a group of mice:

```
> library(CCA)
> data(nutrimouse)
```
