# 6 Regularization Methods in RegressionRidge, Lasso, and Elastic Net

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-9](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-9)

In the previous chapter we provided an overview of simple and multiple linear regression methods. We saw that the estimator of choice was an unbiased one, that is, a “BLUE” estimator. The quality of being *unbiased* seemed like a desirable feature to possess. Indeed, from elementary statistics courses onward, students are regularly taught that an unbiased estimator is one of the most favorable qualities of an estimator, in addition to other characteristics such as consistency, sufficiency, etc.

In some cases, however, especially where the matrix of predictors is ill-conditioned (e.g., collinearity), it may be worthwhile to drop the requirement of an unbiased estimator and instead *adopt an estimator that is biased*. At first glance, this may seem statistically unintuitive and borderline reckless. To actually *prefer* a biased estimator seems to go against all essential statistical teaching for favoring unbiased estimators. However, as we will see, choosing a biased estimator in regression has the effect of driving coefficients of predictors toward or to 0, thus potentially de-emphasizing predictors that are not essential to the regression solution. By driving coefficients to or toward 0, using a biased estimator can facilitate variable selection in multiple regression. In fact, we will demonstrate in this chapter that the residual sums of squares of ordinary least-squares is nothing more than a special case of regularized regression for a specific choice of hyperparameter.

Three popular estimators that are known to regularize a model are the *ridge*, *lasso*, and *elastic net*. Before discussing each of these, a general and broad introduction and overview of the *principle of regularization* is in order. Regularization as a general concept is not exclusively associated with any particular estimator per se, and shows up in many different statistical and machine learning methods. That is, regularization is an *idea*, not any specific particular methodology. This point is perhaps the most important to understand as it concerns regularization.

## 6.1 The Concept of Regularization

The main idea of regularization is getting a “handle” on a model to simplify its complexity so that it potentially generalizes better to new test data and hence minimizes overfitting. Equivalently, we can say that the goal of regularization is to improve performance on the test set by adding a penalty to the training loss (Kroese et al., [2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000202)) so that the learner we do select is one that does not overfit on the training data and that generalizes relatively well on the test data. *Regularization is all about preventing overfitting and increasing generalizability*. It is often associated with so-called *shrinkage* and techniques such as ridge regression and the lasso, but it is important to understand that it is much more general and broader than this. One can regularize a model without implementing any specific algorithm. Regularization, the *concept* at least, is very simple and quite general.

To demonstrate the essence of regularization, consider an exceedingly simple example of regularization in the basic linear model:266

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*] + *ε*[*i*]  
(6.1)

The above models a linear relationship between response *y*[*i*] and predictor *x*[*i*]. But suppose the observed sample data exhibit nothing at all like a linear relationship. Suppose instead the plot of *y*[*i*] on *x*[*i*] is as depicted in [Figure 6.1](#c6.xhtml#f6.1), with a correlation close to 0.

![Figure 6.1 Arbitrary plot of data with estimated Pearson Product-Moment correlation equal to (approximately) 0.Return to text.⏎](images/fig6.1.jpg)

*Figure 6.1* Arbitrary plot of data with estimated Pearson Product-Moment correlation equal to (approximately) 0.[Return to text.⏎](#c6.xhtml#re_f6.1)

Now, consider if we fit the above linear model to this data. Would it fit well? No, and if it does not fit well, it likely will not *generalize* well to test data. To use statistical jargon, even a simple linear model on this data can be considered *overfitting*, and overfitting rarely leads to good generalizability. Hence, one solution is to simplify the model so that it no longer overfits and generalizes better. One way to simplify the model would be to simply constrain the slope parameter to equal 0, or equivalently, not estimate it:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {y\_{i} = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x\_{i} + \\varepsilon\_{i}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\beta\_{0} + \\left( 0 \\right)x\_{i} + \\varepsilon\_{i}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\beta\_{0} + \\varepsilon\_{i}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(6.2)

This “simpler” model is now just an estimate of the intercept (or “bias” term, to use neural network terminology) along with some error, *ε*[*i*]. Simple as this example may be, *we have just engaged in an act of regularization of a statistical model*. The effect of simplifying the model has another implication; it expresses our belief that the true function is much less complicated than the linear function in this case. [Hastie et al. (2009, p. 34)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145) describe this idea beautifully:

> Regularization methods, express our prior belief that the type of functions we seek exhibit a certain type of smooth behavior, and indeed can usually be cast in a Bayesian framework.267

Their point is that on a technical level, penalties (or *regularization*) reflect to some extent *prior belief*, which is a Bayesian idea. In our example of the line turned to intercept only, the penalty is implicit, and reflects our belief that the true function underlying the data is not as “complicated” as including the slope would suggest. It’s much simpler in that the intercept suffices to account for the true function. This is the *idea* or *spirit* of regularization.

> *Regularization can be very informal in practice and can be as simple as deciding to not model the slope in a simple linear regression problem. From a Bayesian point of view, we are imposing our belief that the true functional form underlying the data is simpler than hypothesizing a non-horizontal slope in the regression*.

### 6.1.1 Regularization in Regression and Beyond

Consider for a moment the extent to which the above basic and simple concept might generalize to other modeling activities and methods. For example, when we constrain a parameter estimate in structural equation modeling so as to not overfit and hence improve generalizability, we are, in effect, engaged in model regularization. Likewise, when we decide on a simpler principal component solution instead of a more complex one for the purpose of generalization (such as in *principal components regression*, for instance), we are also regularizing the model. As we will see later, there are a variety of ways of regularizing a neural network, perhaps the most obvious or natural way by reducing the number of hidden layers or the number of nodes. Even *early stopping* of the iterative algorithm in neural networks constitutes a simple way to regularize a neural network.

In general then, anytime a model or method is simplified in some sense, it denotes an act of regularizing that model if such is done in an effort for it to generalize better to test data. In terms of regression, there are three more advanced and common ways of imposing a regularization parameter that go beyond our simple example of constraining the slope above. These include *ridge*, *lasso*, and *elastic net* regression. With the “spirit” of regularization now in place, we now survey these methods.

## 6.2 Ridge Regression

We begin with *ridge regression* because it is among the oldest and most significant and influential of the regularization techniques. These techniques often fall under the umbrella of “shrinkage,” where partial regression coefficients are driven toward or to values of 0. At first glance, it may seem questionable why you might ever want to “shrink” coefficients toward 0, but in the end, shrunken coefficients can greatly simplify, and hence regularize, a model. The ridge penalty (or similar, such as the *lasso*) is also generally known as *weight decay* and the *L*[2] parameter norm penalty and ridge regression is commonly known as *Tikhonov regularization* in many circles ([Goodfellow et al., 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000131)). The lasso penalty is commonly known as *L*[1] regularization. Where the ridge penalty is in squared units, that is, a *quadratic* penalty, the lasso penalty is in absolute value units and is hence nonquadratic. The difference in penalties can have important consequences, especially for data in which the number of cases is greater than the number of variables. For an example of this latter point, see Hastie et al. ([2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 660). An advantage of *L*[1] penalization is that such allows for feature selection through driving weights *to*, rather than simply *toward*, 0.

Ridge (and lasso, elastic net) can be applied to situations where one might have literally thousands of predictors, and hence shrinking becomes a good strategy for simplifying the model and making it more interpretable. However, just as regularization is a wide-ranging concept, so is 268shrinkage. Shrinkage is merely one way in which a model can be regularized. Be sure this is clear, as there is often some degree of misunderstanding that regularization is *equivalent* to shrinkage, but this is not the case. Subset selection, stepwise regression, forward regression, and even less formal techniques are all methods designed to regularize a model as well. *A regularization method need not be associated with shrinkage*.

As mentioned, another benefit to shrinking parameter estimates relates to the ratio of sample size *n* to the number of predictors *p*. If *n* is not that much larger than *p*, there can result inflated variability in the least-squares fit, which can result in overfitting and possibly poor predictions of future observations not used in the training. What is more, if *p* > *n*, there is no longer at all a reliable least-squares estimate, since the variance will be infinite. Under this situation, there exists simply too many ways to project the response variable onto the set of predictors ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). Shrinkage is a tremendously valuable technique in such situations, since by shrinking the estimated coefficients in these cases, both when *n* = *p* and *p* > *n*, we can essentially reduce the variance at the cost of a negligible increase in bias.

### 6.2.1 Mathematics of Ridge Regression

To understand how ridge regression works, first recall ordinary least-squares regression. In least-squares regression, *β*[0], *β*[1], ..., *β*[*p*] are estimated via *β̂* = (*X*^(*T*)*X*)^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*y* such as to minimize the residual sums of squares (RSS) function,

  
$$RSS = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( {y\_{i} - \\beta\_{0} - {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{\\beta\_{j}x\_{ij}}}} \\right)^{2}}$$  
(6.3)

Not surprisingly, in ridge regression we also seek to minimize a quantity, but instead through the ordinary least-squares (OLS) estimator

  
*β̂* = (*X*^(*T*)*X*)^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*y*  
(6.4)

the ridge estimator adds a small quantity *λ* to the trace of *X*^(*T*)*X* such that

  
*β̂*[*r**i**d**g**e*] = (*X*^(*T*)*X*+*λ**I*)^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*y*  
(6.5)

The quantity minimized in ridge regression is similar to that in least-squares regression, but with an extra term added:

  
$$RSS = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( {y\_{i} - \\beta\_{0} - {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{\\beta\_{j}x\_{ij}}}} \\right)^{2}} + \\lambda{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}}$$  
(6.6)

Note that the only difference between the two quantities that are minimized is in (6.6), we have added the trailing term $\\lambda{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}}$, where *β*[*j*]² is simply the square of *β*[*j*] which we are already familiar. However, this quantity is “weighted” by *λ*, which is a *tuning parameter* that is imposed on the sum of the squared regression weights (i.e., $\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}$). Taken together, the trailing term $\\lambda{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}}$ is known as a *shrinkage penalty*. But why add this penalty term to the original residual sums of squares? What is the theoretical consequence of doing so? We explore that motivation now.269

### 6.2.2 Consequence of Ridge Estimator

We first note that the residual sums of squares for ridge regression reduces to ordinary least-squares regression when the value for the tuning parameter is equal to 0, since

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {RSS = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( {y\_{i} - \\beta\_{0} - {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{\\beta\_{j}x\_{ij}}}} \\right)^{2}} + \\lambda{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( {y\_{i} - \\beta\_{0} - {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{\\beta\_{j}x\_{ij}}}} \\right)^{2}} + 0{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( {y\_{i} - \\beta\_{0} - {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{\\beta\_{j}x\_{ij}}}} \\right)^{2}}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

For values of *λ* greater than 0, we see that it has the effect of increasing the value of the residual sums of squares, since we are then adding on at least *some* of $\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}$ to the least-squares residual.

Hence, ridge regression has the *apparent* effect of *increasing the residual sums of squares over what it would have been had we simply used least-squares regression*. This effect can seem contradictory to the purpose of conducting regression in the first place, as up to now, the goal in regression analysis has always been to *minimize* the objective function, which for classical least-squares has typically been the sum of squared errors. But now, with ridge regression, we are purposely adding on a “penalty” term that would seem to have the effect of *increasing* the sums of squared errors.

Why would we want to do this? We should have a good reason for doing so. It turns out that we do, and that is because we are *no longer using the best unbiased estimator.* Instead, ridge regression uses a *biased estimator*. Ridge regression has an explicit analytic solution, and so numerical methods are not required. Numerical methods will be required when we encounter a related technique called the *lasso*, as a closed-form solution for the lasso does not exist.

To understand why using a biased estimator may be advantageous over employing an unbiased one, we need to revisit the bias-variance tradeoff discussed earlier in the book.

### 6.2.3 Revisiting the Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Why Ridge Is Useful

To appreciate why ridge regression is effective and why using a biased estimator has an advantage over an unbiased one, we need to recall the bias-variance tradeoff concept:

  
*E*(*y*[0]−*f̂*(*x*[0]))²\= *V**a**r*(*f̂*(*x*[0])) + \[*B**i**a**s*\[*f̂*(*x*[0])\]\]² + *V**a**r*(*ε*)  
(6.7)

where *E*(*y*[0]−*f̂*(*x*[0]))² is the expected test mean squared error (i.e., MSE) at a given value of *x*, that of *x*[0]. The goal is to get *E*(*y*[0]−*f̂*(*x*[0]))² down or reduced. All else equal in the equality, we see that an increase in \[*B**i**a**s*\[*f̂*(*x*[0])\]\]² will have the effect of increasing *E*(*y*[0]−*f̂*(*x*[0]))², not decreasing it, again, *all else equal*. But here’s the key to understanding ridge regression: *not all else is equal*! For an increase in bias, the hope is that the variance of the function, that of *V**a**r*(*f̂*(*x*[0])), will decrease, which overall, for a constant *V**a**r*(*ε*) implies that *E*(*y*[0]−*f̂*(*x*[0]))² will decrease overall, not *increase*. Cutting right to the chase, *ridge regression works by purposely introducing bias into the estimator to offset a reduction in variance*, which we can summarize succinctly below:270

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} \\left. E\\left( {y\_{0} - \\hat{f}\\left( x\_{0} \\right)} \\right)^{2} = \\,\\downarrow Var\\left( {\\hat{f}\\left( x\_{0} \\right)} \\right) + \\uparrow\\left\\lbrack {Bias\\left\\lbrack {\\hat{f}\\left( x\_{0} \\right)} \\right\\rbrack} \\right\\rbrack^{2} + Var\\left( \\varepsilon \\right) \\right. \\\\ \\left. \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\downarrow E\\left( {y\_{0} - \\hat{f}\\left( x\_{0} \\right)} \\right)^{2} \\right. \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(6.8)

That is, the net effect of using a ridge estimator is desirable because it typically results in a smaller MSE on test data. This last point is important. *The smaller MSE is expected (and desired) on test data, not necessarily training data*.

When performing ridge regression, it is common to recommend standardization of input variables prior to carrying out the procedure, despite the recommendation not being accepted by everyone ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167); [Thisted, 1976](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000356)).

### 6.2.4 A Visual Look at Ridge Regression

Ridge regression can be understood visually and is often referred to as *penalized* least-squares regression. The original motivation for the ridge estimator, as discussed, was the observation made by [Hoerl and Kennard (1970)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000154) that potential instability in the OLS estimator could be tracked by adding a small constant *k* to the diagonal entries of *X*^(*T*)*X* before taking its inverse. This is what results in the *ridge estimator*, or sometimes called the *ridge rule*. This has the effect of regularizing ordinary least-squares by shrinking toward a multiple of the identity matrix ([Friedman, 1989](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000114)).

But what is the significance of adding this small constant *k*? To understand this, consider the depiction in [Figure 6.2](#c6.xhtml#f6.2) (left) featuring that of concentric ovals or ellipses for OLS, along with the search space for ridge estimators. We can see that the ridge estimate lies on the outer oval of the OLS ellipse, for both *β*[1] and *β*[2] (note that *β*[1] and *β*[2] are on the *x* and *y* axes, respectively).271

![Figure 6.2 Concentric RSS ellipses for OLS. The ridge estimate is a shrunken version of the OLS estimate moving coefficients toward 0 as a function of a tuning parameter (left). For a constant concentric ellipse, the ridge estimates for \\beta\_{1} and \\beta\_{2} lie as indicated in the plot where both coefficients \\beta\_{1} and \\beta\_{2} have been shrunken toward, but not to, 0. That is, where the ellipse “touches” the circle (it is a circle or “disk” and not another shape as a consequence of the ridge constraint region) is at a point on the circle unequal to 0. In contrast, the lasso solution (right) generates a shape of a diamond constraint region with sharp edges, and hence the lasso solution for \\beta\_{1} and \\beta\_{2} is more likely to have a given coefficient equal to 0.Return to text.⏎](images/fig6.2.jpg)

*Figure 6.2* Concentric RSS ellipses for OLS. The ridge estimate is a shrunken version of the OLS estimate moving coefficients toward 0 as a function of a tuning parameter (left). For a constant concentric ellipse, the ridge estimates for *β*[1] and *β*[2] lie as indicated in the plot where both coefficients *β*[1] and *β*[2] have been shrunken toward, but not to, 0. That is, where the ellipse “touches” the circle (it is a circle or “disk” and not another shape as a consequence of the ridge constraint region) is at a point on the circle unequal to 0. In contrast, the lasso solution (right) generates a shape of a diamond constraint region with sharp edges, and hence the lasso solution for *β*[1] and *β*[2] is more likely to have a given coefficient equal to 0.[Return to text.⏎](#c6.xhtml#re_f6.2)

The concentric ellipses in [Figure 6.2](#c6.xhtml#f6.2) represent possible and constant values of residual sums of squares for coefficients *β*[1] and *β*[2] for each ellipse. That is, no matter where RSS is on a given particular ellipse, it is the *same* value. Ellipses further away from the estimated coefficients have greater RSS. The OLS estimate (and corresponding RSS) in the plot is that RSS produced in regression for a combination of *β*[1] and *β*[2] values. Notice where the corresponding ridge estimate is; it is at a location where both *β*[1] and *β*[2] values have “shrunk” and are thus smaller than the OLS estimates (situated in the center ellipse), though typically not driven all the way to 0 since geometrically ridge features a *circular constraint*. That is, the circular constraint region is effectively the search space for ridge coefficients. That search is most likely to terminate on an edge of the circular region as shown in [Figure 6.2](#c6.xhtml#f6.2) (left). The lasso, on the other hand, features a *diamond* search space with sharp edges instead (as a consequence of the L1 penalty), which illustrates that coefficients will not only be driven smaller, but may be “shrunk” to 0. That is, the search space is this time within the diamond, which means RSS will intersect a hard edge of the diamond rather than a smooth part of the circular region as in ridge. Hence, the lasso coefficient “lands” on a 0, such as for *β*[1], as the first point that touches the lasso constraint region, that is, the lasso search space. For a more thorough discussion related to interpreting ridge (and lasso) regression this way, see James et al. ([2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)) for a deeper explanation of the geometry of ridge vs. lasso regression.

### 6.2.5 Ridge Regression in Python

Ridge regression can be performed very easily in Python. We create a simple example from *sklearn’s* ridge library:

```
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
import numpy as np
n_samples, n_features = 10, 5
```

Note from the above that we have designated the number of samples equal to 10 and the number of features equal to 5, which we confirm below:

```
n_samples

n_features
```

```
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
y = rng.randn(n_samples)
X = rng.randn(n_samples, n_features)
y
```

Note that the y values consist of a single vector, while the X values below comprise five different variables, each having ten cases (to generate standardized data, one can use StandardScaler(), more on this later):

```
Out[104]:
array([[ 0.14404357, 1.45427351, 0.76103773, 0.12167502, 0.44386323],
          [ 0.33367433, 1.49407907, -0.20515826, 0.3130677 ,-0.85409574],
          [-2.55298982, 0.6536186 , 0.8644362 ,-0.74216502, 2.26975462],
         [-1.45436567, 0.04575852, -0.18718385, 1.53277921, 1.46935877],
[ 0.15494743, 0.37816252, -0.88778575,-1.98079647,-0.34791215],
         [ 0.15634897, 1.23029068, 1.20237985,-0.38732682,-0.30230275],
         [-1.04855297,-1.42001794, -1.70627019, 1.9507754 ,-0.50965218],
         [-0.4380743 ,-1.25279536, 0.77749036,-1.61389785,-0.21274028],

         [ 0.42833187, 0.06651722, 0.3024719 ,-0.63432209,-0.36274117]])
clf = Ridge(alpha = 1.0)
clf.fit(X, y)
Out[146]: Ridge()
```

The default alpha in the above is 1.0. We could adjust it to other values. The smaller the value for alpha (*regularization* or *tuning* parameter), the more the solution will resemble ordinary least-squares regression. Recall that *for an alpha of 0, the two solutions will converge*. As sample size increases and alpha →0, both ridge and linear regression will also converge to generate the same output. With enough training data, the impact of regularization usually also becomes less prominent.

Now, let’s define some new data on each of the five features and predict a value based on that new data. The new data we will define by the name row:

```
row = [0, 2, 3, 4, 5]
yhat = clf.predict([row])
print(‘Predicted: %.3f’ % yhat)
Predicted: 4.059
```

We see that for the above new data on row, the predicted value for y is equal to 4.059.

We now cross-validate the solution. The RepeatedKFold cross-validator in Python performs *k*\-fold *n* times with different randomization in each repetition. We will request ten splits (i.e., “folds”) with three repeats:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedKFold
cv = RepeatedKFold(n_splits=10, n_repeats=3, random_state=1)
grid = dict()
grid[‘alpha’] = np.arange(0, 1, 0.01)
```

The above values from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.01 are values of the regularization parameter alpha. We will now run a *grid search* that scans the parameter values, finding the one that gives the smallest mean absolute error:273

```
search = GridSearchCV(clf, grid, scoring=‘neg_mean_absolute_error’, cv=cv, n_jobs=-1)
results = search.fit(X, y)
print(‘MAE: %.3f’ % results.best_score_)
MAE: -0.620
print(‘Config: %s’ % results.best_params_)
Config: {‘alpha’: 0.13}
```

Above, we see that the *negative mean absolute error* (i.e., MAE) is equal to −0.620 based on the most optimal parameter, equal to an alpha of 0.13.

Python also offers *Bayesian ridge regression*, where regularization parameters are updated systematically. To implement Bayesian ridge regression, see the BayesianRidge() function in Python. Also, for the example featured here, because we drew random data from a standard normal distribution (i.e., the data drawn were on the same *scale*), we did not *standardize* the resulting data to have a mean equal to 0 and standard deviation equal to one. However, such does not imply that standardization would not be worthwhile here. This is especially true in situations where variables occur naturally on *different scales* where one does not want the “importance” of one variable to exceed that of another simply due to the scale on which it is being measured. On the other hand, it is possible that this kind of “Bayesian prior” in terms of the *original scale on which measurements are taken* is precisely what is desired depending on the research setting and context, in which case the decision to standardize or not is a more difficult decision ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). Either way, it is a good idea to compare results both with and without standardization when conducting most regularization methods. If one must choose one option over the other, it is probably a good idea to standardize ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 63) in most cases, but such should not be done without great care and consideration.

Indeed, beyond regularization methods, the decision of whether or not to standardize must be made in many other methods as well (e.g., principal components analysis). Offering a “cookbook” recommendation to “always standardize” is not good statistical teaching, especially without carefully considering whether or not it is desirable that the original variances of the measurement units play a role in the ensuing statistical analyses. Once more with the Bayesian prior concept, sometimes we want those variances to impact the solution, whereas other times we do not. The key point is that neither solution is definitively right or wrong, and the decision to keep measurements in their original units or transform them to standardized units needs to be made on a case-by-case basis.

### 6.2.6 Ridge Regression in R

Ridge regression in R can be performed using the *lmridge* package ([Imdad & Aslam, 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000165)). For an excellent summary of this package, see Ullah et al. ([2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000366)). The package is *outstanding* in its coverage of all things “ridge.” In the following, we fit a ridge regression to the *Hald* data. The data relate to an engineering application that was concerned with the effect of the composition of cement on heat evolved during hardening. What is most relevant about this data for our purposes is that the features are relatively highly correlated and hence well-suited for ridge regression. Consult the package for further details on this specific example.

Let’s first briefly survey the Hald data:

```
> library(lmridge)
> data(Hald)
> head(Hald)
```

We will fit a model where y is hypothesized as a function of predictors X1 through X4:

```

+ scaling = “sc”, K = seq(0, 1, 0.001))
```

The “sc” for scaling scales the predictors to correlation form. The option scaling = “centered” would have simply centered all predictors. The option K = designates the ridge biasing *tuning* parameter, where in the above we chose options 0, 1, 0.001, which means R will compute coefficients starting at 0 up to 1, at steps or increments of 0.001.

## 6.3 Lasso Regression

The ridge regression just featured is only one way that we may shrink parameter estimates. A second popular and modern way is through lasso regression. In lasso regression, the idea of minimizing *E*(*y*[0]−*f̂*(*x*[0]))² over and above what OLS regression would accomplish remains through imposing a penalty term, but this time, instead of the penalty $\\lambda{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}}$ as in ridge, the penalty term is $\\left. \\lambda\\left. \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p} \\right|\\,\\beta\_{j} \\right|$so that we are now minimizing the following:

  
$$\\left. RSS = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left( {y\_{i} - \\beta\_{0} - {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{\\beta\_{j}x\_{ij}}}} \\right)^{2}} + \\lambda{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\left| \\beta\_{j} \\right.} \\right|$$  
(6.9)

That is, instead of the tuning parameter being applied to the sum of squared regression weights, $\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\beta\_{j}^{2}$, it is now applied to the sum of the *absolute value* regression weights, $\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\left| \\beta\_{j} \\right.} \\right|$. Be sure to note however that whether adding a squared term in ridge regression or absolute value term in lasso regression, the general principle is the same, and that is to include a penalty term to the least-squares residual sum of squares to seemingly increase the error function. But again, it is worth asking why we would want to do such a thing. As before with ridge, it becomes “worth it” if such an addition of the penalty reduces MSE on test (not necessarily *train*) data. The only difference between ridge and lasso is the nature of the penalty. In both cases, as lambda *λ* increases, all coefficients in the regression will eventually go to 0, and hence a “stopping point” will be required; otherwise performing ridge or lasso regression would be trivial and meaningless. That is, while we would like to shrink some coefficients to or toward 0, driving all coefficients to 0 would be 277counterproductive. As we will soon see, in practice, the stopping point is typically selected via cross-validation.

According to [Müller and Guido (2017)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000258), ridge is usually the first choice between that of ridge vs. lasso. Lasso might be most useful if you have a large number of predictors and expect only a few of them to be important, so that the rest can drop out. Remember, lasso can be used for variable selection because it drives some coefficients all the way to 0. This is the key distinguishing feature, in an applied sense, between using ridge vs. the lasso.

### 6.3.1 Lasso Regression in Python

We can perform lasso regression in Python using sklearn.linear\_model by importing the lasso function. As with ridge, the tuning parameter is adjusted via alpha():

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
lasso_reg = Lasso(alpha = 0.1)
```

Let’s first build some random data. We will request three columns for X and a single column for y:

```
X = 2*np.random.rand(10, 3)
```

The designation (10, 3) requests 10 rows by 3 columns, and hence 3 variables, each having 10 values:


### 6.3.2 Lasso Regression in R

Lasso regression in R can be fit using glmnet() in the *glmnet* package ([Friedman](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000117) et al., 2023). As was true for *lmridge*, *glmnet* is an outstanding package. The options are endless for performing lasso regression and a host of other regression models. [Hastie et al. (2023)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000141) also published *An Introduction to glmnet*, which is equally outstanding and strongly recommended for getting started with *glmnet*.

We feature an example from the package:

```
> library(glmnet)
> data(QuickStartExample)
> x <- QuickStartExample$x
> y <- QuickStartExample$y
```

There are four predictors in x and a single response in y. We now fit the model (printing only a few cases):

```
> fit <- glmnet(x, y)
> fit
Call: glmnet(x = x, y = y)
```

The number of nonzero coefficients is indicated by DF, with %Dev indicating the percent of deviance explained for various values of lambda, where the higher the deviance, the more that is explained by that particular case. The percent deviance explained is relative to the null deviance, which is a baseline model containing only the intercept term.

The plot() function ([Figure 6.5](#c6.xhtml#f6.5)) reveals the coefficient growth as a function of *λ* and consequently the L1 norm ∑|*β*[*j*]| of the coefficient vector, where the top axis (0–9) shows the number of nonzero coefficient for the given value of L1:

Hence, via cross-validation, we have settled on a set of coefficients that we could deem “final” for our lasso regression, or could have also explored coefficients in the neighborhood of lambda.min. Automating the tuning parameter can further be performed using the *caret* package ([Kuhn, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000208)). Boehmke and Greenwell ([2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000033), p. 133) provide an excellent summary of how to use the *caret* package for this purpose, where a *grid search* over values of lambda for various values of alpha is performed, where the alpha setting indicates whether we have performed ridge, lasso, or elastic net (to be surveyed next). That is, such a search will reveal the model with both the best (i.e., lowest RMSE) alpha parameter *and* lambda combined. A similar approach for searching for both alpha and lambda can be performed using cv.glmnet (see the package for details).

## 6.4 Elastic Net

A third option for shrinking parameters is that of *elastic net*, with penalty equal to

  
$$\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\left( \\alpha \\middle| \\beta\_{j} \\middle| + \\left( 1 - \\alpha \\right) \\right.}\\beta\_{j}^{2} \\right)$$  
(6.10)

Elastic net is considered a compromise of sorts between the ridge and lasso, a kind of “hybrid” of the aforementioned estimators ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). It can be shown that elastic net actually employs a linear combination of the ridge and lasso penalty functions (see [Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 153 for details).

Note that elastic net features two coefficients, *β*[*j*]² and |*β*[*j*]|. To understand the role of *α*, the tuning parameter in this context, note that it is being applied to both *β*[*j*]² and |*β*[*j*]|, both the losses that are used in the ridge and lasso, respectively (i.e., quadratic and absolute function losses). Hence, we can see that the role of *α* is to differentially weight *β*[*j*]² and |*β*[*j*]|. This is why elastic net is interpreted as a “compromise” between ridge and lasso, and such compromise depends on the chosen value for *α* in differentially weighting the ridge and lasso L2 and L1 losses, respectively.

### 6.4.1 Elastic Net in Python

The library scikit-learn can perform elastic net. In what follows we fit an elastic net model on two features:

```
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
X, y = make_regression(n_features=2, random_state=0)
regr = ElasticNet(random_state=0)
```

```
           2.47135869e+02,-1.07140916e+02,-8.57587584e+01,-3.79043198e+01,
          -7.95749661e+01, 1.86961487e+01, 4.93789716e+01, 5.32933539e+00,
          -1.16562784e+02, 5.63423160e+01,-8.36280817e+01, 7.68252760e+01,
```

We fit the elastic net regression and obtain coefficients below:

```
regr.fit(X, y)
Out[689]: ElasticNet(random_state=0)
print(regr.coef_)
[18.83816048 64.55968825]
print(regr.intercept_)
1.4512607561654032
```

We can see that the regression coefficients are equal to 18.84 and 64.56 for each feature, respectively, while the intercept is equal to 1.45. Let’s now obtain a prediction for values of 0 and 0 on each feature:

```
print(regr.predict([[0, 0]]))
[1.45126076]
```

Not surprisingly, we see that the predicted value is equal to the intercept of 1.45 (try other values to see what predicted values you get).

As we did for the lasso, we can use the package *glmnet* to fit elastic net in R. We can also use a recently-proposed package *fasterElasticNet* (Ma et al., 2022) that purports to fit elastic net (and related models) very efficiently.284

## 6.5 Which Regularization Penalty Is Better?

To conclude our discussion of these regularization approaches, it should be noted that neither ridge nor lasso nor elastic net will universally dominate each other. *There is no free lunch!* Lasso might perform better when a few coefficients are close to 0 and the rest quite substantial, where ridge often performs best when all coefficients are approximately equal, or at minimum, of equal importance to the investigator. However, there are no guarantees. The use of *cross-validation* in some capacity is recommended to determine which approach is better for a given data set, with tuning parameters selected via *grid search* on different values and cross-validation employed to observe which gives the lowest *test error*. To reiterate, we want to minimize the *test error*, not necessarily *train error*. This is why cross-validation is so important to choosing an optimal tuning parameter. See [Frank and Friedman (1993)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000108) for a comparison of ordinary least-squares to not only ridge regression, but also principal components regression and partial least-squares.

## 6.6 Least-Angle Regression

As we have seen when surveying variable selection techniques, forward regression selects variables in the candidate pool one at a time that improves model fit. *Least-angle regression* can be seen as a related technique to forward regression as it still selects based on a forward strategy, but does not necessarily select the *entire* variable. Instead, what enters into the selection is as much of the variable that is *merited* to the prediction, not all of it as in traditional stepwise routines. Hastie et al. ([2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), pp. 73–74) describe the algorithm most succinctly:

> At the first step it \[least-angle regression\] identifies the variable most correlated with the response. Rather than fit this variable completely, LAR (least-angle regression) moves the coefficient of this variable continuously toward its least-squares value (causing its correlation with the evolving residual to decrease in absolute value). As soon as another variable “catches up” in terms of correlation with the residual, the process is paused. The second variable then joins the active set, and their coefficients are moved together in a way that keeps their correlations tied and decreasing. This process is continued until all the variables are in the model, and ends at the full least-squares fit.

The algorithm begins with standardizing predictors to have a mean equal to 0 and variance equal to 1 (i.e., *z*\-scores). At this initial step, the residual *r*[*i*] is computed having no predictors in the model, that is, $r\_{i} = y\_{i} - \\overline{y}$, with all coefficients in the regression set to 0. That is, *β*[1] = *β*[2], ..., *β*[*p*] = 0. Next, the predictor having the largest correlation with this residual is entered into the model; however, *not all of it*. The predictor’s weight moves *toward* its least-squares coefficient until another predictor “catches up” and has as much correlation with the current residual as the first predictor. At this point, both *β*[1] and *β*[2] move in the direction of their *joint* least-squares coefficient until another predictor “catches up” to the current residual. The algorithm proceeds in this way until all predictors are entered and hence the least-squares solution is achieved for the model. In the case where the number of predictors is greater than sample size (more specifically, *N*\-1), the algorithm will reach a zero residual condition after *N*\-1 steps ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 74).

Hence, least-angle regression builds up a regression model by piecewise linear “partial” steps, adding single elements at each step by correlating the new variable with the current residual. As another variable “catches up,” the algorithm moves in a direction *equiangular* (i.e., having the 285same angle) to predictors. For this reason, least-angle regression has been called the “democratic” version of stepwise ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). Both the lasso and forward stagewise regression models can be computed through the *least-angle regression algorithm* ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). The key point to emphasize is that in least-angle regression, predictors essentially “catch up” to others in the selection process, then those variables move together. In Python, the Lars estimator can be used to fit a least-squares regression. The LARS lasso can also be used which implements the LARS estimator while driving some coefficients to 0, as is characteristic of the lasso.

## 6.7 Additional Variable Selection Algorithms

Other selection algorithms similar in spirit to the ridge and lasso include the *Dantzig selector* as well as the *Garotte* ([Breiman, 1995](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000046)). But why use different penalties in the first place? That is, why not use the same selection algorithm in all situations regardless of the data? The answer to this question once more lies in the *No-Free-Lunch Theorem*, discussed earlier in the book, which, recall, holds that *no universal algorithm universally dominates all data sets*. That is, one data set may have specific “peculiarities” for which one algorithm capitalizes, while another data set may not ([James et al., 2021](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000169)). Hence, different regularization techniques may generate slightly different results depending on the peculiarities of the given data set and it is virtually impossible to be certain that one algorithm or method will dominate others on any particular data set. Just as no single treatment is guaranteed to “work” on any given individual, no single statistical or machine learning method is guaranteed to dominate all others on any single data set.289

Still, the above admonition does not mean we cannot narrow things down to at least a “preferred” approach in “most” circumstances. According to Izenman ([2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 154), when comparing penalized regression approaches:

> Extensive simulations comparing prediction accuracy under a wide variety of conditions and models … show that the Lasso, which tends to choose too many variables, almost always contains the correct model; the nonnegative garotte tends to select smaller models than the Lasso, and all-possible subsets, while more likely to choose the correct model than the Lasso, selects models that contain the correct model far less often than the Lasso.

# 7 Nonlinear and Nonparametric Regression

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-10](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-10)

The regression methods surveyed thus far in this book have all featured one common assumption: that of the relationship between response variables and explanatory variables being modeled is *linearly related*. Why is linearity the focus of so many statistical methods? Huge books, some well over a thousand pages, are written primarily on linear methods alone. Why the obsession with linearity? We see two primary reasons for this focus on linearity:

1.  *Many phenomena in the sciences can be well approximated by linear methods*. The true function underlying the data may not be (and in fact, is *usually* not) linear, but linear models allow us to *approximate* those unknown functions rather well. In short, linearity “works” in many sciences because, though specifying the exact functional form underlying data is difficult to impossible, linearity is a useful *assumption* to make and makes for a nice *approximation* of scientific reality. The key words here are *assumption* and *approximation*. Very few data, if any, actually fall on a straight line.
2.  A second reason why linearity is popular is because it is *simple* and *convenient*. In the absence of knowing the true functional form, linearity provides reasonable prediction and generality analogous in some sense to why we use means and averages to describe many phenomena, even though such can be grossly misleading at times. Even in its sister discipline, *linear algebra*, linearity is, not surprisingly given its name, assumed in most applications. The convenience of fitting simple, functional forms comes at a price, however. Rarely, if ever, do those functional forms represent empirical *reality*. Reality is usually much more complex, or at least in many cases, we *assume* it is more complex. However, assuming a linear relationship generally guards against overfitting and hence can be more generalizable than if we try too much to model the exact form of the relationship that may underlie the data.

> *Though linear models dominate statistics and science, many, if not most phenomena in science are nonlinear. Seeking alternatives to linearity is often preferred to better capture the reality of scientific processes. Advancements in statistics and machine learning are often geared toward models and algorithms that help better unpack nonlinear features in data. Efforts to detect complex nonlinear patterns are at the heart of cutting-edge statistics and machine learning.*

The truth of the matter is that most if not all relationships are *nonlinear* and may be even more complex than we could even ever model. Having surveyed the linear ground thus far in this book, our goal in this chapter is to survey a few methods that model nonlinear relationships. There are 291three general approaches that we will consider here that seek to capture nonlinearity in data: 1) *polynomial regression*, 2) *regression splines*, and 3) *kernel regression*, which we will first motivate by simple local-averaging.

## 7.1 Polynomial Regression

Recall the classic linear model,

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*] + *ε*[*i*]  
(7.1)

The above model is actually a special case of the more general *polynomial regression model*,

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*] + *β*[2]*x*[*i*]² + *β*[3]*x*[*i*]³ + *β*[4]*x*[*i*]⁴+   ⋅  ⋅ ⋅   + *β*[*p*]*x*[*i*]^(*p*) + *ε*[*i*]  
(7.2)

A polynomial of order *p* can have *p − 1* “bends.” For instance, a straight line of order “1” has *p −* 1 = 1 − 1 = 0 bends, which is what makes it a straight line (i.e., there are no “bends” in a straight line, at least macroscopically). A parabola has a single bend (i.e., 2 − 1 = 1), and so on. A constant-only model (e.g., the mean) implies *p* = 0.

Typically, polynomials of only degrees 1 through 4 are generally used in scientific practice, since the higher the order of the polynomial, the greater the possibility of *overfitting*. That is, while fitting a polynomial of say, degree 10 might provide an exceptional fit to your training data (you may in fact be connecting the dots if your sample size is rather small!), many of those higher degrees are likely simply capitalizing on chance factors or random noise in the training data and hence the fit will not generalize well when validated on test data. That is, a polynomial of excessive order is likely to overfit the data. Recall that when it comes to model validation, it is how the model fits on *test* data that matters most, not how it fits on *training* data.

> *A polynomial of order (or “degree”) p can have p − 1 “bends.” The complexity of a polynomial increases with the number of bends in it. Typically, polynomials of only up to degree 4 are used in scientific practice, as higher-order polynomials are likely to overfit the training data. However, higher-order polynomials may be useful depending on the nature of the scientific material and domain.*

When we are fitting the classic linear model, we are in actuality performing polynomial regression, only that the polynomial is a rather simple one, that of a *line*. That is, the linear equation is simply a special case of the wider polynomial equation where only powers of one are included:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {y\_{i} = \\left\\{ {\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x\_{i}} \\right\\} + \\beta\_{2}x\_{i}^{2} + \\beta\_{3}x\_{i}^{3} + \\beta\_{4}x\_{i}^{4} + \\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\, + \\beta\_{p}x\_{i}^{p} + \\varepsilon\_{i}} \\\\ \\left. \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\downarrow \\right. \\\\ {y\_{i} = \\left\\{ {\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x\_{i}} \\right\\} + \\varepsilon\_{i}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

Another way of thinking of the above is that the linear model is a polynomial model in which all higher powers beyond unity are constrained or set to zero.292

### 7.1.1 Polynomial Regression in Python

We can fit a basic polynomial regression in Python quite easily using numpy.polyfit():

```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

We would like to fit a polynomial to the following data:

```
x = [1,2,3,5,6,7,8,9,10,12,13,14,15,16,18,19,21,22]
y = [100,90,80,60,60,55,60,65,70,70,75,76,78,79,90,99,99,100]
```

We specify a third-degree polynomial ([Figure 7.1](#c7.xhtml#f7.1)):

![Figure 7.1 Third-degree polynomial fit to curvilinear data.Return to text.⏎](images/fig7.1.jpg)

*Figure 7.1* Third-degree polynomial fit to curvilinear data.[Return to text.⏎](#c7.xhtml#re_f7.1)

```
mymodel = np.poly1d(np.polyfit(x, y, 3))
myline = np.linspace(1, 22, 100)
plt.scatter(x, y)
Out[209]: <matplotlib.collections.PathCollection at 0x1af74f20dd0>
plt.plot(myline, mymodel(myline))
Out[210]: [<matplotlib.lines.Line2D at 0x1af77d64cd0>]
plt.show()
import numpy
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(r2_score(y, mymodel(x)))
0.9432150416451026
```

We can see from the R-squared that the proportion of variance explained by the polynomial is approximately 94%. The cubic model (i.e., degree 3) fits better than had we tried a quadratic one:293

```
mymodel = np.poly1d(np.polyfit(x, y, 2))
print(r2_score(y, mymodel(x)))
0.759777160189589
```

Had we fit a model of degree 4 (i.e., quartic), we would have obtained only a slightly larger R-squared than the cubic, which would have probably resulted in overfitting the data:

```
mymodel = np.poly1d(np.polyfit(x, y, 4))
print(r2_score(y, mymodel(x)))
0.9542030834699506
```

Polynomial regression can also be performed in Python using statsmodels.

### 7.1.2 Polynomial Regression in R

We illustrate polynomial regression on the Boston data set. This is data derived from information collected by the U.S. Census Service on housing characteristics and measures in the area of Boston, MA. We will use the *tidyverse* ([Wickham](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000384) et al., 2019) and *caret* ([Kuhn, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000208)) packages. A version of polynomial regression using this data can also be found in James et al. ([2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168), p. 115):

```
> library(tidyverse)
> library(caret)
> data(“Boston”, package = “MASS”)
```

There are a total of 506 observations in the Boston data. We will now split the data 0.8 into train and 0.2 into test:

```
> set.seed(123)
> training.samples <- Boston$medv %>%
+ createDataPartition(p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
> train.data <- Boston[training.samples, ]
> test.data <- Boston[-training.samples, ]
```

We confirm that the data has been split correctly:

```
> nrow(train.data)
[1] 407
> nrow(test.data)
[1] 99
```

The number of rows in the train data is 407 while the number of rows in the test data is 99. Recall we had requested that the train data be 80% of the entire data. The total number of cases is equal to 407 + 99 = 506, of which 407 is 80%.

We will now build the model, a polynomial model of degree 5 on the train data:

```
> model <- lm(medv ~ poly(lstat, 5, raw = TRUE),
+ data = train.data)
```
