```
We can see that all degrees of the polynomial are statistically significant, most importantly the highest degree in this case, which is the fifth degree (p = 0.003421). The model explains approximately 68% of the variance in the response (i.e., Multiple R-squared). Adjusted R-squared is only slightly less at 0.6777.
We now obtain some predictions based on the test data:
```

```
> predictions <- model %>% predict(test.data)
> head(predictions)
      3          6          9          11     14         15
36.25964 31.52683 10.98130 14.57053 24.46163 22.15775
```

We can get an R-squared on the predictions as follows, which we can see is just a bit higher than the explained variance on the train data:

```
> R_squared = R2(predictions, test.data$medv)
> R_squared
[1] 0.6829474
```

We can also test smaller-degree models, such as simply a quadratic model. We can obtain coefficients for this model as follows:

```
> print(lm(medv ~ lstat + I(lstat^2), data = train.data))
Call:
lm(formula = medv ~ lstat + I(lstat^2), data = train.data)
Coefficients:
(Intercept) lstat I(lstat^2)
  42.5736 -2.2673  0.0412
```

295 

The package *polyreg* ([Matloff et al., 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000241)) can also be used to fit polynomial regression models.

### 7.1.3 Polynomial Regression as a Global Strategy

What is the problem with polynomial regression? There is no problem, really, if one wishes to model the entire range of *x*[*i*] by assuming a common functional form. That is, both the classic linear model and polynomial regression fit the data in a very *global* manner, similar in some sense to how the arithmetic mean summarizes a set of data from one end of the distribution to the other. For example, consider the small data set

2, 5, 8, 10, 15, 16, 170, 171, 172

The mean of this data is 63.2. But how well does the mean represent the data? Not that well, since, for example, the data points 170, 171, and 172 are very much greater than the rest of the data and the mean will thus be pulled *upward* because of these more extreme scores:

> 2, 5, 8, 10, 15, 16, **170, 171, 172**

Computing the mean on the above set of data provides a very “global” summary of the data. We may not wish to model the data in this way, whether it is in computing the mean or conducting a regression, and may prefer a more *local* approach.

### 7.1.4 A More Local Alternative

For the above data, we may be better off calculating two averages, one for the data 2, 5, 8, 10, 15, 16, and one for the data 170, 171, 172. In doing so, we are essentially modeling the data at a more *local* level. Though this example is very simple, it demonstrates a strong but obvious point, and that is, *fitting global measures to data provides a global summary of that data*. If the data does not conform to a global representation, then fitting *subsets* of the data more locally may be preferable. Indeed, at its extreme, the most local we could go is to model each data point *individually*, but such would be foolish and detract from the purpose of modeling in the first place, except for extremely small data sets. Exact “curve-fitting” is essentially “connecting the dots,” which, for most purposes, defeats the goal of statistical modeling. In this case, we are not averaging anything; we are simply connecting observations on a descriptive level. The general goal of modeling is to estimate a general function over the data, even if local. The goal is not simply “connecting the dots” on the training data and achieving perfect fit. *Anything less than “connecting the dots,” in most cases, can be considered a very general universal form of the aforementioned and discussed regularization concept as it concerns generalizability and minimizing test error.*

### 7.1.5 Least-Squares Regression Line as a “Floating Mean”: Toward a Localized Approach

To further motivate localized regression approaches, recall that the classic least-squares regression line can be interpreted as a “floating mean” across the range of values of the predictor, *x*[*i*]. That is, the slope *β*[1] in *y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[*i*] + *ε*[*i*], analogous to the mean, is a kind of “summary statistic” because 296the model assumes it is constant across the range of *x*[*i*]. Even if the data suggested a different slope or functional form within a given range of *x*[*i*], the classic least-squares line would not account for this. Likewise for polynomial regression, in which the polynomial is fit across the range of *x*[*i*], essentially ignoring more “local behavior” within intervals of *x*[*i*]. Both linear and polynomial regression *generalize* over *x*[*i*] to provide a summary of the data in terms of model fit.

What if we wished, however, to consider *local variation* more carefully? Perhaps the easiest example is that of a scatterplot that you may have come across in introductory statistics, one featuring the presence of two “groups” within the plot, as in [Figure 7.2](#c7.xhtml#f7.2).

![Figure 7.2 Basic scatterplot on two groups (males vs. females) suggesting a more localized approach to modeling, possibly by fitting an individual slope to each group.Return to text.⏎](images/fig7.2.jpg)

*Figure 7.2* Basic scatterplot on two groups (males vs. females) suggesting a more localized approach to modeling, possibly by fitting an individual slope to each group.[Return to text.⏎](#c7.xhtml#re_f7.2)

Of course, for the data in [Figure 7.2](#c7.xhtml#f7.2), a more localized approach to the regression could be as simple as modeling each group separately, with one slope for males and one slope for females. The locality of the data, in this case, is the *group*. But consider this example carefully and you will see that what we are actually proposing here, at least implicitly, is to recognize the potential for an *interaction* in the plot and not simply a main effect. That is, *spotting the potential of an interaction in this sense is an effort to provide a more localized representation of the data*.

> *A localized representation of data can be as simple as computing different averages by identifying different sets in data, or by modeling interaction terms in a regression (or ANOVA) context.*

#### 7.1.5.1 Zooming in on Locality

What if we take locality to the limit, to the extreme? As mentioned, to do so would be to narrow in on each individual data point in our plot, or, for the example of averages, to simply consider each data point by itself. It doesn’t get much more “local” than considering the case study without producing an average at all!

In the regression context, we could produce interaction terms with increasingly greater degrees of “split” or factor levels in ANOVA in one or more variables. Hence, instead of dividing the 297data into two groups, we could divide them into four or five, for instance. The general principle then in a localized approach to regression (or ANOVA) is that instead of assuming a general functional form across the range of *x*[*i*], we wish instead to “zoom in” and inspect *local variations* within given intervals of *x*[*i*]. This is where localized methods of regression come into play. However, as we survey a few approaches to accomplish this, the reader should take away what we have discussed here: that zooming in locally on data can be as simple as splitting data in different ways or modeling interaction terms in regression or ANOVA. That is, local examination and modeling of data need not necessarily take the form of a sophisticated or advanced modeling strategy.

To understand and motivate local regression, it is imperative to first understand the nature of a *basis function* as it relates to regression and modeling in general. Basis functions are so general that they also open the door to understanding more advanced techniques such as neural networks as well, as there are intimate connections between basis functions and most other statistical and machine learning methods.

## 7.2 Basis Functions and Expansions

A *basis function*, or *linear basis expansion* ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)) is essentially the taking of a function of variable (or matrix, in this case) *X*, which we can express quite generally,

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*b*[1](*x*[*i*]) + *β*[2]*b*[2](*x*[*i*]) + *β*[3]*b*[3](*x*[*i*]) + *β*[4]*b*[4](*x*[*i*])+   ⋅  ⋅ ⋅   + *β*[*p*]*b*[*p*](*x*[*i*]) + *ε*[*i*]  
(7.3)

Note that the above is not polynomial regression; none of the (*x*[*i*]) are raised to exponents other than unity. The actual basis functions, which are functions of *x*[*i*], are *b*[1] through *b*[*p*]. For example, *β*[1]*b*[1](*x*[*i*]) is the same as we would classically have in least-squares in that we are weighting *x*[*i*] by the regression parameter *β*[1], but to be more precise, what is being weighted is not *x*[*i*]; we are instead weighting a *function* of *x*[*i*], and that function is *b*[1](*x*[*i*]). That is, we first weight *x*[*i*] by *b*[1], then weight that product by *β*[1]. The basis function here is *b*[1](*x*[*i*]).

To understand the above more clearly, consider the classic linear model as a special case of where basis functions occur. What basis function is inherent or “natural” in the classic linear model? To see this, we observe

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {y\_{i} = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}b\_{1}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) + \\beta\_{2}b\_{2}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) + \\beta\_{3}b\_{3}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) + \\beta\_{4}b\_{4}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) + \\,\\, \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\,\\, + \\beta\_{p}b\_{p}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) + \\varepsilon\_{i}} \\\\ {y\_{i} = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}b\_{1}\\left( x\_{i} \\right)} \\\\ {y\_{i} = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}\\left( 1 \\right)\\left( x\_{i} \\right)} \\\\ {y\_{i} = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}\\left( x\_{i} \\right)} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

and thus we end up with the classic one-predictor linear model. The basis function, *b*[1](*x*[*i*]) is simply *x*[*i*] with *b*[1] implied or set to 1.

Let’s now consider a primitive though arbitrary basis function simply to extend on this simple definition. Instead of *b*[1](*x*[*i*]) = (1)(*x*[*i*]), suppose the basis *b*[1] were equal to 2, making *b*[1](*x*[*i*]) = (2)(*x*[*i*]). Note that none of this is related to the slope *β*[1]; *the basis function here is simply an “action” directly on* *x*[*i*] *before the partial regression slope is applied to it*. The question for us then, is what should the basis function comprise of? There are many possibilities, and the choice of a basis function will be motivated by the type of model we are considering. It doesn’t take long to realize that one could quite easily write an entire book titled *Basis Functions for Prediction*, which would encompass numerous possibilities and statistical models, which would include simple and multiple 298linear regression, polynomial regression, step functions, regression splines, analysis of variance, and a whole gamut of others. The common thread in all of these models is that they are *identified by their bases*, that is, their transformations of *x*[*i*] *before* weighting by least-squares or other technique; that is, before weighting by the parameter estimates in the given model.

### 7.2.1 Basis Functions and Locality

Among the chief benefits of basis functions is that they allow us to model the data at a more *local level*, much more local than polynomial regression ever could. The use of basis functions also allows us to model the relationship between *y* and *x* nonlinearly by adopting nonlinear basis functions. Because the basis function occurs *inside* of the expression “*β*[1]*b*[1](*x*[*i*])”, we could, in theory, allow *b*[1] to be a whole host of nonlinear functions ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)), which include *Gaussian basis functions* such as the following,

  
$$\\phi\_{j}\\left( x \\right) = \\exp\\left\\{ \\frac{\\left( x - \\mu\_{j} \\right)^{2}}{2s^{2}} \\right\\}$$  
(7.4)

or a *sigmoidal basis function*,

  
$$\\phi\_{j}\\left( x \\right) = \\sigma\\left( \\frac{x - \\mu\_{j}}{s} \\right)$$  
(7.5)

among others, where *s* is the standard deviation in the aforementioned functions. The basis functions we have surveyed thus far have been all *fixed* beforehand; that is, they are not amenable or adaptable to the data. The curse of dimensionality will also limit the utility of fixed basis functions ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)). It will thus be advantageous to consider basis functions that are not fixed. We will encounter such basis functions, that is, those that are *adaptive* or *recursive*, when we survey neural networks later in the book and emphasize the connection between the regression methods of this chapter and neural network approaches.

> *A basis function, or linear basis expansion, weights the predictors in a regression model. Depending on the basis function chosen, this may allow for a more “local” examination of the fit at that particular point or region in the range of predictor values, or, may be limited to a more global representation of the data. In regression, this weighting occurs before weighting by the relevant partial regression slope. The basis functions employed in this chapter are fixed and hence can be quite limiting. Neural network basis functions are generally more adaptive to the data.*

### 7.2.2 Neural Networks as a Basis Expansion: Generalizing the Concept

We mentioned above that we could title an entire book about basis functions or more precisely, *basis expansions*. We emphasized some of the more popular “special cases” of what we would include in such a book, namely simple and multiple regression, and so on. This was meant to 299emphasize how general basis expansions actually are and how many statistical methods can be understood or conceived in terms of basis expansions. Indeed, neural networks can be considered as a basis expansion as well and yet another special case of this wider framework.

In a classic neural network, as we will see later in the book, we take *functions of functions*, otherwise known as *composite functions* from elementary mathematics. Taking composite functions allows us to implement a similar idea of a *basis expansion* as we did just earlier. The general concept we need is that of a *feature extractor* (Murray, 2022):

  
*f*(*x*;*θ*) = *W**ϕ*(*x*) + *a*  
(7.6)

The parameters in the above are *θ* = (*W*,*a*) and if we were to write the classic functional equation, we would omit *ϕ* altogether. The key to the above, however, is the inclusion of *ϕ* which in our earlier regression example was *β*[1]*b*[1](*x*[*i*]) where *ϕ* = *b*[1]. That is,

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {f\\left( x;\\theta \\right) = W\\phi\\left( x \\right) + a} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = Wb\_{i}\\left( x \\right) + a} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

where we now denote *b*[1] as *b*[*i*] to eliminate any confusion in notation. What is the benefit to writing *f*(*x*;*θ*) this way? The answer is its *generality*. The more general form for *f*(*x*;*θ*) allows *ϕ* to be a more *arbitrary* and *general* function. More to the point, we are now permitting the feature extractor to have its own designated parameter, *θ*[2]:

  
*f*(*x*;*θ*) = *W**ϕ*(*x*;*θ*[2]) + *a*  
(7.7)

As we will see when we study neural networks, this allowance of the *feature extractor* to have its own parameter vector will generalize our current idea of basis expansion to much wider possibilities. The general idea is to specify *functions of functions*, which is what neural networks are all about.

We can see then that basis functions are an entirely *general concept*, and the choice of a basis function is essentially theoretically limitless. In the earliest of courses in introductory statistics, basis functions are indeed present in *t*\-tests, ANOVA, regression, and so on; however they are simply not revealed and are usually *implicit* within the given method or procedure. Interactions in ANOVA, for instance, are yet another example of a basis expansion. *Basis expansions essentially enrich the feature space.* Support vector machines are yet another example of a basis expansion, which we survey later in the book.

In what follows and in returning to our discussion of nonlinearity, we focus on a particularly common basis function or expansion that will prove useful for modeling nonlinear regression, that of *regression splines*.

### 7.2.3 Regression Splines and the Concept of a “Knot”

We have discussed so far the benefit of leaving global functions behind and fitting more local functions to data. The general idea is to fit a model locally, or “zoomed in” to different parts of the data. *Regression splines* are a common way to get at the local structure of the data in a regression context.

But how can we define local subsets of the data range? An easy and common way to do so is via *knots*. A *knot* is something that divides areas of the data on *x*[*i*] into intervals, where the coefficients in the model *change* as to reflect a change in the data trend. In general, *the greater the number 300knots, the greater the flexibility of the curve*. As the number of knots increases without bound to infinity, we eventually obtain perfect fit. If we use too many knots, however, we are at risk of overfitting. The selection of the right number is thus crucial and is typically made by cross-validation or possibly simply by visualization. *Smoothing splines*, on the other hand, often use a maximal or near-maximal number of knots instead of that number being arbitrarily selected by the user ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)).

[Figure 7.3](#c7.xhtml#f7.3) depicts the concept of a knot in spline regression, where it is clear that the coefficient of the curve changes in a rather dramatic and somewhat exaggerated way to illustrate the concept.

![Figure 7.3 Concept of a “knot” in spline regression. The location of the change in the coefficient of the curve is the location of the knot. Such is an exaggerated illustration, but clearly indicates that a knot would be useful since the trend in the data suggests a different function from 50 onward.Return to text.⏎](images/fig7.3.jpg)

*Figure 7.3* Concept of a “knot” in spline regression. The location of the change in the coefficient of the curve is the location of the knot. Such is an exaggerated illustration, but clearly indicates that a knot would be useful since the trend in the data suggests a different function from 50 onward.[Return to text.⏎](#c7.xhtml#re_f7.3)

Recall that in the previous chapter we had chosen the tuning parameter in ridge, lasso, and elastic net by cross-validation to implement regularization. The choice of the number of knots can also be considered a form of regularization, and thus the number of knots can be thought of as a tuning parameter. That is, *by reducing the number of knots, thus reducing the chance of overfitting, we are essentially regularizing the model*. Indeed, this whole discussion of splines can actually be formally recast into the wider category of regularization (see [Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), pp. 167–168 for a discussion). It is generally recommended that using 4 to 5 knots equally distributed, say at percentiles 20, 40, 60, etc., is a useful first strategy for their implementation in a typical regression problem ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)).

> *Knots in regression splines define local subsets of a data range where coefficients typically change. The choice of the number of knots in spline regression can yet again be considered an instance of regularizing a model, just as selecting a suitable tuning parameter in ridge and lasso regression was a form of regularization. Hence, the number of knots can be thought of as a tuning parameter.*301

### 7.2.4 Conceptualizing Regression Splines

How should we conceptualize the idea of a regression spline? Regression splines are best represented as a special case of the more general idea of basis functions or basis expansions that we just surveyed. Recall the basis representation developed earlier:

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*b*[1](*x*[1]) + *β*[2]*b*[2](*x*[2]) + *β*[3]*b*[3](*x*[3]) + *β*[4]*b*[4](*x*[4])+   ⋅  ⋅ ⋅   + *β*[*p*]*b*[*p*](*x*[*p*]) + *ε*[*i*]  

where *b*[1] through *b*[*p*] are the basis functions. That is, they are transformations of *x*[*i*] *before* the relevant weighting by *β*[1] through *β*[*p*]. The placement of the knots can, in theory at least, be arbitrarily chosen based on shifts in the function. However, as mentioned, a uniform, equally spaced distribution of knots is usually the more common and initial strategy ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)).

Cross-validation can be used to determine the best number of knots, that which produces the smallest residual sums of squares in the test error. *Cubic splines* are often preferred because these naturally ensure the function is continuous and has continuous first and second derivatives at each knot ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). The number of knots divides the data into one or more *bins*. For example, 4 knots divide the data into 4 + 1 bins. If we increased the number of knots to their limit, we would have the number of knots equal to the number of values for *x*[*i*] or data points. Using *n* knots to represent *x*[*i*] *unique* values results in what is generally known as a *smoothing spline*. Since there is typically not a fixed number of knots determined *a priori*, smoothing splines are usually regarded as *nonparametric*, as the number of splines is a function of the number of data points or values of *x*[*i*] in the data ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259), p. 395).

As noted by [Fox (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), spline regression models can also be considered a “bridge” between the *linear* and *generalized linear model*. In fact, the *generalized additive model* is one that extends the regression spline to the case of multidimensional inputs, assuming an additive form (i.e., no interactions). The generalized additive model can then be extended beyond regression and into classification, in which case one has the full-blown generalized linear model ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)).

### 7.2.5 Problem with Splines and Imposing Constraints

The great thing about splines is that we can be as flexible as we wish. However, too much flexibility entails a cost. For example, consider [Figure 7.4](#c7.xhtml#f7.4). In this case, we are *too* flexible. That is, *we have not imposed enough constraints on the knots*. To remedy this, we begin imposing constraints, such as continuity from left to right to ensure there cannot be a jump (James et al., [2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)). Recall what “imposing a constraint” means; it means we would like the curve to fit, but without, in this case of continuity, a *jump*. That is, we have taken the “jump” out of the possibility in the fitting or estimation of the curve; this is the *constraint* we are imposing.

![Figure 7.4 Imposing the constraint of continuity (right) on the cubic regression spline.Return to text.⏎](images/fig7.4.jpg)

*Figure 7.4* Imposing the constraint of continuity (right) on the cubic regression spline.[Return to text.⏎](#c7.xhtml#re_f7.4)

This idea of imposing constraints on functions is not at all new. Indeed, virtually every statistical model has constraints either implicitly imposed that we cannot see or that the user imposes manually, such as in structural equation modeling where constraints are regularly imposed. As perhaps the simplest of examples, in linear regression the constraint of *linearity* is imposed, meaning that we will fit a functional form to data *with the constraint that it assumes only a linear form*. While this is an obvious example, it is nonetheless powerful and pedagogical; many researchers perform linear regression analysis without the awareness that they have implicitly constrained their predictive *potential* to that of lines at the expense of other curves such as a higher-order polynomial.302

Constraining a spline regression to have no jumps, or other constraints, gives the model less flexibility as when such parameters need to be estimated, in addition to limiting the type of spline fit so that it is scientifically meaningful to the researcher. Hence, if it is unreasonable to assume a jump can occur in one’s data, then constraining there to be no jumps (or other characteristic of the fitted curve) is perfectly reasonable. On the other hand, if such a jump is a reasonable possibility in the data, then imposing such a constraint would be ill-advised and the data should be modeled in some capacity that incorporates the discontinuity. In this regard, the *science* matters a great deal. If a discontinuity is a reasonable expectation for the given scientific data, it may make little sense to constrain it.

### 7.2.6 Polynomial Regression vs. Regression Splines

In our discussion above, we have presented regression splines as a special case of the more general idea of basis functions, and noted they are more local than methods such as polynomial regression. Which provides the better fit? As argued by [James et al. (2013)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168), regression splines often give superior results. Why? The reason that splines often give better results is that each polynomial regression and splines introduce flexibility in a different manner. *Splines typically do it better*. For polynomial regression, flexibility is introduced by increasing the degree of the function (e.g., from linear to quadratic to cubic and so on). Splines, on the other hand, introduce flexibility by keeping the degree fixed and instead increasing the number of knots, which can range from minimal to maximal. Hence, splines are simply more flexible than fitting a global polynomial, even of increasing degree of complexity, which usually means splines will perform better in cross-validation. What is more, as mentioned, regression splines can serve as a bridge to more generalized modeling such as the generalized linear model ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)).

One-dimensional splines can also be generalized to multidimensional splines though these are beyond the scope of this book. Multidimensional splines are a straight generalization of the one-dimensional spline, however ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). For an excellent overview of spline options across a variety of R packages, see [Perperoglou et al. (2019)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000286). We can also use the *spline2* package ([Wang, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000318)) to fit, in addition to natural cubic splines, other splines as well, such as more general *B-splines*, *M-splines*, among others, which we will not detail here (see the package for details). Another popular package for fitting splines in R is that of *gss* ([Gu, 2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000135)). One can also use the *bspline* package ([Sokol, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000341)) for estimating spline regression. The *absorber* package ([Savino, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000324)) is a variable-selection method using b-splines in multivariate nonparametric regression models that can be useful in choosing the “best” variables in a spline regression problem.303

### 7.3 Nonparametric Regression: Local and Kernel Regression

In our quest to model nonlinearity, we have thus far surveyed two possibilities: polynomial regression and regression splines. Polynomial regression provided a global fit to the data, while splines allowed us to model the data at a more local level. However, both approaches were *parametric* in nature, though splines, depending on the type and how we are using the terms parametric vs. nonparametric, are also often considered nonparametric ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 511).

We now briefly survey two nonparametric approaches: 1) *simple local-averaging*, and 2) *kernel regression*. We will see that kernel regression is a generalization of simple local-averaging and the latter can be used to motivate the former. Kernel regression is our primary focus as a nonparametric technique.

To be more precise, kernel regression is a way to model a *non-hypothesized* form of the relationship, which will typically end up being some undesignated nonlinear form. It can be considered a *nonparametric* approach to regression ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)). The nonparametric feature of kernel regression, as is true of kernel methods in general, allows the data to “speak” and tell us of its shape; we do not in advance assume a hypothetical linear or nonlinear form. That is, if the parametric linear model is

  
*y* = *f*(*x*,*θ*) + *ε*  
(7.8)

then the nonparametric linear model is

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {y = f\\left( x \\right) + \\varepsilon} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\, = f\\left( x\_{1},x\_{2},...,x\_{p} \\right) + \\varepsilon} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(7.9)

where now there is no parameter vector, *θ* and instead the form of the relation is learned entirely by the data, *x*[1], *x*[2], ..., *x*[*p*]. *Simple local-averaging* on the other hand, is what is generally regarded as a “naïve” approach to regression where averages within predetermined subsets or bins along the *x*\-axis are established in order to obtain a more *local flavor* in tracing the response variable. Kernel regression can be interpreted as a more general method of simple local-averaging.

### 7.3.1 Motivating Kernel Regression via Local-Averaging

In classical least-squares regression, recall that we typically assume that the conditional distribution of *y*/*x* is Gaussian (i.e., normal). More formally, we model *p*(*y*,*x*|*D*) where *y* is the response, *x* is the predictor, and *D* is the data. That is, in typical classical regression, we are tracing the mean function:

  
*μ* = *E*(*y*|*x*[1],...,*x*[*p*]) = *α* + *β*[1]*x*[1] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *β*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  
(7.10)

Given the assumption that the conditional distribution is normal, consider if we backtracked for a moment and motivated ordinary regression via a naïve approach and dissected the explanatory variable into *bins*, that is, *subsets* of area or *intervals* along the *x*\-axis. Not surprisingly, bias is minimized by making the bins as numerous and as narrow as possible ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)). Sampling variance is minimized by using a small number of relatively wide bins, each with many observations. Hence, as usual, there is a trade-off between bias and variance here, encapsulating the classic *bias-variance trade-off*, as illustrated in [Figure 7.5](#c7.xhtml#f7.5).304

![Figure 7.5 Local-averaging in regression. Bias is minimized by making the bins more numerous and narrow; wide bins (left), narrow bins (right).Return to text.⏎](images/fig7.5.jpg)

*Figure 7.5* Local-averaging in regression. Bias is minimized by making the bins more numerous and narrow; wide bins (left), narrow bins (right).[Return to text.⏎](#c7.xhtml#re_f7.5)

We note in [Figure 7.5](#c7.xhtml#f7.5) that as the bins get progressively narrower, we eventually “zero in” on the actual data points that make up the theoretical regression line as well as the actual points that happen to fall on the sample regression line. Hence, in this extreme version of nonparametric regression where each data point is a mean, we are simply *connecting the means* located within the bins. Clearly, such an approach would usually not be useful, and we are better off increasing the size of each bin. However, if we increase the bin size too much, we miss out on the *locality* of the data we initially were after; *this is the nature of the trade-off*.

What makes this approach *nonparametric* is that no assumptions about the population or form of the relationship are made. Sample size plays a crucial role here as well. As the sample size increases, the intervals become successively narrower, each containing more data, where in the limit as sample size gets larger, the naïve nonparametric regression coincides with the population regression ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)). What happens with this approach when there are many explanatory variables? Not surprisingly, the previously discussed *curse of dimensionality* rears its ugly head. For simplicity, we focus on the case where we only have a single predictor.

A glaring weakness of this approach is that for a bin of a given size, assuming the bin is larger than each single data point, the estimate within each bin will be inexact for surrounding data points. That is, if the bin size contains 20 data points, the mean computed on these 20 data points will be a rather *coarse* representation of locality. Is there a way we can do better than the mean? Is there a way we can represent the data within each interval more “fairly” or precisely? The answer to this will be yes, via *kernel regression*.

### 7.3.2 Kernel Regression – “Locally Weighted Averaging”

Kernel regression seeks to improve on simple local-averaging by attempting to explicitly give more weight to observations that are close to the focal *x*[0] and less weight to more remote values in the training data ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)). What is a “focal *x*[0]”? This is the hypothetical value from which you wish to make a prediction of the response, *y*. This is an attractive idea, as doing so will provide a better representation of the data *within* each interval or “bin” of data. The distance *x*[*i*] from *x*[0] can be represented by ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 529):

  
*z*[*i*] = (*x*[*i*]−*x*[0])/*h*  
(7.11)

The scale factor here is *h* and is the *bandwidth* of the kernel estimator, controlling its degree of smoothness. As an example, suppose the distance (*x*[*i*]−*x*[0]) is equal to 5, with a bandwidth *h* equal to 1, yielding a *z*[*i*] equal to 5. If we increase the bandwidth to 2, then *z*[*i*] is equal to 2.5. The function of *h* then is to *scale* the distance (*x*[*i*]−*x*[0]). For a constant distance, as *h* grows larger and larger, the interval on the *x*\-axis becomes smaller relative to *h* and we obtain a *finer* fit. The 305smoothness of the fitted function is thus largely influenced by the size of the bandwidth, *h*. In general, as *h* increases, the function becomes smoother. Too fine, or too smooth a fit could be detrimental in modeling scientific data, especially if the finer or smoother fit provides too “general” of a modeling approach across the span of the data where perhaps one strategy is more appropriate than another for particular ranges of the data space.

Scaling deviations *x*[*i*] − *x*[0] by the bandwidth *h* is fine, but we can do even better and apply a kernel function to the scaled deviation to obtain final weights, *w*[*i*]:

  
*w*[*i*] = *K*\[(*x*[*i*]−*x*[0])/*h*\]  
(7.12)

Using the above weights *w*[*i*], the fitted value at *x*[0] is computed by weighted local-averaging of the *y*[*i*] values:

  
$$\\left. \\hat{f}\\left( x\_{0} \\right) = \\hat{y} \\middle| x\_{0} = \\frac{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{w\_{i}y\_{i}}}{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}w\_{i}} \\right.$$  
(7.13)

We thus see that kernel regression is effectively a form of *weighted regression*, where the weights feature the use of a kernel.

### 7.3.3 A Variety of Kernels

Note that in our description of kernel regression and the computation of weights, *w*[*i*], we have not yet described the nature of *K*, that is, the *kernel function* we are choosing to use for the given problem and by which we are applying to \[(*x*[*i*]−*x*[0])/*h*\]. Not surprisingly, there are many choices for a kernel function. One choice, perhaps the default, is to use the *Gaussian* (or “normal”) kernel:

  
$$K\\left( z \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}}e^{- z^{2}/2}$$  
(7.14)

where the bandwidth in (7.14) is the standard deviation. As noted by [Fox (2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 530), distances greater than 2*h* from the focal value of *x*[0] receive virtually no weight due to the nature and shape of the normal density.

Following Fox ([2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 530), another possibility is to use the *tricube kernel*,

  
$$K\_{T}\\left( z \\right) = \\left\\{ \\begin{array}{l} \\left. \\left( 1 - \\middle| z \\middle| {}\_{3} \\right)3, \\middle| z \\middle| < \\,\\, 1 \\right. \\\\ \\left. 0, \\middle| z \\middle| \\geq 1 \\right. \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$$  
(7.15)

or the *rectangular kernel*,

  
$$K\_{R}\\left( z \\right) = \\left\\{ \\begin{array}{l} \\left. 1, \\middle| z \\middle| < 1 \\right. \\\\ \\left. 0, \\middle| z \\middle| \\geq 1 \\right. \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$$  
(7.16)

There are other kernels we can choose from, however according to [Fox (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), the choice of kernel function is not that critical in carrying out the regression. There is nothing wrong with trying out a variety of kernels to study their impact on the given regression solution.306

### 7.3.4 Kernel Regression Is Not Nonlinear; It Is Nonparametric

We reiterate that kernel regression should not be considered specifically a nonlinear approach to regression in the same vein as polynomial regression (in terms of modeling nonlinear trends, not the model being nonlinear). Rather, it is a *nonparametric approach*, which implies that it *learns from the data*. If that learned form is linear, then so be it, but the point is that kernel regression does not *a priori* assume a linear or nonlinear form. It is first and foremost nonparametric because it essentially makes no parametric assumptions regarding the shape of the true function. *Local-polynomial regression* extends kernel regression where polynomials are instead fit at the focal value of *x*[0]; however this is beyond the scope of this book. For an excellent discussion of kernel regression (and much of anything else to do with regression), see [Fox (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106).

### 7.3.5 Kernel Regression in R

Kernel regression in R can be fit using the package *gplm* ([Mueller, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000255)). We adapt an example from the package’s documentation below, where we first create data on 1000 observations for variable x:

```
> library(gplm)
> n <- 1000
> x <- rnorm(n)
> head(x)
[1] -0.71040656 0.25688371 -0.24669188 -0.34754260 -0.95161857 -0.04502772
```

We next create m as a function of x and then y as a function of m:

```
> m <- sin(x)
> head(m)
[1] -0.65214204 0.25406776 -0.24419733 -0.34058836 -0.81435593 -0.04501251
> y <- m + rnorm(n)
> head(y)
[1] 0.2638500 1.0546901 -1.1807664 -1.7413758 -0.6540784 -0.3189749
> plot(x,y,col=“gray”)
> lines(kreg(x,y),lwd=2)
```

307 

The squiggly line ([Figure 7.6](#c7.xhtml#f7.6)) is the kernel regression estimate, using the Nadaraya-Watson estimator (see [Nadaraya, 1964](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000262)). See the package for many more functions that can be applied to the kernel regression, including extracting estimated fitted values.

![Figure 7.6 Plot of kernel regression line (right).Return to text.⏎](images/fig7.6.jpg)

*Figure 7.6* Plot of kernel regression line (right).[Return to text.⏎](#c7.xhtml#re_f7.6)

The *gplm* package ([Mueller, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000255)) also features rather sophisticated 3-D visualizations of kernel regression. As an example (see the package for the code), [Figure 7.7](#c7.xhtml#f7.7) is an advanced graphic generated, where the original function is on the left and the estimated function is on the right.

![Figure 7.7 Graphic generated using the gplm package in R with both original (left) and estimated (right) functions.Return to text.⏎](images/fig7.7.jpg)

*Figure 7.7* Graphic generated using the gplm package in R with both original (left) and estimated (right) functions.[Return to text.⏎](#c7.xhtml#re_f7.7)

Kernel regression can also be fit using the *np* package ([Hayfield & Racine, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000148)).

# 8 Generalized Linear and Additive ModelsLogistic and Related Models

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-11](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-11)

Up to now in our discussion of modeling, we have assumed the response variable is more or less *continuous*, or at least “pseudo-continuous,” since no empirical variables are ever truly continuous in the idealistic mathematical sense. Continuity itself is an *abstraction*, a philosophical idea that is expressed mathematically using such things as epsilon-delta definitions in real analysis. More pragmatically, we have assumed the response exhibits a rather wide range of “dense” values and the goal has been to predict a value of the response along this continuum based on one or more predictors. While many of these models have been linear, we have also surveyed a number of nonlinear models. However, in all of these models, response variables have all been assumed to be continuous and treated as such in our analyses. There are many instances in modeling where the response variable is not continuous but is instead *categorical*. Such responses contain mutually exclusive categories instead of a continuum of numerical possibilities. Some responses having this property are naturally occurring (e.g., pass vs. fail), while others can be operationalized by the user into specific categories (e.g., numerical score on a test classified into the binary outcome of pass vs. fail).

How can statistical models deal with binary or categorical responses? Thanks to the theory of the *generalized linear model* ([McCullagh & Nelder, 1989](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000243)), binary and polytomous responses can be situated in the same general framework that we can find classic linear models. The generalized linear model contains the entire family of these models and is the topic of this chapter.

Before surveying the generalized linear model, we should ask an important question from the outset: *Is “binning” a response a good idea*? What are the advantages and disadvantages of doing so? We begin this chapter with a brief survey of the benefits and drawbacks of operationalizing the response as a binary or polytomous outcome.

## 8.1 How to Operationalize the Response

As mentioned, some response variables are naturally categorical. For instance, a salmon fish is either going “upstream” or “downstream,” and cannot be going both (though as we have all seen, they can just seemingly wade in the water without direction at times). When responses take on this quality, leaving the variable “as is” and treating it as binary is an easy decision since leaving it *as is* maintains it in its natural *measured* state. In other cases, however, the researcher may actually choose to bin the variable into mutually exclusive categories. In the machine learning literature, the pseudo-continuity of a variable before “binning” it is sometimes referred to as a *pre-classifier* (Kroese et al., [2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000202)) because it is relatively continuous before forcing those values into categories.309

### 8.1.1 Pros and Cons of Binning

Whether or not to bin a variable is an important decision. Indeed, different operationalizations of a single variable can lead the resulting statistical model to “discover” different effects. As a simple example, the variable *grade* on a class test operationalized as *pass* vs. *fail* may be predictive of final grade, but operationalized as a numerical score may alter the predictive ability. The variable is the same, but how we have operationalized it is now different. What is more, the choice of how to operationalize a variable in analysis of variance (ANOVA) can influence the resulting mean squares and ultimately the rejection of the null hypothesis. There is a whole literature on the influence of operationalizing effects in ANOVA (for example, see [Prentice & Miller, 1992](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000292)).

### 8.1.2 Detecting New Classes or Categories

While we have discussed the pros and cons of binning, it is worth mentioning as well that in machine learning, there are also techniques that actually allow the algorithm to detect new classes or categories based on the algorithm’s examination of the data. Such is referred to as *novelty detection* in machine learning circles, so that instead of classifying cases in one of *C*[*t*] classes, a new class label *C*[*t* + 1] is derived not by the researcher’s judgment or decision of how to bin, but from the actual algorithm discovering the new category. This process sometimes goes by the general concept of *open set recognition* ([Murray, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). In this book, we do not survey methods that detect new categories. We assume the researcher is actively deciding how to operationalize their variables.

## 8.2 The Generalized Linear Model

The motivation behind the generalized linear model (GLM) is to encompass models that have continuous responses such as in classic ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression, but also incorporate models with binary or categorical responses. The GLM is the “parent” to all of these models and essentially features a transformation of binary or polytomous responses into linear and continuous ones. In developing the GLM, it is first best to recall the classic linear model featured earlier in our discussion of regression:

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[1] + *β*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *β*[*p*]*x*[*p*] + *ε*[*i*]  
(8.1)

Note that the above model is *linear in the parameters*, meaning that *β*[0], *β*[1], … *β*[*p*] are all raised to the exponent “1.” Even if *x*[1], for example, was raised to the second power, *x*[1]², the model would still be regarded as a linear model so long as *β*[0], *β*[1], … *β*[*p*] remained raised to a coefficient of one; however, one could say it is no longer linear in the variables. *Linear models require only that coefficients be raised to no terms greater than one*. What basis transformations on the actual variables we perform is inconsequential as it pertains to the linearity or nonlinearity of the actual model in statistical parlance ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)). For example, the following model would rightly be considered *nonlinear* because it is nonlinear in the coefficients, notably the *β*[2]² term:

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[1] + *β*[2]²*x*[2] + *ε*[*i*]  
(8.2)

Note that the following model is also nonlinear because of *β*[2]² but not because of *x*[2]²; it is considered both nonlinear in the *parameter* and *variable*:310

  
*y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[1] + *β*[2]²*x*[2]² + *ε*[*i*]  
(8.3)

### 8.2.1 Intrinsically Linear Models

A useful distinction to make when it comes to linear vs. nonlinear models is that between *intrinsic linearity* vs. *non-intrinsic linearity* (Neter et al., [1996](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000266)). A model that is nonlinear, but that can be linearized through a transformation is often referred to as an *intrinsically linear model*. Perhaps the most classic example of this is the *exponential response*, where if we were to take the log of the exponential in such a model, we would obtain a linear model. That is, we can transform the response into one that is linear. It is intrinsically linear because its nonlinearity is a product only of a transformation. A *non-intrinsically linear model*, on the other hand, is one that cannot be linearized via transformation.

### 8.2.2 General vs. Generalized Linear Models

Many of the models featured thus far in this book can be considered special cases of the wider *general linear model*. Regression and analysis of variance models are indeed special cases of this wider framework. But what defines a general linear model exactly? When we refer to a specific model arising from this “general” framework, we usually mean that the distribution of the error term, *ε*[*i*], has an expected *normal distribution*. The classic linear regression model, *y*[*i*] = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[1] + *ε*[*i*] is one such example where *ε*[*i*] ∼ *N*(0,*σ*[*ε*]²), meaning that the error in the model is expected to be normal, having a mean of 0 and a finite and measurable variance, *σ*[*ε*]². There are many situations, however, where we would not naturally expect the error term to behave this way. One classic and popular example is when the response variable is not continuous but instead *binary*. When a response variable is binary, the expectation of the error term is, not surprisingly, not normal. Nor could we reasonably expect errors to have constant variance ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)).

The difficulty then on a theoretical level is how to deal with error distributions that have a non-normal expectation. They seem to be a different class of models altogether. However, thanks largely (but not exclusively) to the work of [Nelder and Wedderburn (1972)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000265), a wider framework of statistical models was proposed that could encompass even these types of models with non-normal error distributions. Recall that understanding statistics is all about looking for *hierarchies, of* classifying “special cases” of models in the context of higher forms and generalities. This is precisely what these authors accomplished in proposing a framework for modeling that encompasses not only the classic linear model (regression, ANOVA) that features normally distributed error terms, but also models that contain non-normal error terms. This new class of models they called the *generalized linear model*, and hence a vast array of models can be situated in this general framework. That is, *the generalized linear model encompasses models that contain normally and non-normally distributed error terms*.

Essentially, the logic of the generalized linear model is to take an otherwise nonlinear model and make it mimic linearity through what is called a *link function*. Through the link function, the model becomes approximately linear and we can then treat the model more akin to how we would treat a classic linear model. This is the essential logic of the generalized linear model. An important distinction to make here is that it is the *decision surface* that is linearized, not truly the model entirely or necessarily ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)). Generalized linear models such as logistic regression engage in transformations that make them “linear-like” ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106)), such that otherwise nonlinear models can be “linearized” via the transformation (e.g., taking a link function such as the log of the odds in the case of logistic regression).311

One very special case of the generalized linear model that has historically been very popular across virtually all scientific fields, especially medical fields, is the aforementioned *logistic regression model*, which we survey next.

## 8.3 The Logistic Regression Model

The logistic regression model is known as the *conditional Maxent model* ([Mohri et al., 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000253)) in machine learning circles, which is simply the multinomial regression model of which binary regression is a special case. The logistic function is given by the following,

  
$$p\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x}}{1 + e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x}}$$  
(8.4)

where we can work with the formulation in (8.4) and get

  
$$\\frac{p\\left( x \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x \\right)} = e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x}$$  
(8.5)

The left-hand side of (8.5), *p*(*x*)/\[1−*p*(*x*)\] is what is referred to as the *odds*. In words, the odds is the probability of an event occurring, *p*(*x*), relative to the probability that the event does not occur, 1 − *p*(*x*). If the probability of an event occurring is the same as the probability of it not occurring, then the odds are equal to 1.0. For example, suppose *p*(*x*) = 0.5, then it stands that,

  
$$\\frac{p\\left( x \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x \\right)}\\frac{0.5}{1 - 0.5} = \\frac{0.5}{0.5} = 1.0$$  

Suppose we were to take the logarithm on both sides of

  
$$\\frac{p\\left( x \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x \\right)} = e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x}$$  

so that,

  
$$\\log\\left\\lbrack \\frac{p\\left( x \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x \\right)} \\right\\rbrack = \\log\\left\\lbrack e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x} \\right\\rbrack$$  
(8.6)

Recall that taking the log of an exponential function *e* has the effect of bringing the exponent down and so what we have from the above is

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\log\\left\\lbrack \\frac{p\\left( x \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x \\right)} \\right\\rbrack = \\log\\left\\lbrack e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x} \\right\\rbrack} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(8.7)

That is, *the log of the odds is assumed to be a linear function*. The log of the odds goes by the name of the *logit*, and hence once we produce the logit, we are effectively now working with an approximate linear model similar in many respects to the classic linear model of regression. Of course, it is not *exactly* the same, since the units we are working in are no longer the natural units of the original variable, but instead are in units of the *logged odds*, or the *logit*, and hence the interpretation of parameter estimates will be in units of the logit.312

For example, suppose that in the model of (8.7), *β*[1] were equal to 0.8; what would be the interpretation? In classic least-squares regression, the interpretation, as we recall, would be *for a one-unit increase in X, we expect Y to increase by 0.8 units*, given the model under test. In logistic regression, the interpretation is the same, only that the “units” now are not natural units of the original variable, but instead are units of the *logit*, and hence, our interpretation would be *for a one-unit increase in X, we expect the logit of Y to increase by 0.8 logits*, given the model under test.

### 8.3.1 Odds and Odds Ratios

Recall that we said the odds were defined as the probability of an event occurring relative to the probability of the event not occurring, that is,

  
$$\\frac{p\\left( x \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x \\right)}$$  

The *odds ratio* is, as the name suggests, a *ratio of odds*, comparing the odds for one variable, *x*[1], or category of a response, to the odds of another variable, *x*[2], or complement category to *x*[1]:

  
$$OR = \\frac{\\left( \\frac{p\\left( x\_{1} \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x\_{1} \\right)} \\right)}{\\left( \\frac{p\\left( x\_{2} \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x\_{2} \\right)} \\right)}$$  
(8.8)

For example, if the odds are the same for each variable or category, then the odds ratio is equal to one. An odds ratio greater than one implies that the odds for *x*[1] are greater than the odds for *x*[2]. Conversely, an odds ratio of less than one implies that the odds for *x*[1] are less than the odds for *x*[2].

### 8.3.2 Logistic Regression in R

We can use the *blorr* package ([Hebbali, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000151)) for running logistic models. In what follows, we run a logistic regression on the *hsb2* data featuring two hundred observations that were randomly sampled from a survey conducted on high school seniors by the *National Center of Education Statistics*:

```
> library(blorr)
> head(hsb2)
```

We can see that all effects are statistically significant (*p* < 0.01). We can see that the *residual deviance* is quite a bit smaller than the *null deviance*. The residual deviance here is the deviance on which the model is based, which is reflected by the lesser degrees of freedom (196). When we fit the model, we expect the *residual variance to be less than the null deviance*, akin to error sums of squares being smaller than total sums of squares when we fit an ANOVA model.

### 8.3.3 Logistic Regression in Python

## 8.4 Generalized Linear Models and Neural Networks

Recall that in our survey of linear and nonlinear models in previous chapters, we purposely drew a link to neural networks in a way to foreshadow them later in the book. Not surprisingly, we can likewise draw a link between the generalized linear model and that of neural networks. As we will see in a later chapter, neural networks are defined by an *activation function* which models a linear sum in a (typically) nonlinear fashion. Do generalized linear models have such a link function? Yes! The generalized linear model can be given by315

  
*E*\[*Y*|*X*\=*x*\] = *h*(*x*^(*T*)*β*)  
(8.9)

where the function *h* is the *activation function*. Note that the rest of the expression, that of *x*^(*T*)*β*, is simply the generalized linear model component we surveyed earlier. Reduced to a linear model, *x*^(*T*)*β* is simply the systematic portion of a linear model with activation function set at unity, such that *h*(*x*^(*T*)*β*) = 1(*x*^(*T*)*β*) = *x*^(*T*)*β*. In generalized linear models, this *concept* is referred to more generally as the *link function*. Hence, we see that while the generalized linear model is not as deep as neural networks typically are (as we will see later), both generalized linear models and neural networks can be said to feature the unifying notions of *activation* and *link functions*. This point is important, as the *concept* of activation functions is often regarded as “unique” to neural networks. However, they are much more general than they may at first appear. Indeed, prior familiarity with the generalized linear model allows one to better “see” the activation function featured in neural networks. The activation function, most generally, is simply the outer function that is being applied to the inner function, and is usually, *though need not necessarily be*, of nonlinear form. Both the generalized linear model and neural networks are unified by the concept of *composite functions*.

## 8.5 Multiple Logistic Regression

In our survey of logistic regression thus far, we have featured the one-predictor logistic model. As we did in generalizing simple linear regression to multiple, we can likewise generalize the logistic regression model to multiple logistic regression. Going from the one-predictor logistic model to the multiple logistic model is straightforward,

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\log\\left\\lbrack \\frac{p\\left( x \\right)}{1 - p\\left( x \\right)} \\right\\rbrack = \\log\\left\\lbrack e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot + \\beta\_{p}x\_{p}} \\right\\rbrack} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x\_{1} + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot + \\beta\_{p}x\_{p}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(8.10)

where, as before with the one-predictor model, we can write *p*(*x*) as follows:

  
$$p\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot + \\beta\_{p}x\_{p}}}{1 + e^{\\beta\_{0} + \\beta\_{1}x + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot + \\beta\_{p}x\_{p}}}$$  
(8.11)

Interpreting coefficients in a multiple logistic setting is analogous to interpreting them in a multiple regression setting, meaning that coefficients must be interpreted *relative to the model* in which they appear. That is, each coefficient is interpreted in the *context* of other coefficients. For instance, the following interpretation for *β*[1] would be *incorrect*:

> *For a one-unit increase in* *x*[1]*, we expect the logit to change by* *β*[1] *amount.*

The correct interpretation is the following:

> *For a one-unit increase in* *x*[1]*, we expect the logit to change by* *β*[1] *amount,* ***given the other predictors in the model*** .

As always, recall that when interpreting effects in a model, we are never, *ever*, interpreting them in a *vacuum*; they always occur or exist in the *context* of the other variables in the model. This is one of the key features to remember about virtually all statistical modeling as a whole, or any 316narratives for that matter, that *there is always a context to the model you are interpreting, no matter how simple or complex that model may be*. The trailing phrase “given the other predictors in the model” or “given the context of the model” is not *optional* in interpretation; it is *essential* for a correct interpretation of modeling results. *Even in the case of a simple logistic regression with only a single predictor, the trailer “given the context of the model” is still required, even if that context is of no additional predictors. Interpreting univariate or bivariate effects in a multivariate or multivariable model without reference to context is equivalent to misinterpreting effects in the model. All models, as is true of all narratives, are context-dependent.*

### 8.5.1 Multiple Logistic Regression in R

## 8.6 Poisson Regression

While logistic regression assumes the response is binary, Poisson regression assumes the response has a Poisson distribution, which may or may not be skewed depending on the value for *μ*. A Poisson regression is often used when the response variable is a *count*. The distribution of a Poisson variable is the following:

  
$$p\\left( y \\right) = \\frac{\\mu^{y}e^{- \\mu}}{y!}$$  
(8.12)

where *μ* is the mean of *y* and *y*! is equal to *y*(*y*−1)(*y*−2) ⋅  ⋅  ⋅ (1). The Poisson distribution is useful for modeling *y* when such is the number of events occurring during a fixed time interval of a given length. The expectation of *Y* conditioned on *x*, that is, *Y*/*x*, where *x* is a vector of predictor variables, is given by the following where the model coefficients *θ* appear in the numerator, that is, they are in the exponent to the *e* base:

  
*E*(*Y*/*x*) = *e*^(*θ*′*x*)  
(8.13)

Murray (2022) and [Fox (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106) provide good treatments of Poisson regression.

### 8.6.1 Poisson Regression in R

Just as was true for logistic regression, Poisson regression can also be fit using the *glmnet* package (Friedman et al., [2010](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000116)). Below we adapt an easy example from that package:

```
> library(glmnet)
> data(PoissonExample)
> x <- PoissonExample$x
> y <- PoissonExample$y
```

The above provides the data we require for the model, which we now fit, being sure to specify family = “poisson” whereas in logistic regression recall that the family was that of binomial:319

```
> fit <- glmnet(x, y, family = “poisson”)
> plot(fit)
```

In [Figure 8.3](#c8.xhtml#f8.3) the size of coefficients as a function of the L1 norm is plotted. As the penalty increases, the L1 norm *decreases* until the number of nonzero coefficients (top axis) is equal to 0 for an L1 norm equal to 0.
