## 8.7 Generalized Additive Models: A Flexible Nonparametric Alternative

The generalized linear model, with special cases such as logistic and Poisson regression, features “linear-like” or other *parametric* forms. That is, we approach the data with an *a priori* parametric idea or form in mind to fit to the data that particular form or preconceived structure. As emphasized throughout this book, however, there are many times where we do not want to approach the data with a *prior hypothesized structure* in mind. Instead, we would like to “discover” structure or form in the data without preconceived hypothesized ideas about that structure.

We have seen that the general linear model is a special case of the generalized linear model. However, the generalized linear model can be conceived as a special case of an even more general and wider model, that of the *generalized additive model* ([Hastie and Tibshirani, 1986](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000144)), or “GAM” for short, where in this formulation, a precise functional form is not specified *a priori*. In GAM, 322we no longer assume linear forms such as $\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}{\\beta\_{j}x\_{j}}$, even after transformation, but instead generalize this notion to $\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}{s\_{j}\\left( x\_{j} \\right)}$, where instead of linear regression weights *β*[*j*], *s*[*j*] are unspecified functions that are estimated using a nonparametric *scatterplot smoother* (or some other nonparametric form, such as a kernel estimate or spline) and an iterative procedure known as the *local scoring algorithm* ([Hastie & Tibshirani, 1986](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000144)) or *iterative weighted least-squares* ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 575). The reader may recall from our earlier discussion in the book that smoothers are useful in providing a close fit to the data without generally making parametric assumptions *a priori*.

### 8.7.1 Why Use a Smoother Instead of Linear Weights?

The question naturally arises as to why use a smoother (*s*[*j*]) instead of linear weights (*β*[*j*])? What is the motivation for this approach? Like the motivation for the generalized linear model, the goal of the generalized additive model is to *capture nonlinear effects,* but by estimating them *nonparametrically*. Just as in kernel regression surveyed earlier, we wish to not make any parametric assumptions about the form of the relationship and instead want to have the data essentially speak for itself. This is what nonparametric estimation is all about. The idea of a smoother is a nonparametric idea in which we are allowing the data “to speak” in this sense and fit a function that approximates the data as well as possible, but without a prior hypothesized functional form such as we would have in the classic linear model estimated by least-squares, for instance. This is a hallmark of machine learning such that many analyses are *data-driven* (i.e., loosely, *nonparametric*) instead of *hypothesis-driven* (i.e., loosely, *parametric*). Generalized additive models, even in their own right, are pedagogically useful if for nothing else than understanding and appreciating how various models can be contextualized as special cases of others.

It can also be shown that GAMs can be likened to a neural network with a logistic activation function ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). Further, generalized additive models can also be interpreted as extensions to both the class of additive models, and as we have already seen, the class of generalized linear models.

> *The big idea of the generalized additive model is to use a nonparametric smoother (or some other nonparametric structure) to explore nonlinearity in the relationship between the response and covariates. Whereas the generalized linear model assumes some functional form (i.e., a linear form), the generalized additive model uses the data entirely to determine fit and hence makes no* a priori *parametric assumptions of what class of parametric functions will fit best. The generalized linear model can thus be considered a special case of the wider nonparametric generalized additive model.*

### 8.7.2 Deriving the Generalized Additive Model

To understand and appreciate how the generalized additive model arises, we begin once more with what is most familiar, that of the standard linear model, where the expectation of *y* is conditional on predictors *x*[1], *x*[2], ..., *x*[*p*]:323

  
*E*(*y*|*x*[1],*x*[2],...,*x*[*p*]) = *β*[0] + *β*[1]*x*[1] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *β*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  
(8.14)

The generalized additive model makes the classic linear model a special case of

  
$$E\\left( y \\middle| x\_{1},x\_{2},...,x\_{p} \\right) = s\_{0} + {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}{s\_{j}\\left( x\_{j} \\right)}}$$  
(8.15)

The distinction between models is that *s*[*j*](*x*[*j*]) replaces *β*[*j*](*x*[*j*]) and are now *smooth functions*. These functions *s*[*j*](*x*[*j*]) are also typically standardized ([Hastie & Tibshirani, 1986](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000144)) such that *E*(*s*[*j*](*x*[*j*])) = 0. The functions *s*[*j*](*x*[*j*]) are estimated, as mentioned, via scatterplot smoother or some other nonparametric device. The word “smooth” here generally refers to the idea of “nonparametric” because it implies the local area of the data being “smoothed” by a flexible curve instead of a rigid *a priori* (typically *parametric*) structure (e.g., a line or other curve). Cubic smoothing splines or the kernel smoothers that we saw earlier in the book are special cases. GAMs, however, place no restriction on what *can* be used, and hence the family of potential nonparametric functions is much wider. The algorithm used for estimating parameters in a generalized additive model is then tasked with estimating all the *p* functions in the data, whatever we have chosen those functions to be.

### 8.7.3 GAM as a Smooth Extension to GLLM

As we have seen, the generalized additive model is entirely general in the sense that it can subsume a variety of forms. Parametric structures are hence a special case of the wider GAM framework. The general linear model is easily cast as a GAM and so is the generalized linear model also a special case of the wider generalized additive model. Since in this chapter we are focused on the generalized linear model, we now detail such a bit more deeply.

Recall that in a generalized linear model, the linear predictor, now in the language of the generalized additive model, is given by

  
$$\\eta = s\_{0} + {\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{p}{s\_{j}\\left( x\_{j} \\right)}}$$  
(8.16)

where in the above, *s*[1](⋅),  ⋅  ⋅ ⋅,*s*[*p*](⋅) are now, in the GAM, *smooth functions*, which are not in parametric form but will instead be estimated nonparametrically. The intercept, *s*[0] is analogous from the generalized linear model to the GAM. Where the models differ is that in the classic “non-smooth” generalized linear model, *s*[*j*](*x*[*j*]) was simply *β*[*j*](*x*[*j*]) where *β*[*j*] were the linear weights as in regression. That is, the GAM applies a flexible smooth function to predictors *x*[*j*] instead of setting them as linear as in the classic generalized linear model. As [Hastie et al. (2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), pp. 296–297) note, *s*[1](⋅),  ⋅  ⋅ ⋅,*s*[*p*](⋅) do not need to consist exclusively of nonlinear terms but may also contain linear and other possibilities. The possibilities are virtually endless in the GAM. For instance, [Hastie et al. (2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 297) give the case of the following model,

  
*g*(*μ*) = *x*^(*T*)*β* + *α*[*k*] + *f*(*z*)  
(8.17)

which is considered *semiparametric*, where *x* are variables modeled linearly, and *z* *nonparametrically*. The GAM easily accommodates such a model, whereas the general linear model or the generalized linear model would have difficulty doing so without alteration.324

Other possibilities may consist of including qualitative variables or interaction terms as other examples. There is no real limit to the possibilities of combining parametric and nonparametric style inputs in the GAM and such decisions will be made in part based on the prior experience of the researcher but also on what the actual data have to say. While the generalized additive model is nonparametric, we note that deciding on what nonparametric “objects” to include in the model is still a decision that must be made by the researcher. Whether to include a kernel or spline or whether to mix linear and nonlinear terms is still up to the researcher. Hence, *nonparametric models learn from the data almost exclusively, but what tool does the learning is still a decision the researcher must make*.

There are numerous algorithms that can be used to fit GAMs. Some of the more popular include the *backfitting algorithm* and the *Newton-Raphson procedure* ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 299). Iterated weighted least-squares can also be adapted for GAMs and combined with the backfitting algorithm, the so-called IWLS-backfitting procedure ([Fox, 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106), p. 576). Likelihood-ratio chi-square tests along with deviance can be used to assess model fit. Generalized additive models can also be extended to handle multinomial responses. For details, see [Hastie et al. (2009)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145) and [Fox (2016)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000106).

### 8.7.4 Generalized Additive Models and Neural Networks

Once again, we can draw a link between models, this time generalized additive models and neural networks. We can relate the generalized additive model to neural networks in the following way. Suppose we take our earlier function,

  
$$\\eta = s\_{0} + {\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{p}{s\_{j}\\left( x\_{j} \\right)}}$$  
(8.18)

and now take a *function of this function*,

  
$$\\eta = g\\left( {s\_{0} + {\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{p}{s\_{j}\\left( x\_{j} \\right)}}} \\right)$$  
(8.19)

The formulation in (8.19) for *η* is essentially that of *g*(*f*(*x*)); that is, we are taking, in a general sense, a *composite function*, which, as we will see in our discussion of neural networks later, allows us to use backpropagation via the chain rule in calculus. Once more, as we do in several other places in the book, in appreciating the nature of neural networks it is helpful to see what other methods can be conceived as related or even special cases of that more global framework or approach. We encourage the reader to return to this and other sections in the book where we relate models to neural networks once we discuss and develop them more thoroughly later.

### 8.7.5 Linking the Logit to the Additive Logistic Model

We have seen that generalized additive models are a way to deal with nonlinearities in our data via nonparametric estimation. Perhaps not surprisingly at this point, there is a natural connection between the logit link function and the additive logistic regression model ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). Consider the logit once more, that is, the log of the odds,325

  
$$\\log\\left( \\frac{\\mu\\left( x \\right)}{1 - \\mu\\left( x \\right)} \\right) = \\alpha + \\beta\_{1}x\_{1} + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot \\beta\_{p}x\_{p}$$  
(8.20)

where now *μ*(*x*) is the probability of the event of interest (e.g., survival) and 1 − *μ*(*x*) the probability of its complement (e.g., death). The *additive logistic regression model* exchanges each linear term by a more general and to-be-defined functional form *f*[1] through *f*[*p*], generating the following function:

  
$$\\log\\left( \\frac{\\mu\\left( x \\right)}{1 - \\mu\\left( x \\right)} \\right) = \\alpha + f\_{1}x\_{1} + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot f\_{p}x\_{p}$$  
(8.21)

As before, not all of the *f*[1]*x*[1] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅ *f*[*p*]*x*[*p*] need to be nonlinear. As was the case where the generalized additive model replaced terms in the general linear model with nonparametric estimates, the generalized additive model likewise replaces the parametric terms in the logistic generalized linear model with smooth nonparametric estimates.

The package *mgcv* ([Wood, 2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000391)) can be used in R for fitting generalized additive models.

## 8.8 Overview and Recap of Nonlinear Approaches for Nonlinear Responses

The purpose of this chapter thus far has been to introduce and survey ways of modeling and accounting for nonlinearity or unknown structure in data where the response variable is something other than a continuous variable and instead binary or polytomous. As mentioned from the outset, while many or even most statistical models are linear in nature, many if not most scientific *phenomena* are *nonlinear* or at minimum, unknown, such that we may be better off allowing the data to “speak for itself.” A powerful way to understand the range of nonlinear and nonparametric methods is to consider how far we wish to depart from linearity to capture nonlinear effects. In this section, we provide a global review of the strategies we have surveyed so far. To set things up for this review, consider the basic scatterplot ([Figure 8.5](#c8.xhtml#f8.5)) with a single response variable and two predictors.326

![Figure 8.5 Generic scatterplot of y as a function of x and z.Return to text.⏎](images/fig8.5.jpg)

*Figure 8.5* Generic scatterplot of y as a function of x and z.[Return to text.⏎](#c8.xhtml#re_f8.5)

The central question we wish to ask is:

> *What are the options for modeling this data where y is hypothesized as a function of x and z?*

We now review and summarize the ways of modeling such data discussed in this and the previous chapter, which include *linear*, *nonlinear*, as well as *nonparametric* approaches. For each of the following, we encourage the reader to keep the plot in [Figure 8.5](#c8.xhtml#f8.5) in mind to help conceptualize how each of the following approaches would address this data:

1.  1\. *Linear Regression* – This classic approach will ignore any nonlinearity in the data and simply model a linear function to the data points. This can be a useful strategy if we are not that concerned about any nonlinear trend that may or may not be present in the data. Linear regression can be interpreted as a special case of the *general linear model*, which in turn can be considered a special case of the more *general nonlinear model* framework.
2.  2\. *Principal Components Regression* – In this approach, we generate principal components on the predictor side and use those component scores to predict the response variable. Recall that one limitation to this approach is that the components generated on the predictor side are not those necessarily maximally related to the variance in the response. That is, *there is no guarantee that the components generated vary in the directions of the response*. Still, this approach can be useful for reducing the data on the predictor side. However, the approach is still linear and will inadequately address any nonlinearities in the data. For the data depicted in [Figure 8.5](#c8.xhtml#f8.5), the approach would not be fruitful since we only have two predictors. However, given a much larger number of predictors, dimension reduction on the predictor side before predicting the response may be an effective strategy.
3.  3\. *Partial Least-Squares Regression* – As was the case for principal components regression, we seek to reduce the set of predictors to a smaller set that can be used for prediction of the response. In doing so, PLS, unlike PCR (principal components regression), attempts to incorporate both the response and predictor sides of the equation.
4.  4\. *Multivariate Reduced-Rank Regression* – Many models can be conceived as a special case of the wider reduced-rank regression problem. This context is more pedagogical than applied, as most models we will fit will not go by this name.
5.  5\. *Regularization* (*ridge*, *lasso*, *elastic net*) – This approach seeks to regularize the model by the concept of *shrinkage*, where one or more predictors have weights driven toward (or *to*) 0. This serves to simplify the model so that predictors that are not essential are minimized in importance. While the ridge estimator will drive weights *toward* 0, lasso will drive them exactly *to* 0, making lasso a kind of variable-selection procedure. Elastic net can be interpreted as a kind of compromise between the ridge and the lasso.
6.  6\. *Least-Angle Regression* – This takes a linear and stepwise approach, but instead of including variables at each step, estimated parameters are increased in a direction *equiangular* (in part, motivating the name *least-angle*) to each one’s correlations with the residual. That is, least-angle regression only includes that “part” of a predictor that is “next up” in terms of importance (at least, *statistical* importance) at each step.
7.  7\. *Canonical Correlation Analysis* – This relates each side of the equation just as in bivariate linear correlation, where each side is a set of variables. A Pearson Product-Moment correlation is a special case of the canonical correlation where each side of the equation consists of very simple linear combinations, those of only a single variable. That is, the “variate” in this case is a single variable on each side.327
8.  8\. *Polynomial Regression* – This seeks to model a polynomial that is more general than a degree 1 polynomial (line). This is a *global approach* that seeks to capture the *global nonlinearity* or trend of the data. Linear models can be considered a special case of the wider and more general polynomial regression problem. Linear regression can generally be considered a special case of polynomial regression.
9.  9\. *Regression Splines* – In this approach, we choose splines as a *basis expansion* for our predictors. Regression splines are not *equivalent* to a basis expansion, but are merely a special case. Splines, as was the case for polynomial regression, are meant to capture nonlinearities in the data, but do so at a more *local level*. The locality of splines is what makes them so attractive and useful. Splines feature the use of “knots” that are employed to capture the local and nonlinear segments of the data trend. It is generally regarded as a nonparametric technique as it uses the data (not the model) to determine the fit; however, elements of regression splines can also make them partially parametric.
10.  10\. *Kernel Regression* – This approach also seeks to model the data more locally using a kind of weighted regression and a kernel to draw focus to focal values in the regression while at the same time incorporating values of nearby or “neighboring” points. Kernel regression is a kind of weighted-average regression that extends notions of naïve nonparametric regression.
11.  11\. *Generalized Linear Models* – These employ a link function to “linearize” an otherwise nonlinear response such as one that is binary or polytomous. The response may also be categorical or count data, for which a Poisson link is an option. Many other link functions are available. The general linear model can be considered a special case of the generalized linear model where the link is the identity function.
12.  12\. *Generalized Additive Models* – These models feature nonparametric “smoothers” that generalize many other models, including the generalized linear model and polynomial models. The choice of what nonparametric smoother to use is left up to the researcher; however, common ones are smoothing splines, kernels, or many others. Pedagogically, the generalized additive model is very useful for conceptualizing a host of other models as special cases and in turn can also be considered a simplified version of neural networks.

## 8.9 Discriminant Analysis

Recall that we briefly introduced discriminant analysis toward the end of our discussion of the multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) model earlier in the book. There, we said that we would recap and extend on our discussion of the model later in the book when we introduced the generalized linear model. We discuss discriminant analysis here in this chapter on generalized linear models because it belongs to the types of models used for classification such as binary logistic regression and can be conceptualized as a special case of the generalized linear model with a binary response. Recall that the reason we originally introduced discriminant analysis in the context of MANOVA is that it shares many technical similarities with the MANOVA model and is often used as a follow-up analysis to the MANOVA procedure. Whereas in MANOVA we sought mean vector differences on a linear combination of response variables, in discriminant analysis we turned the problem around and sought to classify observations into groups based on a linear combination of predictors.

In the machine learning and statistical learning literatures, the presentations of discriminant analysis are rarely, if ever, related to multivariate analysis of variance. At least authors usually make no mention of the connection. Discriminant analysis is seen purely as a classification technique, one of the many *classifiers* featured in a wider discussion of multivariate and machine learning algorithms. We find the omission of multivariate analysis of variance in these contexts 328unfortunate and a clear missed pedagogical opportunity. Because this is a book on both multivariate statistics *and* machine learning, we have chosen to take both approaches, where earlier in the book we discussed discriminant analysis in the context of MANOVA and where here we focus on the machine learning paradigm of discriminant analysis as purely a classifier without any mention of MANOVA.

We begin by discussing the most “optimal” strategy for classification, which is that of using Bayes. As we will see, *Bayes is best* when it comes to classification. For reasons that we will discuss, using Bayes for classification is often not possible, and hence our second choice will be to implement the discriminant analysis model to *approximate* the Bayes boundary.

As we will also see, linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is yet another example of a statistical methodology in which *generative assumptions* (such as linearity) greatly simplify the learning process and can afford greater predictability. This is the reason why developing the discriminant analysis model is worthwhile; otherwise we would be content with using such procedures as *k-nearest* *neighbors* which, as we will see, essentially makes no prior parametric assumptions about the data. The principle here is that, once more, *making generative assumptions simplifies the problem and in cases where those assumptions are satisfied, doing so yields great benefit*. In cases where assumptions are not satisfied, nonparametric approaches are fair competitors to parametric ones.

> *Generative assumptions can greatly simplify the problem of modeling. If those assumptions are not met, however, nonparametric approaches can be useful, and in many cases are more appropriate competitors.*

### 8.9.1 Bayes Is Best for Classification

Recall the nature of Bayes’ theorem discussed earlier in the book,

  
$$p\\left( y = k \\middle| x = x\_{i} \\right) = \\frac{\\pi\_{k}f\_{k}\\left( x\_{i} \\right)}{\\sum\\limits\_{l = 1}^{K}{\\pi\_{1}f\_{l}\\left( x\_{i} \\right)}}$$  
(8.22)

where *p*(*y*\=*k*|*x*\=*x*[*i*]) is the *posterior probability* of *y* equaling a particular class *k* given some particular value of *x* = *x*[*i*]. The numerator in Bayes’ theorem, *π*[*k*]*f*[*k*](*x*[*i*]) contains the *prior probability*, *π*[*k*], multiplied by the density function of *x*[*i*], *f*[*k*](*x*[*i*]) = *p*(*x*\=*x*[*i*]|*y*\=*k*). Note that the final result of Bayes essentially “inverts” this conditional probability, that is, from *p*(*x*\=*x*[*i*]|*y*\=*k*) to *p*(*y*\=*k*|*x*\=*x*[*i*]). In a nutshell, this is the goal of Bayesian analysis in a simple problem such as this, to “flip” or invert conditional probabilities.

Recall also that Bayes is not simply an “equation” or “rule” (i.e., “Bayes rule”) as above and how it can be “casually” represented in elementary statistics, but is more generally a *philosophy* of how theory or belief should be revised in light of data or experience more generally. As we did earlier in the book, a more general way of writing Bayes’ theorem is the following:329

  
$$p\\left( T \\middle| D \\right) = \\frac{p\\left( T \\right) \\cdot p\\left( D \\middle| T \\right)}{p\\left( T \\right) \\cdot p\\left( D \\middle| T \\right) + p\\left( \\overline{T} \\right) \\cdot p\\left( D \\middle| \\overline{T} \\right)}$$  
(8.23)

where now *p*(*T*|*D*) is the probability of the theory *T* given data *D*. That is, given the numerator *p*(*T*) ⋅ *p*(*D*|*T*), the prior probability multiplied by the likelihood, we seek to “flip” *p*(*D*|*T*) to *p*(*T*|*D*).

Why is Bayes so important? Why do we continuously hear about Bayes in statistics and science? Why are there entire *books* written on Bayesian statistics and Bayesian philosophy? Aside from the fact that Bayes’ theorem has a very long history and is the cornerstone of a branch of statistics appropriately called *Bayesian statistics*, in our current context of classification it is especially important and meaningful because the Bayes’ boundary, or more generally, the Bayes *classifier* has the lowest error rate out of all classifiers ([Cover and Hart, 1967](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000070); [James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)), *under the assumption that all terms in Bayes’ theorem can actually be defined and measured*. Under such conditions, as summarized by Cover and Hart ([1967](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000070), p. 23), “The Bayes risk serves as merely a reference – the limit of excellence beyond which it is not possible to go.”

Long story short, Bayes’ theorem is an optimal sought-after result when it comes to classifying outcomes. It is the theoretical *ideal*. It is what we would wish for all the time if we had the choice. For the 0−1 loss (binary) problem, the Bayes classifier has us classifying to the most probable class using the conditional (discrete) distribution. The error rate generated is called the *Bayes rate* and is the “holy grail” of error rates. Many other methods, both in statistics and machine learning, such as the *k-nearest-neighbor approach*, are meant as direct *approximations* to the Bayesian ideal. They are “second choices” to using a Bayes boundary. *Bayes is always first choice and is always best*. However, nearest-neighbor approaches can have tremendous value in approximating Bayes. Indeed, it has been shown that the nearest-neighbor probability of error, *R*, for a classification problem with *M* categories, is bounded below by the Bayes probability of error, *R*′, and above by *R*′(2−*M**R*′/*M*−1)). As Cover and Hart have found, “*any* other decision rule based on the infinite data set cut the probability of error by at most one half. In this sense, half of the available information in an infinite collection of classified samples is contained in the nearest neighbor” (p. 27).

### 8.9.2 Why Not Always Bayes?

If Bayes is so wonderful, why not just use it all the time? Ideally, we would use Bayes for virtually all classifier problems. The problem, however, is that the terms needed for Bayes are usually not known. For instance, we do not know the term *f*[*k*](*x*[*i*]) in Bayes, and hence, we need a second approach to *estimate* it. The linear discriminant analysis model, and other approaches, are used as *approximations* to the Bayes classifier. However, only when observations are multivariate Gaussian with equal covariance matrix between classes is linear discriminant analysis the estimated Bayes classifier ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). Hence, our discussion of discriminant analysis should be “housed” in the context of trying to approximate Bayes, but all the while remembering that Bayes is regarded as the optimally desired approach if the terms in Bayes are available. In fictitious toy problems where terms may be available, *all else constant*, one would virtually always choose Bayes over discriminant analysis or any other classifier because it will provide the lowest of error rates. In reality, however, techniques such as discriminant analysis or competitors will usually be employed. Hence, we may say that Bayes is best; however, pragmatic concerns, including variations on sample size availability, will usually suggest a competing methodology such as the linear discriminant analysis model.330

### 8.9.3 Linear Discriminant Analysis Model

We have said that we do not typically know *f*[*k*](*x*[*i*]) in the Bayesian formulation. We would like to estimate it. To estimate it, however, we need to make some model assumptions about it. We begin by assuming that *f*[*k*](*x*[*i*]) has a normal density. That is, we assume:

  
$$f\_{k}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\sigma\_{k}}\\exp\\left( {- \\frac{1}{2\\sigma\_{k}^{2}}\\left( x\_{i} - \\mu\_{k} \\right)^{2}} \\right)$$  
(8.24)

where the right side of (8.24) is the normal density and *k* is the class or group number. Each class has a mean *μ*[*k*] and variance *σ*[*k*]². In the current setting, there are only two groups on the response variable since it is binary classification, and hence *k* = 2. The density for the first group is thus equal to:

  
$$f\_{1}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\sigma\_{1}}\\exp\\left( {- \\frac{1}{2\\sigma\_{1}^{2}}\\left( x\_{i} - \\mu\_{1} \\right)^{2}} \\right)$$  

and for the second (notice the change in subscripts from 1 to 2),

  
$$f\_{2}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\sigma\_{2}}\\exp\\left( {- \\frac{1}{2\\sigma\_{2}^{2}}\\left( x\_{i} - \\mu\_{2} \\right)^{2}} \\right)$$  

An important assumption made in the classic discriminant analysis model, one which we will relax later when we consider quadratic discriminant analysis, is that the standard deviation or variance is *constant* across both groups or levels on the response variable. That is, we assume

  
*σ*[1]² =  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  = *σ*[*k*]²  
(8.25)

We will also assume equality of covariances between responses, which, along with the assumption of equality of variances, yields the *equality of covariance matrices assumption*. This is essentially the same assumption we encountered earlier in our original discussion of MANOVA and discriminant analysis earlier in the book, which as we saw we can evaluate using the *Box M test*.

### 8.9.4 How LDA Approximates Bayes

Here is the trick to understanding how the normal density can be used to approximate Bayes. We desire Bayes in the end, so we substitute in the previous normal densities for the Bayes densities we wish to estimate, those of *f*[*k*](*x*[*i*]), where the numerator is the density for the specific class we are modeling and the denominator is the sum of the classes, mimicking the structure of Bayes,331

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {p\\left( y = k \\middle| x = x\_{i} \\right) = \\frac{\\pi\_{k}f\_{k}\\left( x\_{i} \\right)}{\\sum\\limits\_{l = 1}^{K}{\\pi\_{l}f\_{l}\\left( x\_{i} \\right)}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\frac{\\pi\_{k}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\sigma\_{k}}\\exp\\left( {- \\frac{1}{2\\sigma\_{k}^{2}}\\left( x\_{i} - \\mu\_{k} \\right)^{2}} \\right)}{{\\sum\\limits\_{l = 1}^{K}\\pi\_{l}}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\sigma\_{}}\\exp\\left( {- \\frac{1}{2\\sigma\_{}^{2}}\\left( x\_{i} - \\mu\_{l} \\right)^{2}} \\right)}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(8.26)

where *μ*[*k*] and *σ*[*k*]² is the mean and variance for class *k*, the class we are modeling, where again, we assume *σ*[*k*]² is constant across classes. When we now take the log of equation (8.26), it can be shown that it is equivalent to assigning the observation to the class for which the following gives the largest quantity:

  
$$\\delta\_{k}\\left( x\_{i} \\right) = x\_{i} \\cdot \\frac{\\mu\_{k}}{\\sigma^{2}} - \\frac{\\mu\_{k}^{2}}{2\\sigma^{2}} + \\log\\left( \\pi\_{k} \\right)$$  
(8.27)

But what is (8.27)? What is this function? This function is called the *linear discriminant function*. At a technical level, the linear discriminant function approximates the Bayes classifier by estimating *π*[*k*], *μ*[*k*], and *σ*², and substituting these into (8.27). Once we have those values estimated, the approximation to the Bayes classifier is complete.

### 8.9.5 Estimating the Prior Probability and Parameters of the Discriminant Function

The estimate for the prior probability *π*[*k*] can come from several sources, including simply the opinion or educated guess of the investigator. Recall that in Bayesian theory, the prior is essentially a *belief* espoused by the investigator. This isn’t to suggest it is wise to have *irrational* beliefs about the prior, only that ultimately the prior can be set by the preference of the researcher. Most commonly, the prior is derived from prior knowledge or previous research of the problem under study, that is, from substantive knowledge of the particular problem. In the absence of such information, and in reality probably the most common way of estimating the prior in practice, we can obtain an estimate of *π*[*k*] via

  
*π̂*[*k*] = *n*[*k*]/*n*  
(8.28)

where *n*[*k*] is the number of cases in class or group *k* and *n* is the total number of cases. This can be seen as a “default” method or starting point to estimating the prior, but it should be emphasized that such priors can be “tweaked” in line with, again, what the researcher knows about the specific problem under consideration. Recall that by their nature, priors are *subjective probabilities* and hence there are no strict rules about them. Of course, if you advance an irrational prior, then few will take it seriously. The benefit of specifying the prior on an individual/personal basis is that any biases or even *irrationality* in the estimate is open for others to see. This is a strength of Bayesian approaches in general such that *they reveal your degree of belief, even if your degree of belief is irrational*.332

In the discriminant function of (8.27), recall we also required values for *μ*[*k*] and *σ*², that is, the mean for each class and the variance of the classes. These can be estimated by

  
$${\\hat{\\mu}}\_{k} = \\frac{1}{n\_{k}}{\\sum\\limits\_{i}x\_{i}}$$  
(8.29)

and

  
$${\\hat{\\sigma}}^{2} = \\frac{1}{n - K}{\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{\\sum\\limits\_{i}\\left( x\_{i} - {\\hat{\\mu}}\_{k} \\right)^{2}}}$$  
(8.30)

where *n*[*k*] is the number of cases in class *k* and *n* − *K* is the total sample size minus the total number of classes. We can see that *σ̂*² is essentially a variance estimate across classes, pooling across classes *k* = 1 to *K*.

All of the aforementioned principles apply equally to the case of multiple predictors. That is, in the case of more than a single predictor (*as different from multiple response categories*), instead of the univariate Gaussian distribution, we require the *multivariate Gaussian*, which recall is given by

  
$$f\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\left. \\left( 2\\pi \\right)^{p/2} \\middle| \\Sigma \\right|^{1/2}}\\exp\\left( {- \\frac{1}{2}\\left( x - \\mu \\right)^{T}\\Sigma^{- 1}\\left( x - \\mu \\right)} \\right)$$  
(8.31)

where the only difference now is that we require a mean vector *μ* and covariance matrix *Σ* instead of only a mean *μ* and variance *σ*² as we required in the univariate case. This is so because now we have several predictor variables, and hence in each classification category there is a mean *vector* instead of simply a mean, and a covariance *matrix* instead of simply a variance (try sketching the multivariate LDA cells on paper).

The classification will assign *x* = *x*[*i*] to the class for which the following multivariate discriminant function is the largest:

  
$$\\delta\_{k}\\left( x \\right) = x^{T}\\Sigma^{- 1}\\mu\_{k} - \\frac{1}{2}\\mu\_{k}^{T}\\Sigma^{- 1}\\mu\_{k} + \\log\\pi\_{k}$$  
(8.32)

A comparison of the univariate discriminant function in (8.27) to that of the multivariate in (8.32) will reveal their similarities, especially if we keep in mind that *Σ*^( − 1) is serving in place of *σ*².

## 8.10 Multiclass Discriminant Analysis

In multiclass discriminant analysis where we have more than two categories on the response, we can use a *Mahalanobis distance* metric to best separate classes from each other and provide a linear projection of dimensionality up to *k* − 1, where again *k* is the number of groups or levels on the response variable. Why is the dimensionality limited to *k* − 1 dimensions? Why not exactly *k*? The reason for this can be easily understood through the following simple example. Suppose you are asked to guess which hand behind my back holds the marble. You require only a single “discriminator” to make the selection. If not in the left hand, then it must be in the right, or vice versa. When we generalize to more than two groups, there is always one less the number of groups for which a “rule” can be established for a similar reason (*a weighted sum of predictors, the reverse of the MANOVA 333problem*; see Eq. (8.35)). The “discriminator” is a rule that separates classes, and hence having a number of discriminators equal to the number of classes would make little sense. *The purpose of a discriminator is to differentiate between at least two objects. Discriminating between a single object makes no sense*. *Hence the reason why for k groups, only k − 1 discriminant functions are required.*

## 8.11 Discriminant Analysis and Dimensionality in a Simple Scatterplot

The dimensionality aspect of discriminant analysis is perhaps best understood using an example from introductory statistics. Consider the bivariate scatterplot of data in [Figure 8.6](#c8.xhtml#f8.6).

![Figure 8.6 Scatterplot of data where x, the sole predictor and hence “linear combination” composed of only a single variable, discriminates well between males and females.Return to text.⏎](images/fig8.6.jpg)

*Figure 8.6* Scatterplot of data where x, the sole predictor and hence “linear combination” composed of only a single variable, discriminates well between males and females.[Return to text.⏎](#c8.xhtml#re_f8.6)

We can see in the plot that there are two groups: one group is male while the other is female. In this simple plot, we have the *concept* of a discriminating *dimension*; in this case, that dimension is made up of only a single variable. That is, the function, made up of a single variable, typically with an intercept, *separates well*. We see that it separates males from females along a *rule* (weighted sum of predictors) defined by the dimensionality of *x*. The dimension is simple in this case, but it’s still a dimension. To reiterate, *the dimension in this case is made up of only a single variable*. The extension to a more complicated and traditional LDA is that each dimension is made up of more than a single variable; it is composed of a *linear combination* or *composite* of variables.

If you keep this simple example in mind, you will always appreciate discriminant analysis as not only a “classifier,” but also as a means of *reducing the dimensionality* of data, similar in some respects, but by no means *equivalent*, to principal components analysis. The simple scatterplot featured in introductory statistics with two groups appearing in the plot could have been the starting point to discussing discriminant analysis because once we move on to considering *t*\-tests and such in elementary statistics, we are in fact engaged at some level in at least the *concept* of discriminant analysis as the two techniques will share technical similarities, especially as we venture into multivariate *t*, which is Hotelling’s *T* ² ([Rencher & Christensen, 2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295)). *That “simple” t-test in “stats 101” was, in the end analysis, a first conceptual “opportunity” and preview of discriminant analysis*.

As in traditional analysis of variance, we seek to minimize within-scatter and maximize between-scatter of the classes. The discriminant function guarantees that the separation is *maximal*. 334By “maximal” we mean that the function separates better on the given data than any other function we could have used in the parametric family (e.g., linear models). It accomplishes this by finding the projection that maximizes the ratio of the following, called the *Rayleigh coefficient* (sometimes called *Rayleigh quotient*):

  
$$\\max\\limits\_{a} = \\frac{a^{T}{Ha}}{a^{T}{Ea}}$$  
(8.33)

where *H* and *E* are hypothesis and error matrices respectively, and *a* are coefficients or *coordinates* ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 116) of the estimated linear combination, or more precisely, linear discriminant function.

We can perform some algebra on (8.33) and obtain

  
*a*′(*H**a*−*λ**E**a*) = 0  
(8.34)

We seek to know the values of *a* (other than 0) that maximize values for *λ*. The solutions are found by

  
(*E*^( − 1)*H*−*λ**I*)*a* = 0  
(8.35)

The solutions for *λ* and *a* are the corresponding eigenvalue and eigenvectors of the discriminant function(s). Large eigenvalues are associated with discriminant functions that are “important” (*statistically*, not necessarily *substantively*) and essentially doing a lot of “work” in separating classes. *They are not variances in the context of LDA (in PCA, eigenvalues will be variances)* and hence are best considered measures of “importance” of the given discriminant function. Smaller eigenvalues are associated with less important functions. Such measures of importance can help us in deciding how many functions to keep from our analysis. If an analytical solution for discriminant analysis is unavailable or a gradient descent solution is preferred, gradient descent can be performed where reduction of error occurs by taking partial derivatives of the error *E* with respect to coefficient weights *a*[1], *a*[2], ..., *a*[*p*],

  
$$\\nabla\_{a}E = \\left\\lbrack {\\frac{\\partial E}{\\partial a\_{1}},\\frac{\\partial E}{\\partial a\_{2}},...\\frac{\\partial E}{\\partial a\_{p}}} \\right\\rbrack^{T}$$  
(8.36)

where at each step, weights *a*[*i*] are updated,

  
$$\\Delta a\_{i} = - \\eta\\frac{\\partial E}{\\partial a\_{i}}$$  

where *η* is the learning rate, and hence new weights are computed by *a*[*i*] = *a*[*i*] + *Δ**a*[*i*] ([Alpaydin, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000009)).335

## 8.12 Quadratic Discriminant Analysis

In the linear discriminant analysis above, recall that we assumed Gaussian distributions as well as equal covariance matrices among populations. More formally, we assumed that any given observation comes from a given class *k* such that

  
*x*[*i*] ∼ *N*(*μ*[*k*],*Σ*[*k*])  

That is, we assume the covariance matrices *Σ*[*k*] are the *same* from population to population. What if, instead, we did not make this assumption, but allowed *flexibility* such that covariance matrices between populations were permitted to be *unequal* instead of *constrained* to be equal? Note our use of the word “flexibility” here, which means that instead of imposing the constraint/condition that the covariance matrices are equal, we will allow for unequal covariance matrices between populations and to incorporate these differences into our modeling. Allowing for this inequality has the effect of modeling a nonlinear or irregular (i.e., quadratic, in this case) decision boundary, and hence whereas classical LDA uses only class centroids to determine membership, QDA will use more than a single “prototype” (i.e., class centroids as well as covariance matrices). Indeed, LDA is known as a *prototype classifier* ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)).

When we allow for differing covariance matrices, we will then assign *x* = *x*[*i*] to the class for which the following function is the largest, where one can readily see the relevant substitutions,

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} \\left. \\delta\_{k}\\left( x \\right) = - \\frac{1}{2}\\left( x - \\mu\_{k} \\right)T\\Sigma\_{k}^{- 1}\\left( x - \\mu\_{k} \\right) - \\frac{1}{2}\\log \\middle| \\Sigma\_{k} \\middle| + \\log\\pi\_{k} \\right. \\\\ \\left. \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = - \\frac{1}{2}x^{T}\\Sigma\_{k}^{- 1}x + x^{T}\\Sigma\_{k}^{- 1}\\mu\_{k} - \\frac{1}{2}\\mu\_{k}^{T}\\Sigma\_{k}^{- 1}\\mu\_{k} - \\frac{1}{2}\\log \\middle| \\Sigma\_{k} \\middle| + \\log\\pi\_{k} \\right. \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(8.37)

For a brief but excellent discussion of why the assumption of equal covariance matrices matters and the essential difference between linear vs. quadratic discriminant analysis, consult James et al. ([2021](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000169)). Simplified, the argument essentially goes like this: for example, with *p* = 3 predictors, the covariance matrix looks as follows:

  
$$\\sum{= \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {\\sigma^{2}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{cov}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{cov}} \\\\ {{cov}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\sigma^{2}\\mspace{6mu}\\,\\,\\,\\,{cov}} \\\\ {{cov}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{cov}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\sigma^{2}\\,\\,\\,\\,} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack\\,\\,}$$  
(8.38)

Notice that for *p* = 3 predictors, there are six parameters to estimate, or more generally, *p*(*p*+1)/2 parameters. That is, *p*(*p*+1)/2 = 3(3+1)/2 = 6. Even if we have *k* = 3 groups, we still have only six parameters to estimate since we are assuming *Σ*[*k*] is constant across groups. However, what if we designated a *separate* covariance matrix per group? This would imply that we have *p*(*p*+1)/2 parameters *per group*, which yields *k**p*(*p*+1)/2. Thus, for the *k* = 3 group problem, we will now have 3(6) = 18 parameters to estimate, which is a lot more than in the linear case. The assumption of equal covariance matrices induces linearity, which means the LDA model is *less flexible* since a great number of parameters are *a priori fixed*. That is, because of the equality condition, once we know one covariance matrix, we know them all. In the quadratic case, we are freeing this parameter to be different for each covariance matrix. Freeing and fixing parameters is a commonality in virtually all modeling. Nothing would stop us, for instance, from fixing or equating only a *few* parameters in the wider discriminant analysis framework, thereby building a more “customized” 336model. Presumably, such action would be based on theory or prior information. In the absence of such information, LDA or QDA are usually sufficient as “off the shelf” methods.

QDA then, is the more *general model*, where LDA can be conceptualized and shown to be a special case of QDA where the assumption of equal covariance matrices is imposed. The linear case is essentially a special case of the wider quadratic case in which quadratic terms are canceled due to shared covariance ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)). Instead of *k**p*(*p*+1)/2 parameters to estimate in QDA, the linearity in *x* implies there to be only *k**p* coefficients to estimate since we only have to count a single covariance matrix in our estimation, not a number equal to however many groups we have on the response (in our earlier example, that number was 3). While QDA is more flexible, it has been found that classification rules for QDA usually require larger sample sizes than for its LDA counterpart and may also be more sensitive to parametric assumptions overall. For a discussion, see [Wald and Kronmal (1977)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000378). Indeed, it should be emphasized as well that maximal separation is not necessarily equivalent to *maximal classification*, as classification incorporates additional considerations (e.g., see [Rencher & Christensen, 2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295)).

## 8.13 Regularized Discriminant Analysis

As we have seen, *linear* discriminant analysis is so popular, on a technical level, in part due to the assumption that covariance matrices are equal and linear separation is a good way to simplify the problem. It is a very easy and facilitating assumption to make about parametric structure. We have seen that by assuming equality of covariance matrices, it lessens the number of parameters that need to be estimated. Hence, even if the assumption is violated and covariance matrices are different to some extent, one convenient way to *regularize* in this setting is to simply and forcefully set them as equivalent, or to *pool* them. As [Friedman (1989, p. 167)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000114) notes:

> Even if the population class covariance matrices are substantially different, the decrease in variance accomplished by using the pooled covariance estimate can sometimes lead to superior performance, especially in small-sample settings. This is a large part of the reason for the success and popularity of linear discriminant analysis.

By *pooled covariance estimate* above is simply meant an average of covariance matrices and hence reducing the number of parameters that need to be effectively estimated. Recall that in general, when you simplify a model, you essentially regularize it as it is usually less prone to overfitting. However, doing so also risks the introduction of potential bias. Indeed, “regularizing” a linear regression equation to simply consist of an intercept is very unlikely to provide a good estimate of a bivariate relationship. In other words, over-regularizing usually *underfits* the data.

For details on how regularization can be done much more thoroughly in discriminant analysis beyond this simple trick, see [Friedman (1989)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000114). Hastie et al. ([2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), Chapter 18) also discuss discriminant analysis for the case in which the number of cases is greater than the number of variables, the so-called *diagonal LDA classifier*, where within-class covariance matrices are diagonal, thus implying independent predictors. Mixture models in discriminant analysis are also a possibility, 337which combine several densities (typically Gaussian) and can be estimated via the EM algorithm to obtain maximum likelihood estimates.
