# 10 Decision Trees, Bagging, Random Forests and Committee Machines

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-13](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-13)

Thus far in this book we have surveyed a number of *learners*. A *strong learner*, as can be said of an intelligent human being, adapts relatively quickly to new data (or *experience* more generally) and adjusts how it does things as the incoming data call for it. One touch of the hot stove psychologically conditions the individual to stay away from hot stoves – perhaps forever. A “close call” and near traffic accident on a winter road conditions you to forever drive with more care in winter, or even perhaps in all seasons. If we had the choice, *we would usually prefer strong learners*.

A *weak learner* learns much more slowly. This is the individual who has five DUI arrests yet still risks the lives of others and “never learns” (and probably belongs forever in jail). More statistically, a weak (also called a *base*) classifier is one that correctly classifies just over 50% of the time, that is, a bit better than chance ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). Even though we would like all learners to be strong, the truth is that many (perhaps most) times, we are confronted with weak learners. Given this is the case, the question then becomes the following:

> *How can we take a series of weak learners and combine them to produce a stronger one?*

This is what this chapter is all about. It is about how to take a number of weak learners, combine them in *some capacity*, and generate a much stronger learner. Perhaps the most amazing thing here is that by combining weak learners, we generate a *stronger learner*. This in itself is quite a remarkable idea. There are even times when choosing a set of weak learners dominates a single strong learner. Hence, though we in general prefer strong learners, sometimes combining weaker learners is actually more efficient. Five “close calls” with the hot stove (set of weak learners) may teach you to avoid hot stoves better than a single experience (strong learner) in which you undergo an actual burn.

> *Given the choice, we would generally prefer all learners be strong learners. However, by combining weak learners, it becomes possible to generate a stronger learner. Combining a set of weak learners can actually be preferable in some cases over a single stronger learner.*

## 10.1 Why Combining Weak Learners Works: Concept of Variance Reduction Using Averages

It is well known in statistics that *averaging reduces variance*. That is, when one repeatedly guesses the average income of a population, one “centers” in on a figure at the expense of a lot of variability around that figure.369

So-called *ensemble* methods or *committee machines* combine weak learners to produce stronger ones, ones that are more *stable* than not. Unstable predictors or classifiers have high variance (due to overfitting) and low bias. As we will see, methods such as *decision trees* suffer from high variance such that if we tweak the data slightly, we are likely going to see a significant change in the outcome. This is what suffering from high variance means. It means if you *perturbate* (i.e., “change”) the data in different ways, even if rather slight, it results in much *perturbated* outcomes, as [Figure 10.1](#c10.xhtml#f10.1) illustrates.

![Figure 10.1 Example of pertubating a data set. Original data set (left). Pertubated data set by adding random points (right).Return to text.⏎](images/fig10.1.jpg)

*Figure 10.1* Example of pertubating a data set. Original data set (left). Pertubated data set by adding random points (right).[Return to text.⏎](#c10.xhtml#re_f10.1)

Decision trees and neural networks are relatively unstable methods, whereas methods such as linear regression and discriminant analysis are much more stable, having low variance and higher possibility of bias. Even with these techniques, however, *committee machines* can be used to combine learners to produce a more stable estimator. The stability is reflected in how well the learner generalizes to new test data, and hence, committee machines or *ensemble* *methods*, as they are sometimes called, can also be interpreted as a form of regularization ([Goodfellow et al., 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000131)). For example, [Perrone and Cooper (1993)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000287) have proposed producing committees of neural networks instead of selecting the single neural network with the best generalization performance. Indeed, it can be shown that the error generated by a committee of networks is less than or equal to the error generated by an average of those networks. Again, this is quite remarkable in and of itself – *a team of mediocre players performs better than a single stronger player; a pack of weaker wolves performs better than a single strong wolf.*

Hence, and perhaps somewhat paradoxically and unexpectedly, the instability of an algorithm can actually be desirable, in a sense, or at minimum not detrimental, and thus an important tool that can be used to exploit and improve the accuracy of that learning algorithm. Both *bagging* and *boosting*, as we will see, actually exploit this relative weakness, the weakness being the instability, in order to create a more accurate learning method. Weak(er) learners can be combined to generate a stronger one. By perturbing the learning set, these methods generate an “ensemble” of different base predictors or classifiers which are then combined into a single combined predictor or classifier. How successful is this combination? The success will depend in part on the degree of instability in the individual base predictors. Bagging has been shown to be beneficial when combining learners that tend to overfit the data and are relatively unstable (Kroese et al., [2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000202)).370

On the opposite end, as mentioned, a procedure is said to have low variance if it yields similar results on distinct data sets or even subsets of the same dataset. That is, if you perturbate the data somewhat, it still generally leads to a similar outcome. Recall the bias-variance trade-off that has dominated this book thus far, which we remind here:

> *Good learners have low bias and low variance; however, as one decreases, the other is likely to increase; hence the trade-off.*

Before we consider committee machines in more detail, we need to survey the important topic of *decision trees*. We start with decision trees for two reasons: 1) decision trees are important in their own right and constitute a rather simple way to understand the statistical influence of predictors, and 2) our discussion of bagging and boosting will center around decision trees. As we will see, averaging several decision trees is a prime example of constructing a committee machine, though averaging and combining other procedures also has similar effects.

## 10.2 Decision Trees

Statistical learning methods based on decision trees have gained tremendous popularity due to their simplicity, intuitive representation, and to some extent, predictive accuracy, though often they come in second when compared to many other learning methods. Of all statistical learning methods, decision trees, a member of the tree-based family of algorithms, have been regarded as perhaps the most useful of so-called “off-the-shelf” procedures for data mining. In the context of regression, regression trees were first introduced by [Morgan and Sonquist (1963)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000254) using a computer program called *Automatic Interaction Detection* (AID). For a history of decision trees, consult Ripley ([1996](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000301), Section 7.4). As we will discuss shortly, boosting and bootstrap aggregation (*bagging*) can improve the efficiency of decision trees and other learning methods.

In [Figure 10.2](#c10.xhtml#f10.2) is a basic decision tree, one that we will revisit shortly.

![Figure 10.2 Example of a basic decision tree on the iris data.Return to text.⏎](images/fig10.2.jpg)

*Figure 10.2* Example of a basic decision tree on the iris data.[Return to text.⏎](#c10.xhtml#re_f10.2)

The *root node* in the decision tree is the unique starting point of the tree, and where the tree ends is referred to as the *terminal node*. Along the way down the tree, branches are created that represent splits in the given variable. Of course, not all nodes are terminal. A nonterminal node splits into two daughter nodes, which creates a binary split. If the variable is binary, then defining the nature 371of the split is easy (e.g., 0 vs. 1). If the variable is continuous, however, it is made discrete and binary, such as split at the median, for example. A single-split tree with only two terminal nodes is called a *stump*. The set of all terminal nodes is called the *partition of the data*.

Decision trees have a lot of benefits to them. For one, they can handle very large datasets. They can also handle a mixed bag of predictors, that of *quantitative* and *qualitative*. They can be used both for regression (where targets or response variables are *continuous*) and classification problems (where targets or predictors are *categorical*). They handle missing data quite easily and in general, trees are relatively easy to interpret, especially if the tree is small. Downsides to decision trees include the fact that larger trees can be difficult to interpret and the predictive performance of decision trees is often not as good as competing methods. Further, deep trees (i.e., those without pruning, also known as *saturated trees*) are often too heavily reliant on the training data used to construct them. Small changes in training data can result in a dramatic change in the resulting tree. Because decision trees often exhibit high variance, committee machines such as *bagging*, *boosting*, and *random forests* have come into vogue and are especially useful when applied specifically to decision trees.

### 10.2.1 How Should Trees Be Grown?

We have demonstrated a simple decision tree above, but how do we grow such a tree? How do we go about creating the relevant nodes and branches? At each node, the tree-splitting algorithm needs to decide which variable is “best” in terms of providing a split. That is, at each node, the algorithm needs to select a variable that provides differentiation with regard to the response variable. We must consider every possible split over all variables present at the given node, then enumerate all possible splits, evaluate each one, and decide which is ideal in some sense ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 285). If the variable at which a split is contemplated is ordinal or continuous, the number of possible splits at a given node is one fewer than the number of its distinctly observed values. If the variable is nominal or categorical, the set of possible splits at that node for that variable is the set of all subsets.

### 10.2.2 Optimization Criteria for Tree-Building

As is true with virtually all statistical methods, we should require a condition to optimize in creating the relevant branches for the trees. Since we cannot consider *every* partition of the predictor space (such would take too long and have too many possibilities), we need to adopt an overall approach to doing so. One approach that is often taken is a *top-down*, *greedy approach*, referred to as *recursive binary splitting* or more generally *recursive partitioning* ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)) which seeks to minimize the following criterion:

  
$$\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}\\left( y\_{i} - {\\hat{y}}\_{s\_{j}} \\right)^{2}$$  

which the reader will recognize as the familiar *residual sums of squares criterion* (RSS) where *y*[*i*] are observed values and *ŷ*[*s*[*j*]] are predicted values within a given subsection of the decision surface for a combination of predictors. The predictor which results in the greatest reduction in RSS is chosen at each step. This process continues for each predictor and space until some criterion to stop the process is attained. The stopping criteria may include a consideration of sample size limitations. That is, tree splitting may continue until there is minimal *n* at each split, enough to halt the algorithm.372

### 10.2.3 Why Not Multiway Splits?

In our construction of decision trees, note that we are performing *binary* splits at each node. But why not perform splits containing more than two possibilities? While it is also possible to split a tree node into more than two groups, generally referred to as *multiway* or *multivariate* splits, it generally produces inferior results when compared to the simpler binary split. As well, multiway nodes can often be difficult to interpret ([Aggarwal, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000005); [Alpaydin, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000009)). The major reason for this is that multiway splits can lead to too many nodes near the tree root that have only a few data points, thus leaving insufficient data for later splits. Therefore, instead of attempting multiway splits, the generally preferred strategy is for numerous binary splits.

At times, it can be beneficial to preprocess the data before fitting a tree. This includes standardization of the data. Trying out both solutions, raw and standardized, may be advantageous to learn of any effects due to standardizing scores prior to building a tree.

> *Minimizing residual sums of squares is a common criterion for choosing a predictor at each step of building a decision tree. The algorithm is “greedy” in that by minimizing RSS at a given split, it does not consider longer-term consequences for branches to follow.*

### 10.2.4 Overfitting, Saturation, and Tree Pruning

A single decision tree fit to data is likely to overfit the data because it is built too specific to the particular data set. This would be akin to fitting a regression curve (not limited to a line) a bit too closely to a scatterplot of points. Of course, the consequence of this is that an overfit tree is likely to not perform that well on test data for reasons we are already familiar with.

If the tree is grown to the point where none of the nodes can be split any further, the tree is said to be *saturated*. That is, saturated trees have exhausted their potential for performing splits. Especially in high-dimensional space, it is very easy to allow the tree to grow extremely large, and if we allow it to grow to the point of saturation, it can actually become unwieldily large. So, how does one prevent overfitting? In the earlier days of decision trees, tree growers attempted to restrict the growth of the tree by implementing so-called “stopping rules” to prevent overfitting. However, as shown by [Breiman et al. (1984)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000045), such stopping rules are not generally advised and perhaps counter-intuitively, the preferred solution is often to build a very large tree and then perform what is known as *pruning* to obtain a *subtree* ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 308). That is, it can be shown that building a saturated tree and then *scaling back* the tree is often preferable to early stopping or trying to, more generally, *regularize* the tree too early.

How to prune then becomes a crucial process. Indeed, much of the research in the evolution of decision trees has not been so much about how to grow a tree, but rather *how to prune it back*. The general problem to overcome in pruning is that *pruning generates bias*. Why is this the case? Consider that when we prune a tree, we are now imperfectly estimating the data, the same way a regression line imperfectly estimates a swarm of data in a scatterplot. Another approach might be to forego tree pruning entirely and simply grow many trees quite large (via resampling) and then take an average of the trees to reduce variance. As we will see later, this technique of averaging is referred to as *bagging*, which is a short name for *bootstrap aggregating*. Not surprisingly, the “best” pruned tree would be the one that performs best on *cross-validation*. Doing so, however, 373would involve entertaining many different trees. Hence, we need an alternative strategy for pruning and selecting a smaller set of trees for consideration.

> *Decision trees are easily subject to overfitting. Implementing “stopping rules” to prevent the tree from growing too large is usually not the ideal solution. The preferred solution is often to allow the tree to grow to saturation and then prune it back.*

### 10.2.5 Cost Complexity or Weakest Link Pruning

The procedure of *cost complexity pruning*, which also goes by the name of *weakest link pruning*, is one way of providing us with the subset of trees we require when pruning. Instead of considering every possible tree, we consider only a sequence of trees that will be indexed by a nonnegative tuning parameter *α*. Tuning parameters, of course, are not new by now, as we have seen them repeatedly in other procedures such as ridge and lasso regression. For each value of the tuning parameter *α*, we will obtain a *subtree* such that the following criterion is minimized:

  
$$\\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}\\left( y\_{i} - {\\hat{y}}\_{s\_{j}} \\right)^{2}} + \\alpha \\middle| T \\right|$$  
(10.1)

The number of terminal nodes is indicated by |*T*| of the given tree *T*. The tuning parameter *α* controls the trade-off between the subtree’s complexity and its fit to the training data ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)). We can see that as *α* increases, it results in a relatively large increase in the overall error *especially when there are several terminal nodes to the tree* (|*T*|) since |*T*| multiplied by a larger number than not in *α* will result in a larger product *α*|*T*| than not. Informally, what this means is that if you want a lot of nodes to your tree, *then there is a cost to doing so*, since we would expect RSS to decrease with increasing number of nodes unless we invoked a penalty. This idea parallels that of multiple regression where the addition of more predictors, without a penalty, generally decreases residual sums of squares. Recall the goal is to minimize $\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}\\left( y\_{i} - {\\hat{y}}\_{s\_{j}} \\right)^{2}$ which means smaller values are preferred to larger values. The choice of *α* is generally made through cross-validation or an independent sample test set where an independent test set may be preferable to cross-validation if the data set is large enough and can be split accordingly. It should be emphasized as well that for any value of the penalty, there may be more than a single minimizing subtree which makes selection of the “best” tree in this situation a bit more challenging. As values for *α* increase away from zero, the decision tree gets “pruned” and so obtaining an ideal value for *α* is of paramount importance ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168), p. 309).

> *For increasing values of* *α**, the product* *α*|*T*| *increases, where* *T* *is the number of terminal nodes. That is, as the complexity of the tree increases,* *α*|*T*| *serves as a penalty and increases RSS. Hence, if the nodes included in T are not “worthwhile” in reducing RSS sufficiently, then penalized RSS will end up increasing rather than decreasing.*374

## 10.3 Classification Trees

In our survey of decision trees thus far, we have discussed only those of regression trees. Decision trees, not surprisingly, are also applicable to classification. Classification trees are used to predict *qualitative* or *categorical* responses instead of *continuous* responses as was the case for the regression trees just surveyed. As for regression trees, *recursive binary splitting* is used to build the tree. However, in assessing the quality of the tree, we cannot use RSS as the quantity to minimize since RSS is applicable to continuous measures only.

What to use for estimating error rates instead of RSS? An alternative for classification trees is the *classification error rate*:

  
*E* = 1 − max[*k*](*p̂*[*m**k*])  
(10.2)

where here *p̂*[*m**k*] is the proportion of observations (on the *training* data) in the *m*th region of the tree that are classified in the class denoted by *k* (James et al., [2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)). Hence, (10.2) is the fraction of observations in error for the given class. The classification error rate is not always a perfect measure of the quality of the tree, however. A problem with the classification error rate is that it is not sensitive enough of a measure for growing a tree ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168), p. 312). That is, it is a bit too “crude” of a measure. We require other measures to help in assessing the build of our tree. These two measures are the *Gini index* and the *deviance*, which we now discuss.

### 10.3.1 Gini Index

The *Gini index* is a measure that can be used in place of, or to supplement the classification error rate and can take the place of residual sums of squares in the regression tree context. It is a measure of *node purity* (also often called node *impurity*), defined by

  
$$G = {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{{\\hat{p}}\_{mk}\\left( 1 - {\\hat{p}}\_{mk} \\right)}}$$  
(10.3)

which is a measure of total variance across the *k* classes, where recall *p̂*[*m**k*] is the proportion of training observations in the *m*th region that are from the *k*th class. As a measure of total variance across the classes, the index takes on a smaller-than-not value the closer the *p̂*[*m**k*] values are to 0 or 1. That is, when *p̂*[*m**k*] is equal to 0, then *G* reduces to

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {G = {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{{\\hat{p}}\_{mk}\\left( 1 - {\\hat{p}}\_{mk} \\right)}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{0\\left( 1 - 0 \\right)}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = 0} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

On the other extreme, when *p̂*[*m**k*] = 1, then375

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {G = {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{{\\hat{p}}\_{mk}\\left( 1 - {\\hat{p}}\_{mk} \\right)}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{1\\left( 1 - 1 \\right)}}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = 0} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

A smaller-than-not value for the Gini index indicates that a node contains predominantly observations from a single class ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)). The variance is maximized as *p̂*[*m**k*]→0.5 across the classes, which equals 0.5(0.5) = 0.25 per class. Any deviation from this maximum, for instance, 0.4(1 − 0.4) = 0.24 produces a lesser product and hence contributes less variance to the sum ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)). For *p̂*[*m**k*] = 0.1, for instance, the given product is 0.1(0.9) = 0.09 which is quite small indicating hardly any variance across the classes. This again is why *p̂*[*m**k*]→0.5 maximizes the variance of the classes.

An alternative to the Gini index is *cross-entropy* or *deviance*, defined by

  
$$D = - {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{{\\hat{p}}\_{mk}\\log{\\hat{p}}\_{mk}}}$$  
(10.4)

Recall that *p̂*[*m**k*] is bound between 0 and 1, which implies that  − *p̂*[*m**k*]log *p̂*[*m**k*] must be equal to or greater than 0 (James et al., [2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168), p. 312). Entropy takes on a value close to 0 for *p̂*[*m**k*]′*s* approaching 0 or 1. That is, as was the case for the Gini index, overall *node purity* is suggested by a small *D* ([James et al., 2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)). Entropy can be interpreted as the minimum number of bits of information required to encode the class code of an instance or observation ([Alpaydin, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000009)).

> *The Gini index and entropy are very similar to one another. Both attempt to provide a measure of how much variance exists across the classes. They can both be regarded as measures of node purity.*

### 10.3.2 Decision Trees in R

We will use the *tree* package in R and code ([Ripley, 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000302)) to compute a decision tree on the iris data:

```
> library(tree)
> ir.tr <- tree(Species ~., iris)
> ir.tr
```

The code Species ~., iris requests a tree based on sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width on the iris data. The output below details the splitting decisions made at different points in the tree. What will be most useful is the summary given at the end of the output, not the specific details of the splitting:

```
node), split, n, deviance, yval, (yprob)
* denotes terminal node
1) root 150 329.600 setosa ( 0.33333 0.33333 0.33333 )
  2) Petal.Length < 2.45 50 0.000 setosa ( 1.00000 0.00000 0.00000 ) *
  3) Petal.Length > 2.45 100 138.600 versicolor ( 0.00000 0.50000 0.50000 )
    6) Petal.Width < 1.75 54 33.320 versicolor ( 0.00000 0.90741 0.09259 )
      12) Petal.Length < 4.95 48 9.721 versicolor ( 0.00000 0.97917 0.02083 )

```

376 

We see above the residual mean deviance (0.1253) as well as the misclassification error rate of 0.02667. We now plot the tree ([Figure 10.3](#c10.xhtml#f10.3)), where pretty = 0 keeps the level names of factor splits unchanged (see the package for how this parameter can be adjusted):

![Figure 10.3 Plot of decision tree on the iris data. Tree without labels (left). Tree with labels (right).Return to text.⏎](images/fig10.3.jpg)

*Figure 10.3* Plot of decision tree on the iris data. Tree without labels (left). Tree with labels (right).[Return to text.⏎](#c10.xhtml#re_f10.3)

```
> plot(ir.tr)
> text(ir.tr, pretty=0)
```

We can also obtain the misclassifications of the tree:

```
> ir.tr1 <- tree(Species ~., iris)
> misclass.tree(ir.tr1)
[1] 4
```

377 

The number 4 agrees with the misclassification error rate reported above. We also see that the number of terminal nodes agrees with the tree we generated. That is, the endings of each branch terminate with either *setosa*, *versicolor*, *versicolor*, *virginica*, *virginica*, or *virginica*.

We now prune our original tree, which will allow us to observe misclassification error rate as a function of tree size:

```
> cv.iris = cv.tree(ir.tr, FUN=prune.misclass)
> cv.iris
$size
[1] 6 4 3 2 1
$dev
[1] 8 8 11 95 112
```

The output $dev refers to the cross-validation error rate (“misclass” in the plot below). We see that it is equal at a value of 8 for trees of size 6 and 4 terminal nodes, as we can more easily see in the plot in [Figure 10.4](#c10.xhtml#f10.4) (plot (cv.iris, type = “b”) will produce a similar plot):

![Figure 10.4 Misclassification error as a function of size of decision tree.Return to text.⏎](images/fig10.4.jpg)

```
> plot(cv.iris)
```

We now obtain the pruned tree with 4 nodes ([Figure 10.5](#c10.xhtml#f10.5)):

![Figure 10.5 Pruned decision tree on the iris data.Return to text.⏎](images/fig10.5.jpg)

*Figure 10.5* Pruned decision tree on the iris data.[Return to text.⏎](#c10.xhtml#re_f10.5)

```
> prune.ir.tr = prune.misclass(ir.tr,best = 4)
> plot(prune.ir.tr)
> text(prune.ir.tr)
```

378 

We now obtain misclassifications on the tree,

```
> prune.ir.tr = prune.misclass(ir.tr, best = 4)
> misclass.tree(prune.ir.tr)
[1] 4
```

The number of misclassifications is equal to 4. Note that had we chosen a much more crude tree, say with 2 nodes, the misclassification error rate would have skyrocketed, such as in the following where we request only 2 nodes (best = 2):

```
> prune.ir.tr = prune.misclass(ir.tr, best = 2)
> misclass.tree(prune.ir.tr)
[1] 50
```

The package *rpart* ([Therneau et al., 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000355)) can also be used to fit decision trees. We will fit a tree to the iris data:

```
> library(rpart)
> iris.rpart <- rpart(formula = Species ~., data = iris, method = “anova”)
> iris.rpart
n= 150
node), split, n, deviance, yval
    * denotes terminal node
1) root 150 100.0000000 2.000000
  2) Petal.Length< 2.45 50 0.0000000 1.000000 *
  3) Petal.Length>=2.45 100 25.0000000 2.500000
    6) Petal.Width< 1.75 54 4.5370370 2.092593
      12) Petal.Length< 4.85 46 0.9782609 2.021739 *
      13) Petal.Length>=4.85 8 2.0000000 2.500000 *

> library(rpart.plot)
```

379 

Percentages of sample size in respective nodes are depicted in [Figure 10.6](#c10.xhtml#f10.6). We note from the figure that a tree size of 3 or 4 gets the relative error down to fairly low levels, where “cp” on the *x*\-axis is the cost complexity parameter ([Therneau et al., 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000355)). In general, setting cp to a smaller value will generate a fuller tree ([Boehmke and Greenwell, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000033)). See the package for further details regarding the computation of cp.

There has been some research done on multivariate responses for decision trees (Canete-Sifuentes et al., [2021](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000053), [Zhang & Ye, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000402)). Survival trees ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)), also known as *conditional inference* *trees*, have also been advanced. *Multivariate adaptive regression splines* (MARS), due to [Friedman (1991)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000115) is a generalization of recursive partitioning and is a nonparametric regression approach which uses basis functions. For details, see Izenman ([2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 311). Work has also been done on *Bayesian additive regression trees* (Chipman et al., [2010](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000061)).

## 10.4 Committee Machines

As mentioned at the outset of this chapter, “committee machine” is a general term referring to combining weaker learners to generate a stronger learner. By far the most popular and useful of committee machines are those of *bagging* and *boosting*.

## 10.5 Overview of Bagging and Boosting

We have so far in this chapter discussed decision trees and have focused on their construction. We have emphasized that a single tree, especially if not pruned, likely significantly overfits the data. That is, it is easily subject to random perturbations in the data such that if we changed a few data points here or there, the outcome of the tree would be different. In statistical learning theory, as we 380know by now, this is referred to the method having *high variance*. Note carefully this is not the *data* having high variance. We are referring here to the *method*. The data are what they are. We are more interested in evaluating the *method* used to evaluate the data. Unstable methods are usually not preferred to more stable ones. Decision trees are not the only statistical method that is unstable, but in what follows, we will use them as an example in our discussion of bagging and boosting.

How can we reduce the variance of an otherwise unstable method? Though there are many ways of accomplishing this reduction in variance, two methods are often used: *bagging* and *boosting*; however, boosting prioritizes reducing *bias* over reducing variance. Bagging, which is short for *bootstrap aggregating*, is random and probabilistic. By essentially averaging bootstrapped samples, one could get different bagging results depending on the given sampling procedure. Boosting, on the other hand, is not random or probabilistic. It is instead *systematic* or *deterministic*. Boosting generates predictable non-random perturbations of the training data by successive reweighting of the training set, where the most current and updated weights depend on misclassification history. We survey boosting shortly. First, we more fully develop the idea of bagging.

### 10.5.1 Bagging

Bagging is essentially a procedure of taking many bootstrapped samples and then aggregating (averaging) them. By averaging results, the goal is to reduce variance. For example, as already discussed, in a typical decision tree, any *particular* tree likely suffers from high variance, which basically means that a given tree is subject to random fluctuations in the data. That is, if we perturbed the data somewhat, the resulting tree would be different. By averaging trees (or whatever method we are using), the hope is to reduce the overall variance. In fact, the success of bagging actually depends on how originally unstable the data are; *the more unstable, the more perturbing the data set causes a change in prediction, the more advantageous it is to bag to improve accuracy* ([Breiman, 1996](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000047)). Be sure to understand what we have just said. We emphasize that *the more unstable a learning method, the more it stands to benefit from aggregating*. If the learning method is stable, bagging will, in general, be less efficient. In fact, for relatively stable methods, bagging has been found to work less well and has been found to actually *degrade* the performance of stable procedures ([Breiman, 1996](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000047)).

### 10.5.2 A Familiar Example: Bagging Samples and the Variance of the Mean

The simplest conceptual example of bagging would be to designate a sample of say, 100 observations, bootstrap 10 samples, on each compute a sample mean, then average those means. The average of those averages $\\mu\_{\\overline{y}}$ will have less variance than any of the individual averages, $\\overline{y}$. *Averaging (in this case, of means) reduces variance*. If each of the subset samples has a variance equal to *σ*², then the variance of those means, as is well known, is equal to *σ*²/*n*, with standard error $\\sigma/\\sqrt{n}$.

Hence, when we think of bagging, it is convenient to simply think of the word *averaging*. *Averaging reduces variance*. As an analogy, imagine taking betting predictions for a sporting event from one forecaster vs. ten forecasters. If you averaged the results from ten forecasters, the prediction would have less variance. On average, the forecast might be more “stable” than if you relied on the prediction of a single, stronger forecaster. This is the idea of bagging, except that we will apply it to bootstrapped samples instead of to actual empirical divisions of the data. In theory, if we had enough data, we could feasibly take segments of the data and average results, but usually, 381we do not have enough data to do this. This is why bootstrapping is utilized in bagging – *because of an insufficient amount of real data*.

### 10.5.3 A Deeper Look at Bagging

Let us look more closely into how bagging works. First, we begin with the most ideal and fanciful but unrealistic of situations. Suppose we apply a statistical learning method to some data and compute a function on many different empirical subsets of that data. Let’s suppose for a moment that we were able to partition the data perfectly and have all subsets of the data represented. Then, the average of all those subsets would be the following:

  
$${\\hat{f}}\_{avg}\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{1}{B}{\\sum\\limits\_{b = 1}^{B}{{\\hat{f}}^{b}\\left( x \\right)}}$$  

where *B* is the number of subsets that we are drawing and computing on each a function on *x*. The estimated function is *f̂*^(*b*)(*x*). Thus, *f̂*^(*b*)(*x*)/*B* is the average of all those computed estimated functions. But why is this situation unrealistic? It is so because we are likely to not have access to all partitions of the data, or, the number of partitions of the data would likely simply be too large to be practical. Data is usually expensive (at least in some fields), and so the idea of having large partitions of data available may not be pragmatic. However, it should be emphasized that if this were possible, it would be the ideal situation to shoot for. *Real data is always better than simulated data*.

The way around the above problem will be to bootstrap samples from the only sample we do have and compute the average of all such bootstrapped samples:

  
$${\\hat{f}}\_{bag}\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{1}{B}{\\sum\\limits\_{b = 1}^{B}{{\\hat{f}}^{\*b}\\left( x \\right)}}$$  

Notice that the only thing that has changed is where before *f*[*a**v**g*](*x*) was the average of all partitions of the training data, now *f̂*^( \* *b*)(*x*) is the average of all the *bootstrapped* samples. Hence, we are averaging a subset of all samples via the bootstrap procedure. That is, we are *aggregating the bootstrapped samples*. This is precisely what bagging means. *It simply means taking an average of functions via bootstrapping*. For a good theoretical discussion of just why bagging works on a technical level superseding our intuitive conceptual explanation, see Breiman ([1996](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000047), p. 129). Breiman justifies that the degree of instability in the method is paramount to determining whether bagging will or will not be effective.

> *Bagging is simply taking an average of bootstrapped samples. The reason for taking bootstrapped samples is that dividing up the data into many divisions is impractical. Dividing the actual empirical data into subset samples would, theoretically, be our first choice, however, if practical.*

When working with decision trees, bagging can combine hundreds or even thousands of bootstrapped trees. Think of what this means for a moment – we have a single sample, we bootstrap many samples from this sample, and on each, we compute a separate decision tree. We then average the results of all the decision trees we compute. Each tree alone suffers from high variance, 382but when we bag (i.e., average) all of the bootstrapped trees, *we reduce variance*. As already discussed, bagging is especially useful when dealing with predictors that tend to overfit the data, such as in decision trees, where the unpruned tree structure is very sensitive to small changes or perturbations in the training set.

### 10.5.4 Out-of-Bag Error

Once we bag, we would like to know how well the bagging procedure performed. We need a way of evaluating the results of the bagging. To properly evaluate, it would make little sense to validate on the bagged decision trees (or whatever statistical learning method we used). This would be akin to evaluating how well a boxing fighter performs on practice opponents; it is not a true test of the boxer’s skill.

To evaluate the goodness of bagging, *we require observations that were not part of the bagging procedure*. That is, as with other cross-validation, we require a kind of *test set* on which to evaluate bagging. Observations that were not part of the bagging procedure are referred to as *out-of-bag (OOB) observations.* These are the observations that are part of the training set, but not used to generate the given bagged tree. In spirit, they serve the same purpose as in typical cross-validation; however, the out-of-bag observations are simply the set of observations (roughly 1/3; James et al., [2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168)) in the training data not used in generating the given bootstrapped tree.

### 10.5.5 Interpreting Results from Bagging

When we bag, there is no easy way to interpret the result since now we have a number of trees rather than a single tree. Hence, while bagging does tend to improve prediction accuracy, as is true of so many machine learning algorithms, it does so generally at the expense of *interpretability*. There is simply no easy way to combine trees and read off the “meaningfulness,” in some sense, of the individual predictors.

The situation is not entirely hopeless, however. There are some measures of importance that can be used. For bagging regression trees, as already discussed, a decrease in RSS can be used to evaluate the importance of a predictor due to its split inclusion. A large decrease in RSS suggests the given predictor is valuable to the decision tree. In a classification context, decreases in the *Gini index* can be used in a similar way to evaluate the importance of a given variable. Large decreases in the Gini index suggest the variable under consideration may be important.

It should be emphasized as well that bagging does not always improve performance and relies very much on the base models being *unstable*. There are some situations where bagging will not improve performance or prediction. For instance, [Buja and Stuetzle (2000)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000050) found bagging to, at times, increase bias; however, the increase or decrease in mean squared error was contingent upon the given statistic and its distribution. There is no free lunch, and hence bagging on one data set may perform better or worse than bagging on another.

### 10.5.6 Bagging in R

Many packages can be used to bag in R such as *baguette* ([Kuhn, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000209)). Bagging for classification in R can be performed using *ipred* ([Peters & Hothorn, 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000288)) and *rpart* ([Therneau et al., 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000355)). Below we feature an example from the package *ipred*, which uses data on breast cancer from the package *mlbench* ([Leisch & Dimitriadou, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000216)) featuring various characteristics of cells:383

```
> library(ipred)
> library(MASS)
> library(survival)
> data(“BreastCancer”, package = “mlbench”)
> head(BreastCancer)
```

 
|  || Id || Cl.thickness || Cell.size || Cell.shape || Marg.adhesion || Epith.c.size |

| 1 || 1000025 || 5 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 2 |

We now bag the following model in a single step, where *class* is modeled as a function of cell characteristics:

```
mod <- bagging(Class ~ Cl.thickness + Cell.size
          + Cell.shape + Marg.adhesion
          + Epith.c.size + Bare.nuclei
          + Bl.cromatin + Normal.nucleoli
+ Mitoses, data=BreastCancer, coob=TRUE)
```

The designation coob=TRUE instructs to use the out-of-bag error rate. We now print the results from the bagging:

```
print(mod)
Bagging classification trees with 25 bootstrap replications
Call: bagging.data.frame(formula = Class ~ Cl.thickness + Cell.size +
    Cell.shape + Marg.adhesion + Epith.c.size + Bare.nuclei +
    Bl.cromatin + Normal.nucleoli + Mitoses, data = BreastCancer,
    nbagg = 100, coob = TRUE)

```

We can see that the out-of-bag misclassification error estimate is equal to 0.0381. That is, the classifier only misclassifies approximately 3.8% of cases on unseen data. This result is consistent with what Breiman ([1998](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000048)) found on these same data. The number of bootstrap replications is 25 by default. We can change that number by including nbagg = 100 just before the coob = TRUE statement:384

```
mod <- bagging(Class ~ Cl.thickness + Cell.size
          + Cell.shape + Marg.adhesion
          + Epith.c.size + Bare.nuclei
          + Bl.cromatin + Normal.nucleoli
          + Mitoses, data=BreastCancer, nbagg = 100, coob=TRUE)
```

## 10.6 Random Forests

We have seen how bagged trees (or whatever statistical learning method we are using) can help reduce variance in the method by averaging results. The question now is, *can we improve on bagging?* It turns out that we can. The technique of *random forests* is yet another committee machine. Random forests take bagging to the next level, seeking to improve upon it. To appreciate how random forests improve on bagging, we first need to consider what is lacking in bagging in the first place.

### 10.6.1 The Problem with Bagging Decision Trees

We know that in building decision trees, overfitting can occur because the nodes will contain the “best option” at each split. That is, a decision tree is, in a sense, *optimized* to produce the best outcome and hence is capitalizing on the training data a great deal. Thus, we can expect trees to be *similar* in many respects when bagged because each tree is built with the same optimization strategy in mind. Of course, if you build trees with the same optimization, this will quite naturally and quickly lead to overfitting.

*Random forests* are an ingenious way to combat the overfitting problem of combining decision trees. How they do this is by introducing a *randomization feature* into each node split in an effort to combat overfitting. That is, each node is split in a random manner where a random sample of predictors is chosen as split “candidates” from the full set of possible predictors. This improves over bagging alone because when we bag, if there is, say, one strong predictor, most of the trees developed will use this strong predictor in the top split, and hence, *all bagged trees will look similar, which produces predictions that are highly correlated*. Where bagging reduces variance and potentially bias for full-grown trees, a random forest reduces the correlation between 385tree-structured classifiers. That is, random forests essentially *decorrelates* the trees through this randomization process. Random forests forces each split to consider only a *subset of the predictors*, which is what “decorrelates” the trees.

> *The problem with bagging decision trees is that the trees are correlated. Averaging many highly correlated quantities reduces variance, but not as much as averaging many uncorrelated quantities. Random forests overcomes this problem by introducing a randomization process regarding how predictors are chosen at each split.*

### 10.6.2 Equivalency of Random Forests and Bagging

The observant reader may have noticed that there is a certain condition in which random forests must be equivalent to bagging. Indeed, random forests have a natural relationship to bagging *when the random forest is built using the number of trees equal to the number of predictors*. Under this condition, *random forests equate to bagging*. Random forests then can be considered, in this context, simply a *special case* of bagging where a randomization feature is introduced, or vice versa, one can also consider bagging a special case of random forests where no randomization feature is implemented.

> *Random forests can be considered a special case of bagging in which a random sample of decision trees are selected from the bootstrapped “bagged” samples in an effort to decorrelate the trees. When all predictors are used in the random forest and hence there is no randomization element, this then reduces to bagging.*

### 10.6.3 Random Forests in R

The package *randomForest* ([Liaw & Wiener, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000221)) can be used to build a random forest in R. We demonstrate on the iris data, where we combine an ensemble of trees (see package for more details on this example):

```
> library(randomForest)
> data(iris)
> rf1 <- randomForest(Species ~ ., iris, ntree=50)
> rf2 <- randomForest(Species ~ ., iris, ntree=50)
> rf3 <- randomForest(Species ~ ., iris, ntree=50)
```

We can look at each of the 50 trees before combining them. For instance, for rf1, we have:386

```
> rf1

          Type of random forest: classification
              Number of trees: 50
No. of variables tried at each split: 2

```

| setosa || 50 || 0 || 0 || 0.00 |

We see from the above that the out-of-bag error estimate is 4.67%, and we see from the confusion matrix that a few cases have been misclassified. Following Liaw and Wiener ([2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000221)), we now combine all of the individual random forests into a single ensemble, where we note now the number of trees is equal to 150 (i.e., 50 + 50 + 50 trees):

```
> rf.all <- combine(rf1, rf2, rf3)
```

## 10.7 Boosting

Boosting is another committee machine that again essentially operates on combining weak learners, analogous to how bagging averages many bootstrapped samples. However, boosting does this *systematically* and *deterministically*, not randomly. As explained by James et al. ([2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168), p. 321) in reference to boosting with regression trees:

> Each tree \[or single predictive tool, more generally\] is grown using information from previously grown trees. Boosting does not involve bootstrap sampling; instead, each tree is fit on a modified version of the original data set.

Boosting, in general, is what is known as a *slow learner*, which in general, performs better than fast or greedy learners. An analogy to boosting would be you and your friend drawing a picture. Suppose you get the picture started and your strengths are on full display, but also your weaknesses. For instance, suppose you are good at drawing the general shapes of objects, but not so good at filling in some of their more specific characteristics. After you are finished doing what you can, your friend steps in and focuses specifically on drawing the elements that you were poor at drawing, including giving specific attention to errors that you made in your contribution. The combination of both of you generates a rather strong painting even though you were both weak at drawing particular individual elements of the painting.

Another prototype example for understanding how boosting works is the spam e-mail paradigm described by Izenman ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 511). Suppose we wish to know whether an e-mail is spam or not before opening it. If the e-mail contains the word “money,” this by itself is a weak identifier because identifying it as spam might appear as random and misclassify the result. In other words, this is a *weak classifier*. Indeed, another classifier that is weak is one that classifies as spam if the e-mail contains the word “credit,” for instance. Taken on their own, weak classifiers are not very good and are bound to misclassify many cases. However, as was the case for bagging, *if we combine these weak classifiers, we may be able to substantially improve classification*. This is what is behind the idea of boosting. In this example, classification based on the word “money” will be imperfect and rather weak, but the second classifier trained will try to make up for the error generated by the first classifier. When combined, they make a pretty decent classifier. Boosting relies on the assumption that each of the weak hypotheses has accuracy that is just a bit better than chance levels. This assumption is generally referred to as the *weak learning condition* ([Schapire, 2001](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000325)).

We draw on James et al. ([2013](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000168), p. 323) quite heavily as well as Bishop ([2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032), p. 658) in giving a formal, if not brief, summary treatment of boosting. Suppose in a regression tree problem *f̂*(*x*) is the estimated function. At the initial step of the algorithm, we will set *f̂*(*x*) = 0 and residuals *r*[*i*] = *y*[*i*], that is, residuals equal to the values of the response variable in the training data. We then fit a regression tree with *d* splits to the training data. We call this tree *f̂*^(*b*). We then update the original function *f̂*(*x*) = *f̂*(*x*) + *λ**f̂*(*x*) with a shrunken (weighted) version of the new tree:

  
*f̂*(*x*) = *f̂*(*x*) + *λ**f̂*^(*b*)(*x*)  
(10.5)

where in (10.5) *λ* is a shrinkage parameter regulating the rate of learning, which notice is being applied to the new tree, *f̂*^(*b*)that has *d* splits. Next, we update residuals by389

  
*r*[*i*′] = *r*[*i*] − *λ**f̂*^(*b*)(*x*[*i*])  
(10.6)

This process is repeated for all *b* models and the final boosted model is produced, which is the sum of *all* weighted estimated functions, *f̂*^(*b*),

  
$$\\hat{f}\\left( x \\right) = {\\sum\\limits\_{b = 1}^{B}{\\lambda{\\hat{f}}^{b}\\left( x \\right)}}$$  
(10.7)

Hastie et al. ([2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 341) show that boosting is a simple example of an additive model and yet another instance of a *basis expansion*. There are many boosting algorithms in existence. However, one particular algorithm has historically dominated boosting, that of *AdaBoost*, short for *adaptive boosting* and generally used to classify into one of two binary categories ([Schapire, 2001](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000325)). The algorithm works by modifying probabilities of drawing instances as a function of error similar to the generic boosting algorithm described earlier ([Alpaydin, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000009)). AdaBoost has been found to be equivalent to forward stagewise additive modeling where an *exponential loss* function is minimized ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). Gradient boosting, and extensions, are more general than AdaBoost where additional loss functions can be minimized. See [Izenman (2008)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167) for details.

### 10.7.1 Boosting Using R

In R, we can use the package *ada* ([Culp et al., 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000073)) for AdaBoost for binary responses. A very popular package for gradient boosting in R is *gbm* ([Ridgeway](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000298) et al., 2024).

We adapt the example for boosting on the iris data in the *ada* package:

```
> library(ada)
> data(iris)
```

We will drop the *setosa* variable from the data:

```
> iris[iris$Species!=“setosa”,] ->iris
```

By dropping setosa, we will have removed 50 cases from the data set, so that the new data set should contain 100 cases. We can confirm this by requesting the dimension (dim()) of the new data:

```
> n <- dim(iris)[1]
> n
[1] 100
```

We assigned the dimension (dim) of the data because we are going to use n in what follows. We will sample 60 observations (i.e., .6\*n; [Culp et al., 2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000073), p. 5):390

```
> trind <- sample(1:n, floor(.6*n), FALSE)
> trind
```

```
> iris[,5]<- as.factor((levels(iris[,5])[2:3])[as.numeric(iris[,5])-1])
```

We are now ready to fit the trees. The following will fit eight-split trees (Culp et al., [2016](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000073), p. 5). We specify the number of iterations to equal 20 (iter=20) and set the shrinkage parameter (nu) equal to 1:

We note the confusion matrix results in perfect classification. We can also see from the above output that the out-of-bag error is equal to 0.017 for iteration = 6. As iterations increase, overfitting becomes a concern. These results can be visualized to observe fluctuations on the training error across iterations ([Figure 10.8](#c10.xhtml#f10.8)). Note that by iteration 9, the training error has bottomed to 0, which agrees with the output above. We note as well that *kappa* ([Figure 10.8](#c10.xhtml#f10.8)), which measures the agreement between observed and predicted classification, is also maximized by iteration 9 (these figures are reported in the above output, train.err1 = 9, train.kap1 = 9), where TRUE, TRUE controls the reporting of training and kappa curves:

391

Now, we add the testing data and evaluate both training and testing error:

```
> gdis=addtest(gdis, iris[teind, -5], iris[teind, 5])
> plot(gdis, TRUE, TRUE)
```

We can see from the left plot in [Figure 10.9](#c10.xhtml#f10.9) that the training error decreases while the testing error remains relatively constant until it elevates toward the end of the iterations, likely due to overfitting. The *kappa accuracy* reflects the extent to which there is agreement between the observed classification and the predicted classification. We see from the plot that kappa increases on the train data as the number of iterations increases, which is what we would expect, as the higher the kappa score, the greater the degree of agreement. Kappa decreases, however, on the test data as we near the final iteration, which is likely again a sign of overfitting.

![Figure 10.10 Variable importance measures for different features on the iris data.Return to text.⏎](images/fig10.10.jpg)

*Figure 10.10* Variable importance measures for different features on the iris data.[Return to text.⏎](#c10.xhtml#re_f10.10)

```
> varplot(gdis)
```

We can see from [Figure 10.10](#c10.xhtml#f10.10) that in the boosted sample, *sepal length* is most important, followed by *sepal width*. See Hastie et al. ([2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml#c10)) for the computation of variable importance in this context. Re-running the model at various iterations may be useful both to regulate overfitting and also to observe changes in variable importance.

Whereas bagging and boosting combines weak “base” learners to produce a stronger learner, so-called *stacked models* seek to combine weak to strong learners into an even stronger one via optimizing the weighting of each model, a so-called *super learner*. This is generally referred to as *stacking* or *stacked generalization* ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). Stacked learners will often outperform individual base learners. [Breiman (1996, p. 51)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000047) summarizes the benefits of stacking:

> The results show that stacking can produce predictors with substantially reduced prediction errors. Stacking never does worse than selecting the single best predictor. We note that the biggest gains came when dissimilar sets of predictors were stacked, i.e., subset selection and ridge regressions. The more similar the predictors, the less advantage there is in stacking.

In R, we can use the package *h2o* ([Fryda et al., 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000120)) for model stacking. For details on stacked generalization, see [Hastie et al. (2009)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145).393
