# 11 Principal Components Analysis, Blind Source Separation, and Manifold Learning

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-14](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-14)

In this chapter, we survey the method of *principal components analysis*, or “PCA” for short, as well as other related techniques. As we will see, principal components analysis can be interpreted as a special case of more general methods that generally fall under the name of *blind source separation* and *manifold learning*. PCA can be regarded, in fact, as a special case of manifold learning where in the case of PCA the manifold is *linear*. The more general manifold can take on nonlinear shapes and most often the phrase “manifold learning” will refer to *nonlinear dimensionality reduction*. Virtually all dimension-reduction techniques can be crudely classified into *linear* vs. *nonlinear*.

The motivation for PCA is to take a set of observed variables and generate linear combinations of those variables. Substantively, PCA is often advertised as being able to “discover” underlying dimensions of data. However, as we will learn in this chapter, the word “discovery” is potentially misleading and problematic. All that PCA can guarantee, for certain, is to derive linear composites of variables that maximize variance in the original variables. Whether those composites are meaningful in any substantive sense is not a question that can be answered by PCA and is only answerable by the user with reference to scientific theory and the domain of application. What is more, is that maximizing variance in observed variables may not result in dimensions that are in any way *interesting*. This is an important point, as there are many other competing techniques that claim to discover more interesting patterns in data and have their own criteria for doing so other than maximizing variance. In short, *maximizing variance in components does not necessarily imply those components will be of value or interesting in themselves*. They may, from a substantive point of view be entirely meaningless given current theory or application. Indeed, from a scientific point of view, the results of any dimension-reduction or manifold learning technique should be interpreted with caution as it is entirely possible that the given algorithm “causes” interesting geometric patterns or trends that in the end are not supported by the data (Meila & Zhang, [2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000247)).

Principal components is only one of many techniques that seek to reduce the dimensionality of data. That is, PCA is *a* (i.e., only *one*) dimension-reduction technique; it is not *equivalent* to dimension reduction. In its most general sense, dimension reduction may be said to be taking observed data in a high-dimensional context and reducing that data to a lower-dimensional context but ensuring that it still conveys similar information (Nanga et al., [2021](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000263)). That is, a good dimension-reduction technique should retain essential properties of the original data. If the information contained in the lower dimensions is misleading or at odds with the information at a higher dimension, then the reduction may lead to faulty interpretation. Hence, this is one important reason for understanding the nature of the dimension-reduction technique one is using as the conclusion provided by one technique may differ from the conclusion reached from another. *Dimension reduction is as much a function of the method as it is of the data*. A question worth asking is if the visualization of one technique is different from another, which then is most *correct*? The only answer to this question is that none are “correct”; they simply accomplish different things.395

Most dimension-reduction techniques are nonparametric in nature ([Murray, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)), which essentially implies that they focus heavily on the training data often without attempting directly to generalize to out-of-sample data. These include techniques such as the aforementioned *PCA*, but also *classical multidimensional scaling*, *kernel PCA*, *Isomap*, *Laplacian Eigenmaps* ([Belkin & Niyogi, 2003](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000026)), and *t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE)*, *non-negative matrix factorization* (*NMF*), among others. Alternative names for PCA include *Karhunen-Loeve transform* ([Karhunen, 1947](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000181)), *empirical orthogonal functions*, *common principal components analysis* ([Flury](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000105), 1998), and others. The different names are largely due to the same method being developed in various disciplines or as special cases or extensions of classic PCA. For instance, the Karhunen-Loeve transform features the option of using class information on data before applying PCA to each class, then takes an average of class PCA ([Alpaydin, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000009)). This is similar to *common PCA* where similar components are hypothesized to arise in different data sets. Hence, not all names are *identical* to classic PCA, but at their core are still “PCA.” Once more with jargon in statistics and machine learning, one can know a given method well but fail to “recognize” it in a given field because it is named something different!

Many dimension-reduction techniques are justified based on a fundamental theorem, the *Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma*. It holds that for a number of points in high-dimensional space, such points can be mapped to a much lower dimension with an upper limit to how much pairwise distances can be distorted. That is, the lemma essentially holds that dimension reduction can be performed while still preserving fundamental properties of the data. For further details on the lemma, consult Mohri et al. ([2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000253), p. 354).

## 11.1 Dimension Reduction and Jargon

As we have mentioned, what can make dimension reduction challenging is that many of the same techniques have evolved in various scientific fields under somewhat different names and for different purposes. For instance, in psychometrics, one may wish to produce orthogonal linear combinations to represent attitudes of respondents, whereas in more physical applications such as images in information theory, this same idea translates to the *compression* of an image. The same technique can almost have unrecognizable and diametrically opposed applications. While this can be said of virtually any technique and not just dimension-reduction ones, the jargon is especially “rich” in dimension analysis.

However, just as is true for simple arithmetical operations such as addition, it is not *what* is being added that matters when it comes to understanding addition; it matters more in understanding what addition *does*. The technique must be studied, at least to some extent, from an abstract point of view exclusive of application. Only in that sense can one understand what the technique actually accomplishes without being “swayed” by what we “wish” it to accomplish to satisfy our *Freudian id* on this or that data set.

If dimension reduction is so vast a subject, why begin with PCA? We begin with PCA simply because it is generally considered the most common and oldest method of the family of dimension-reduction methods, having its origins with Karl Pearson in 1901. It is also the easiest (though deceptively simple) to understand and hence forms a good grounding for understanding other more advanced techniques as extensions or derivatives of essential PCA. Since the time of Pearson, several other dimension-reduction methods have been developed, PCA now considered only a *special case* of a wider family of blind source separation techniques ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). Many of the more modern techniques feature latent variables which are analogous to hidden variables in neural networks ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)) and are also featured extensively in exploratory and confirmatory factor-analytic models as well as structural equation models. In its most general interpretation, 396blind source separation involves separating out signals from noise, such that the signals extracted possess certain mathematically desirable properties, such as orthogonality in the case of classical PCA and many versions of exploratory factor analysis, or independence in the case of independent components analysis or independent factor analysis.

Principal components analysis can also be considered purely from an essential linear algebra point of view, equivalent to *best subspace approximation* using the singular value decomposition, or “SVD” for short (more precisely, *reduced SVD*). Singular value decomposition itself dates back to [Beltrami (1873)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000027) and is a method for obtaining eigenvalues and eigenvectors from a matrix, mathematical objects that are at the very crux of PCA. SVD is able to decompose via factorization of a rectangular matrix *X* such that

  
*X* = *V**D**W*^(*T*)  
(11.1)

where *X* in a statistical application is a data matrix of observations on a number of variables, *V* and *W* contain orthonormal columns (i.e., orthogonal and of length equal to one), and *D* is a diagonal matrix ([Jolliffe, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174), p. 44). From the SVD, singular values and singular vectors can be obtained of even rectangular matrices, and hence SVD can be considered a pathway to generating principal components.

We can also conceptualize PCA as a *rotation*, such that PCA transforms or rotates empirical data by deriving new axes from which the data are projected onto these new axes. These new axes are the *eigenvectors* of the rotation. The *best basis theorem* states the best orthonormal basis is given by the leading eigenvectors of the transformation.

Whether one uses eigen analysis or SVD to compute principal components will result in the same components, though SVD is often preferred due to computational benefits (Murray, 2022). For extremely large dimensional problems, a *randomized SVD algorithm* (Murray, 2022) can be used to handle increasingly large dimensional data. In Python, for instance, *sklearn* features a randomized solver. PCA is also associated with the *Eckart-Young* and *Schmidt-Mirsky* theorems in mathematics as these both account for the mathematics that underlie the dimension-reduction technique.

> *In modern statistics and machine learning, there are a whole host of dimension-reduction techniques. What unites them all is the attempt to “uncover” a lower-dimensional manifold from higher-dimensional data. That data could be attributes on a scale or an image that needs to be “decoded” by color, or even sound signals from a musical symphony.*

## 11.2 Deriving Classic Principal Components Analysis

As mentioned, classical PCA has its roots with Pearson in 1901. The term “principal component” was coined by Hotelling in 1933. Classical PCA is motivated as follows. Suppose we have a set of observed variables *x*[1] through *x*[*p*]. From these observed variables, we wish to produce linear combinations of these variables that have desirable statistical properties. Recall more generally the nature of a linear combination from our earlier review of linear algebra:397

  
*l*[*i*] = *a*[1]*y*[1] + *a*[2]*y*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *a*[*p*]*y*[*p*]  

where a linear combination *l*[*i*] is a *weighted sum of products* and where *a*[1] through *a*[*p*] are the weights applied to observed variables *y*[1] through *y*[*p*]. For our data on *x*[1], ..., *x*[*p*], the linear combination becomes

  
*z*[*i*] = *a*[1]*x*[1] + *a*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *a*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  

where now *z*[*i*] is the name of the linear combination and *x*[1] through *x*[*p*] are the observed variables. A principal component is a unique kind of linear combination such that the weights *a*[1] through *a*[*p*] correspond to values of allied eigenvectors extracted from an eigen analysis performed on the covariance or correlation matrix of variables *x*[1], ..., *x*[*p*]. Hence, if we denote the weights *a*[1] through *a*[*p*] by *e*[1] through *e*[*p*] to denote eigenvector weights, the first principal component is defined as

  
*z*[1] = *e*[1]*x*[1] + *e*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *e*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  
(11.2)

The first principal component possesses an important property; *it is the linear combination that accounts for the most variance in the observed variables*. What this means is that the variance of the resulting *z*[*i*] will have *maximum variance* compared to any other linear combination that we could have derived from the data. If you think about this for a moment, you might agree that it is a favorable quality to have for a linear combination. It suggests that instead of needing *x*[1], ..., *x*[*p*] variables, perhaps we could account for a great deal of the variance in those observed variables by considering only the first principal component. That is, the first component makes up a large proportion of those observed variables.

However, the first principal component will likely not account for *all* of the variance in the variables. To account for more, we will have to consider the second and successive principal components.

More formally, if the total variance *E*|*x*−*μ*|² is defined by

  
$$\\left. E \\middle| x - \\mu \\middle| {}\_{2} = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{p}{{var}x\_{i} =}}{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{p}\\sigma\_{ii}^{2}} = {tr}\\Sigma \\right.$$  
(11.3)

where *t**r**Σ* is the sum of variances *σ*[*i**i*]² along the main diagonal, PCA essentially constructs orthogonal variables (i.e., linear combinations) the variance of which, in totality, equal *t**r**Σ*.

> *The first* *principal component is that which accounts for maximal amount of the variance in the original variables as possible. Ensuing components will account for increasingly less variance.*398

### 11.2.1 The Second Principal Component

The second principal component is that linear combination that accounts for maximal variance in the variables, as was true for the first component, but with an additional important property, that it accounts for variance *not captured by the first* *principal component*. How can we express this idea mathematically? Recall that in linear algebra, linear combinations that account for different sources of *information* (in a sense) more generally in the original variables are called *orthogonal*. Hence, the second principal component is that linear combination accounting for maximal variance in the observed variables but *orthogonal* to the first component:

  
*z*[2] = *e*[1]*x*[1] + *e*[2]*x*[2] +  ⋅  ⋅  ⋅  + *e*[*p*]*x*[*p*]  

where now *e*[1], *e*[*p*] represent elements of the second eigenvector. More precisely, the eigenvectors are orthogonal, the components are uncorrelated, though it is fine to use the terms “uncorrelated” and “orthogonal” interchangeably in this context so long as one is aware of the difference. We need not stop there! We can continue to derive principal components from our data each accounting for a successive amount of variance unaccounted for by prior components. Note that in our development of classical PCA, we have applied the technique to the entire training data at once. That is, we have assumed the entire training data is readily available. An alternative to this approach is known as *incremental PCA* ([Lippi & Ceccarelli, 2019](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000224)), where the updated covariance matrix *Σ*[*n* + 1] is based on the “old” covariance matrix, *Σ*[*n*]. That is, incremental PCA adds new observations (the  + 1 in *n* + 1) to the covariance matrix and thus has computational advantages over traditional PCA. The benefit is that not all data has to be saved in memory and the algorithm can be applied when the data set is expected to grow quickly or if the stationary data set is itself very large, too large to fit into memory at once ([Lippi & Ceccarelli, 2019](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000224)). Incremental PCA is available in Python in sklearn via IncrementalPCA.

### 11.2.2 PCA as a Least-Squares Technique and Minimizing Reconstruction Error

As is the case with most statistical methods, there is more than a single interpretation of principal components analysis. Our interpretation thus far has been via eigen analysis or SVD, but we can also interpret it as a least-squares technique similar to that of least-squares regression, with which we are already familiar. Instead of projecting from higher-dimensional space to lower-dimensional space such that we minimize the sum of squared errors in a response as in the typical ordinary least-squares regression, in PCA we also seek a projection, but this time from higher-dimensional space to lower-dimensional space such that the sum of squared *perpendicular distances* are minimized, where “perpendicular” is equivalent to *orthogonal*.

For example, in Figure 11.1 is a projection from two-dimensional space to a single *hyperplane* such that the orthogonal squared data distances from the principal component are minimized.399

![Figure 11.1 Hyperplane that minimizes squared orthogonal distances and maximizes variance in the original variables. Such a hyperplane is called a principal component.Return to text.⏎](images/fig11.1.jpg)

*Figure 11.1* Hyperplane that minimizes squared orthogonal distances and maximizes variance in the original variables. Such a hyperplane is called a principal component.Return to text.⏎

In fact, in the typical PCA analysis, we seek to minimize what is known as the *reconstruction error* ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). Not coincidentally, it can be shown that the reconstruction error is minimized when the resulting components are eigenvectors of an eigen analysis of the covariance matrix. Details of the derivation can be found in [Bishop (2006)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032) and [Murphy (2022)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259). The average reconstruction error is given by:

  
$$l\\left( W,Z \\right) = \\frac{1}{N}{\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left| \\middle| x\_{n} - Wz\_{n} \\middle| \\right|^{2}}$$  
(11.4)

where *x*[*n*] are the original data points, *z*[*n*] are the derived data points based on the projection, and *W* is an orthogonal matrix. The optimal solution (i.e., *l*(*W*,*Z*), which is a *loss*, is minimized) is obtained when *Ŵ* = *U*[*L*], where *U*[*L*] are the eigenvectors of a covariance matrix, and hence by definition for a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues, orthogonal. Note that *W**z*[*n*] is essentially trying to produce the least amount of deviation from *x*[*n*] and under the most ideal of circumstances where the reconstruction of data based on the obtained eigenvectors (i.e., loosely, components) is perfect, then *l*(*W*,*Z*) = 0. Minimizing this reconstruction error is equivalent to maximizing the variance in the variables (Murray, 2022) which was the original interpretation of PCA we started out with. Again, as is the case with most statistical methods, there are a variety of different ways to derive the PCA technique, where in this case it can be shown that minimizing the reconstruction error is *mathematically equivalent* to maximizing the variance of the data projected by the components solution. Different ways of perceiving a statistical or machine learning technique from various angles and perspectives can pay dividends in truly understanding it in depth.

In addition to PCA being computed by eigen analysis or (truncated) SVD, components can also be gotten by the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and has advantages over eigen analysis such that it is often faster ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)).400

### 11.2.3 Choosing the Number of Derived Components

Under most conditions of a well-behaved matrix, the number of components that we can obtain is equal to the number of observed variables subjected to the components analysis. That is, if *x*[1], ..., *x*[*p*] consists of say, 100 variables, then under usual (and most common) conditions, the number of components computed on these variables will equal 100. In brief, *a PCA on observed variables does not, by itself, reduce the information in the data*. In the case of the 100 variables, *choosing* less than 100 computed components is where the actual *data reduction* occurs, else all the PCA has done is disproportionately load most variance hopefully onto the first few components. What this means is that PCA is simply “packaging” (or *re-packaging*) the variance of observed variables into successive linear combinations. But it is not truly dimension “reduction” in an applied sense until we select less than the total number of components generated. This is the logic of PCA as a dimension-reduction technique. PCA is first and foremost only a *transformation*.

### 11.2.4 Why Reconstruction Error Is Insufficient for Choosing Number of Components

As a result of PCA attempting to account for as much variance in the variables as possible, when choosing the number of dimensions (components) to retain, one cannot simply use the *reconstruction error* or *variance explained* as a guide, since the more components one keeps, the more variance one will explain and the smaller will be the consequent reconstruction error. This is somewhat analogous to the effect of adding more predictors in a multiple regression – variance explained will virtually always increase (except in very unusual situations of zero correlation), and hence choosing the “best” regression model based on variance explained alone is not a good strategy. This limitation of using reconstruction error as a guide will also resurface when we consider cluster analysis later in the book and seek a measure to justify the number of clusters to retain. Since reconstruction error typically and necessarily reduces as the number of clusters increases, reconstruction error is not a sufficient measure for making decisions on how many clusters to retain.

To determine the number of components to keep, one should primarily use substantive judgment in addition to statistical indicators, and in the end, a bit of common sense. For example, if the first two components explain 70% of the variance, but the third component only explains an additional 1%, then obviously the two-component solution will dominate under *most* circumstances (depending on the substantive nature of the investigation). Graphical measures such as the *scree plot* can be used to visualize both the reconstruction error as well as the variance explained, and one typically looks for a “bend” in such plots to indicate where the reconstruction error (or variance explained) suddenly “drops.”

> *PCA, under most circumstances, will generate as many components as there are variables. The actual “data reduction” occurs by selecting the first few components to account for as much of the variance in the variables as possible, or equivalently, minimizes the reconstruction error. Choosing the number of components to keep or maintain is largely dependent on the research or scientific context and often based on user judgment.*

### 11.2.5 Constraints on Components

Recall that we mentioned that the eigenvector weights *e*[1] through *e*[*p*] were applied to observed variables in order to generate components. In deriving these components, we shall impose the 401constraint on these eigenvector weights so that the *sum of their squares is equal to unity*. That is, the sum of squared eigenvector weights we will set equal to one,

  
$${\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}e\_{i}^{2}} = 1$$  
(11.5)

When we impose such a condition on each component, the component is said to have been *normalized*. There is no absolute requirement that the sum needs to be 1; it could in theory be any other constant positive value. Setting it equal to 1 implies that the length of the component is equal to unity. But why impose such a constraint at all? The purpose of this constraint is such that if we did not impose at least *some* constraint on the loadings, then in theory we could allow the component’s variance to increase without bound. By imposing this constraint, or other positive constant for the variance, we are assured that the variance of the component will not simply be a reflection of increasingly large eigenvector weights.

As we have seen throughout this book, constraints such as the above are not atypical in statistical or machine learning methods. It is a regular occurrence in mathematical modeling more generally that some quantities are fixed or constrained to particular values so that other variable quantities can be more freely estimated under these constraints. Constraints such as these, in the end, *simplify problems*.

### 11.2.6 Centering Observed Variables

Observed variables are also often (though need not *necessarly* be) centered before being subjected to the components analysis, so that each variable has a mean equal to 0. By *centering* here we simply mean subtracting the mean of each observed raw variable. For example, if the observed variable is *x*[*i*] with mean $\\overline{x}$, then centering the variable means generating $x\_{i} - \\overline{x}$ for each observation. The reader will recognize centering here as a precursor to computing *z-*scores where the centered deviation is then further divided by the standard deviation, *s*. As a simple example of centering, consider the following vector of data in R having original raw mean equal to 6.2:

```
> v <- c(0, 4, 8, 9, 10)
> mean(v)
[1] 6.2
```

To center this data, we simply subtract the mean from each observation:

```
> v.center <- v - mean(v)
> v.center
[1] -6.2 -2.2 1.8 2.8 3.8
```

We can then easily confirm that, within rounding error, the mean of the centered data is equal to 0:

```
> mean(v.center)
[1] -1.775489e-16
```

402 

### 11.2.7 Orthogonality of Components

As mentioned already, one of the attractive features of components analysis is that derived components are guaranteed to be orthogonal (i.e., eigenvectors) and uncorrelated to one another. Recall what orthogonality means, it means derived components are at *right angles*, or *perpendicular* to one another (that of 90 degrees). From a substantive point of view, orthogonality ensures that each component accounts for, or *explains* a differing proportion of variance in the variables and that there is no overlap. It is important to emphasize that orthogonality is not the same as *statistical independence*. *Statistical independence is, in a sense, a stronger property than orthogonality in this case and principal components will only be both orthogonal and independent if the data are multivariate normal*. For components to be both orthogonal and independent beyond the assumption of multivariate normality one must go beyond traditional PCA and instead perform an *independent components analysis*, to be discussed later. Assuming all components are nonzero, however, orthogonality of components will imply *linear independence* (as opposed to *statistical* independence).

> *Classic principal components analysis ensures orthogonality of components but does not guarantee their statistical independence. Statistical independence is the stronger property in this case, reserved for the technique of independent components analysis.*

### 11.2.8 Proportion of Variance Explained by Each Component: Covariance vs. Correlation Matrices

Having computed components in decreasing order of variance explained, a natural question worth asking now is: how much variance is actually accounted for by each component? Recall that components analysis does not *change* the amount of variance in the original variables. It merely reconstructs that variance along new dimensions (called the *components*, which are in effect, *eigenvectors* of the transformation). Hence, it stands that *the total variance in the totality of components should be equal to the total variance in the original variables.* That is, when we sum up the variance accounted for by all of the components, that sum should equal the total variance in the original variables. In a covariance matrix, that sum of variance will equal the sum of variances across all observed variables. In a *correlation matrix*, that sum will equal to the total number of *variables* because in a correlation matrix, the variance contributed by each variable is equal to one. Whether one analyzes a covariance or correlation matrix can result in quite vastly different outcomes. Principal components analysis is not invariant to type of matrix analyzed. This fact may at first seem to go against intuition, such that one might have assumed or expected that both the covariance and correlation matrices would yield similar results, or at minimum, one result would be a trivial transformation of the other. However, this is not the case. A PCA performed on a correlation matrix will usually yield *different* eigenvalues and eigenvectors than a PCA performed on a covariance matrix.

Given this distinction, the question becomes: which matrix to analyze? While some hold the covariance matrix is more in spirit with PCA (e.g., see [Rencher & Christensen, 2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295)), others recommend that PCA should virtually always be performed on the *standardized* covariance matrix, otherwise known of course as the *correlation matrix* ([Bilodeau & Brenner, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000030); Murray, 2022). Of course, there is no harm in trying both solutions and comparing them. The important point, however, is to recognize that performing PCA on one versus the other will, in general, not produce the same result. Principal components analysis also requires at least *some* covariance (or 403correlation) among pairs of variables. In the absence of such covariance, that is, if all covariances or correlations are equal to 0 and only variances remain along the main diagonal, PCA will be of little use. At most, PCA will simply generate components that are a reflection of the original variables but in descending order of variance ([Chatfield & Collins, 1980](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000057)). For now, we will assume we are working with the covariance matrix. Given that the eigenvalues are variances of each component, then the following relation should then hold:

  
∑*s*² = ∑*λ*[*i*]  
(11.6)

That is, the sum of variances of the original variables should equal the sum of eigenvalues from the components analysis. We can easily demonstrate this on empirical data. Consider some data on *x*, *y*:

```
> x <- c(2.5, 0.5, 2.2, 1.9, 3.1, 2.3, 2.0, 1.0, 1.5, 1.1)
> y <- c(2.4, 0.7, 2.9, 2.2, 3.0, 2.7, 1.6, 1.1, 1.6, 0.9)
```

The variances of each variable are the following:

```
> var(x)
[1] 0.6165556
> var(y)
[1] 0.7165556
```

The sum of these variances is

```
> sum(var(x), var(y))
[1] 1.333111
```

When we compute the components analysis on the covariance matrix from this data, we obtain via eigen analysis eigenvalues of 1.284 and 0.0491, which when summed total 1.3331, which we note is the same total as that generated by summing the original variances of the variables. Hence, we have demonstrated through empirical data that PCA has not *changed* the variance in the variables, it has merely *reconstructed* the variance onto new dimensions instead of on the original variables. *The variance accounted for by the new components is the same variance in the original variables*. This is why again we dislike the idea of PCA “discovering” dimensions. We prefer say that PCA is simply *reorganizing* the variables onto dimensions that are mathematically assured by the decomposition. For the majority of data sets and well-behaved matrices, PCA *will* generate components. It is whether such components can be *interpreted* and whether they are meaningful that is the *real* question of interest.

### 11.2.9 Principal Components as a Rotation of Axes

We have seen that principal components analysis can be explained by eigen analysis or by reference to a least-squares argument in which squared perpendiculars are minimized instead of vertical distances. The real “mystery” of principal components analysis lies in eigen analysis. Once we accept that eigen analysis can be performed, it is a relatively simple matter to accept that we can generate components. It is the substantive understanding of these components that then matters. 404What we mean by this is that if one truly wants to understand PCA, one needs to truly understand eigen analysis.

Our understanding of PCA can also benefit from understanding some of its geometry. Geometrically, PCA is nothing more than a rotation of the original Cartesian axes. To demonstrate such a rotation, consider once more our data on PCA ([Smith, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000340)):

```
> x <- c(2.5, 0.5, 2.2, 1.9, 3.1, 2.3, 2.0, 1.0, 1.5, 1.1)
> y <- c(2.4, 0.7, 2.9, 2.2, 3.0, 2.7, 1.6, 1.1, 1.6, 0.9)
```

We now generate a dataframe from these vectors as well as the corresponding covariance matrix:

```
> data <- data.frame(x, y)
> data
```

 
|  || X || y |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 2.5 || 2.4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 || 0.5 || 0.7 |
| 3 || 2.2 || 2.9 |
| 4 || 1.9 || 2.2 |
| 5 || 3.1 || 3.0 |
| 6 || 2.3 || 2.7 |
| 7 || 2.0 || 1.6 |
| 8 || 1.0 || 1.1 |
| 9 || 1.5 || 1.6 |
| 10 || 1.1 || 0.9 |

```
> cov(data)
```

 
|  || X || y |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X || 0.6165556 || 0.6154444 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Y || 0.6154444 || 0.7165556 |

Next, we perform an eigen analysis on this data to extract eigenvalues and eigenvectors from the covariance matrix:405

```
> eigen(cov(data))
eigen() decomposition
$values
[1] 1.2840277 0.0490834
$vectors
```

 
|  || \[,1\] || \[,2\] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \[1,\] || 0.6778734 || \-0.7351787 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \[2,\] || 0.7351787 || 0.6778734 |

We note the first eigenvalue is equal to 1.284 with eigenvector 0.6779, 0.7352 (the eigenvectors corresponding to each eigenvalue are in *columns* above, not rows). The second eigenvalue is equal to 0.0491 with eigenvector −0.7352, 0.6779. But what do these eigenvectors represent? We can consider them to be *factors of rotation* of the original axes ([Young, 2023](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000401)). The eigenvectors are first and foremost *vectors*, and as such, can be easily plotted in space (Figure 11.2).

![Figure 11.2 First and second principal components accounting for all of the variance in the variables. The two components are mutually orthogonal.Return to text.⏎](images/fig11.2.jpg)

*Figure 11.2* First and second principal components accounting for all of the variance in the variables. The two components are mutually orthogonal.Return to text.⏎

Note carefully that each eigenvector appears to account for the scatter of points. The first eigenvector, from bottom left to upper right, seems to account for *most* of the variance in the data. This is not a surprise, since the first eigenvalue is equal to 1.284 and is much larger than the second of 0.0491. The proportion of variance accounted for by the first eigenvector is 1.284/(1.284 + 0.0491) = 0.96, or 96%. Clearly, the first eigenvector (component) is accounting for the majority of the variance in the original variables.

We can also see that the angle between the eigenvectors is one of 90 degrees. That is, the rotation of the original axes did not change the angle between them but instead kept it as orthogonal as were the original basis Cartesian axes. In linear algebra, this type of transformation is regarded as a *rigid rotation* of the axes and we have simply found an optimal new *basis* from which to project the data. Mathematically, this is all that PCA accomplishes.

### 11.2.10 Principal Components, Discriminant Functions, Canonical Variates: Linking Foundations

As mentioned at the outset of this book, if there is a common theme running throughout most of it, one of many, it is that of *dimension reduction*. Even the analysis of variance, long before we knew it in undergraduate statistics, on a deeper theoretical level could be said to be generating new dimensions on which data can be projected. It may thus appear to the reader at some point that many of the methodologies surveyed in this book and beyond are performing a similar task. Indeed, dimension reduction is common to most in one way or another, though there are of course important differences regarding how various methods go about such a task.

Recall that we had said earlier in the book that discriminant functions were underlying dimensions such that they maximized separation between groups. Successive dimensions were 406uncorrelated to one another. Both discriminant analysis and principal components analysis execute a “flavor” of dimension reduction, but they go about it in different ways. For one, in PCA, dimensions are obtained that maximize *variance*, not maximize *separation between groups*. Second, while discriminant functions are uncorrelated to one another, they are typically not orthogonal, while principal components are uncorrelated *and* orthogonal. Components have the stronger property of orthogonality ([Rencher & Christensen, 2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295)). This is also true of canonical variates in canonical correlation; *they are uncorrelated but not orthogonal*. As mentioned earlier, components can be made independent (or nearly so), but that requires independent components analysis and not classical PCA. PCA only ensures that components are uncorrelated, which is a weaker property than statistical independence ([Jolliffe, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174), p. 396).

A second feature that distinguishes PCA from linear discriminant analysis (LDA) (and canonical analysis) is that obtaining components does not involve the computation of an inverse matrix. In discriminant analysis, we were required to obtain eigenvalues and eigenvectors from *E*^( − 1)*H* and hence *E*^( − 1) had to exist. In PCA, no such inverse is computed. Of what consequence is this fact? Recall that inverses exist only for matrices that are *nonsingular*. A singular matrix has determinant equal to 0, which also implies or equates to linear dependence among select rows or columns. However, if the computation of an inverse is not required, then this implies that *PCA can be performed on a covariance matrix that is singular*. Under this condition some eigenvalues will equal 0 ([Rencher & Christensen, 2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295)). In such a case, these components are to be ignored, as they explain zero variance. A second case in which singularity can arise is when the number of observations is less than the number of variables. PCA can still be performed on such data, whereas LDA or canonical analysis on such data would, analytically, be problematic.

### 11.2.11 Principal Components in Python

We consider a very easy example of PCA in Python on fictional data:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
X = np.array([[-1, -1], [-2, -1], [-3, -2], [1, 1], [2, 1], [3, 2]])
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X
Out[95]:
array([[-1, -1],
      [-2, -1],
      [-3, -2],
      [ 1, 1],
      [ 2, 1],
      [ 3, 2]])
pca.fit(X)
Out[72]: PCA(n_components=2)
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
[0.99244289 0.00755711]
```

We see from the above that the proportion of variance explained by the first component is 0.99, while the proportion of variance explained by the second component is 0.0075. Clearly, the first 407component is most important to the analysis. Note that the cumulative sum of the proportions equals 1 (i.e., 0.99244289 + 0.00755711 = 1.0).

As mentioned earlier, *incremental PCA* can be beneficial when the data are so large that it cannot fit in memory at once, and can be fit using IncrementalPCA. Heatmaps can also be used to visualize components (see [Müller & Guido, 2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000258), pp. 148–149 for examples).

### 11.2.12 Principal Components in R

Conducting a basic PCA in R is very easy. For example, we can use the *Rdimtools* package ([You & Shung, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000400)) on the iris data:

```
> library(Rdimtools)
> data(iris)
> set.seed(100)
```

Below we will sample 50 observations from numbers 1 through 150:

```
> subid = sample(1:150, 50)
```

We then create the matrix X made up of variables 1 through 4 (in columns) in the iris data, which are the plant features (i.e., sepal length, sepal width, etc.), followed by the designation of species (i.e., label):

```
> X = as.matrix(iris[subid,1:4])
> label = as.factor(iris[subid,5])
```

We now conduct the PCA, requesting two dimensions (ndim = 2):

```
> PCA <- do.pca(X, ndim=2)
> PCA
$Y
```

 
|  || \[,1\] || \[,2\] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \[1,\] || 1.50866388 || \-0.491302038 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \[2,\] || 1.90078112 || \-0.156616064 |
| \[3,\] || \-2.65041514 || \-0.245114259 |
| \[4,\] || 1.18816125 || 0.114116172 |
| \[5,\] || 0.13988863 || \-0.543760253 |

The above are the component scores resulting from the PCA (only the first five scores are shown). Next, we are given the variances associated with each component:

```
$vars
[1] 3.8646558 0.2000033
$projection
```

 
|  || \[,1\] || \[,2\] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \[1,\] || 0.37088025 || 0.63842394 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \[2,\] || \-0.08806873 || 0.72546180 |
| \[3,\] || 0.84794544 || \-0.24184196 |
| \[4,\] || 0.36834802 || 0.08736427 |

408 

We can see that the variance of the first component is 3.86 while the variance of the second component is 0.200. The component weights (eigenvectors) are given next which are to be read vertically for each component. We can obtain a visualization of the projected component scores (Figure 11.3, left):

![Figure 11.3 Principal component scores (left) and Laplacian score (right) on the same data, revealing quite different patterns. Dimension reduction using variable techniques will often generate quite disparate results.Return to text.⏎](images/fig11.3.jpg)

*Figure 11.3* Principal component scores (left) and Laplacian score (right) on the same data, revealing quite different patterns. Dimension reduction using variable techniques will often generate quite disparate results.Return to text.⏎

```
> plot(PCA$Y, pch = 19, col = label, main = “PCA”)
```

Incidentally, we encourage the reader to try a competing alternative to the above PCA simply to get a glimpse and appreciation of how drastically the dimension reduction (or “embedding,” a term we will use shortly) can change as a function of method employed for the data reduction. For example, had we conducted a *Laplacian Score*, we would have obtained the plot to the right of the above PCA (Figure 11.3, right). Instead of do.pca(), we code do.lscore():

```
> lap = do.lscore(X, ndim=2)
> plot(lap$Y, pch = 19, main = “Laplacian score”)
```

Clearly, as is evident from the two different methods of dimension reduction, the expression “*what you find in data is largely a function of what you use to do the finding*” rings true!

Curvilinear component analysis is yet another option and can be fit by R with the package *ProjectionBasedClustering* ([Thrun](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000357) & Ultsch, 2021).409

### 11.2.13 Cautionary Concerns and Caveats Regarding Principal Components

Principal components analysis can seem like a relatively simple procedure, but it has a lot of hidden complexities associated with it that often bypass the novice. In statistics, PCA is probably the simplest procedure that has the most complexity associated with it and things that can “trip you up” if you’re not careful. *Its simplicity is deceiving*. Understanding PCA is actually quite challenging, which might explain why there are entire books devoted to the subject. The graduate student learning PCA for the first time, concluding it is an “easy” procedure simply lacks the experience to appreciate its “latent” (pun intended!) complexity. We list a few of the more common caveats below. These are things you should be well aware of before using or interpreting the technique. Some we have already mentioned elsewhere in the chapter, and we emphasize here again only to reiterate their importance:

1.  1\. *Principal components are not scale-dependent*. That is, whether the PCA is performed on the covariance or correlation matrix usually results in different findings. Variables with greater variance will have greater influence on the PCA solution than variables with lesser variance. The typical way to get around this issue is to scale variables so that they all have the same variance, which amounts to analyzing the correlation matrix instead of the covariance matrix. While this may seem like a good solution to be adopted in all circumstances, if variables are not originally conceived to be of equal importance (almost in the sense of a Bayesian prior), then the covariance matrix should be analyzed over the correlation matrix ([Chatfield & Collins, 1980](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000057), p. 71) as the analysis of covariance matrices is more in the spirit of PCA ([Rencher & Christensen, 2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295)).
2.  2\. *The first* *principal component, as mentioned, is the one with the largest variance*. However, this does not necessarily imply that it is the component of *most interest*. There is no guarantee that the first principal component will be more theoretically interesting than the second, or the third, etc. It is the “best” component only in the sense of maximizing variance. Other components may be preferred based on their correlation with other variables or how they perform in ensuing regression analysis for instance, or even how they cluster in a cluster analysis ([Marden, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000239)). Variance explained is only one criterion that should be used in addressing the “importance” or “relevance” of a component.
3.  3\. *Principal components will under most circumstances generate as many components as there are original variables*. PCA, under most circumstances, will necessarily generate components. However, there is absolutely no requirement that the components obtained are meaningful or useful. The fact that you ran a PCA on variables and obtained components is not a “finding.” It is a mathematical *certainty* that existed long before you performed the components analysis. Whether you believe the transformation is in some sense “interesting” will likely depend on your substantive science and even philosophy of mathematics. That is, if the components look “meaningless” now substantively, does the mathematical transformation still imply they are nonetheless “real?” This isn’t a statistical question, it is one of the *philosophy of mathematics*. If you believe mathematics corresponds to “reality,” then regardless of whether you can “make sense” of the components or not you may still believe them to nonetheless “exist.” This is an exceptionally interesting topic, but far beyond the scope of this book.
4.  4\. *Related to #3, components are only as good or interesting as the input variables subjected to the components analysis*. Hence, the first and primary concern of interest is subjecting PCA to a set of variables that is inclusive of all the variables you wish to analyze. If the data set is not interesting or you leave out important variables from the ensemble of variables, conducting a PCA on such data will likely be limiting, or your components analysis will be misspecified.410
5.  5\. *It is possible, even if unlikely, that a PCA generates eigenvalues that are equal or near equal in size*. Further, population eigenvalues are usually not exactly equal to eigenvalues generated by the sample. Inferential tests for eigenvalues exist (e.g., [Camargo, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000052)), but are rarely used. Tests have been developed and usually require the normality assumption ([Collins & Chatfield, 1980](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000057); Peres-Neto et al., [2005](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000285)).
6.  6\. Components derived in PCA depend more on the *ratios* of correlations in a correlation matrix than the correlations themselves. As noted by Collins and Chatfield ([1980](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000057), p. 67), dividing all off-diagonal correlations by a constant greater than 1 reveals that the eigenvalues change but that the eigenvectors, which implies the components as well, do not.
7.  7\. PCA does not assess the dimensionality of the variables; it assesses the *linear dimensionality* of the variables. If the data are nonlinear, which amounts to the underlying manifold being nonlinear, then classical PCA will fail to capture this nonlinearity. As discussed later, techniques such as *kernel PCA* will be more effective at uncovering a nonlinear underlying manifold.
8.  8\. Related to the previous point (#7), PCA is, in its most general sense, a type of *manifold learning* where the manifold is assumed to be linear. Nonlinear techniques may be more effective at uncovering the true manifold. *A failure to uncover meaningful components using PCA should never be taken as conclusive evidence that deeper dimensionality is nonexistent underlying the variables*. Such interesting dimensionality may indeed exist, but it may be *nonlinear* in form, a structure that PCA will be limited in uncovering.

## 11.3 Independent Components Analysis

In the classical PCA just discussed, we required components to be linear functions and orthogonal to one another. We sought to reduce the rank of the matrix of observed variables into one of smaller rank, but that accounted for most of the variance in the original variables, preferably in the first few components. The fact that the components were orthogonal to one another was a key feature of principal components analysis.

In *independent component analysis* (ICA), we require components (i.e., the *latent variables*) to be mutually independent and typically non-Gaussian ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). That is, the goal in ICA is to find a linear representation of non-Gaussian data so that the components are statistically independent, and if not perfectly so, then *as independent as possible*. *This is a different requirement than simply requiring orthogonality*. As noted by [Jolliffe (2002)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174), the links between classical PCA and independent components analysis are, perhaps surprisingly, not that strong, and ICA is closer in relation to factor analysis than it is to components analysis.

The ICA model ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)) can be stated as follows:

  
*X* = *f*(*S*) + *e*  
(11.7)

where *X* is a vector of random observed “manifest” variables, *S* is an unobservable random vector variate of sources whose components are independent latent variables, each having zero mean, and *e* is a random vector representing noise, for instance, in the measurements taken on *X*. The key point is that the independence of the sources implies that each individual source signal is hypothesized to be generated by a process unrelated to any other source signal ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)). Without *e*, the model is referred to as *noiseless ICA*. When *e* is included, we refer to the technique as *noisy ICA*.411

In ICA, projected points *P* are obtained as a product of the original data *D* and an unmixing matrix *M*^(*u*), where the mixing matrix is equal to *M*. Hence, *P* = *D**M*^(*u*). ICA essentially looks for rotations of data that have (approximately) independent coordinates. This will necessarily be true for all rotations from samples from multivariate normal distributions ([Venables & Ripley, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000376), p. 313), and hence ICA will not be of most interest for such a “trivial” situation. Instead, ICA is most valuable and useful for data arising from distributions that are not normal, that is, *non-Gaussian*.

### 11.3.1 Principal Components vs. Independent Components Analysis

How does independent component analysis relate to PCA? It stands that there should be some relation between them, and indeed there is. PCA can be considered *a special case of ICA*, where PCA yields orthogonal components while ICA generates independent components.

Jolliffe ([2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174), p. 396) best summarizes the difference between PCA and ICA:

> PCA has as its main objective the successive maximization of variance, and the orthogonality and uncorrelatedness constraints are extras, which are included to ensure that the different components are measuring separate things. By contrast, independent components analysis (ICA) takes the “separation” of components as its main aim. ICA starts from the view that uncorrelatedness is rather limited as it only considers a lack of linear relationship, and that ideally components should be statistically independent. This is a stronger requirement than uncorrelatedness, with *the two only equivalent for normal (Gaussian) random variables* \[emphasis added\]. … This is much closer to the set-up for factor analysis, and it is this “model” that ICA generalizes.

Jolliffe goes on to emphasize that simply because ICA is most appropriate in non-Gaussian contexts, this does not imply that classical PCA assumes normality, since it does not. One need not make any distributional assumptions to conduct a PCA as it is simply a mathematical decomposition of variance. If one chooses to make inferences of components to populations, then that is a different matter that would require corresponding parametric assumptions.

Hence, whereas PCA seeks to find or uncover a reduced-rank representation of variables, ICA attempts to represent data as independent sub-elements. ICA tries to separate the *signals* in one’s data, while PCA attempts to “load” the data onto the first few important or “principal” components. These are two quite different objectives. The reader will better appreciate how ICA is more similar to factor analysis when we survey factor analysis later in the book. Factor analysis is a proper statistical *model* and thus includes an error term, making it comparable to ICA. In PCA, no such error term is typically included nor is any statistical “model-like” structure advanced.

> *PCA and ICA are not the same technique. PCA seeks a lower-dimensional linear representation of the variables, whereas ICA seeks to separate the observed data into independent signals. Independence is a stronger property than uncorrelatedness under the assumption of non-Gaussian distributions.*

As a simple example of independent components analysis, consider Figure 11.4.412

![Figure 11.4 The objective behind independent components analysis is to “unmix” signals in a data set such that the resulting “source signals” are as independent as possible.Return to text.⏎](images/fig11.4.jpg)

*Figure 11.4* The objective behind independent components analysis is to “unmix” signals in a data set such that the resulting “source signals” are as independent as possible.Return to text.⏎

We begin with a *mixed signal*. The goal of ICA is to essentially “unmix” the signals. In sound analysis, for instance, a variety of components make up any sound, and ICA has been found useful for unmixing those composite sounds (e.g., “black box” recordings following an airplane crash). Independent components analysis can also prove useful in “unmixing” mixtures of image components in a picture.

For further details on ICA, see [Izenman (2008)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167). For an excellent discussion that summarizes the primary features of ICA and elaborates greatly on the required assumptions (and why they are necessary), see [Hyvärinen and Oja (2000)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000162). For a concise discussion of the differences between PCA and ICA, see Jolliffe ([2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174), p. 396). *Kernel ICA* is a relatively recent development ([Bach & Jordon, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000016)) at least in comparison to classical PCA and is discussed in Izenman ([2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), pp. 575–576). Independent components analysis can be fit using Python’s Fast ICA algorithm. In R, the package *ica* ([Helwig, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000152)) can perform ICA as well as the package *e1071* ([Meyer](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000251) et al., 2023).

We feature an example in R from the package *ProjectionBasedClustering* ([Thrun et al., 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000357)), where the Hepta data (three-dimensional) contain pre-defined clusters but with different variances:

```
> library(ProjectionBasedClustering)
> data(Hepta)
> Data = Hepta$Data
> Proj=ICA(Data)
```

## 11.4 Probabilistic PCA

In classical PCA, there is an absence of an associated probabilistic model for the data. That is, classical PCA is not probabilistic in any way; it is merely a mathematical transformation of the variables onto new axes such that it establishes a new *basis* (i.e., one that is orthogonal) from which the data are projected. As many writers on PCA have emphasized, PCA is not a “model” per se, it is simply a rotation of axes on which data are projected in correspondence to this rotation. Components are not obtained with reference to any kind of density-estimation framework. Be sure to note that in this distinction we are referring to the *construction of the components*, not the *estimation* of the components in the population. As mentioned, inferential procedures for components analysis do exist but are rarely used, with users preferring visualization techniques (e.g., scree plots) and eigenvalue magnitudes as aids to determining how many components to retain. When inference is employed, the inferential aspect of PCA makes components analysis probabilistic, but only in that particular sense of inference, not in the sense of actually deriving the components via eigen analysis.

It is possible, however, to derive the PCA approach based on a probabilistic formulation even without regard to estimation. Probabilistic PCA was first proposed by [Tipping and Bishop (1999)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000361) to provide an alternative approach to PCA, one that is probabilistic and thus exists in a density-estimation framework ([Tipping & Bishop, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000361)).

We give the case of *probabilistic PCA*, which can also be regarded as a special case of factor analysis, where *W* is a loading matrix and where the covariance matrix *S* can be written as

  
*S* ∼ *W**W*^(*T*) + *σ*²*I*  
(11.8)

Notice the noise term *σ*²in the probabilistic model. Classic principal components analysis is a special case of probabilistic PCA as *σ*²→0, or at minimum is infinitesimally small and essentially converges to zero. Noise dimensions are also uncorrelated, which above is indicated by *σ*²*I*, since in the identity matrix only values of 1 lie along the main diagonal and zeroes everywhere else. The inclusion of *σ*²*I* as the “error term” here instead of only *σ*² simply denotes the fact that we are working in the context of several variables and hence require a matrix representation.

The principal axes of probabilistic PCA can be derived as maximum-likelihood parameter estimates computed by the usual eigen-decomposition approach. There is no closed-form solution and hence parameter estimates for *W* and *σ*²*I* must be obtained iteratively ([Tipping & Bishop, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000361)). We can also approach the construction of components via an iterative, computationally efficient expectation-maximization approach. For details, see [Murphy (2022)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259). For an excellent introduction to the probabilistic PCA model from the ground up starting with classic non-probabilistic PCA, see [Tipping and Bishop (1999)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000361) who provide a very good overview.

### 11.4.1 Motivation for Probabilistic PCA

Why seek out a probabilistic approach to PCA in the first place? Why add a noise term similar to how factor analysis includes an error term? There are at least a couple benefits to doing so over the simpler and more conventional PCA approach:

1.  1\. Using a probability model allows us to extend the scope of conventional PCA and may also be useful in cases of missing data. It also allows for a comparison with other probabilistic approaches which dominate statistics, facilitating statistical testing and allowing for the application of Bayesian approaches ([Tipping & Bishop, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000361)).415
2.  2\. Probabilistic PCA can be utilized as a constrained Gaussian density model ([Tipping & Bishop, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000361)). This allows for the efficient computation of maximum-likelihood estimates directly from the data principal components.

### 11.4.2 Probabilistic PCA in R

Probabilistic PCA can be performed in R using the *Rdimtools* ([You & Shung, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000400)) package. The following is an example, adapted from the package (p. 184), that compares probabilistic PCA (PPCA) to PCA on the iris data:

```
> library(Rdimtools)
> data(iris)
> set.seed(100)
> subid = sample(1:100, 50)
> X = as.matrix(iris[subid,1:4])
> label = as.factor(iris[subid,5])
```

The above samples 50 observations from the data 1 through 100 (i.e., subid = sample(1:100, 50)), denotes variables 1 through 4 as X and the label as the fifth variable. We print a few of the first observations for X and label:

## 11.5 PCA for Discrete, Binary, and Categorical Data

Up to now, we have assumed that the data subjected to PCA is numerical and relatively continuous in nature. This is fine, so long as the data in one’s study adheres to this nature. However, oftentimes data come in a variety of forms that are hardly continuous. For example, binary (e.g., yes vs. no) data are common in polling, and categorical data (e.g., A, B, C) are quite popular as well.

Can PCA be used for data of different types? According to Jolliffe ([2002, p. 339](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174)), the answer is “yes”:

> When PCA is used as a descriptive technique, there is no reason for the variables in the analysis to be of any particular type … the variables could be a mixture of continuous, ordinal or even binary (0/1) variables. It is true that variances, covariances and correlations have especial relevance for multivariate normal data *x*, and that linear functions of binary variables are less readily interpretable than linear functions of continuous variables. However, the basic objective of PCA – to summarize most of the “variation” that is present in the original set of p variables using a smaller number of derived variables – can be achieved regardless of the nature of the original variables.

While PCA can be conducted on a mixture of variables, *multiple correspondence analysis* (MCA) is usually the preferred technique for dimension reduction using categorical data, as PCA is most often used for dimension reduction featuring numerical measurements. [Kalantan and Alqahtani (2019)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000179) also feature a method of PCA for mixed data. Murphy ([2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259), p. 670) gives the case of PCA for categorical data.418

## 11.6 Nonlinear Dimension Reduction

### 11.6.1 Kernel PCA

As we have seen, classical or “standard” principal components analysis allows for linear dimensionality reduction. However, we must ask the question of how often the true dimensionality of the variables or data lies in a subspace that is precisely linear. Probably not that often just as most data subjected to regression models are hardly linear, which is why techniques such as polynomial regression, splines, and other nonlinear and nonparametric approaches were surveyed earlier in the book. Though linearity is a useful *approximation* for dimension reduction, the true underlying dimensionality of most sets of variables is probably *nonlinear*. That is, the true manifold is likely, in the end, a *nonlinear* structure, not a linear one. We emphasize again that the linear vs. nonlinear underlying dimensionality always refers only to the set of variables you are working with and have included in your set of chosen variables. Dimension analysis, as is the case with any mathematical technique, can only operate on the set of variables you have subjected to analysis. All analyses are on what might be called *restricted universes* of variables and their respective interrelationships. This seems like an obvious point to make, but is one worth emphasizing: *a PCA, or any statistical method can only provide results on the variables on which it is analyzed! If you leave out important variables, your entire analysis will be misspecified. What you “find” is entirely related to what you supply the “machine” doing the searching. All is context-dependent all of the time.*

*Kernel principal components analysis* (KPCA) allows one to generalize standard PCA to *nonlinear dimensionality reduction*. As we will see, it is one of many nonlinear options to choose from when it comes to uncovering nonlinear dimensions.

### 11.6.2 How KPCA Works

Recall that the big idea of using kernel methods in general, not just for PCA (but for example, support vector machines), is that data that may not be separable in its current feature space may benefit from being projected into higher dimensions. For example, instead of having variables *x*[1] and *x*[2] only, an enlargement of the feature space might be *x*[1], *x*[2], *x*[1]², *x*[2]². *This enlargement of the feature space makes the data more linearly separable*. This is the very essence of what kernel methods, and kernel PCA in particular, seek to accomplish. Through the calculation of a kernel, we can then apply PCA in higher-dimensional space without ever having to really go there. When you think about it, this is truly a marvel! Indeed, kernel methods can be applied to many algorithms that can be formulated in terms of inner products in the feature space.

> *By projecting data that is nonlinear into higher-dimensional space, we make otherwise nonlinear data in the data space more linearly separable in the feature space. This is the essence of how kernel PCA (and other kernel methods) work.*

To further unpack how kernel PCA may be useful, consider Figure 11.7 consisting of data in two dimensions. Clearly, the data are not linearly separable. That is, we cannot draw a line through the data to separate the circles from the crosses. A more complex decision surface would provide much better separability. Mapping the problem from two dimensions to higher, we make the problem linearly separable, and it now looks as in Figure 11.8.419

![Figure 11.7 Data in two dimensions for which the data are obviously not linearly separable.Return to text.⏎](images/fig11.7.jpg)

*Figure 11.7* Data in two dimensions for which the data are obviously not linearly separable.Return to text.⏎

![Figure 11.8 Mapping data to higher dimensions via kernels makes it more linearly separable.Return to text.⏎](images/fig11.8.jpg)

*Figure 11.8* Mapping data to higher dimensions via kernels makes it more linearly separable.Return to text.⏎

The mapping from two dimensions to higher dimensions has made the data linearly separable, and thus a linear method can now be applied to the transformed “kernelized” data. This is the essence of kernelizing data in the context of PCA, that of transforming the data via kernels so that otherwise nonlinear data becomes linearly separable in the feature space and an “ordinary” PCA can then be applied to the transformed “kernelized” data.420

### 11.6.3 Kernelizing and Computational Complexity

There is another benefit to kernelizing. When we move from two dimensions to three, or, more generally, from lower dimensions to higher, such can seriously increase computation time. For smaller problems, this is usually not a problem, but for larger dimensionality tasks it becomes prohibitive. Hence, an immediate problem with high dimensionality is that of *computational complexity*. We would like to get around this problem and still capitalize on the benefits of working in higher-dimensional feature space. If we can compute in lower-dimensional space but actually work in higher-dimensional space, such would be ideal. This is precisely what the kernel trick allows us to do in terms of facilitating computation. That is, we can take advantage of higher-dimensional representations *without having to actually work in those higher configurations*. Instead, we can remain in lower dimensions and nonetheless conduct our analyses there. This is accomplished by computing *kernels*, which even though computed in lower dimensions, contain information about higher-dimensional representation.

The above result is due to *Mercer’s theorem*, which the reader may recall was discussed earlier in the book in relation to support vector machines. In brief, *the computational complexity of kernel PCA does not one-to-one increase with the dimensionality of the feature space* (Schölkopf et al., [1998](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000327), p. 4), and so even if we are working in very high-dimensional space theoretically, the computational complexity can be “tamed” somewhat by computing in a lower-dimensional space. This is thanks to the fact that we can compute kernels to represent this higher-dimensional inner product (Hilbert) space, and the fact that kernels are relatively simple to compute. Again, kernelizing is a marvel!

What is more, with kernel PCA no nonlinear optimization is involved. We can simply solve an eigenvalue-eigenvector problem as we would in traditional PCA *but now on the kernelized data*. The benefit of this is that getting “stuck” in local optima, in this case, *minimums*, is not a problem as it might be using other nonlinear methods. That is, *global optima* can be attained in kernel PCA ([Belkin & Niyogi, 2003](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000026), p. 1374). Clearly, kernel PCA has computational benefits to employing direct nonlinear methodologies.

> *The kernel trick allows us to work and compute in lower dimensions but benefit from higher-dimensional representation. The advantage of this is to both account for potential nonlinearity in the data but also to simplify computation time since we do not have to actually access the higher-dimensional space or surfaces in order to account for it. This is more generally known as the “kernel trick” and is due to Mercer’s theorem.*

### 11.6.4 Reconstruction Error in Kernel PCA

As was the case for classic PCA, the goal in kernel PCA will be to minimize the reconstruction error. It should make sense as to why this goal has not changed when moving from classical PCA to kernelized PCA; both methods are essentially doing the same thing, but simply on different transformations of the variables and data. At first glance, it may appear that enlarging the feature space would *increase* the dimensionality in which we need to compute. However, contrary to what we may expect, this is not what occurs, thanks again to the *kernel trick*. As we have emphasized, due to the kernel trick, we will not actually have to do any calculations in the higher-dimensional feature space. *Computation of kernels occurs in the original lower-dimensional space of the data*. As summarized by Hastie et al. ([2009, p. 547](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)):421

> Kernel PCA expands the scope of PCA, mimicking what we would obtain if we were to expand the features by non-linear transformations, and then apply PCA in this transformed feature space.

To add to all this, the higher-dimensional space could very well turn out to be *infinite dimensional*. This is why it’s called a “trick,” because we can simply compute kernels in lower dimensions and learn something of the higher dimensions without actually doing complex computations in higher dimensions. By analogy, it would be somewhat like being able to add two numbers, a very simple operation, to learn more about how the numbers relate in very complex ways (e.g., whether the distance between the numbers is a prime number). *The kernel trick allows for a simple computation to represent a much more complex reality or “space” behind those numbers*. Inexact analogy to be sure, but approximates the idea somewhat in spirit. The takeaway message is that the kernel trick is a *big deal* in statistics and machine learning.

### 11.6.5 The Matrices of Kernel PCA

Mathematically, kernel PCA relies on the fact that principal components can be obtained from a data matrix *X* by computing inner products of that data matrix,

  
*K* = *X**X*^(*T*)  
(11.9)

Eigen analysis is then performed on the double-centered version of *K*, where *K̃* is now equal to

  
*K*[*c*] = (*I*−*M*)*K*(*I*−*M*)  
(11.10)

and where *M* = 11^(*T*)/*N* which serves to center *K* ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 547). That is, we are computing a kernel matrix *K̃* that contains all pairwise dot products between data points. The double-centering here ensures the mean of every row and column is equal to 0. Whereas classical PCA uses the covariance matrix and scales regarding the number of input dimensions, kernel PCA scales with respect to the number of *data points* rather than dimensions in that the eigen analysis occurs on the *K̃* matrix and not the covariance matrix as in PCA.

As is true when using kernels, a variety of kernels are available, such as the *radial kernel* and others. However, the choice of kernel is critical, and the expression “*what you find is a function of what you put in*” is very relevant here; one kernel over another can drastically generate different findings (for an example of this, see Hastie et al., [2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 549). What does the eigen problem look like? Recall classic eigen decomposition:

  
*A**x* = *λ**x*  

For kernel PCA, *A* is now the kernel matrix *K̃*, and by simple substitution ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032), p. 588) the eigenvalue problem becomes,

  
*A**x*\=*λ**x*→*K̃**x*\=*λ**N**x*  
(11.11)

or as simply422

  
*K̃**x* = *λ̃**x*  

if *λ̃* = *λ**N* ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167), p. 611). Note that we are performing eigen analysis on the *K̃* matrix and not the covariance or correlation matrix as in traditional PCA ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)). Once we have the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, we can now project the data onto each new dimension.

> *Kernel PCA can be conceptualized as an “ordinary” PCA, but instead of weighted by input variables by values of the eigenvector, it is the kernel of the data points that is weighted by values of the eigenvector. Hence, KPCA simply replaces the variables (dimensions) with the kernel of observations, so that the kernel trick can “do its magic.”*

### 11.6.6 Classical PCA as a Special Case of Kernel PCA

We have seen that kernel PCA allows for nonlinearity. Hence, it stands that with some constraints imposed, classical linear PCA should be able to be obtained and operationalized as a *special case* of kernel PCA. Indeed, it should be evident from our earlier discussion that classical PCA must simply be a special case of KPCA ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032), p. 589) in which the *kernel is the linear kernel*. This is powerful insight. *In general, many linear methods can be regarded as special cases of a more general nonlinear framework*. The set of nonlinear statistical “possibilities” is much wider than the smaller set of linear models, and hence linear methods are a subset of that wider set, not only in the case of kernel PCA in relation to PCA but for most statistical methods in general.

### 11.6.7 Kernel Trick Is Not Simply about Cost

The kernel trick is useful since it saves on computational cost in accessing the higher-dimensional feature space. However, it should be emphasized that that is not the only reason for its utility. The primary benefit to using kernel methods is not only as a way around computational complexity. To reiterate, *the kernel trick allows us to work in higher dimensions without knowing the specific details of that dimensionality. That is its key benefit*. Hence, though often kernel methods in general are advertised or evaluated for their computational properties in “accessing” higher dimensionality, applying kernel methods in general is far from simply a way to ease computation. Even if the computations are laborious, which they can be in computing dot products of large matrices, kernel methods are useful since they allow access to those higher dimensions in the first place. *In general, kernel methods allow access to higher dimensionality while working in lower dimensions, often all for a more reasonable computational cost than if we were to access those higher dimensions directly.*

### 11.6.8 Kernel PCA in Python

We will perform kernel PCA in Python using the KernelPCA function:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import KernelPCA
X = np.array([[-1, -1], [-2, -1], [-3, -2], [1, 1], [2, 1], [3, 2]])
X
Out[24]:
array([[-1, -1],
     [-2, -1],
     [-3, -2],
     [ 1, 1],
     [ 2, 1],
     [ 3, 2]])
```

423 

We will request a kernel PCA for two components using a *radial basis function* (i.e., kernel = “rbf”):

```
kernel_pca = KernelPCA(n_components = 2, kernel =“rbf”, gamma = 0.03)
```

We have requested two components (n\_components = 2) as well as the radial basis kernel (kernel = “rbf”). We have also set gamma equal to 0.03, which is the kernel coefficient for the radial basis function (rbf).

```
final = kernel_pca.fit_transform(X)
print(final)
[[-0.3149893 -0.17944928]
[-0.46965347-0.0475298 ]
[-0.62541667 0.22697909]
[ 0.3149893 -0.17944928]
[ 0.46965347-0.0475298 ]
[ 0.62541667 0.22697909]]
```

The above are the two components resulting from the kernel PCA. Of course, the result looks very similar to what we might have obtained had we performed a classic PCA (i.e., two columns of eigenvectors), but remember that because it is a kernelized PCA, eigenvectors were computed on transformed “kernelized” data, not the original (and typically centered) data we would ordinarily use for a traditional PCA.
