The package *ProjectionBasedClustering* ([Thrun et al., 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000357)) can also be used for performing *t*\-SNE.

## 11.17 Manifold Learning and Beyond

This chapter has been about dimension-reduction techniques, that is, to find a lower-dimensional embedding from higher-dimensional data. Dimension reduction can be seen as a special case of the wider *blind source separation* or *manifold learning* paradigm. The focus of the chapter was first on principal components analysis since it is the simplest of the dimension-reduction techniques, the most used, and understanding it is the gateway to understanding extensions of the PCA approach as well as more modern techniques for dimension reduction.

In the following chapter, we will discuss yet another approach to dimension reduction, that of the *exploratory factor analysis model*. Though we have mentioned exploratory factor analysis in the current chapter, it is such an extensive and popular technique that it merits its own chapter.

PCA has its origins with Pearson in 1901 and Hotelling in 1933. As discussed in the chapter, a limitation of PCA is that it can only extract *linear components* and also can be sensitive to multivariate outliers. *Robust PCA* ([Locantore et al., 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000228)) and *Expectation Robust PCA* ([Serneels & Verdonck, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000332)) have been proposed as a means for dealing with outlying data. Other methods of PCA include *Local PCA*, *Generalized PCA*, and *Multi-linear PCA*. *Principal Components Analysis* by [Jolliffe (2002)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174) is perhaps misnamed, as it provides an extensive survey of not only PCA but also many other techniques related to PCA. These include *discriminant analysis*, *canonical correlation*, and even *neural networks*.

In our survey of dimension reduction and manifold learning, it is important to realize that we have merely skimmed the surface. As is the case with most statistical and machine learning topics, entire books and monographs have been written on the topic, many of which we have not had time or space to treat in this book. For instance, *latent semantic analysis* (LSA) is yet another dimension-reduction technique, this time for finding an embedding of words to decipher semantic meaning and thus specifically designed for text data. It is essentially an SVD on text data. As an example, suppose an author uses a group of words that have a “dark” tone to them. Do these words have an underlying dimension? LSA might be useful in uncovering such dimensionality. Many of these techniques are in one way or another related to SVD, and much statistical research has been targeted toward demonstrating parallels and equivalencies.

*Non-negative matrix factorization* is another dimension-reduction technique that once more creates a new basis for data that is originally in high dimensions. Such a basis is also guaranteed to be non-negative, which is where NMF gets its name. That is, the components and coefficients are non-negative ([Müller](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000258) & Guido, 2017). However, in NMF, the basis will not necessarily be orthonormal as is the case in PCA, however orthogonal versions of NMF have also been proposed ([Yang & Xu, 2021](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000397)). However, like PCA, “vanilla” NMF is restricted to uncovering only linear dimensions. Essentially, NMF reduces the data down to a non-negative weighted sum and may lead to more interpretable components than PCA. The procedure is effective at providing semantic interpretability for text analysis and dimension reduction (see [Aggarwal, 2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000005), p. 191).

At a more advanced level, sometimes manifolds contain loops (e.g., torus or circle) in them which makes traditional dimensionality much more difficult, if not prohibitively challenging. Techniques for reducing the dimensionality of such complex manifolds have been suggested ([Lee & Verleysen, 2005](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000214)). For an excellent overview of various dimension-reduction techniques and where current developments stand, see [Nanga](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000263) et al. (2021).459

# 12 Exploratory Factor Analysis

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-15](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-15)

In the previous chapter, we surveyed the method of principal components analysis, or PCA, as well as many extensions, derivatives, and special cases of the PCA method, including nonlinear approaches. The theme of all of these techniques was that of *dimension reduction* and could be considered special cases of an even more general problem, that of *manifold learning*. Whether it was principal components, multidimensional scaling, or other reduction technique, the overarching goal was to learn something about the hypothesized underlying lower-dimensional manifold that might subsume the observed data. That is, the goal was to seek out a lower-dimensional *embedding*. The purpose of PCA, in particular, was to uncover dimensionality in the variables by transforming from one *basis* to another such that the new variables (called *components*) have desirable properties, the most significant of which was to maximize variance. The first principal component was that which maximized the variance in the variables, and each component thereafter maximized a decreasing proportion of the variance. Components were constrained to be *orthogonal* to one another and the hope was to explain most of the variance in the variables by the first few components. Other techniques such as *independent components analysis* (ICA) held the stronger property that components be independent and not only uncorrelated. ICA was useful for such things as extracting the independent sources of variation from signals, speech, or images and proved especially useful for so-called *blind source separation* problems. Both classical PCA and ICA are examples of dimension-reduction techniques such that we believe the true (or at least our working hypothesis) dimensionality of the data lies in a lower *subspace* than in the original empirical representation. We noted that if the true dimensionality, or true manifold underlying the data was not linear, then a classical PCA could actually mislead more than it could enlighten. In this respect, PCA does not uncover *the* dimensionality underlying a set of data; it uncovers the *linear* dimensionality.

In this chapter, we survey the technique of *exploratory factor analysis* (EFA). Factor analysis is yet another dimension-reduction technique that we could have easily included as one of the several approaches surveyed in the former chapter. As we will see later, principal components analysis can actually be conceived mathematically as a special case of the wider factor analysis model. And though factor analysis is sometimes mistakenly conflated with PCA as being equivalent, it should be emphasized at the outset that *factor analysis is not the same as PCA*. First, factor analysis models *observed* variables as a function of *latent* variables, whereas PCA models components (loosely, “latent variables”) as a function of observed variables. Second, most versions of factor analysis hypothesize a *probabilistic model* that naturally includes an error or noise term, whereas classical PCA does not. In classical PCA, there is no “noise,” whereas in classical factor analysis, observed variables are modeled as a function of factors *plus* an error term. The advantage of factor analysis being probabilistic is, for one, that we can build more complex models such as *mixture* and *nonlinear factor analysis models* ([Murray, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). Some software programs such as SPSS 461routinely provide PCA results first before delivering on factor analysis findings and can lead some researchers to believe PCA results are *equivalent* to those of factor analysis, which, as we have noted, are not.

## 12.1 Why Treat Factor Analysis in Its Own Chapter?

Since we have said that factor analysis can be conceived as just another dimension-reduction technique, why devote a separate chapter to it instead of including it in the former chapter? There are a few reasons for treating factor analysis independently in a distinct chapter. These reasons include the fact that factor analysis has a long tradition in many social sciences (e.g., psychology) as a *centerpiece methodology*, and in many courses on multivariate analysis in the social sciences is given maximal attention as a methodology in its own right. Factor analysis grew out of a research context that initiated a tremendous amount of growth and innovation in what are generally referred to as *latent variable models*. Originally founded by Charles [Spearman (1904)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000344) in psychometrics, the concept of a *latent variable* formed the very bedrock of many techniques that grew out of factor analysis, such as *structural equation modeling*, which we survey in the following chapter.

Hence, factor analysis has its own unique historical lineage and germination and arose to address very specific substantive research problems where defining and tapping into constructs proved quite challenging, difficult, and, at many times, contentious. For reasons such as these, to treat it only on a technical level as an alternative to PCA or yet as just another approach to dimension reduction, we believe, would be a mistake. Despite its controversy historically, it is well-deserving of its own chapter for its devoted emphasis on the *measurement problem* which has dominated the social sciences in which it first arose and is responsible for giving birth to numerous other latent variable modeling techniques.

Toward the end of the chapter we will draw links between it and other techniques to show how factor analysis relates to these other dimension reduction and manifold learning methods, especially as contextualized in modern machine learning. As we will see, in a machine learning context, factor analysis can be best conceived as yet another *autoencoder*, more specifically a *variational autoencoder* due to its inclusion of an error or “noise” variable. Before we generalize to such lengths, however, we begin with the model from the bottom up by noting conceptual parallels it has, not with principal components, but instead with the classic *regression model*.

## 12.2 Common Orthogonal Factor Model

The common orthogonal factor model is given by

  
*x* = *μ* + *Λ**f* + *ε*  
(12.1)

where *x* is a vector of observed, or “manifest” variables that we seek to “explain” by the factor model, *μ* is an overall mean of the observed variables, *Λ**f* are weights or “loadings” in *Λ* applied to a vector of factors in *f* and *ε* is a vector of errors, that is, variation unexplained by the factor model. Of special note here is *f*, a vector of *unobserved* variables, not *observed* variables as in *x*. This is what is so special about the factor model, such that it attempts to account for observed variables by hypothesizing unobserved underlying variables. Note that this is not what occurs in PCA. Principal components analysis simply undergoes a rotation of axes resulting from an eigen decomposition; there is no *model equation* per se as in factor analysis. Note as well that *ε* is a vector of unobserved variables just as it was in the classic linear model. The vector *ε* is usually 462hypothesized to contain “specific” or “unique” variances, that is, variation that is unaccounted for by the latent variables in the factor model.

### 12.2.1 Factor Analysis Is a Regression Model

One of the first things to note about the factor analysis model is that it is, in actuality, a *regression model*, but not the classic regression of previous chapters. Defining it as a regression model simply means we are modeling an observed response by weighted predictors, that is, *regressing the observed responses on the weighted set of predictors*, but this is a very general idea; what is specifically being regressed on what will determine the exact *type* of regression model. Hence, concluding that factor analysis is a regression model only implies that it has a regression *characteristic* to it, no more. To appreciate the differences between the factor analysis model and that of classical least-squares regression, it behooves us to compare them side-by-side:

*x* = *μ* + *Λ**f* + *ε*   *y* = *x**β* + *ε*

We note similarities and differences between the models; both models have an observed vector as output of the function; in the factor analysis model, that vector is *x* while in the regression model that vector is *y*. Both models contain an *error* or *noise* term, *ε*. Where the models differ is in the middle terms of each equation. In regression, note that we are weighting an observed vector *x* by *β* whereas in the factor analysis model, we are weighting *unobserved* factors *f* by *Λ*. Both models are regression models, but *the factor analytic model contains unobserved factors as an explanatory variable*, whereas the regression model contains observed variables as explanatory variables. This is the key difference between the models.

> *The factor analysis model is a regression model, however unlike the classic regression model in which observed variables are regressed onto other observed variables, the factor analysis model features observed variables regressed onto unobserved factors or so-called latent variables.*

### 12.2.2 Assumptions Underlying the Factor Analysis Model

As in virtually all statistical modeling, models come with them a set of assumptions, assumptions that if not satisfied, can drastically weaken the application of the model and the conclusions that can be drawn when applying it to data. For the common factor analytic model, the assumptions are generally that *E*(*f*) = 0, that is, the mean of factors is equal to 0, and *E*(*f**f*′) = *I*, the covariance of factors is an identity matrix. Note that this is only an assumption of the *orthogonal factor model*. When we relax this assumption and allow factors to covary, such gives rise to the *oblique factor model*.

We also usually assume the errors have a mean equal to 0, that is, *E*(*ε*) = 0, and we assume the errors do not covary. We also typically assume that the covariance between the error term and the factors is equal to 0, that is, *E*(*ε**f*′) = 0. When we consider the confirmatory factor analytic model in the following chapter, we will see how these assumptions are not set in stone and can be relaxed such as to generate a factor model that is much more flexible.

### 12.2.3 Implied Covariance Matrix

The factor analysis model we have described implies the following structure to the covariance matrix,463

  
*Σ* = *Λ**Λ*′ + *ψ*  
(12.2)

That is, the covariance of observed variables is equal to *Λ**Λ*′ loadings plus a matrix of errors. The above equality is *implied* by defining the factor analysis model as we did earlier such that we can reproduce the covariance matrix *Σ* based on *Λ**Λ*′ + *ψ*. Recall that we said errors were uncorrelated, which implies that *ψ* will be an identity matrix, with values of one along the main diagonal and zeroes everywhere else. Given that *ψ* is set this way, this further implies that the covariances in *Σ* must be accounted for by the contents of *Λ*. Contrast this for a moment to PCA in which there is no *ψ* term to “explain” the covariance matrix, which implies that PCA will attempt to not only explain covariances, but also variances ([Alpaydin, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000009)). Another way of looking at this is to allow *ψ* to be in the PCA set-up, but set it to zero, that is, *ψ* = 0 for the PCA model but *ψ* ≠ 0 for the factor analysis model. As we will discuss later, if all error variances are assumed to be equal, that is, *ψ* = *ψ**Ι* (i.e., *isotropic error*), PCA becomes the aforementioned *probabilistic PCA* of the previous chapter, which, in the sense of the error structure, is more similar to factor analysis than it is to components analysis.

To understand and appreciate further why the above covariance identity holds, see [Denis (2021a)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000087) or [Johnson and Wichern (2007)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173). The important point for our immediate purposes here is to appreciate that the covariance matrix can be “deconstructed” into the above as a result that follows from the very definition of the factor model. The equality in (12.2) implies that if we can estimate the contents of *Λ*, we can “account for” the covariance of observed variables, that is, the factor analytic model attempts to reconstruct the covariance matrix through its estimation of factors.

Is this idea new to factor analysis? Not at all! In virtually all modeling, we are trying to *reconstruct* something in terms of something else, some *translation* or *reorganization* of data or variables. This is what is behind most function statements (i.e., the left side and right side of equality signs in model equations) in statistical models as we are simply trying to account for something that is already observed, which in this case, is the covariance matrix. In factor analysis, we are trying to reproduce the observed covariance matrix based on the specification of the factor analytic model. In the case of linear regression, it was the observed vector of response values that we were trying to reproduce via our model equation. In the case of discriminant analysis, it was the binary or multi-coded response that we were, again, attempting to reproduce. In the case of neural networks, as we will see later, it is the continuous or categorical outcome, and so on with most other kinds of modeling. *Many models, whether in multivariate statistics or machine learning, attempt to reconstruct, in some sense, an outcome*. *How well they reconstruct that outcome is measured by how well the model “fits.” In many applications, the model serves as a “narrative” for how the data were generated just as physicists, for example, try to find a narrative for how the universe began or psychologists a narrative for how neurotic behavior arises. Those narratives are typically (though not necessarily always ideally) expressed via mathematical frameworks.*

## 12.3 The Problem with Factor Analysis

What would a model be if it did not come with some baggage? Perhaps more than any other statistical method, factor analysis comes with it a legacy of criticism and perhaps even more, a legacy of *misunderstanding*. The major criticism of factor analysis is that *factor loadings are not unique*. What this means is that we can change the factor loadings (through a *rotation* of the factor solution, as we will see later), and still reproduce the same covariance matrix. Both original factor loadings and transformed loadings (by an orthogonal matrix) can reproduce the same covariance matrix ([Rencher & Christensen, 2012](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295)). Hence, the factor analyst is often left with trying to decide which are the “correct” loadings. The correct loadings will often be determined by which solution 464makes the most *substantive* sense to the researcher, which can make factor analysis seem a bit too subjective for some and historically is often a reason for some of the disdain for factor analysis by critical audiences.

Full details about why this is the case can be found in [Denis (2021a)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000087), but for now we cut right to the chase to the end result. The bottom line is that we can introduce an orthogonal matrix *T* such that the following holds:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {x - \\mu = \\Lambda f + \\varepsilon} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\Lambda{TT}'f + \\varepsilon} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(12.3)

That is, by simply including *T**T*′ into the factor model, we obtain an equivalent representation of *x* − *μ*. The substantive implication of this is that the loadings we obtain in factor analysis are not *unique* and are subject to an orthogonal matrix. Substantively, such implies that if a researcher does not “like” the factor solution they obtained, they can modify it (via *rotation*) until they find a solution they do like! Had the solution been unique, then the factor analyst would be “stuck” with the loadings produced.

### 12.3.1 The Problem Is the Users, Not the Method

To conclude this thought on the chief difficulty with factor analysis, we should emphasize that first and foremost, there is nothing “wrong” with factor analysis. The lack of uniqueness of its loadings may be a limitation of the technique, but all statistical methods, when considered carefully and in much detail, can be said to have limitations. The key is to *recognize* those limitations, be acutely aware of them, and not conclude from the methodology more than is warranted. This is the real danger of not understanding a statistical method, that one will draw more conclusions from it than are warranted by the model. Hence, the chief problem as it concerns factor analysis is more to do with how it is *applied* and *interpreted*. That is, the problem is usually with the *users* of the method not interpreting factor analysis *ethically*.

The author has time and time again seen the factor analytic model *misapplied*, *misused*, *misinterpreted*, and substantive conclusions drawn from applications of the model that violate the model’s assumptions and are simply not epistemologically supported. But again, this can be said to be true of the use of most statistical methods at times. *Too often researchers believe statistics tell them something about data that it simply cannot*. With factor analysis, especially when applied to social data, the problem of misunderstanding is usually compounded. *It is often more important to understand and appreciate what a statistical model will not tell you than it is to learn what it can tell you about reality.*

### 12.3.2 Factor Analysis Generalizes to Machine Learning

Historically, factor analysis was slow to gain acceptance by the mathematics community. Some mathematical statisticians had disdain for the method due to some of its perceived technical pitfalls (such as loadings not being unique) but likely also due to the academic turf war it may have initiated with psychology where the method was originally conceived ([Chatfield & Collins, 1980](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000057)). Some books on multivariate analysis would even refuse to cover the technique at all and pretend as though it didn’t exist!

With the arrival and meteoric rise of machine learning however, along with the data science “revolution,” factor analysis has enjoyed a resurgence in virtually *all* fields, not just those in social science in which it has always been quite popular. Today, factor analysis and its many derivatives 465and extensions is simply another method in the arsenal of the statistician or computer scientist. For example, *generative topographic mapping* (Bishop et al., [1998](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000031)), a form of nonlinear factor analysis and alternative to self-organizing maps ([Kohonen, 1982](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000196)) is featured in machine learning and builds on the foundation of latent variable models, an idea originally popularized by factor analysis. Indeed, the concept of latent variables is a powerful one and though the *idea* of latent variables is not due to factor analysis per se ([Mulaik, 1987](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000257)), factor analysis is responsible for operationalizing the construct and putting it on a technical foundation. Factor analysis has also helped give rise to the field of psychometrics. For instance, *item response theory*, also known as *latent distribution theory*, *item characteristic curve* (ICC), and *item characteristic function* (ICF), or *latent trait analysis* ([Mair, 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000237)) all build on the basic factor model. A good overview and summary of these models are provided by [Mahmud (2017)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000236).

Hence, we argue that to simply conclude that factor analysis is problematic and should be avoided is a well-outdated viewpoint, especially in the context of the rise of computer science and machine learning where it has found tremendous application. What is not an outdated viewpoint is that unless one is willing to study, understand and appreciate some of the more salient theoretical underpinnings and caveats of the method, one stands a much greater chance of misunderstanding and misusing factor analysis and concluding from the method much more than is epistemologically warranted.

## 12.4 Factor Estimation

As with virtually all statistical methods, we require a way to estimate parameters of the model. Though there are numerous estimation methods in EFA, classical estimation methods include *principal factor* (or *principal axis factoring*) as well as *maximum likelihood*, which we now (very) briefly survey.

### 12.4.1 Principal Factor (Principal Axis Factoring)

To understand the principal factor method of estimation, it is first necessary to revisit PCA and define what is meant by a *communality*. Given that we are working with the correlation matrix, the main diagonal in a PCA will contain *unit variances* as a result of each variable initially contributing one “unit” of variance to the PCA. In the *principal factor* approach, also known as *principal axis factoring*, the residual matrix is minimized and features replacing the initial communalities along the main diagonal in the correlation matrix with weights that are derived from the given variable being regressed on remaining variables subjected to the factor analysis. That is, each communality weight is given by

  
$${\\hat{h}}\_{i}^{2} = R\_{i}^{2} = 1 - \\frac{1}{r^{ii}}$$  
(12.4)

where *ĥ*[*i*]² is the estimated communality for variable *i*, *R*[*i*]² is the coefficient of determination for regressing variable *i* on all other variables being subjected to the given factor analysis, and *r*^(*i**i*)is the *i*th diagonal element of the inverse of the correlation matrix *R* ([Rencher & Christensen, 2012)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000295). If the covariance instead of the correlation matrix is analyzed, then (12.4) becomes

  
*ĥ*[*i*]² = *s**s*[*i**i*]*R*[*i*]²  
(12.5)

where *s**s*[*i**i*] is the *i*th diagonal element of the covariance matrix, *S*.466

### 12.4.2 Maximum Likelihood

The most common approach for estimating factors is, perhaps not surprisingly, that of maximum likelihood. It is easiest to carry out *maximum likelihood* (ML) estimation via the Expectation-Maximization algorithm (Choi et al., [2010](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000062); [Rubin & Thayer, 1982](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000316)). As was the case for the orthogonal factor model, the ML estimator is also invariant under rotation, and hence any rotation will generate the same ML estimates (Choi et al., [2010](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000062)). As we will see later, this is not unconditionally true for all factor analysis models. For instance, imposing an *l*[1] penalty on the factor model, yielding sparse “lasso” factor analysis, is not rotationally invariant (Choi et al., [2010](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000062)).

To obtain the maximum likelihood estimator for factor analysis, we first need to define the log-likelihood function in a multivariate context:

  
$$\\left. \\ln L\\left( \\mu,\\Sigma \\right) = - np\\ln\\sqrt{2\\pi} - \\frac{1}{2}n\\ln \\middle| \\Sigma \\middle| - \\frac{1}{2}\\left( n - 1 \\right)\\text{tr}\\left( \\Sigma^{- 1}S \\right) - \\frac{1}{2}n\\left( \\overline{y} - \\mu \\right)'\\Sigma^{- 1}\\left( \\overline{y} - \\mu \\right) \\right.$$  
(12.6)

The maximum likelihood estimator for *μ* is $\\overline{y}$ and the assumed covariance structure for the population covariance matrix *Σ* is *Λ**Λ*′ + *Ψ*, from which we can rewrite the log-likelihood function as

  
$$\\left. \\ln L\\left( \\Lambda,\\psi \\right) = - np\\ln\\sqrt{2\\pi} - \\frac{1}{2}n\\ln \\middle| \\Lambda\\Lambda' + \\psi \\middle| - \\frac{1}{2}\\left( n - 1 \\right)\\left. \\text{tr\[(}\\Lambda\\Lambda' + \\psi \\right)^{- 1}\\left. S \\right\\rbrack \\right.$$  
(12.7)

It can be shown that maximizing the log-likelihood function is equivalent to minimizing the following fit function,

  
*F*[*M**L*]\=ln|∑(*θ*)|+tr(*S*∑^( − 1)(*θ*))−ln|*S*|−*p*  
(12.8)

and upon substituting the orthogonal factor model, we obtain

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} \\left. \\left. F\_{ML} = \\ln \\middle| {\\sum\\left( \\theta \\right.} \\right) \\middle| + \\text{tr}\\left( S{\\sum{}^{- 1}}\\left( \\theta \\right) \\right) - \\ln \\middle| S \\middle| - p \\right. \\\\ \\left. \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\ln \\middle| \\Lambda\\Lambda' + \\Psi \\middle| + \\text{tr}\\left( S \\middle| \\Lambda\\Lambda' + \\Psi \\middle| {}\_{- 1} \\right) - \\ln \\middle| S \\middle| - p \\right. \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(12.9)

## 12.5 Factor Rotation

Recall we had said earlier that factor loadings are not unique, or, put another way, they are unique *but only up to an orthogonal rotation*. Recall that a square matrix *T* is orthogonal if *T**T*^′ = *T*^′*T* = *I*. Given this quality of the factor model, it stands that we can reproduce the same covariance matrix *Σ* but with alternative loadings. This translates into rotating the factor solution virtually at will yet still reproducing the same covariance matrix, *Σ*. The image in [Figure 12.1](#c12.xhtml#f12.1) depicts the idea of a factor rotation where we see the original axes *x*[1] and *x*[2] rotated to new axes *y*[1] and *y*[2], respectively:467

![Figure 12.1 Concept of a factor rotation. The new axes (y\_{1} and y\_{2}) are rotated from the old (x\_{1} and x\_{2}).Return to text.⏎](images/fig12.1.jpg)

*Figure 12.1* Concept of a factor rotation. The new axes (*y*[1] and *y*[2]) are rotated from the old (*x*[1] and *x*[2]).[Return to text.⏎](#c12.xhtml#re_f12.1)

A *clockwise* rotation features multiplying the factor loadings in *Λ* by the matrix *O*[1],

  
$$O\_{1} = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {\\cos\\phi\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\sin\\phi} \\\\ {- \\sin\\phi\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\cos\\phi} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  

whereas a *counterclockwise* rotation of *Λ* features multiplication by the matrix *O*[2],

  
$$O\_{2} = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {\\cos\\phi\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, - \\sin\\phi} \\\\ {\\sin\\phi\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\cos\\phi} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  

The new rotated loadings we now denote by *Λ*[*R*] and it can be shown that these new rotated loadings *provide the same fit to the covariance matrix as the unrotated loadings*. Recall our original deconstruction of the covariance matrix *Σ* presented earlier:

  
*Σ* = *Λ**Λ*′ + *ψ*  

It can be shown that with the new loadings *Λ*[*R*], the same covariance matrix can be reproduced:

  
*Σ* = *Λ*[*R*]*Λ*[*R*]′ + *ψ*  
(12.10)

It is for this reason that loadings in the orthogonal factor model are not unique. We can rotate the loadings quite freely and still generate the same covariance (or correlation) matrix. There are numerous ways of rotating factors in factor analysis. In what follows we survey a couple of the more popular methods in use.

### 12.5.1 Varimax Rotation

The varimax rotation is given by468

  
$$\\left. V = {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{p}\\left( l\_{ij}^{2} - \\overline{l\_{j}^{2}} \\right.} \\right)^{2}$$  
(12.11)

where *l*[*i**j*]² are the squared loadings *i* to *p* for a given factor, and $\\overline{l\_{j}^{2}}$ is the average squared loading across the *p* variables (i.e., across the *observed variables*, not factors). The name *varimax* derives from the fact that it maximizes these sum of squared loadings for each factor. How is such a maximum achieved? It attains a maximum by driving larger weights to be even larger and smaller weights to be even smaller, creating *heterogeneity* in the estimated weights in a manner that maximizes their squared sum. Varimax rotation has the benefit of clarifying factor structure since the larger weights will, hopefully, be more indicative of what the factor is “made up of” (in some sense) compared to the smaller weights that poorly indicate the factor structure. In his original use of factor analysis, Thurstone called this idea that of establishing *simple structure* ([Thurstone, 1954](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000358)).

### 12.5.2 Quartimax

The quartimax rotation is given by

  
$$\\left. Q = {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m}\\left( l\_{ij}^{2} - \\overline{l\_{j}^{2}} \\right.} \\right)^{2}$$  
(12.12)

where now the sum of squared loadings, *l*[*i**j*]², is maximized *across* factors *j* = 1 through *m*, having the effect of maximizing the variance due to observed variables rather than the factor variance as was the case for varimax. That is, maximizing *across* factors instead of *within* factors as varimax does has the effect of maximizing *variable* variance in place of the *factor* variance maximized by varimax.

Regardless of which of the above rotations we perform, the same correlation (or covariance) matrix is reproduced. To reiterate, this point is key to understanding the indeterminacy problem of factor analysis. One could, in theory, rotate the solution until one finds the solution they “prefer” without any consequence on the structure or makeup of the covariance matrix. Clearly, this will lead to the analyst’s subjective preference for a given solution, one that naturally accords with what the analyst was “hoping” to see.

## 12.6 Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity

A factor analysis, not surprisingly, requires there to be correlations greater than 0 in *R*, the correlation matrix. Prior to conducting a factor analysis then, one might wonder whether performing the EFA on the correlation matrix is worthwhile. That is, we may question whether there is *sufficient* correlation in the matrix on which to conduct the factor analysis. Of course, nothing prevents us from trying an EFA on a matrix with even minimal correlation. However, tests exist to evaluate the feasibility of doing so prior to doing the factor analysis and might also help explain why the ensuing factor analysis did not quite work out as the investigator had originally hoped.

*Bartlett’s test of sphericity* is one such test that seeks to evaluate the “appropriateness” of the data as it concerns factor analysis and is given by469

  
$$\\left. \\chi^{2} = - \\left\\lbrack {\\left( n - 1 \\right) - \\frac{\\left( 2p + 5 \\right)}{6}} \\right\\rbrack\\ln \\middle| R \\right|$$  
(12.13)

where *p* is the number of variables, *n* is the number of observations, and ln|*R*| is the natural logarithm of the determinant of the correlation matrix. For any given problem,

  
$$- \\left\\lbrack {\\left( n - 1 \\right) - \\frac{\\left( 2p + 5 \\right)}{6}} \\right\\rbrack$$  

will be a constant, and hence what determines the size of *χ*² will be a function of *R*, more specifically the determinant of *R*, |*R*|, where the latter can be considered a measure of *generalized variance* ([Johnson & Wichern, 2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000173)). Rejecting the null in this case suggests the matrix under analysis is not an identity matrix, which implies there exists sufficient correlation in *R* to carry on with the analysis. A failure to reject the null here does not “prove” the matrix to be an identity matrix, but it may cast doubt on whether performing the factor analysis is worthwhile. As with all significance tests, however, since Bartlett’s will be influenced by sample size, researchers are sometimes encouraged to perform the factor analysis regardless of what is reported by Bartlett’s, especially if sample size is fairly large. On a practical level, performing the factor analysis can’t hurt either way, and at worst, the investigator may simply not find any meaningful factor structure from the analysis.

### 12.6.1 Factor Analysis in Python

We can perform factor analysis in Python using FactorAnalyzer():

```
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
```

Let’s create some data:

```
data = np.array([[0, 5.90], [.90, 5.40], [1.80, 4.40], [2.60,
4.60], [3.30, 3.50], [4.40, 3.70], [5.20, 2.80], [6.10, 2.80],
[6.50, 2.40], [7.40, 1.50]])
data
Out[108]:
array([[0. , 5.9],
      [0.9, 5.4],
      [1.8, 4.4],
      [2.6, 4.6],
      [3.3, 3.5],
      [4.4, 3.7],
      [5.2, 2.8],
      [6.1, 2.8],
      [6.5, 2.4],
      [7.4, 1.5]])
```

We will import factor\_analyzer as well as Bartlett’s test of sphericity and the chi\_square value for computing Bartlett’s:

```
import factor_analyzer
from factor_analyzer.factor_analyzer import calculate_bartlett_sphericity
```

Recall that Bartlett’s test evaluates the null hypothesis that the correlation matrix is an identity matrix. As an example, for a three-variable problem,470

  
$$H\_{0}:R = I = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 0\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 0} \\\\ {0\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 1\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 0} \\\\ {0\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 0\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, 1} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  

The alternative hypothesis is that *H*[1] : *R* ≠ *I*. When we run Bartlett’s test of sphericity, we obtain:

```
chi_square_value, p_value=calculate_bartlett_sphericity(data)
chi_square_value, p_value
Out[35]: (23.012894934627763, 1.609184226770749e-06)
```

The *p*\-value is very small (1.609…-06), suggesting that we can reject the null hypothesis that the correlation matrix is an identity matrix. We infer that there *is* a degree of correlation in the matrix, probably enough to try a factor analysis.

We also wish to import the KMO test, which stands for the *Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy*, a measure used for evaluating the utility for conducting a factor analysis in the sense of providing an estimate of the proportion of variance in variables that might be “due” (in some sense) to underlying factors ([Denis, 2021b](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000088)):

```
from factor_analyzer.factor_analyzer import calculate_kmo
kmo_all, kmo_model=calculate_kmo(data)
kmo_model
Out[36]: 0.5
```

Values of 0.70 or higher are generally preferred, however values as small as 0.5 are sometimes regarded as sufficient. Either way, a result on the KMO test should not discourage you from running a factor analysis even if the result is somewhat less than 0.5; the worst that can happen here is that your factor analysis does not “pan out” as you had hoped.

We now conduct the factor analysis using the ‘minres’ approach, which stands for *minimum residual* (see [Comrey (1962)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000067) for details on the approach). The number of factors we will request is equal to 1 (n\_factors=1):

```
from factor_analyzer import FactorAnalyzer
fa = FactorAnalyzer(rotation=None, method = ‘minres’, n_factors=1)
fa.fit(data)
Out[112]: FactorAnalyzer(n_factors=1, rotation=None, rotation_kwargs={})
fa.loadings_
Out[113]:
array([[-0.98816761],
[ 0.98816761]])
fa.get_communalities()
Out[114]: array([0.97647522, 0.97647522])
```

We see that the loadings from the factor analysis are −0.988 and 0.988, with each communality equal to 0.97. Factor analysis can also be performed using Python’s *sklearn*.

## 12.7 Independent Factor Analysis

Recall in our more general discussion of principal components earlier in the book, we surveyed the method of independent components analysis, which required components to not merely be uncorrelated but rather *independent*. ICA was featured as one method in the wider blind-source separation and manifold learning problem. Most applications of ICA, however, did not feature an error term and are regarded as *noiseless ICA*. As [Attias (1999, pp. 2–3)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000015) notes, however, not including a noise term limits the ability of ICA to recover components:

> As the noise level increases, the performance of ICA algorithms deteriorates and the separation quality decreases, as manifested by cross-talk and noisy outputs. More importantly, many situations have a relatively small number of sensors but many sources, and one would like to lump the low-intensity sources together and regard them as effective noise, while the separation sources focuses on the high-intensity ones. There is no way to accomplish this using ICA methods … Our IFA \[independent factor analysis\] algorithm reduces to ordinary FA when the model sources become Gaussian, and performs principal component analysis (PCA) when used in the zero-noise limit … IFA therefore generalizes and unifies ordinary FA, PCA and ICA and provides a new method for modeling multi-variable data in terms of a small set of independent hidden variables … IFA amounts to fitting those data to a mixture model of co-adaptive Gaussians.

Hence, the classic factor analysis model, principal components, and independent principal components can all be conceived in a sense as special cases of the wider independent factor analysis model. The IFA model will look as it did in the classic version of the EFA model,

  
*x* = *μ* + *Λ**f* + *ε*  
(12.14)

but with the important caveat that factors will now be constrained to be *independent*, not only *uncorrelated* as in the common factor analysis model. The independent latent variables have flexible distributions modeled by mixtures of Gaussians ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)) and hence while common exploratory factor analysis can be thought of as a low-rank version assuming a Gaussian distribution, independent factor analysis distinguishes itself from this as it features non-Gaussian distributions with Gaussian densities as essentially a “special case” ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)).

The loading matrix *Λ* in IFA is regarded as the *mixing* matrix and as was true of ICA, is responsible for blending in of the various sources. The EM algorithm is typically used to maximize the log-likelihood of the observed data with respect to the parameters of the generative model that account for the data ([Attias, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000015)). As is the case with common factor analysis, in independent factor analysis the number of latent variables and observed variables can differ ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032)).474

The independent factor analysis model has not seen much development as a unique method since its inception nor does it appear extensively in the literature. This may be due to the ICA model dominating applications ([Izenman, 2008](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000167)).

## 12.8 Nonlinear Factor Analysis and Autoencoders

We have emphasized that the classic factor analysis model is linear in the parameters. One way to relax this assumption is to allow the mapping of variables to unobserved variables to be a *nonlinear model*. We remind ourselves at this point that classic PCA can be conceptualized as an *autoencoder*, where recall an autoencoder is a kind of *transformer* that encodes input into output but does not necessarily reduce the dimensionality of the input. Factor analysis can also be conceived as such, and hence conceptualizing nonlinear factor analysis is best done via an autoencoder, more specifically what is called a *variational encoder*, which is best thought of as a probabilistic version of a deterministic autoencoder ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). Factor analysis is a variational encoder due to its inclusion of an error term, *ε*. It is also a *generative model*, which implies that we can create new data (e.g., factor scores) from it, whereas the traditional classic autoencoder is deterministic ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)).

### 12.8.1 Unpacking the Autoencoder

Recall that an autoencoder features two components, the *encoder* is *x*→*z* while the *decoder* is *z*→*x*. In the current context, observed variables *x* are encoded into one or more latent variables, while latent variables can be decoded back into observed variables. Unpacked, encoding *x* into *z* with a weighting matrix *W* corresponds to *z* = *W*[1]^(*T*)*x*, while decoding *z* corresponds to *x̂* = *W*[2]^(*T*)*z*, where the distance *x* − *x̂* is minimized ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). In a classical PCA, the encoding and decoding stages will be linear maps and *W* will be constrained to be orthogonal. In a nonlinear factor analysis or a (nonlinear) neural network, the encoding and decoding will be nonlinear and depending on whether we wish factors to be uncorrelated or not we will place constraints on *W*. Eigenvectors of the covariance matrix in *W* are chosen such that the above reconstruction error is minimized.

The key to nonlinear factor analysis then is that the mapping from *x*→*z* contains nonlinear functions, which may include such things as *interaction terms* or *polynomials*, or virtually any other nonlinear function. Note that this may sound somewhat like multiple regression, but recall that in multiple regression, there is no real “encoding,” unless we think of predictors in *x* being “encoded” into a fitted vector, *ŷ*, but such is not traditionally how autoencoders are usually conceived or conceptualized.

### 12.8.2 Factor Analysis as a Neural Network

Because an autoencoder can be conceived as a special type of neural network, the nonlinear maps from *x*→*z* and *z*→*x* applied to factor analysis can also be thought of as a *neural network* in which the mapping is some nonlinear *activation function*. Hence, we see once more the generality of specific approaches such as factor analysis as special cases of a wider neural network framework. Not surprisingly, as is the case with other nonlinear methods surveyed in this book, imposing a nonlinear encoder can detect patterns and shapes in data that a classic linear factor analytic model or principal components cannot ([Japkowicz & Gluck, 2000](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000170)). According to Japkowicz et al. ([2000](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000170), p. 1):

> While linear autoassociators emulate PCA and thus exhibit a flat or unimodal reconstruction error surface, autoassociators with nonlinearities in their hidden layer learn domains 475by building error reconstruction surfaces that, depending on the task, contain multiple local valleys.

Nonlinear factor analysis can also be conceived as a *deep latent Gaussian model* (Rezende et al., [2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000297)). The origins of nonlinear factor analysis go back to [Bartlett (1953)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000021), though at the time it could not be conceived as an autoencoder or neural network, since these conceptualizations are relatively recent. For a thorough review of nonlinear factor analysis, see [Amemiya and Yalcin (2001)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000010).

## 12.9 Probabilistic “Sensible” PCA (Again)

We have already surveyed *probabilistic PCA* in the context of PCA. We now survey it in the context of the factor analytic model. Probabilistic PCA, or *sensible PCA* as it is sometimes known ([Roweis, 1998](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000314)), contains noise along the main diagonal of the correlation matrix whereas classical PCA on the correlation matrix contains values of unity along the main diagonal. As explained by [Roweis (1997, p. 5)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000313):

> If we require **R** \[correlation matrix\] to be a multiple *ε**I* of the identity matrix (in other words the covariance ellipsoid of **v** is spherical) but do not take the limit as *ε*→0 then we have a model which I shall call sensible principal components analysis or SPCA … the scalar value *ε* on the diagonal of **R** the global noise level.

The key to the above is not taking *ε*→0 in the limit as one would in a classical orthogonal PCA model. Allowing *ε* ≠ 0 permits at least *some* error along the main diagonal of *ψ* yielding the following probabilistic PCA reconstruction of *Σ* which looks a lot like factor analysis:

  
*Σ* = *Λ**Λ*′ + *ψ*  
(12.15)

This is why PCA is sometimes cast as the limiting case of a linear-Gaussian model, equivalent to the classical factor analysis model as the error or “noise” becomes extremely small and in the limit goes to zero.

So, what is the difference between probabilistic PCA and factor analysis then? It would seem they are the same since they both contain error terms. They are slightly different, however. The key difference lies in the restrictions placed on the error term. In the factor analysis model, recall that *ψ* was constrained to have *σ*²*I* along its main diagonal. That is, *σ*²*I* translates to values of noise *ε* along the main diagonal of *R*. However, *σ*² *did not need to be constant (i.e., the same number) along the main diagonal*. In probabilistic PCA, however, *ψ* is constrained to have *σ*²*I* along its main diagonal and it is required for *ψ* to be *isotropic* or *spherical*, which means it must be *proportional* to the identity matrix ([Bishop, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000032), p. 584). Since the identity matrix has values of one along the main diagonal, this implies that *ψ* *must have errors that are equal to one another*. This is why probabilistic PCA is considered a special case of factor analysis, where factor analysis allows, as Lawrence ([2005](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000211), p. 1784) puts it, a “richer error term” which simply means in this context that the error term need not be *constant*. That is, the covariance matrix need not be spherical in classic factor analysis. In probabilistic PCA, it is required to be so.

## 12.10 Mixtures of Factor Analysis: Modeling Local Linearity

Instead of assuming a linear mapping to unobservable latent variables, as is true of other methods, we can relax this assumption and model things more *locally*. That is, we can assume that locally the model is linear, and then combine all these local model segments to approximate a curved 476manifold. Of course, this concept is not new, we have come across this idea of *local approximation* many times throughout this book (such as in locally linear embedding). In the current context, when one sums together local linear approximations, one gets a better picture of the overall curved manifold, somewhat analogous in concept to the idea of fitting many tangent lines to get the “fit” of a curve in calculus. In essence, a mixture of factor analyzers devotes a factor analysis to each of individual groups or clusters. It is perhaps best described by Ghahramani and Hinton ([1997](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000128), p. 1):

> we present an EM learning algorithm for a method which combines one of the basic forms of dimensionality reduction – factor analysis – with a basic method for clustering – the Gaussian mixture model. What results is a statistical method which concurrently performs clustering and, within each cluster, local dimensionality reduction.

First, we recall the factor analysis model, omitting the mean, *μ*,

  
*x* = *Λ**f* + *ε*  

For the mixture model, where now *f* = *z*, the generative model is the following,

  
$$P\\left( x \\right)\\left. = {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m}{\\int{P\\left( x \\right.}}} \\middle| z,w\_{j} \\right)P\\left( z \\middle| w\_{j} \\right)P\\left( w\_{j} \\right)dz$$  
(12.16)

and where *w*[*j*] are the different mixing distributions such that

  
*p*(*z*|*w*[*j*]) = *p*(*z*) = *N*(0,*I*)  

which reads that the conditional probability of *z* given *w*[*j*] is equal to the unconditional probability of *z*, of which both are normally distributed. Following Ghahramani and Hinton ([1997](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000128), p. 4), each factor for each mixing distribution will also have its own mean,

  
*p*(*x*|*z*,*w*[*j*]) = *N*(*μ*[*j*]+*Λ*[*j*]*z*,*ψ*)  
(12.17)

which is unlike in traditional factor analysis, where the mean was constant across all factors (i.e., *x* = *μ* + *Λ**f* + *ε*).

The mixture of factor analyzers is estimated using the EM algorithm. For details, see [Ghahramani and Hinton (1997)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000128). If the error structure happened to follow that of the probabilistic PCA model just surveyed, then the model becomes a *mixture of probabilistic PCA models*. Indeed, probabilistic PCA is a special case of the above model when, as we saw, the error matrix is spherical ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)). The covariance matrix for the mixture model will have *mkp + p* parameters whereas the classic nonmixture factor analysis had *mp*(*p* + 1)/2, where *m* is the number of factor analysis models to use in the mixture model, *k* is the number of factors to extract in each of those factor analyses, and *p* is the number of variables in *x*.

## 12.11 Item Factor Analysis

Item factor analysis, or IFA, is the factor analysis model adapted to analyzing multivariate *categorical* data, which proves especially useful for modeling item-level response data on surveys and questionnaires. These data are often *binary* or *polytomous* or otherwise *categorical* in nature and thus the classic maximum-likelihood factor analysis model ,which assumes continuous variables 477can cause issues ([Everitt & Dunn, 2001](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000096)). Indeed, performing such a traditional factor analysis on data that is not continuous can result in very disparate findings when compared to performing it with an alternative estimation method. See Everitt and Dunn ([2001](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000096), p. 286) for a comparison of output.

[Muthén and Kaplan (1985)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000260) compared estimators for factor analysis of non-normal skewed variables, which included binary and categorical variables, and which included *maximum likelihood*, *generalized least-squares* (GLS), and *asymptotically distribution-free* (ADF) *generalized least-squares*, as well as a categorical variable estimator. They found that ML and GLS standard errors were typically biased downward, but that for ADF no bias was found and the CVM (*categorical variable estimator*) worked well for skewed variables that had been dichotomized. For further details, see [Muthén and Kaplan (1985)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000260).

[Urban and Bauer (2021)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000369) proposed a deep artificial neural network for exploratory item factor analysis, who also showed that other factor analytic models such as nonlinear factor analysis may be subsumed under their novel algorithm. Software-wise, *Mplus* ([Muthén & Muthén, 2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000261)) has especially good capabilities for fitting factor analysis models featuring binary or categorical indicators. Item factor analysis can also be fit using the *OpenMx* package in R (Boker et al., [2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000035)).

## 12.12 Sparse Factor Analysis

Recall that a *sparse* model is one in which there is a purposeful effort to simplify the model by driving coefficients *to* or *toward* values of 0 in the same spirit as estimators such as ridge and lasso regression surveyed earlier in the book. In one sense, we have already surveyed a sparse-like factor analysis model when we introduced the *varimax rotation*, whose objective, recall, was to drive large coefficients to be larger and small coefficients to be smaller as to approximate *simple structure* for each factor. The sparse factor analysis likewise aims to increase the sparsity of the factor model by introducing penalization or regularization methods that drive coefficients to or toward 0, as to simplify and clarify the factor structure.

[Drton et al.](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000091) (2024) detail algebraically sparse factor analysis models as models that set or hypothesize some or many of the coefficients (i.e., *factor loadings*) equal to 0. Other approaches do not necessarily set weights equal to zero, but instead “encourage” ([Murphy, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000259)) them to equal 0 through regularization, such as an *l*[1] penalty (Choi et al., [2010](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000062)). Penalties of course have a Bayesian flavor in a sense because we are influencing the size of weights *a priori* and thus having a corresponding influence on prior probabilities. [Frühwirth-Schnatter et al. (2024)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000119) detail *sparse Bayesian factor analysis* for the case where the number of factors is unknown with what are known as *spike-and-slab priors* on the factor loading matrix. The use of such priors drives some factor loadings to 0, which allows the model to be identified. Setting weights to 0 to help identify a model is also a common analytical choice in the structural equation models of the following chapter.
