# 13 Confirmatory Factor Analysis, Path Analysis, and Structural Equation Modeling

DOI: [10.4324/9781003376941-16](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003376941-16)

In the previous chapter, we surveyed the exploratory factor analysis (EFA) model and learned that in the classic factor analysis model, observed variables were being hypothesized as linear functions of unobserved latent variables. We also surveyed some of the very many derivatives and extensions of the classic EFA model, which included nonlinear factor analysis and other possibilities, which ranged from models emanating from statistics and social science to more modern advances in machine learning.

In the current chapter, we develop the full structural equation model, which can be said to consist of elements common to both factor analysis and regression. First, we consider the confirmatory version of factor analysis, appropriately called *confirmatory factor analysis* in which the researcher has a specific factor pattern or hypothesis they would like to test instead of conducting a purely exploratory search as in EFA. What a confirmatory test reduces to, on a technical level, is a more deliberate *fixing and freeing of model parameters* than in its exploratory counterpart. However, as we will see, distinctions between what makes a model exploratory vs. confirmatory can be quite blurry. We then introduce the structural equation model, which can be conceptualized as a series of (typically) linear equations, however nonlinear structural equation modeling is also a possibility and we briefly survey those as well.

The origins of structural equation modeling are twofold. The measurement model of SEM can be said to have begun with Charles [Spearman (1904)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000344), while the structural portion of SEM has its roots primarily with Sewall [Wright (1918)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000392) who developed the method of *path analysis*. Path analysis features networks among observed variables and hence is largely seen as a precursor, historically, to the arrival of structural equation models. Combining the measurement model with that of the structural components of path analysis gives rise to the full structural equation model. Jöreskog ([1970](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000176), [1973](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000177)) is usually credited with the first true SEM model ([Tarka, 2018](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000353)) although researchers, especially in sociometrics, were running structural equation modeling in the 1950s and 60s. It was Jöreskog, however, who is primarily responsible for pioneering cutting-edge estimation methods for SEM.

## 13.1 What Makes a Model “Exploratory” vs. “Confirmatory”?

Exploratory factor analysis models are named as such because the user does not typically have any idea in advance regarding how many factors may result from the analysis. This is the *exploratory* nature of the model; the user is diving into the data without any preconceived *theory* as to the number of factors that may result. At first thought, this may seem like an unrealistic proposition, since researchers usually have at least *some* idea of what may come out of their factor analyses before conducting them. That is, the Bayesian prior is typically not *uniform*, even in exploratory analyses.480

The way to improve on the above exploratory idea of a factor analysis model is to have a *pre-conceived structure* of what to expect from the factor analysis. In this case, the researcher has a pre-established theory in mind and wishes to evaluate that specific hypothesized structure. *Confirmatory factor* *analysis* in this case is a viable option, where the model allows the researcher to virtually control and specify almost every parameter of the model. That is, the user can *fix*, *free*, or even *equate* estimated parameters with other model parameters and obtain measures of model fit assessing how well or how poorly her model stood up to the data.

A step above the confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) model is the full-blown structural equation model, which in addition to hypothesizing specific latent structures, also hypothesizes relationships among latent structures. For example, the SEM model allows a researcher to hypothesize one latent structure as a predictor of another, and many more possibilities. Many discussions of CFA in the literature are “housed” within the wider SEM framework, and hence it is for this reason that we focus primarily on SEM in this chapter. Confirmatory factor analysis is best understood as a special case of the wider SEM framework.

## 13.2 Why “Causal Modeling” Is Not Causal at All

Hume once defined causality as

> We may define a cause to be an object followed by another, … , where, if the first object had not been, the second never had existed.
> 
> (Hume, 1748, Section VIII)

Since the time of Hume, philosophical work on causality has filled volumes, books, and academic careers. The study of causality is a full-time job and truth be told, nobody is still quite sure what causality even means. There are several different versions and interpretations of the meaning of causality (e.g., see [Bollen, 1989](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000037)). Exploring the nature of causality alone in this book would take up at least a chapter if not more, and hence, we do not go there. It will be enough, however, to reject the idea of structural equation models having anything *intrinsically* and *necessarily* to do with causality.

### 13.2.1 Misguided History

If modern causality goes back to Hume, the study of causality itself can be said to go back to the ancient Greeks. The development of statistical regression took place primarily in the late 1880s and early 1890s with the original work of Francis Galton, followed by Karl Pearson and his student, George Udny Yule. Did these pioneers refer to regression models as being causal? Not explicitly, but they did at times use the word *causal* when describing the relationships among the response and predictor variables. However, nowhere did these pioneers ever give regression the power or “license,” *unequivocally*, to make causal claims or draw causal conclusions from non-experimental designs.

Fast-forward to 1917 with the work of Sewall Wright on path analysis, well documented elsewhere (e.g., see [Denis & Legerski, 2006](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000085)). Wright was interested in the generational transmission of color in the guinea pig. From the very inception of Wright’s path models, for which he named the coefficients from such models *causal coefficients*, opposition to such claims of causation surfaced almost immediately. As argued in [Denis and Legerksi (2006)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000085), path models, and their eventual offspring, structural equation models, have no more philosophical authority to claims of causation than the regression models invented in the 1890s. *Causality has nothing to do with the model; it has everything to do with the objects and variables that are being modeled*.481

To illustrate the above point, consider a figure ([Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#f13.1)) from Wright’s original guinea pig diagram (left) where he traced what he called the *causal* paths from parent to offspring.

![Figure 13.1 Early path diagram by Wright (left). Replacing guinea pig names with arbitrary variable names (right).Return to text.⏎](images/fig13.1.jpg)

*Figure 13.1* Early path diagram by Wright (left). Replacing guinea pig names with arbitrary variable names (right).[Return to text.⏎](#c13.xhtml#re_f13.1)

Obviously, in the context of parents giving birth to guinea pigs, color transmission was a heritable, biological reality. That is, the fact that offspring had a similar color as their parents could be explained by what was known at the time of heritable influences. Naming such paths “causal” did no harm, as the genetic transmission from parent to offspring agrees more or less with the idea of causality. However, suppose we now replaced the guinea pigs in the picture with simply abstract variables (right): *X*, *Y*, *W*, and *Z*. Could we now make an analogous causal claim? Does it make any sense to claim that *W* causes *Z*, for instance? Surely not! After all, we do not even know what these variables even *are*. They are entirely *abstract*.

From this simple example and comparison, it is clear to see that the model alone could never infer causality. Ascribing causal “power” to the statistical *model* instead of to the *variables* on which the model is applied is nothing less than faulty reasoning. *There is nothing inherently causal about a path model or a structural equation model or any other statistical model*. The only conceivable possible exception to this is if all variables in the entire *universe* and all residuals (and their relationships) were able to be included in the model such that the model was fully (and unreasonably on a pragmatic level) specified. Then, it *may* make more sense to speak of the model as causal regardless of the substantive natures of variables used in the model. But of course, such is a fanciful reality that will never be achieved. It is simply unattainable and unrealistic. Hence, identifying or associating causality with the path or structural equation model, or with *any* model for that matter, is simply illogical. Causality is a *scientific* issue, not a *statistical* one.

### 13.2.2 Baron and Kenny (1986)

We fast-forward for a moment to Baron and Kenny’s seminal and highly cited 1986 publication, *The Moderator-Mediator Variable Distinction in Social Psychological Research: Conceptual, Strategic, and Statistical Considerations*. In it, the authors wished to emphasize the difference between moderators and mediators, which is a noteworthy contribution. They offer the following definition of a moderator:482

> In general terms, a moderator is a qualitative (e.g., sex, race, class) or quantitative (e.g., level of reward) variable that affects the direction and/or strength of the relation between an independent or predictor variable and a dependent or criterion variable (p. 1174).

Of course, the above definition, taken *literally*, is somewhat problematic. Statistical moderators have no license whatsoever to *affect* the direction or strength of anything. The word “affect” usually implies “to have an influence on” or similar. As discussed when we surveyed moderation earlier in the book, statistical moderators are simply unable to do such a thing; *substantive moderators*, perhaps, but not *statistical ones*. Calling a variable a *statistical moderator* does not by itself imply that it moderates anything.

Why bring up Baron and Kenny at all here in a discussion of path analysis and structural equation models? We do so for the reason that mediation and moderation models can easily be cast as structural equation models, and hence addressing the causality issue here in relation to SEM models is mandatory. To be fair to Baron and Kenny, they do later in their seminal paper discuss such things as experimental controls and manipulation where causality may possibly be inferred, but the point we wish to make here is that defining moderation or mediation with any kind of *action words* encourages the student (and even researcher!) to falsely and illogically ascribe powers to statistical techniques that they simply do not possess. Some sciences, such as psychology, have a long history of inferring and concluding far “too much” from what a statistical paradigm is philosophically able to provide. We believe that this is in part because in some subfields, carrying out *experimental designs*, where claims of causality may be more reasonable, can be tremendously challenging or impossible due to ethical and other constraints. One cannot randomly assign age, for instance, and hence, many designs in these fields and areas are necessarily *correlational* in nature. Even given these interpretational constraints, however, this may not be enough to stop researchers’ “Freudian id” from stepping in and concluding more from the statistical analysis than what may be warranted.

## 13.3 Is the Variable Measurable? The Observed vs. Unobserved Distinction

Structural equation modeling distinguishes between *observed* or *manifest* vs. *unobserved* variables. With a little thought, the distinction here, like many terms in statistics, gets fuzzy and blurry very quickly, and once more we end up studying the philosophy of these distinctions rather than simply defining them. Still, we must do our best to attempt some definitions here so we can move on and not get stuck in philosophical quicksand.

Essentially, an *observed variable* is any variable for which we can, at least in theory, obtain a direct *measurement*. For instance, height would be regarded as an observed variable. We can easily measure it and have well-defined units to describe it (e.g., inches, feet, etc.). If we are unable to obtain such a *direct* measurement of a variable and need or desire to infer its existence based on other measurable variables, then that variable is usually regarded as *unobserved*. The most classic example of a latent variable is that of intelligence (IQ). Intelligence is a *construct* for which it is difficult or even impossible to measure without inferring it based on other criteria, such as IQ tests, clinical interviews, etc., and hence, to measure something called “IQ,” one must *indicate* it via other more observable variables. Consequently, these observed variables are often referred to as *indicators* for the reason that they *indicate* the unobserved variable.

With this distinction in mind, and again with a little critical thought, it does not take long to realize that all variables are, at least philosophically, *unobservable*, though some variables are less unobservable than others. As an example, consider height once more. Is height observable or unobservable? If we measure your height to be 70 inches, we have, psychometrically, not measured your *true* height. We have merely a *measurement* of your height as an *indicator* of what your 483true height might be. Height is thus an unobservable variable but one might argue it is much less unobservable than a variable such as IQ. Likewise, though one’s weight is regarded as observable, in the end, weight is also an unobservable construct for which the measurement of weight is but an attempt to “tap into” the construct. This is how, when we push these ideas and distinctions to their philosophical limits, we come to realize that all variables are essentially *unobservable*, but some less so than others. However, for the purpose of building and analyzing path and structural equation models, we will consider the less unobservable variables to be observable and have the capacity of being directly measured. Variables such as height, weight, distance, temperature, biometric pressure, and so on, we will consider to be observable and easily measured variables. Variables such as IQ, self-esteem, happiness, depression, self-actualization, and so on, we will consider to be unobservable or *latent* variables that must be indicated by more observable ones.

## 13.4 Path Analysis: Extending Regression and Previewing SEM

Thus far, we have discussed path analysis informally. We now present the model a bit more formally. Path analysis is essentially a structural equation model that features only observed variables without the *direct* inclusion of unobservable or latent variables. The path model does include residual or *error* variables, however, and these are, by their nature, *latent*. They are considered unobservable because we cannot literally *see* or easily measure what might be “inside” such residual variables, or know precisely what it is composed of, implying it must be indicated by more observable variables. This meets the definition of a latent variable. An equivalent interpretation of a path model is as an extension of the classic regression models surveyed earlier in the book.

[Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#f13.2) is a very simple example of a path model (adapted from [Denis, 2021a](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000087)) where IQ from one generation is hypothesized to predict IQ of the next.

![Figure 13.2 Basic path diagram featuring parental IQ predicting offspring IQ. Used with permission of John Wiley & Sons - Books, from Applied Univariate, Bivariate, and Multivariate Statistics by Daniel J. Denis, © 2021; permission conveyed through Copyright Clearance Center, Inc.Return to text.⏎](images/fig13.2.jpg)

*Figure 13.2* Basic path diagram featuring parental IQ predicting offspring IQ. Used with permission of John Wiley & Sons - Books, from Applied Univariate, Bivariate, and Multivariate Statistics by Daniel J. Denis, © 2021; permission conveyed through Copyright Clearance Center, Inc.[Return to text.⏎](#c13.xhtml#re_f13.2)

We see in [Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#f13.2) that parent IQ is a predictor of its offspring’s IQ, which is then a predictor of the next generation’s IQ. In the figure, d1 and d2 are *residual* or *error* variables and contain variance unexplained by the predictor preceding it. These typically will have path coefficients set to 1, while other parameters of the model (e.g., path coefficients along arrows) will need to be estimated.

Path models can be useful to researchers and scientists because they allow more complex hypotheses to be stated that are otherwise difficult or even impossible to operationalize and test in classic regression models. As emphasized already, however, they do not allow for concluding causality any more than the typical regression model. In the model of IQ transmission, it probably would not be wrong to conclude that parental IQ is at least a *partial cause* of IQ in offspring, but that causal statement is made as a result of heritable evidence of IQ transmission, not because we are using a path model. *The causal statement is supported by the variables used in the model, not the fact that we are using a path analysis*. This distinction is very important.484

### 13.4.1 Exogenous vs. Endogenous Variables

An *exogenous* variable is one emanating from outside of the system and has no arrows pointed toward it. In [Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#f13.2), parental IQ is one such exogenous variable. An *endogenous* variable has at least one arrow pointing toward it, such as offspring IQ in the path diagram. [Figure 13.3](#c13.xhtml#f13.3) is another example of a path model, this one featuring hypothesized relationships between parental intelligence, environment, and child’s IQ. The only endogenous variable in this model is that of child’s IQ, as both parental intelligence and environment are exogenous.

![Figure 13.3 Example of a path model, featuring child’s IQ as a function of parental intelligence and environment.Return to text.⏎](images/fig13.3.jpg)

*Figure 13.3* Example of a path model, featuring child’s IQ as a function of parental intelligence and environment.[Return to text.⏎](#c13.xhtml#re_f13.3)

In the diagram are correlations (*r* = 0.6036, *r* = 0.4771*, r* = 0.7653), however the theorized relationships include parental intelligence and environment *predicting* child’s IQ. The two-sided arrow between parental intelligence and environment is what is generally referred to as an *unanalyzed* relationship, which simply means only the correlation is being modeled and not the estimation of a directional path of one variable onto another. The path from parental intelligence (*a*), for instance, is regarded as an *analyzed* relationship because it is not two-sided but instead hypothesizes a directional relationship, that of parental intelligence predicting child’s IQ.

## 13.5 Confirmatory Factor Analysis Model

Having briefly surveyed the path analysis model, we now provide an overview of the confirmatory factor analysis model. Recall once more that the common factor analysis model of the previous chapter was an *exploratory* one, meaning that the user typically entered a number of variables into the model without presumably any hypothesis as to how many factors might be present in the data or what the nature of those factors may be. On a technical level, this translates to there being fewer constraints imposed on the model and any that were included were implicit and part of the model’s “default” parameterization. The user did not typically fix, free, or constrain any parameters at will. Of course, a user with some computational experience could alter the exploratory model and re-parametrize it, but the point we are making is that classic factor analysis is generally not amenable to such *precise* model specification. It is an “out-of-the-box” model and we simply run it on data to see what comes out.

In contrast to the exploratory model, the confirmatory factor analysis model is one in which the user typically has, *a priori*, a theory as to how many factors may result from the analysis and which observed variables should load onto which factors. That is, the researcher comes to the model with a *theory* already in mind and is ready to specify the model in great detail in terms of what parameters get estimated, which do not, and other aspects of the model. In this way, the user has much more freedom in modeling because she can essentially fix and free parameters in line with the theory she wishes to evaluate. *Confirmatory factor analysis yields all the power and freedom of modeling to the user*. Of course, one can fix and free parameters in other statistical models as 485well and hence, this idea is not unique to CFA models or the wider structural equation modeling framework that generalizes them. For example, in analysis of variance (ANOVA), not testing an interaction term is essentially fixing that parameter estimate to 0, just as not modeling a quadratic term in polynomial regression is implicitly fixing that parameter estimate to 0. Statistical modelers are *implicitly* fixing parameters every day, even if they are only running a simple *t*\-test! In an SEM model, however, the fixing and freeing of parameters is a prerequisite to even running the model and allows greater specification of the user’s theory.

A simple one-factor confirmatory factor analysis model has the same model equation as we saw in the previous chapter for exploratory factor analysis:

  
*x* = *Λ**f* + *ε*  
(13.1)

where as before, *x* are observed variables, *f* are latent factors, *Λ* is a loading matrix, and *ε* is a matrix of errors. The number of factors in *f* is prespecified by the researcher. The following is a model with a two-factor structure hypothesizing factors *f*[1] and *f*[2]:

$\\begin{array}{l} {\\,\\,\\,\\text{x}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\text{=}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\Lambda\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\text{f}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\text{+}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\varepsilon} \\\\ {\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} x\_{1} \\\\ x\_{2} \\\\ x\_{3} \\\\ x\_{4} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{ll} \\lambda\_{11} & 0 \\\\ \\lambda\_{21} & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\lambda\_{32} \\\\ 0 & \\lambda\_{42} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} f\_{1} \\\\ f\_{2} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack + \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} \\varepsilon\_{1} \\\\ \\varepsilon\_{2} \\\\ \\varepsilon\_{3} \\\\ \\varepsilon\_{4} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack} \\\\ \\end{array}$

which yields the following equations:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {x\_{1} = \\lambda\_{11}f\_{1} + 0f\_{2} + \\varepsilon\_{1}} \\\\ {x\_{2} = \\lambda\_{21}f\_{1} + 0f\_{2} + \\varepsilon\_{2}} \\\\ {x\_{3} = 0f\_{1} + \\lambda\_{32}f\_{2} + \\varepsilon\_{3}} \\\\ {x\_{4} = 0f\_{1} + \\lambda\_{42}f\_{2} + \\varepsilon\_{4}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

Note that only *x*[1] and *x*[2] are hypothesized to “load” on *f*[1] as reflected by the loading matrix *Λ* constraining the loading estimates for *x*[3] and *x*[4] to 0. The key distinction in the confirmatory model in comparison to the exploratory model of the previous chapter is in precisely specifying the nature of the factor matrix, *f*, and hence attempting to “confirm” a very *specific* hypothesized factor structure through the precise specification of parameters.

## 13.6 Structural Equation Models

Having briefly surveyed path analysis and confirmatory factor analysis, we are now ready to survey the full structural equation model. The full structural equation model is given by

  
*η* = *B**η* + *Γ**ξ* + *ζ*  
(13.2)

where *η* is a latent endogenous vector, which we note appears on both sides of the equation. Contrary to classic linear models in which a variable only appears on one side of the equation, in the SEM model, *η* are allowed to predict one another, which is why we see it both on the left side and right side of the model (in *B**η*). This parameterization allows a latent variable to predict another latent variable in an SEM model. The exogenous variables are in the vector *ξ*, weighted by 486coefficients in *Γ*, and *ζ* is a vector of latent errors, also known as *disturbances* in the SEM literature. All parameter estimates for the model are contained in matrices *B* and *Γ*.

Assumptions for the model in (13.2) include *E*(*η*) = 0, *E*(*ξ*) = 0, and *E*(*ζ*) = 0, as well as latent errors being uncorrelated with latent exogenous variables. For further details on this classic SEM parameterization, see [Bollen (1989)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000037).

### 13.6.1 Covariance Modeling

Recall that in prior methods surveyed in this book, the goal was essentially to reproduce some function of the data. In regression, we sought to reproduce the response *y* by estimating predicted values, *ŷ*. In SEM and covariance models in general, the goal is also to reproduce some function of the data, but this time, it is the *observed covariance matrix* that we will attempt to reproduce by choosing which parameters to estimate and which to keep fixed. This is not that different from the factor analysis model in which the end goal, mathematically, was to regenerate the covariance or correlation matrix via specification of the model; *the “better” the model, the more precisely we should be able to reproduce the covariance or correlation matrix*.

Covariance modeling comprises an enormous class of models. [Bollen (1989)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000037) has shown that from the following simple equality, a whole host of models can be deduced as special cases,

  
*Σ* = *Σ*(*θ*)  
(13.3)

where the above reads that *Σ* (the covariance matrix) is a function of model parameters contained in the vector *θ*. That is, *Σ*(*θ*) is the *implied model-based covariance matrix* that regenerates the observed covariance matrix, *Σ*. Choosing which parameters to *fix* and which to *free*, along with other model specification considerations, will determine how well the model fits the data. Note once more that this is exactly the same thing we do in other models from regression to ANOVA and beyond; the only difference is that such specifications in those models, at least the finer ones, are often not made as *explicit*. The equality in (13.3) is far-reaching, and special cases of it at their most fundamental level simply require decisions made by the user in conjunction with the types of variables and data they are working with in any given context. As Bollen ([1989](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000037), p. 2) summarizes:

> The simplicity of this equation \[i.e., *Σ* = *Σ*(*θ*)\] is only surpassed by its generality. It provides a unified way of including many of the most widely used statistical techniques in the social sciences. Regression analysis, simultaneous equation systems, confirmatory factor analysis, canonical correlations, panel data analysis, ANOVA, analysis of covariance, and multiple linear indicator models are special cases of *Σ* = *Σ*(*θ*).

The value of *Σ* is unknown, and hence we estimate *Σ* via *S*, the sample covariance matrix. We desire the distance between *S* and *S*(*θ*) to be as small as possible, that is, to be *minimized*, where *S*(*θ*) is the sample covariance matrix *implied* by the estimated model parameters. *Discrepancy functions* are a wide class of functions from which can be selected a specific function to minimize distance between *S* and *S*(*θ*). One such discrepancy function is that of the familiar *ordinary least-squares* that minimizes the distance between observed and fitted values of *y*. Other types of models feature the minimizing or maximizing of other discrepancy functions. In covariance modeling using maximum likelihood (ML), for instance, we wish to minimize the following fitting function *F*[*M**L*] ([Bollen, 1989](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000037), p. 107):487

  
*F*[*M**L*]\=log|∑*θ*|+tr(*S*∑^( − 1)(*θ*))−log|*S*|−(*p*+*q*)  
(13.4)

When *S* = *S*(*θ*), *F*[*M**L*] = 0. That is, as (*S*−*S*(*θ*))→0, *F*[*M**L*]→0, and perfect model fit is achieved, since the difference between the sample covariance matrix *S* and that implied by the model, *S*(*θ*), is equal to 0. It turns out that (*n*−1)*F*[*M**L*] ∼ *χ*² (where *n* is sample size), which can be used for evaluating the following global null hypothesis,

  
*H*[0]:∑=∑(*θ*)  
(13.5)

where the above null hypothesis *H*[0] reads that the population covariance matrix *Σ* is equal to that population covariance matrix implied by the specified parameters, that is, ∑(*θ*). The above null is evaluated against the alternative hypothesis *H*[1],

  
*H*[1]:∑≠∑(*θ*)  
(13.6)

which reads that the population covariance matrix *Σ* is unequal to that implied by the model parameters in *θ*. Equivalently, under the null hypothesis, ∑−∑(*θ*) = 0, and hence if the model fits *perfectly*, the expectation for *χ*² is 0. The extent to which the model does not fit is the extent to which ∑−∑(*θ*) ≠ 0. If you look at the null hypothesis closely, you will see that contrary to traditional null hypothesis testing in which we wish to reject the null, in SEM, we wish to actually *not* reject the null hypothesis. That is, *a null that is supported by the data is a favorable outcome in SEM*, which goes against how traditional null hypothesis testing is classically interpreted. This fact is important, since if you reject the null in SEM, it suggests your estimated model is *not* consistent with the covariance matrix, meaning that it does not reproduce it well, which further implies the fit between the covariance matrix based on the data is not in line with the covariance matrix implied by the model.

### 13.6.2 Evaluating Model Fit

As with most supervised learning models, we desire a measure to assess or evaluate how well the model fits the empirical data. In ordinary least-squares, that measure of model fit is typically *R*², *R*[*a**d**j*]² or some other model selection measures such as *AIC* or *BIC*. In SEM, we also require measures of model fit to assess the extent to which our designated model parameters reproduce *S*, the sample covariance matrix. As in regression and other models, there are numerous ways of assessing fit in structural equation models. Measures of model fit in SEM are typically divided into two broad categories, those assessing *overall* or *absolute* model fit, and those evaluating *incremental fit*, sometimes called *relative fit* measures. Overall measures of model fit assess the model in its entirety without reference to a competing model, whereas incremental or relative measures of fit evaluate a model relative to some reference or competing model, usually a null or baseline model, to evaluate how well the hypothesized model performs relative to the baseline model.

Why not just use *χ*² as a measure of model fit? Recall that (*n*−1)*F*[*M**L*] ∼ *χ*² and the expectation for *χ*² under *H*[0] is equal to 0 under a perfectly fitting model. Hence, it might at first glance seem reasonable to simply use *χ*² as a measure of model fit such that the extent to which *χ*²→0 is the extent to which the model is increasingly well-fitting and the extent to which *χ*² > 0 is the extent to which the model fits poorly. That is, the extent to which *χ*² is statistically significant might be taken as a measure of increasingly poor model fit. While this approach at first glance sounds reasonable, it is very problematic, and overall, *χ*² alone makes for a poor measure of model fit in 488SEM. Recall that as *n* increases, achieving *p* < .05 (or some other arbitrary significance level) for *χ*² is assured other than under the restriction that *χ*² = 0. So long as *χ*² > 0 is true, and it most often will be, statistical significance of *χ*² and more importantly, lack thereof, should not be in any real way interpreted as a measure of “effect,” especially for increasing *n*.

Of course, this idea is not new and was discussed earlier in the book; *p-values are not effect sizes*. That is not to say a user should not utilize *χ*² as an initial assessment of fit, only that *χ*² alone will usually not tell the user what they really want to know, which is a measure of effect that is *independent* of the influence of sample size. In the measures that follow, both overall measures and incremental fit indices are measures of effect size (or of “fit” more generally) that are not influenced by the magnitude of *n* in the way that *χ*² is to a large extent a function of sample size.

### 13.6.3 Overall (Absolute) Measures

Some of the more common measures of overall fit include *root mean square residual* (RMR), its standardized counterpart, the *standardized root mean square residual* (SRMR), and the *root mean square of approximation* (RMSEA). We now briefly survey each of these.

The *root mean square residual* (RMR) is given by

  
$${RMR} = \\left\\lbrack {2{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{q}{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{i}\\frac{\\left( s\_{ij} - s\_{{}\_{ij}}^{'} \\right)^{2}}{q\\left( q + 1 \\right)}}}} \\right\\rbrack^{1/2}$$  
(13.7)

where *s*[*i**j*] is an element of the observed covariance matrix *S*, *s*[*i**j*]^′ is an element of the model-implied covariance matrix *S*(*θ*), and *q* is the number of observed variables in the model. Essentially, RMR assesses the extent to which elements of the observed covariance matrix differ from those of the implied by taking their (squared) difference, (*s*[*i**j*]−*s*[*i**j*]^′)². The extent to which that difference is larger than not is the extent to which RMR will also be large, which would be increasingly indicative of a poorly fitting model. The best-fitting model would have *s*[*i**j*] − *s*[*i**j*]^′ = 0, which would then imply an RMR of 0. Note that all else in the formulation are simply constants, as well as squaring and taking the square root. That is, the most meaningful part of the formula is contained in (*s*[*i**j*]−*s*[*i**j*]^′).

One drawback of RMR is that *s*[*i**j*] is computed on *raw scores*, and hence analogous to how the size of a covariance can be misleading due to the extent of variance in one or both variables, RMR can likewise be small or large, not solely due to the extent of effect present, but instead due to magnitudes of variance in the variables. Solving the scale issue with RMR is the *standardized root mean square residual* (SRMR) which first standardizes residuals *s*[*i**j*] − *s*[*i**j*]^′ via the product of standard deviations, *s*[*i*]*s*[*j*],

  
(*s*[*i**j*]−*s*[*i**j*]^′)/*s*[*i*]*s*[*j*]  

yielding

  
$${SRMR} = \\left\\lbrack {2{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{q}{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{i}\\frac{\\left\\lbrack \\left( s\_{ij} - s\_{ij}^{'} \\right)/s\_{i}s\_{j} \\right\\rbrack^{2}}{q\\left( q + 1 \\right)}}}} \\right\\rbrack^{1/2}$$  
(13.8)

where now the only functional part of the formula continues to be in the numerator, only that now the deviations (*s*[*i**j*]−*s*[*i**j*]^′) have been standardized. As a result of RMR and SRMR being an analysis of residuals from the model, smaller values than not are indicative of better-fitting models. Values 489of 0.08 or less usually indicate reasonable to increasingly good fit for SRMR, though of course any model fit measure computed on data is often only as good as what competing research has found in the given area of investigation. As was true for effect sizes in simpler regression and ANOVA models for instance, effects should always be evaluated relative to other findings in the area under investigation. If you achieve a value for SRMR of 0.05 but all of your colleagues in the same area of investigation are achieving SRMR values of 0.0001 with their models, no criteria or “guidelines” can save you from concluding that your model may not be worth keeping.

The root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) is given by

  
$$\\text{RMSEA} = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n - 1}\\left( \\frac{\\chi\_{m}^{2} - df\_{m}}{df\_{m}} \\right)}$$  
(13.9)

Recall that (*n*−1)*F*[*M**L*] ∼ *χ*² and thus the statistical significance of an SEM model is based on *χ*², where now *χ*[*m*]² is the chi-square resulting from the model. Recall also that smaller than not values for *χ*[*m*]², all else equal, are indicative of an increasingly well-fitting model. Whenever a parameter is estimated, it “costs” a degree of freedom. Ideally, we would wish to achieve a superb model fit without spending too many degrees of freedom. “Spending” a lot of degrees of freedom and estimating everything in the model is suggestive of a poor theory guiding the SEM (and will likely lead to identifiability issues for the model as well, though a discussion of identifiability is beyond the scope of the current text). Estimating everything under the sun, as we know by now, is also an exercise in *overfitting*.

With the above in mind, we can now see how RMSEA works; as the distance *χ*[*m*]² − *d**f*[*m*] gets larger relative to the value of *d**f*[*m*], RMSEA grows in magnitude. The only way this happens is if *χ*[*m*]² is larger than not, which recall, would be suggestive of an increasingly poor fit. A better fit is indicated by increasingly smaller values of *χ*[*m*]². Note as well that the fraction 1/(*n*−1) is inconsequential here and is not the *functional* part of the formulation, it simply serves to “average” the ratio (*χ*[*m*]²−*d**f*[*m*])/*d**f*[*m*]. Values for RMSEA in the approximate range of 0.01, 0.05, 0.08 are generally indicative of excellent, good, and relatively poor fitting models. However, once more, context matters and one should never rely *absolutely* on *relative* guidelines in any field, including statistics.

### 13.6.4 Incremental Fit Indices

We now briefly survey a few of the more common measures of incremental fit. These measures, recall, evaluate model fit not in absolute or global terms, but instead relative to some baseline or null model.

The *normed-fit index* (NFI) is given by,

  
$$\\Delta\_{1} = \\frac{\\chi\_{b}^{2} - \\chi\_{m}^{2}}{\\chi\_{b}^{2}} = \\frac{F\_{b} - F\_{m}}{F\_{b}}$$  
(13.10)

where *χ*[*b*]² is the baseline model and *χ*[*m*]² is the hypothesized model. Since *χ*² ∼ (*n*−1)*F*[*M**L*], *F*[*b*] − *F*[*m*] is the difference between the corresponding fitting functions, *F*[*b*] for the baseline model and *F*[*m*] for the model under test. The baseline model has more restrictions (i.e., on parameter estimates) than the fitted model, and so the difference *F*[*b*] − *F*[*m*] is a reflection of how much the fitting function *decreases* due to the proposed model. The better fitting the proposed model, the smaller is the value of *F*[*m*] and the difference *F*[*b*] − *F*[*m*] increasingly approximates simply *F*[*b*]. Recall that smaller 490values than not for *F*[*m*] are indicative of an increasingly better model fit. Ideally, if the model fit perfectly, then *F*[*m*] would equal 0, and thus *Δ*[1] would equal 1, as easily demonstrated,

  
$$\\Delta\_{1} = \\frac{\\chi\_{b}^{2} - \\chi\_{m}^{2}}{\\chi\_{b}^{2}} = \\frac{F\_{b} - F\_{m}}{F\_{b}} = \\frac{F\_{b} - 0}{F\_{b}} = \\frac{F\_{b}}{F\_{b}} = 1$$  

On the opposite end of things, if there is no model improvement, then *F*[*b*] = *F*[*m*] and so

  
$$\\Delta\_{1} = \\frac{\\chi\_{b}^{2} - \\chi\_{m}^{2}}{\\chi\_{b}^{2}} = \\frac{F\_{b} - F\_{m}}{F\_{b}} = \\frac{0}{F\_{b}} = 0$$  

Values of 0.95 and greater are typically indicative of well-fitting models, not in absolute terms, but relative to a baseline model, which is usually the null model but need not necessarily be so.

A measure of model fit related to *Δ*[1] is that of Bollen’s *ρ*[1] ([Bollen, 1989](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000037)), which is essentially the same as the NFI, but with one important difference in that it scales *Δ*[1] relative to degrees of freedom:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {\\rho\_{1} = \\frac{\\left( F\_{b}/df\_{b} \\right) - \\left( F\_{m}/df\_{m} \\right)}{\\left( F\_{b}/df\_{b} \\right)}} \\\\ {\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\, = \\frac{\\left( \\chi\_{b}^{2}/df\_{b} \\right) - \\left( \\chi\_{m}^{2}/df\_{m} \\right)}{\\left( \\chi\_{b}^{2}/df\_{b} \\right)}} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  
(13.11)

Under the most ideal of situations assuming perfect fit, *F*[*m*] = 0 and thus *F*[*m*]/*d**f*[*m*] will also equal 0 regardless of *d**f*[*m*]. Under the condition that *F*[*m*] > 0, which will most often be the case, *F*[*m*] is essentially *penalized* by how many degrees of freedom *d**f*[*m*] it required to reduce *F*[*b*] to *F*[*m*]. *Strong theories require spending less degrees of freedom to achieve increasingly smaller* *F*[*m*] *that do weaker theories*. We can see then that *ρ*[1] rewards the fitting of models that “spend” a smaller number of degrees of freedom, all else equal, to achieve the same reduction from *F*[*b*] to *F*[*m*]. That is, *ρ*[1] rewards models that are *parsimonious* and result from a well-specified theory such that the researcher clearly had a good framework for what parameters to estimate to result in maximal decrease in *F*[*m*]. Such will be reflected in a ratio *F*[*m*]/*d**f*[*m*] smaller than not, which means less and less is being subtracted from the baseline ratio *F*[*b*]/*d**f*[*b*]. As (*F*[*m*]/*d**f*[*m*])→0, *ρ*[1]→1.0 indicating perfect fit. Values for *ρ*[1] generally in the neighborhood of 0.95 or greater are usually regarded as indicating good to excellent fit.

The *Tucker-Lewis index* (NNFI) is given by

  
$$\\rho\_{2} = \\frac{\\left( \\chi\_{b}^{2}/df\_{b} \\right) - \\left( \\chi\_{m}^{2}/df\_{m} \\right)}{\\left( \\chi\_{b}^{2}/df\_{b} \\right) - 1}$$  
(13.12)

A comparison of *ρ*[1] to *ρ*[2] reveals that (*χ*[*b*]²/*d**f*[*b*]) − (*χ*[*m*]²/*d**f*[*m*]) is no longer being compared to (*χ*[*b*]²/*d**f*[*b*]) but instead to (*χ*[*b*]²/*d**f*[*b*]) − 1. Values of 0.95 and greater are suggestive of increasingly good model fit.

Lastly, the *comparative fit index* (CFI) is given by491

  
$$\\text{CFI} = 1 - \\frac{\\max\\left( \\chi\_{m}^{2} - df\_{m},0 \\right)}{\\max\\left( \\chi\_{b}^{2} - df\_{b},\\chi\_{m}^{2} - df\_{m},0 \\right)}$$  
(13.13)

The CFI follows a similar logic to that of *ρ*[1], but instead of taking ratios as for *ρ*[1], we are subtracting *d**f*from *χ*², that is, *χ*[]² − *d**f*for both baseline and model *χ*². CFI values in the range of 0.90 to 0.95 indicate good fit.

The aforementioned measures of model fit, whether absolute or relative, are just a very small sample of model fit measures available in SEM. Specialists in SEM continue to publish new measures it seems almost yearly, all of which offer different ways to assess and evaluate model fit. An understanding of these most common ones, however, opens the door to understanding many variations and gets the proverbial “foot in the door” to the vast area of model fit statistics in SEM.

## 13.7 Structural Equation Modeling with Nonlinear Effects

Most structural equation models, as we have seen thus far with so many models in statistics and machine learning, assume *linearity in the parameters*. They are a complex network of otherwise *linear models*. As we know by now, assuming linearity can provide relatively good generalizability of findings and hence relatively low variance. However, if the true relationship underlying the data is *nonlinear*, then assuming linearity can seriously bias the model as well as bias parameter estimates generated based on such a restrictive assumption. Indeed, entire trends or features in the data can be missed if attempting to fit more complex models is not attempted ([Kelava & Brandt, 2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000184)).

For example, a linear SEM model may fail to detect a quadratic effect entirely, which may otherwise prove to be very important to the investigator on a scientific level. And since structural equation models can increase in complexity very quickly, exploratory visualization of such models is much more difficult or even impossible compared to visualizing much simpler models, for example a scatterplot where one might immediately detect nonlinearity simply by observing the trend in the corresponding plot. Visualization of multivariate data, especially in complex models such as SEM or neural networks as we will see later in the book, can prove daunting to say the least. This implies that detecting nonlinearity in such data can be equally challenging.

When structural relationships are, in fact, nonlinear, but nonetheless fit using a linear model, many issues arise, the most serious of which is that latent endogenous variables can no longer be assumed to be normally distributed as they are assumed so in linear SEM models ([Klein & Muthén, 2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000188)). This implies that parameter estimates cannot be determined based solely on the covariance structure of the data ([Vegelius & Jin, 2021](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000374)). A failure to include nonlinear effects in a structural equation model when such effects are present, as mentioned, can result in biased estimators (Rdz-Navarro & Yang-Wallentin, [2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000294)).

There has been much work in the development and estimation of nonlinear structural equation models. [Klein and Muthén (2007)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000188) developed a nonlinear structural equation model using a *quasi-maximum-likelihood* approach for estimation, which when evaluated in simulation studies produced robust standard errors and was relatively computationally inexpensive. [Bollen (1996)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000038) proposed a two-stage least-squares approach (2SLS), and more recently Holst and Budtz-Jorgensen ([2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000156)) have also proposed a two-stage least-squares estimation method. An efficient maximum-likelihood *latent moderated structural equations* approach has also recently been advanced ([Klein & Moosbrugger, 2000](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000189); [Umbach et al., 2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000367)).

### 13.7.1 Example of a Nonlinear SEM

The following is an example of a nonlinear SEM model, one without an intercept but featuring an interaction term,492

  
*η* = *γ*[1]*ξ*[1] + *γ*[2]*ξ*[2] + *ω*[12]*ξ*[1]*ξ*[2] + *ζ*  
(13.14)

where the interaction term is given by *ω*[12]*ξ*[1]*ξ*[2], and hence *η* is said to be a nonlinear function of *ξ*[1] and *ξ*[2], which implies *η* has an expectation that will be *non-Gaussian*. One way to deal with this nonlinearity historically has been to treat the product term *ξ*[1]*ξ*[2] as a separate latent variable and construct so-called “indicators” based on products of original indicators ([Vegelius, 2022](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000375)). That is, the new variable becomes *ξ*[3] = *ξ*[1]*ξ*[2] (e.g., see [Kenny & Judd, 1984](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000185)). The inclusion of product terms, however, can lead to relatively smaller communalities as well as larger sampling fluctuation and multicollinearity in addition to the aforementioned nonnormal error terms ([Klein & Muthén, 2007](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000188)).

An example of a more complex model, one that not only includes an interaction term but also quadratic terms, is the following ([Kelava & Brandt, 2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000184)):

  
*η* = *α* + *γ*[1]*ξ*[1] + *γ*[2]*ξ*[2] + *γ*[3]*ξ*[1]*ξ*[2] + *γ*[4]*ξ*[1]² + *γ*[5]*ξ*[2]² + *ζ*  
(13.15)

where now the quadratic terms are given by *γ*[4]*ξ*[1]² and *γ*[5]*ξ*[2]² in addition to the aforementioned interaction term, *ξ*[1]*ξ*[2]. Due to the fact that interaction terms and quadratic terms are often correlated, [Klein and Muthén (2007)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000188) proposed including quadratic effects to rule out spurious interaction effects, which gave rise to the more general nonlinear SEM model,

  
*η* = *α* + *Τ**ξ* + *ξ*′*Ω**ξ* + *ζ*  
(13.16)

in which the quadratic term is now indicated by *ξ*′*Ω**ξ* and where the corresponding measurement equations for the latent variables are the following:

  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {x = \\tau\_{x} + \\Lambda\_{x}\\xi + \\delta} \\\\ {y = \\tau\_{y} + \\Lambda\_{y}\\eta + \\varepsilon} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

The model assumes that *x* is multivariate normal, *δ* and *ε* are multivariate normal and mutually independent where *E*(*δ*) = 0 and *E*(*ε*) = 0. The covariance assumptions include *C**o**v*(*δ*,*ξ*′) = 0 and *C**o**v*(*ε*,*ξ*′) = 0, *C**o**v*(*ζ*,*ξ*′) = 0, *C**o**v*(*ζ*,*δ*′) = 0, and *C**o**v*(*ζ*,*ε*′) = 0. For further details on the specification of this model, see [Klein and Moosbrugger (2000)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000189).

Nonlinear models in SEM can be fit using the package *nlsem* ([Umbach et al.](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000367), 2017). Consult Umbach et al. ([2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000122)) for an introduction and details about the package.

### 13.7.2 Structural Equation Nonparametric and Semiparametric Mixture Models

We have thus far surveyed the general nonlinear SEM model featuring parametric approaches to its estimation. An alternative and promising approach to estimating nonlinear SEM models is that of using a *semiparametric* approach (SEMM), first proposed by [Bauer (2005)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000025) featuring mixture modeling. The central idea behind mixture modeling in this context is to represent what is a nonnormal distribution as a combination of typically normal densities ([Kelava et al., 2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000184)). The density of the nonnormal distribution is then computed as a weighted sum of the (typically) normal densities. We say “typical” because the SEMM allows for flexible approximations of nonnormal distributions ([Umbach et al., 2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000367)). The nonparametric component of these models, as is true of other nonparametric models studied in this book, better allows the data to “speak for themselves” 493as it were rather than have an *a priori* functional form imposed on them such as the classic linearity or similar assumption about parametric form.

A mixture density of American adults (males vs. females) is a classic example of a mixture density where each distribution contributes to the mix. Essentially, and most generally, a mixture density is a type of combination, or crudely, an *average* of other normal or nonnormal densities. In traditional non-mixture maximum-likelihood SEM, multivariate normality is typically assumed for the indicators *x*, *y* of the model, where each of *x*, *y* are vectors corresponding to a number of observed or “manifest” indicator variables. That is,

  
*f*(*x*,*y*) = *N*(*μ*,∑)  

where *μ* and ∑ are the implied mean and covariance structures. The mixture model can be considered as a simple extension of the above,

  
$$f\\left( {x,y} \\right) = {\\sum\\limits\_{g = 1}^{G}w\_{g}}N\\left( \\mu\_{g},\\sum\_{g} \\right)$$  
(13.17)

where *g* = 1 through *G* are now the number of mixture components, *w*[*g*] are mixture probabilities and where each component is distributed multivariate normal, *N*(*μ*[*g*],∑[*g*]). The sum of *w*[*g*] must equal one to ensure it is a proper density. Each of the *g* = 1 through *G* mixture components will then have their own individual SEM model ([Kelava et al., 2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000184), p. 471),

  
*η*[*g*] = *B*[*g*]*η*[*g*] + *α*[*g*] + *Γ*[*g*]*ξ*[*g*] + *ζ*[*g*]  

where we now note the subscript *g* to denote the given model under consideration (e.g., *g* = 1 would be the first model, and so on). Most often, at least some of the parameters across the mixture models are constrained to be equal so that identification of the model is possible (Kelava et al., [2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000184)). However, the model is still yet linear in the parameters. To make it a *semiparametric nonlinear model*, which of course is our ultimate goal here, the model becomes

  
*η*[*g*] = *B*[*g*]*η*[*g*] + *α*[*g*] + *Γ*[1*g*]*ξ*[*g*] + *Γ*[2*g*]*h*(*ξ*[*g*]) + *ζ*[*g*]  
(13.18)

where the nonlinear terms are included in *Γ*[2*g*]*h*(*ξ*[*g*]) and for generality, their exact nature is not specified specifically in this formulation. That is, *h*(*ξ*[*g*]) could include product terms, quadratic terms, and so on, which implies the model has become nonlinear in *h*(*ξ*[*g*]). For further details on this model, see [Kelava et al. (2014)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000184), which is an exceptionally clear and well-written summary of mixture models and nonlinearity in SEM.

Other mixture models are seen operating where finite mixtures of linear SEMs are used to approximate unknown nonlinear relationships of the latent variables ([Umbach et al., 2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000367)). Since the semiparametric approach does not *a priori* designate the *type* of functional relationship between latent variables, curvilinear relationships can be modeled between latent variables ([Umbach et al., 2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000367)). Song et al. ([2014](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000343)) propose nonparametric estimation of multiview latent variable models as special cases of Bayesian networks. In R, the aforementioned package *nlsem* can also be used to fit semiparametric SEM models. Once more, consult Umbach et al. ([2017](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000367)) for details.

SEM models can also accommodate longitudinal data. Such models usually go by the name of *latent curve modeling*, *latent growth curves*, and *latent trajectory modeling*, among others. See [Bollen and Curran (2006)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000039) for details. [Liu (2023)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000227) provides a comprehensive review of longitudinal 494models in SEM as well as R packages for fitting them. [Liao et al. (2020)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000220) propose a *generalized structural equation model* that incorporates neural networks in their estimation. [Sol and Baras (2022)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000342) combine a neural network approach with structural equation modeling in modeling activity trackers.

## 13.8 Caveats Regarding SEM Models

In concluding our discussion of structural equation models, we feel it relevant to clarify a few items of confusion that often arise for those trying to understand these models for the first time.

The first is that SEM models are often marketed as accounting for *measurement error*, presumably because they include unique *error terms* for variables as well as more than a single indicator of a construct, such as is typically the case in simpler models. Including error terms and more indicators than not usually lowers the error with which a construct is measured (or *indicated*). However, if one uses poor indicators, minimizing measurement error is not the chief concern; *the priority instead will be to choose better indicators*. That is, accounting for and minimizing measurement error is only as relevant as the quality of indicators used in reducing said measurement error. For example, measuring heart rate with a stethoscope has relatively little measurement error. Including a second indicator of heart rate or level of cholesterol would not reduce measurement error, but would instead simply make for a relatively poorly defined or indicated latent variable. That is, measurement error can be reduced in SEM but only if indicators are chosen carefully and wisely. *Structural equation models do not unconditionally reduce measurement error. They simply account for it better than many classical statistical models.*

A second caveat is regarding the aforementioned issue of causality. *SEM models have nothing, by themselves, to do with causality*! If the *context* of the model is reasonable, then one *may* be able to infer causality, but by themselves, SEM models are not any more causal than any other statistical or mathematical model or abstract mathematical system. The fact that SEM models often go by the name of *causal models* is not due to their ability to impart or impose causality via their structural relations or parameter estimates. They are named causal models largely for historical reasons and also because researchers often use them on data networks they *believe*, *a priori*, represent *causal processes*. However, the causality assumption arises from the nature of the *science*, not the *statistical method*. For Wright’s pioneering work on path analysis, assuming a causal process in the generational transmission of color in the guinea pig made good sense because it had a scientific biological “organic” basis. *Causality is primarily a design and scientific issue, not a statistical one*.

A third caveat is regarding *context*. As we have discussed throughout this book, all models are *context-dependent*, which means that any relations we observe in a model depend on other variables included or not included in the model. Since perfect specification of a model is rarely if ever possible, virtually all SEM models constructed will be incomplete and hence all parameter estimates will be to some extent, *biased*. All modeling (not just SEM) is but an *approximation* to reality. It could very well be that including an extra few variables in the model results in a vastly different model, so it is essential that when planning an SEM model, or any other model for that matter, the researcher ensures that all instrumental variables are included in the model as to minimize the extent to which it is misspecified.495

## 13.9 SEM Models in R

As mentioned in our discussion earlier, the package *nlsem* ([Umbach](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000367) et al., 2017) in R fits nonlinear structural equation models as well as mixture models. It will also fit special cases of these models which are traditional linear SEM models.

The package *modsem* ([Slupphaug, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000339)) can be used in conjunction with the *lavaan* package ([Rosseel](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000311), 2012) for testing interactions between latent variables. As an example from the package’s documentation, we briefly consider the following three latent variables where we wish to test the corresponding latent interaction term (XZ).

```
> library(modsem)
> m1 <- ‘
+ X =~ x1 + x2 + x3
+ Y =~ y1 + y2 + y3
+ Z =~ z1 + z2 + z3
+ Y ~ X + Z + X:Z’
```

Above we have created the three latent variables, where X is indicated by x1, x2, and x3, Y by y1, y2, and y3, and Z by z1, z2, and z3 ([Slupphaug, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000339)). Below we fit the model and request a summary:

```
> est1 <- modsem(m1, oneInt)
> summary(est1)
```
