$$P\_{n}\\left( x \\right) = f\\left( x\_{0} \\right) + f'\\left( x\_{0} \\right)\\left( x - x\_{0} \\right) + \\frac{f''\\left( x\_{0} \\right)}{2!}\\left( x - x\_{0} \\right)^{2} + \\cdot \\cdot \\cdot + \\frac{f^{(n)}\\left( x\_{0} \\right)}{n!}\\left( x - x\_{0} \\right)^{n}$$  
(15.16)

and for which (15.16) is called the *n*th Taylor polynomial for *f* at *x*[0]. The approximation for points *near* *x*[0] is given by *x* − *x*[0], and the approximation is rarely perfect, yielding a remainder term *f* − *P*[*n*] (i.e., the actual function minus the approximation). If we allow the degree *n* of the polynomial to go to infinity, that is, *n*→∞, then the Taylor polynomial becomes simply a *Taylor series*. That is, a Taylor series is simply a Taylor polynomial of infinite degree. Put differently, a Taylor series is the limiting sum of a Taylor polynomial as *n*→∞.

Though a bit more complicated and involved than the simple Taylor series featured here, the essential idea is analogous in neural networks. Approximating functions is what neural networks, in the end, actually *do*. Often these functions are unknown and must be “learned” from the data. This is, in part, the *nonparametric* element of neural networks.

## 15.12 Neural Networks and Projection Pursuit

There is often a link drawn in the literature between neural networks and a nonparametric technique called *projection pursuit* ([Friedman & Tukey, 1974](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000112); [Friedman & Stuetzle, 1981](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000111); [Kruskal, 1969](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000204)). Understanding the latter can provide a window into better understanding neural networks. As the name suggests, in projection pursuit we are “pursuing” the best means by which to make a projection. The primary qualification for the pursuit is that the projection be in some sense, *interesting*. The original conception of projection pursuit was formulated by Kruskal ([1969](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000204), [1972](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000205)).

More to the point, projection pursuit is the search in a potentially nonlinear structure of high-dimensional data lower-dimensional linear projections ([Posse, 1995](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000291)). It is considered nonparametric since nonparametric estimators (*smoothers*) are used in the estimation process. Many excellent examples of projection pursuit can be found in [Posse (1995)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000291). Projection pursuit is primarily a visualization technique with limited output as is traditional with methods such as principal components analysis ([Laa & Cook, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000210)).

Projection pursuit itself was first coined by [Friedman and Tukey (1974)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000112) in what is an exceptionally well-written paper “A Projection Pursuit Algorithm for Exploratory Data Analysis,” but as mentioned had its origins somewhat earlier with [Kruskal (1969)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000204). Friedman and Tukey introduced the method as an algorithm that seeks to find one- and two-dimensional linear projections of multivariate data that are relatively highly revealing:

> Mapping of multivariate data onto low-dimensional manifolds for visual inspection is a commonly used technique in data analysis. The discovery of mappings that reveal the salient features of the multidimensional point swarm is often far from trivial. Even when every adequate description of the data requires more variables than can be conveniently perceived (at one 556time) by humans, it is quite often still useful to map the data into a lower, humanly perceivable, dimensionality where the human gift for pattern recognition can be applied.
> 
> ([Friedman & Tukey, 1974](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000112), p. 1)

Interestingly, Friedman and Tukey chose not to treat nonlinear dimension reduction techniques stating that they are more difficult to interpret but also for their computational complexity, a problem that has since been overcome by the modern uprise in computing power. Projection pursuit uses a *projection index* as a quantity that needs to be optimized in the search for interesting projections. Hence, we see immediately that *principal components analysis can be regarded as a special case of projection pursuit where the index is that of maximizing variance of orthogonal linear combinations*.

Components analysis, as we have seen, is by far not the only way to project data. For instance, returning to a simpler example, one could project data via ordinary least-squares. Most of the indexes used in projection pursuit are built around detecting departures from known distributions, such as multivariate normality, or projections that are best able to distinguish between groups ([Laa & Cook, 2020](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000210)). As [Jolliffe (2002)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174) notes, most projection pursuit techniques begin by assuming that multivariate normality is the *least* interesting basis for a projection, and hence many indices in the projection essentially measure deviations from this “uneventful” status. Numerically, the actual index is a scalar computed in the *d*\-dimensional space and is maximized over all possible *d-*dimensional projections of a data set. A number of indexes are discussed in [Laa and Cook (2020)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000210). For a concise summary of projection pursuit, see Jolliffe ([2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000174), pp. 219–221).

### 15.12.1 Projection Pursuit Regression and Relation to Neural Networks

The model for *projection pursuit regression*, which can be considered a special case of the wider more general projection pursuit framework, can be stated as follows:

  
$$y\_{i} = \\beta\_{0} + {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{r}{f\_{j}\\left( \\beta\_{j}^{T}x\_{i} \\right) + \\varepsilon\_{i}}}$$  
(15.17)

where the model looks pretty much the same as we would expect from a typical linear regression model,

  
$$y\_{i} = \\beta\_{0} + {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{r}{\\left( \\beta\_{j}^{T}x\_{i} \\right) + \\varepsilon\_{i}}}$$  

However, note the key difference, the inclusion of *f*[*j*] in the projection pursuit of (15.17). For convenience, we will drop the error term *ε*[*i*] for now and simply focus on the systematic portion of the model. In projection pursuit, we can have numerous functions *m* through *M* and hence we account for these via summation,

  
$$\\left. y\_{i} = {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{M}{f\_{j}\\left( \\beta\_{j}^{T} \\right.}}x\_{i} \\right)$$  

and seek to minimize the following error function557

  
$${\\sum\\limits\_{i}^{N}\\left\\lbrack \\left. y\_{i} - {\\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}{f\_{j}\\left( \\beta\_{j}^{T} \\right.}}x\_{i} \\right) \\right\\rbrack}^{2}$$  
(15.18)

We can think of *β*[*j*]^(*T*) in projection pursuit as containing *directions* instead of merely scalars as we might typically think of such in ordinary regression ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)) though it definitely does not hurt to think of these weights as directions in classical regression as well. In projection pursuit, *f*[*j*](*β*[*j*]^(*T*)*x*[*i*]) is called a *ridge function*, with its direction determined by values in *β*[*j*]^(*T*). We note that essentially the only difference between this and the classic linear model is the inclusion of *f*[*j*], where these are a *collection* of unknown smoothing functions (i.e., “unknown” until they are “learned” from the data). That is, in *f*[*j*](*β*[*j*]^(*T*)*x*[*i*]) we are taking a function *f*[*j*] of another function *β*[*j*]^(*T*)*x*[*i*] and hence once more, we are taking a *composite function* just as we do in a neural network. The number of these smoothing functions we will take is a *flexible hyperparameter*. When that number is one the model is sometimes referred to as a *single index model* ([Hastie et al., 2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)). Cross-validation can be used to determine an optimal number of smoothing functions. Its value can also be determined based on how much each successive term improves the model in terms of visualization.

We can see that the projection pursuit model is entirely general. Indeed, as noted by [Hastie et al. (2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145), p. 390), “the operation of forming nonlinear functions of linear combinations generates a surprisingly large class of models.” The link to neural networks is rather obvious then, such that in neural networks we are taking, as we saw, *(typically) nonlinear functions of linear (or nonlinear) combinations*. In projection pursuit, we could do the same if we chose a linear function instead of smoothing functions. That is, with a bit of generality, projection pursuit can be conceptualized as a layered neural network where *f*[*j*] essentially becomes the activation function. Once we make *f*[*j*] a classic activation function such as the sigmoid function instead of smoothing functions, projection pursuit essentially becomes analogous to a simple neural network.

One key difference between projection pursuit and neural networks, however, is that the activation function in the former can be different for each hidden unit and is typically estimated *nonparametrically*, where in neural networks such are usually prespecified parametric functions. However, this does not make neural networks entirely parametric, since they are especially useful when we have no theoretical preconceptions about the data. That is, neural networks “learn” from the data, which is a very “nonparametric” idea. And while it is technically possible to assign a *unique* activation function to each hidden unit in a neural network, it is not the norm.

[Sarle (1994)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000322) perhaps distinguishes best between the parametric vs. nonparametric debate as it pertains to neural networks:

> With a small number of hidden neurons, an MLP \[multilayer perceptron\] is a parametric model that provides a useful alternative to polynomial regression. With a moderate number of hidden neurons, an MLP can be considered a quasi-parametric model similar to projection pursuit regression … An MLP with one hidden layer is essentially the same as the projection pursuit regression model except that an MLP uses a predetermined functional form for the activation function in the hidden layer, whereas projection pursuit uses a flexible nonlinear smoother. If the number of hidden neurons is allowed to increase with the sample size, an MLP becomes a nonparametric sieve that provides a useful alternative to methods such as kernel regression and smoothing splines. MLPs are especially valuable because you can vary the complexity of the model from a simple parametric model to a highly flexible, nonparametric model.
> 
> (p. 5)558

Differences between the two methods also include the fact that parameters in a neural network are typically estimated *simultaneously* where in projection pursuit regression they are usually fit *successively* for each hidden unit ([Klinke & Grassmann, 2000](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000192)). Though not an exact analogy, the optimal number of hidden units in a neural network can be likened to the number of terms to add in a projection pursuit.

Thus, projection pursuit is often considered an historical and conceptual “precursor,” especially pedagogically, to understanding neural networks, and according to Hastie et al. ([2009](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000145)), projection pursuit was not widely used at the time of its inception largely due to computational requirements for obtaining a solution, computational “roadblocks” that have long been overcome with modern computing advances. Perhaps had more computing power existed back in the day of projection pursuit, these models would have a more significant legacy. Pedagogically, however, projection pursuit is very valuable in putting neural networks and other models (e.g., PCA and generalized linear models) into proper context. Indeed, a generalized version of PPR, aptly named *Generalized Projection Pursuit Regression* ([Roosen & Hastie, 1993](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000307)) has been proposed that is similar in structure to the generalized linear model paradigm of McCullagh and Nelder ([1989](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000243)) in its use of link functions and that allow for binary responses.

Lastly, it can be shown that as the number of smoothing functions increases without bound to infinity, for an appropriate set of functions in *f*[*j*], as was the case for neural networks, projection pursuit regression can approximate virtually any continuous function and is considered a *universal approximator*. How many smoothing functions to include in the approximation? There are different recommendations regarding this. For example, [Friedman et al. (1984)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000113) found that adding more terms than necessary then using a backward selection algorithm helps avoid getting stuck in local minima. [Roosen and Hastie (1993)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000307) have found that adding terms to maximize generalized cross-validation then pruning back somewhat may be an effective strategy.

Having compared projection pursuit to neural networks, it is also useful to recap where we began this discussion, in that projection pursuit can be understood as a higher-order and more general framework to principal components analysis. Such emphasizes that the latter is but only one *type* of projection, not *the* unique projection or dimensionality reduction of data. As we have seen throughout our discussion of dimension reduction techniques, what one technique might reveal from the data another technique may do better. There is no such thing as finding the *unique* dimensions of one’s data; *what you find is as much to do with what tool you use to do the finding*, which, incidentally is why some dislike statistics in the first place as it is perceived to provide no “hard” truths, a misguided perception based on an incomplete understanding of the subject.

> *Principal components analysis is only one type of projection of the data. Projection pursuit (and by extension, neural networks) makes this clear – how you project your data will, to a large extent, determine what you find, and thus “see” from that data.*

Projection pursuit in R can be performed using the R package *tourr* (Wickham et al., [2011](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000382)). It can also be performed using ppr() in R.

## 15.13 Summary, Warnings, and Caveats of Neural Networks

Neural networks can be easily misunderstood by the uninitiated. Their very name can encourage newcomers to give them powers they may not have, or at minimum, exaggerate the powers they actually do have. Neural networks are tremendously useful, but in learning them for the first time, it is important to understand exactly what they *are* and what they are *not*. Throughout this chapter 559we have issued many caveats and warnings about neural networks. We summarize, and in some cases extend on those caveats and warnings in what follows.

### 15.13.1 Neural Networks Are Not Biological Nor Are They Machines

A first obvious point is that though neural networks were motivated by psychological and biological entities in the brain, they themselves have nothing to do with psychology or biology! They have everything to do with *abstract mathematics*. What is more, though they, like virtually all other statistical or machine learning methods are run on high-speed computers, there is nothing about neural networks themselves that have anything to do with computers or other “machines.” A neural network can, at least in theory and with enough time, be fit by pencil and paper just as any other mathematical technique. “Enough time” is more lifetimes than anyone might ever have, hence the benefit of using computers.

Why is this point so relevant? It is so because too often some users get into the habit of drawing conclusions from data based on the *jargon* of the statistical or machine learning method. As we discussed earlier in the book, in social statistics, for instance, all too often researchers will surprisingly conclude that such and such variable *mediates* or *moderates* another and impose an *action quality* on those words when no action is necessarily supported by the research design or the *organicity* of the variables used in the modeling. As emphasized throughout this book, *physical action of any sort can never be implied or concluded from the application of a statistical model alone, whether those models are of mediation, moderation, or neural networks*. The statistical or machine learning model never “knows” the kind of data or research design to which it is being applied; all models are able to do is process the data fed to them. *Models are entirely abstract entities*. So-called *action statements* must come from the *design* or *science*, not the *statistics*.

### 15.13.2 Neural Networks Need Not Be Nonlinear

As we have discussed, neural networks are typically *nonlinear* models. However, they need not necessarily be so. The special case, as we have seen, is the *linear* activation function. Of course, imposing a linear activation function minimizes the power of neural networks, and hence most neural networks are nonlinear. However, to say that they *necessarily* need to be nonlinear, or to *necessarily* associate nonlinearity with neural networks is a pedagogical shortcoming, as a linear neural network also, technically, counts as a neural network. Part of the confusion is simply in how writers and researchers choose to define a neural network, often as nonlinear. However, newcomers should be aware of this distinction.

### 15.13.3 Neural Networks Are (Mostly) Nonparametric

One question often asked about neural networks is whether they are *parametric* or *nonparametric*. In truth, they are a bit of both. For one, a user determining the number of nodes to have in a network is a *parametric-like* move. However, others regard the choice of the number of hidden neurons to include as essentially making neural networks nonparametric, especially as sample size increases. The debate as to whether neural networks are parametric or nonparametric is ongoing and is unlikely to be resolved anytime soon. This is due mostly to the wide variety of neural network possibilities and more precisely, how one operationalizes a specific given implementation of a neural network.560

We recall that the traditional statistical definition of *parametric* holds that assumptions are made about the underlying population from which the sample data was drawn. Some say that since neural networks typically require no parametric assumptions about distributions, means, variances, or even correlation of errors ([King, 1999](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000186)), we can conclude that neural networks are essentially, and *mostly*, nonparametric models. The problem with this characterization, however, is that the user is able to freely impose conditions that do imply distributional assumptions to some extent, as well as through regularization techniques (such as weight sharing) that strongly resemble “parametric-like” actions. Hence, in the final analysis, neural networks *can* be nonparametric just as they *can* take on parametric features, depending on how the user sets up the network as well as any assumptions the user makes regarding the population to which the network is being applied.

In the end then, on the nonparametric to parametric *spectrum*, neural networks probably fall somewhere in between, and where exactly depends on the given neural network under consideration.

### 15.13.4 Including More Layers Leads to Increased Approximation on the Training Data

In general, adding more layers to a neural network results in increased approximation accuracy of the underlying function, at least on the training data. However, this may lead to poor generalizability on test data and hence, overfitting. Even simple neural networks do well in approximating functions. For instance, Hornik et al. ([1989](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000158)) found that a neural network using arbitrary squashing functions could approximate virtually any function provided enough hidden units are supplied. The take-away here is that even though one can achieve accuracy by adding successive layers, the true test, as always, is on the *test data*, not the *training data*. By analogy once more, nobody cares much about how much you practiced your piano before the concert. They evaluate you based on your *actual performance*.

## 15.14 Neural Networks in Python

We can quite easily build a simple neural network in Python using *sklearn* for data on X = \[\[0., 0.\],\[1., 1.\]\] and response y = \[0, 1\] having two layers, where the first layer has five neurons and the second, two:

```
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
X = [[0., 0.], [1., 1.]]
y = [0, 1]
clf = MLPClassifier(solver=‘lbfgs’, alpha=1e-5,
... hidden_layer_sizes=(5, 2), random_state=1)
>>> clf.fit(X, y)
Out[222]:
MLPClassifier(alpha=1e-05, hidden_layer_sizes=(5, 2), random_state=1,
   solver=‘lbfgs’)
```

The neural network has now been fit for classifying values on y.

```
clf.predict([[2., 2.], [-1., -2]])
Out[223]: array([1, 0])
```

We see that the new observations are classified into groups 1 and 0 respectively. The alpha parameter serves as a regularization term and helps avoid overfitting (try adjusting it and rerunning the model).561

For further details on the above example, see *scikit-learn.org* as well as [Müller and Guido (2017)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000258) for more examples using MLPClassifier as well as plotting decision boundaries. We encourage the reader to modify the layer sizes (hidden\_layer\_sizes=(5, 2)) as well in the above example to observe the corresponding impact on the ensuing class predictions.

## 15.15 Neural Networks in R

We adapt a very simple example of a neural network from the package *neuralnet* (Fritsch et al., 2019) for a binary classification problem on the iris data. An introduction to the package is provided by [Günther and Fritsch (2010)](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000136). The package is excellent for fitting neural networks and contains many more options than we are able to cover here. In our example below, we merely demonstrate how a neural network can be quickly fit. We encourage the reader to consult the package for further details.

For the current example, we model *setosa* (binary, “yes” vs. “no”) as a function of *petal length* and *petal width*:

```
> library(neuralnet)
> nn <- neuralnet(Species == “setosa” ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width, iris, linear.output = FALSE)
> nn
```

We obtain selective output, which reports the error function used (*sse*) and the activation function (*sigmoid* or “logistic”).

```
$err.fct
function (x, y)
  1/2 * (y - x)^2
[1] “sse”
$act.fct
function (x)
  1/(1 + exp(-x))
attr(,”type”)
[1] “logistic”
```

We proceed with obtaining a plot of the network and note the error has been reduced to 0.012565 ([Figure 15.11](#c15.xhtml#f15.12)).

![Figure 15.11 Plot of neural network on the iris data.Return to text.⏎](images/fig15.12.jpg)

*Figure 15.11* Plot of neural network on the iris data.[Return to text.⏎](#c15.xhtml#re_f15.12)

```
> plot(nn)
```

562 

We can specify a custom activation function for the network other than the sigmoid function that is used as default. Here, as demonstrated in the package, we fit the same model but with a predefined *softplus* activation function (act.fct = softplus):

```
> softplus <- function(x) log(1 + exp(x))
> nn <- neuralnet((Species == “setosa”) ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width, iris, linear.output = FALSE, hidden = c(3,2), act.fct = softplus)
```

We have also specified the structure of hidden layers to be three and two (hidden = c(3,2)) moving left to right across the network (i.e., the first hidden layer has three nodes and the second, two nodes).

A plot of the network follows ([Figure 15.12](#c15.xhtml#f15.13), left).

![Figure 15.12 Neural networks with various numbers of layers and nodes along with estimated error.Return to text.⏎](images/fig15.13.jpg)

*Figure 15.12* Neural networks with various numbers of layers and nodes along with estimated error.[Return to text.⏎](#c15.xhtml#re_f15.13)

```
> plot(nn)
```

563 

We now run the same model but with only a single hidden layer having five nodes ([Figure 15.12](#c15.xhtml#f15.13), right).

```
> nn <- neuralnet((Species == “setosa”) ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width, iris, linear.output = FALSE, hidden = 5, act.fct = softplus)
> plot(nn)
```

Next we fit a model with two hidden layers, each with five nodes, for which we are able to get the error down to 0.003624 ([Figure 15.13](#c15.xhtml#f15.14)).

![Figure 15.13 Neural network with two hidden layers each with five nodes.Return to text.⏎](images/fig15.13_1.jpg)

*Figure 15.13* Neural network with two hidden layers each with five nodes.[Return to text.⏎](#c15.xhtml#re_f15.14)

```
> nn <- neuralnet((Species == “setosa”) ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width, iris, linear.output = FALSE, hidden = c(5, 5), act.fct = softplus)
> plot(nn)
```

A host of other output and functions are available in the package, such as computing confidence intervals for weights via confidence.interval() and obtaining AIC and BIC statistics, these latter two statistics requiring specifying likelihood = TRUE (error function = negative log-likelihood):564

```
> neuralnet(Species == “setosa” ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width, iris, likelihood = TRUE, linear.output = FALSE)
```

| steps || 95.000000000 |
| aic || 10.018847072 |
| bic || 25.072023543 |
| Intercept.to.1layhid1 || 5.558388265 |
| Petal.Length.to.1layhid1 || \-0.085917885 |
| Petal.Width.to.1layhid1 || \-7.246933549 |
| Intercept.to.Species == “setosa” || \-4.875343467 |
| 1layhid1.to.Species == “setosa” || 10.044111027 |

We see that AIC and BIC are equal to 10.02 and 25.07, respectively.

The package *nnet* ([Venables & Ripley, 2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000376)) also fits neural networks. For a good example using the package, see Venables and Ripley ([2002](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000376), p. 342). The *keras* package ([Allaire & Chollet, 2024](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000008)) is a very extensive package for fitting neural networks in R and comes highly recommended. Efforts to visualize what is going on in the “black box” of neural networks have also been advanced (Yosinski et al., [2015](#ref.xhtml#re_CIT000399)) and is a currently expanding area of research in machine learning.

## 15.16 Chapter Review Exercises

1.  1\. Describe the *McCulloch-Pitts neuron*, and compare and contrast it to *Rosenblatt’s perceptron*, then compare and contrast both of these to a classic multiple regression model.
2.  2\. Describe and explain how neural networks are *composite functions*.
3.  3\. Compare and contrast the *activation function* in neural networks to the *link function* in the generalized linear model.
4.  4\. Distinguish between a *saturating* vs. *non-saturating* activation function.
5.  5\. What is the general problem with the *ReLU* activation function and how does the *leakyReLU* attempt to address this problem? Explain and illustrate.
6.  6\. Describe how neural networks are trained by the process of updating parameter weights.
7.  7\. Describe three methods to prevent *overfitting* of neural networks.
8.  8\. Explain what the *universal approximation theorem* has to do with neural networks.
9.  9\. Compare and contrast neural networks to *projection pursuit*.
10.  10\. Does a neural network need to be *nonlinear*? How about *nonparametric*? Justify your answer.
11.  11\. Run a neural network in R on the iris data using the example in the chapter as a guide, but instead of the species *setosa*, use the species *virginica* as the outcome variable. Compare and contrast your results to those in the chapter.

565

# Concluding Remarks

This book has featured an overview of multivariate statistics and machine learning, well suited for an introductory text at the advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate level for students primarily in the social or natural sciences. The goal of the book has been to survey methods from these two merging and overlapping areas in the context of the new data science zeitgeist of the 21st century. The primary motivation behind the book was based on the premise that traditional statistics courses for specialists in science are *no longer enough* and should now incorporate features of machine learning as to emphasize the commonalities between *statistics*, *machine* *learning*, and *data science* more generally, within a scientific context of *research design* and *measurement*.

The book aimed to provide a bird’s eye “big picture” foundational view of a wide gamut of methods and techniques, building on a reasonable mix of requisite *theory*, *application*, and *computation* suitable for an introductory course with relatively minimal assumed prerequisites. The book placed great emphasis on unifying *themes* and *foundations* to understanding statistics and machine learning, demonstrating how many techniques and methods can be understood or conceptualized as special cases of wider and more inclusive approaches. A good scientist must understand the quantitative tools they use in addressing the richness of their data, for what one “finds” in their data can to a significant and often surprising extent be a function of what methodological or statistical “lens” was used to do the searching. *The strengths and limitations of the microscope are sometimes just as relevant in a scientific context as what is being observed under it*. It is hoped that this message has been well-received and that the reader has gained renewed awareness of how influential *context* is to the application of quantitative methods in what is essentially and most globally, *the art of generating narratives from experience*.

As also emphasized throughout the text, virtually all methods discussed have book-length treatments in their own right as well as often long and complex histories of development in professional journals and related publications. Hence, it should be recognized that our overview of these methods has simply *scratched the surface* into the richness and complexities of these data-analytic approaches. Still, it is hoped that the book has provided the student or professional a means to get into these techniques as a *starting point* and as a way to better understand and appreciate the *foundations* of the current quantitative landscape in which they practice their science.
